record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is not attested in the classical philological tradition; no primary Arabic lexical root 'ابز' is recognized in the canonical sources.
record.haqiqah_literal: No literal physical meaning is attested in Asās al-Balāghah or the classical lexical corpus.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: لا يوجد أصل معجمي بهذا الضبط في لسان العرب أو المفردات.
canonical_definition.english: No lexical root with this consonantal sequence is attested in Lisān al-ʿArab or Al-Mufradāt.

record.ontological_core: The root أ-ح-د denotes absolute, indivisible oneness — the negation of multiplicity, composition, and partition. Its foundational physical origin is the notion of a single, isolated unit that admits no second, no plurality, and no internal division.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal meaning is 'one' in the strict sense of absolute singularity — that which is neither paired nor composed, neither divisible nor repeatable. It is the pure unit that excludes all others.
record.majaz_scholastic: In philosophical and theological usage, الأحد is the divine attribute of absolute unity (al-Aḥadiyyah), signifying that God is one without composition, without parts, without multiplicity, and without any second. It is distinguished from الواحد: the latter denotes oneness in contrast to duality, while الأحد denotes oneness that excludes all relation and plurality absolutely. In logic and metaphysics, it is applied to the indivisible point, the unique individual, and the first principle.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأحد: الواحد الذي لا ثاني له، ولا يقبل القسمة ولا التركيب، ولا يوصف به غيره تعالى في الأحدية المطلقة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Aḥad: the One who has no second, who admits neither division nor composition, and none other than God is described by it in absolute oneness.

mufradat.text: أحد يستعمل على ضربين: أحدهما: في النفي فقط (4). والثاني: في الإثبات. فأما المختص بالنفي فلاستغراق جنس الناطقين، ويتناول القليل والكثير على طريق الاجتماع والافتراق، نحو: ما في الدار أحد، أي: لا واحد ولا اثنان فصاعدا لا مجتمعين ولا مفترقين، ولهذا المعنى لم يصح استعماله في ومن تخطئ يعمر فيهرم للموت كأس فالمرء ذائقها وعظموا بأحد الآحاد وأحد في النفي ذو انفراد بعاقل، ومثله عريب كما هنا من أحد قريب الإثبات، لأن نفي المتضادين يصح، ولا يصح إثباتهما، فلو قيل: في الدار واحد لكان فيه إثبات واحد منفرد مع إثبات ما فوق الواحد مجتمعين ومفترقين، وذلك ظاهر الإحالة، ولتناول ذلك ما فوق الواحد يصح أن يقال: ما من أحد فاضلين (1)، كقوله تعالى: فما منكم من أحد عنه حاجزين [الحاقة/ 47]. وأما المستعمل في الإثبات فعلى ثلاثة أوجه: الأول: في الواحد المضموم إلى العشرات نحو: أحد عشر وأحد وعشرين. والثاني: أن يستعمل مضافا أو مضافا إليه بمعنى الأول، كقوله تعالى: أما أحدكما فيسقي ربه خمرا [يوسف/ 41]، وقولهم: يوم الأحد. أي: يوم الأول، ويوم الاثنين. والثالث: أن يستعمل مطلقا وصفا، وليس ذلك إلا في وصف الله تعالى بقوله: قل هو الله أحد [الإخلاص/ 1]، وأصله: وحد (2)، ولكن وحد يستعمل في غيره نحو قول النابغة: 10- كأن رحلي وقد زال النهار بنا بذي الجليل على مستأنس وحد (3) أخذ الأخذ: حوز الشيء وتحصيله، وذلك تارة بالتناول نحو: معاذ الله أن نأخذ إلا من وجدنا متاعنا عنده [يوسف/ 79]، وتارة بالقهر نحو قوله تعالى: لا تأخذه سنة ولا نوم [البقرة/ 255]. ويقال: أخذته الحمى، وقال تعالى: وأخذ الذين ظلموا الصيحة [هود/ 67]، فأخذه الله نكال الآخرة والأولى [النازعات/ 25]، وقال: وكذلك أخذ ربك إذا أخذ القرى [هود/ 102]. ويعبر عن الأسير بالأخيذ والمأخوذ، والاتخاذ افتعال منه، ويعدى إلى مفعولين ويجري مجرى الجعل نحو قوله تعالى: لا تتخذوا اليهود والنصارى أولياء [المائدة/ 51]، أم اتخذوا من دونه أولياء [الشورى/ 9]، فاتخذتموهم سخريا [المؤمنون/ 110]، أأنت قلت للناس: اتخذوني وأمي إلهين من دون الله [المائدة/ 116]، وقوله تعالى: ولو يؤاخذ الله الناس بظلمهم [النحل/ 61] فتخصيص لفظ المؤاخذة تنبيه على معنى المجازاة والمقابلة لما أخذوه من النعم فلم يقابلوه بالشكر. ويقال: فلان مأخوذ، وبه أخذة من الجن، وفلان يأخذ مأخذ فلان، أي: يفعل فعله ويسلك مسلكه، ورجل أخيذ، وبه أخذ كناية عن الرمد. والإخاذة والإخاذ: أرض يأخذها الرجل لنفسه (1)، وذهبوا ومن أخذ أخذهم وإخذهم (2).

record.ontological_core: A deictic-temporal particle whose foundational semantic function is to point to an indeterminate future time; it is not a lexical root with a concrete physical origin but a grammatical operator (adāt) denoting futurity, and it may acquire conditional force when construed with a following verb.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal function of إذا is to designate any future time (al-zamān al-mustaqbal), whether indefinite or specified by context; it is the temporal particle of futurity, as opposed to إذ, which designates past time.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and grammatical usage, إذا may be invested with the meaning of condition (sharṭ) and thereby govern the jussive (jazm) in poetry predominantly; it does not function as a conditional particle unless joined with ما, as in إذ ما. It is also used in logical and theological discourse to mark temporal contingency and future-oriented hypotheticals, without denoting a concrete entity or accident.

canonical_definition.arabic: إذا يعبر به عن كل زمان مستقبل، وقد يضمن معنى الشرط فيجزم به، وذلك في الشعر أكثر؛ و«إذ» يعبر به عن الزمان الماضي، ولا يجازى به إلا إذا ضم إليه «ما».
canonical_definition.english: Ifā denotes any future time, and it may be invested with conditional meaning, in which case it governs the jussive—this being more frequent in poetry; whereas idh denotes past time, and it is not used conditionally unless joined with mā.

derivations.english_translation: if; when (future); then (in conditional constructions)

mufradat.text: إذا يعبر به عن كل زمان مستقبل، وقد يضمن معنى الشرط فيجزم به، وذلك في الشعر أكثر، و«إذ» يعبر به عن الزمان الماضي، ولا يجازى به إلا إذا ضم إليه «ما» نحو: 11- إذ ما أتيت على الرسول فقل له (1) أرب الأرب: فرط الحاجة المقتضي للاحتيال في دفعه، فكل أرب حاجة، وليس كل حاجة أربا، ثم يستعمل تارة في الحاجة المفردة، وتارة في الاحتيال وإن لم يكن حاجة، كقولهم: فلان ذو أرب، وأريب، أي: ذو احتيال، وقد أرب إلى كذا، أي: احتاج إليه حاجة شديدة (2)، وقد أرب إلى كذا أربا وأربة وإربة ومأربة، قال تعالى: ولي فيها مآرب أخرى [طه/ 18]، ولا أرب لي في كذا، أي: ليس بي شدة حاجة إليه، وقوله: أولي الإربة من الرجال [النور/ 31] كناية عن الحاجة إلى النكاح، وهي الأربى (3)، للداهية المقتضية للاحتيال، وتسمى الأعضاء التي تشتد الحاجة إليها آرابا، الواحد: إرب، وذلك أن الأعضاء ضربان: - ضرب أوجد لحاجة الحيوان إليه، كاليد والرجل والعين. - وضرب للزينة، كالحاجب واللحية. ثم التي للحاجة ضربان: حقا عليك إذا اطمأن المجلس - ضرب لا تشتد الحاجة إليه. - وضرب تشتد الحاجة إليه، حتى لو توهم مرتفعا لاختل البدن به اختلالا عظيما، وهي التي تسمى آرابا. وروي أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال: «إذا سجد العبد سجد معه سبعة آراب: وجهه وكفاه وركبتاه وقدماه» (1). ويقال: أرب نصيبه، أي: عظمه، وذلك إذا جعله قدرا يكون له فيه أرب، ومنه: أرب ماله أي: كثر (2)، وأربت العقدة: أحكمتها (3).

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root is the bodily organ of hearing — the ear — conceived as the locus of auditory apprehension. From this concrete anatomical nucleus, the root radiates outward to denote the act of listening, the granting of permission (since one who is heard is thereby admitted), and the act of proclamation or warning (since a summons is issued to be heard).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the ear as a bodily member (al-jāriḥah), together with its homologue in inanimate objects — the loop or handle of a vessel, the ear of a pot, and the like — by virtue of structural resemblance. It also denotes the concrete act of hearing and listening (al-istimāʿ), and the verbal noun al-adhān and al-adhān signifying that which is heard.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root is transferred (mustaʿār) to designate a person who listens excessively and credulously, so that he is called 'an ear' — as in the Qurʾānic 'They say: He is an ear' (Q 9:61), meaning his listening conduces to your good. It is further employed for the faculty of apprehension and intellection (al-ʿilm) insofar as hearing is the primary conduit of knowledge among us, as in 'Grant me leave' (Q 9:49) and 'And when your Lord proclaimed' (Q 14:7). The verb adhina denotes to listen, to grant permission, and to proclaim or warn; taʾadhdhana signifies to give prior notice of evil or to announce a matter — as when the sultan's herald proclaims something, he has thereby 'taʾadhdhana' it. The Qurʾānic 'in their ears is a heaviness' (Q 6:25) is an allusion to their ignorance, not to any defect in their hearing.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأذن: الجارحة، وشبه به من حيث الحلقة أذن القدر وغيرها، ويستعار لمن كثر استماعه وقوله لما يسمع. وأذن: استمع. والأذن والأذان لما يسمع، ويعبر بذلك عن العلم، إذ هو مبدأ كثير من العلم فينا. وأذنته بكذا وآذنته بمعنى.
canonical_definition.english: Al-adhun: the bodily organ [of hearing]; the loop of a pot and the like are likened to it by virtue of structural resemblance; and it is metaphorically applied to one who listens excessively and accepts whatever he hears. Adhina means 'he listened.' Al-adhan and al-adhān denote that which is heard, and by this is expressed the notion of knowledge, since hearing is the origin of much of our knowledge. Adhantuhu bi-kadhā and ādhantuhu are synonymous [i.e., 'I informed him of such-and-such'].

mufradat.text: الأذن: الجارحة، وشبه به من حيث الحلقة أذن القدر وغيرها، ويستعار لمن كثر استماعه وقوله لما يسمع، قال تعالى: ويقولون: هو أذن قل: أذن خير لكم [التوبة/ 61] أي: استماعه لما يعود بخير لكم، وقوله تعالى: وفي آذانهم وقرا* [الأنعام/ 25] إشارة إلى جهلهم لا إلى عدم سمعهم. وأذن: استمع، نحو قوله: وأذنت لربها وحقت* [الانشقاق/ 2]، ويستعمل ذلك في العلم الذي يتوصل إليه بالسماع، نحو قوله: فأذنوا بحرب من الله ورسوله [البقرة/ 279]. والأذن والأذان لما يسمع، ويعبر بذلك عن العلم، إذ هو مبدأ كثير من العلم فينا، قال الله تعالى: ائذن لي ولا تفتني [التوبة/ 49]، وقال: وإذ تأذن ربكم [إبراهيم/ 7]. وأذنته بكذا وآذنته بمعنى. والمؤذن: كل من يعلم بشيء نداء، قال تعالى: ثم أذن مؤذن أيتها العير [يوسف/ 70]، فأذن مؤذن بينهم [الأعراف/ 44]، وأذن في الناس بالحج [الحج/ 27]. والأذين: المكان الذي يأتيه الأذان (1)، والإذن في الشيء: إعلام بإجازته والرخصة فيه، نحو، وما أرسلنا من رسول إلا ليطاع بإذن الله [النساء/ 64] أي: بإرادته وأمره، وقوله: وما أصابكم يوم التقى الجمعان فبإذن الله [آل عمران/ 166]، وقوله: وما هم بضارين به من أحد إلا بإذن الله [البقرة/ 102]، وليس بضارهم شيئا إلا بإذن الله [المجادلة/ 10] قيل: معناه: بعلمه، لكن بين العلم والإذن فرق، فإن الإذن أخص، ولا يكاد يستعمل إلا فيما فيه مشيئة به، راضيا منه الفعل أم لم يرض به (2)، فإن قوله: وما كان لنفس أن تؤمن إلا بإذن الله [يونس/ 100] فمعلوم أن فيه مشيئته وأمره، وقوله: وما هم بضارين به من أحد إلا بإذن الله [البقرة/ 102] ففيه مشيئته من وجه، وهو أنه لا خلاف أن الله تعالى أوجد في الإنسان قوة فيها إمكان قبول الضرب من جهة من يظلمه فيضره، ولم يجعله كالحجر الذي لا يوجعه الضرب، ولا خلاف أن إيجاد هذا الإمكان من فعل الله، فمن هذا الوجه يصح أن يقال: إنه بإذن الله ومشيئته يلحق الضرر من جهة الظالم، ولبسط هذا الكلام كتاب غير هذا (3). والاستئذان: طلب الإذن، قال تعالى: إنما يستأذنك الذين لا يؤمنون بالله [التوبة/ 45]، فإذا استأذنوك [النور/ 62]. و«إذن» جواب وجزاء، ومعنى ذلك أنه يقتضي جوابا أو تقدير جواب، ويتضمن ما يصحبه من الكلام جزاء، ومتى صدر به الكلام وتعقبه فعل مضارع ينصبه لا محالة، نحو: إذن أخرج، ومتى تقدمه كلام ثم تبعه فعل مضارع يجوز نصبه ورفعه (4) أنا إذن أخرج وأخرج، ومتى تأخر عن الفعل أو لم يكن معه الفعل المضارع لم يعمل، نحو: أنا أخرج إذن، قال تعالى: إنكم إذا مثلهم [النساء/ 140].

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ارش is the infliction of a wound or injury (jarḥ) upon the body, from which arises a compensatory claim or indemnity for that injury.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of wounding or injuring (jarḥ) and the taking of compensation (arsh) for that wound.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and legal usage, the term is extended metaphorically to denote the indemnity or financial compensation (arsh) paid for a wound or injury, and by further extension, any monetary compensation for damages. It is also used in the context of reconciliation or settlement (ṣulḥ) where a payment is made to resolve a dispute.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأَرْشُ: دِيَةُ الجِرَاحَاتِ، وَقَدْ أَرَشَ يَأْرِشُ أَرْشًا إِذَا جَرَحَ وَأَخَذَ الأَرْشَ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Arsh: the indemnity for wounds; one says arasha ya'rishu arshan when he wounded and took the indemnity.

entries.text: تقول: أجل من الحرش، أن يجرح ويؤخذ بالأرش.

record.ontological_core: The root ازج (ʾ-z-j) denotes the foundational physical act of joining, pairing, or bringing two things into close conjunction, with a secondary concrete sense of a narrow, constricted passage or a thing tightly bound.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the joining or pairing of two things, or a narrow, constricted place or passage; also used for a tightly bound or compressed object.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, it denotes the conjunction or coupling of abstract entities, such as the pairing of ideas, the union of substances, or the conjunction of premises in logic; in theology, it may refer to the hypostatic union or the conjunction of divine attributes with the essence.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأَزْجُ: الضِّيقُ، وقيل: هو الجَمْعُ بين الشيئين، والأَزَجُ: الفَجُّ الضَّيِّقُ بين الجبال.
canonical_definition.english: Al-azj: narrowness; also said to be the joining of two things; al-azaj: a narrow mountain pass.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is the waist-wrapper or loincloth (al-izār) that a person binds around the waist as a covering garment; from this concrete act of girding and enclosing derives the sense of surrounding, supporting, and strengthening.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the izār: the garment wrapped around the waist, also called izārah and miʾzar; it denotes the act of wearing such a wrapper and the manner of girding it (al-izrah), as in the phrase 'he is excellent in his manner of wearing the izār' and 'for every Arab tribe there is an izrah by which they gird themselves.'
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphor, the izār is used as a euphemism for the wife, since she is as closely attached and covering as the waist-wrapper. From the physical act of girding, the root extends to the sense of strengthening and supporting: 'he girded his back with it' means he fortified him; 'he supported me against it' means he backed and aided me; and 'one who supports and cooperates' is derived from the same image of mutual backing. The theological and ethical usage centers on the idea of God strengthening and supporting the believer, and of humans supporting one another in truth and justice.

canonical_definition.arabic: أصل الأزر: الإزار الذي هو اللباس، يقال: إزار وإزارة ومئزر، ويكنى بالإزار عن المرأة. وشد به أزره، ومعه من يؤامره ويؤازره. وأردت كذا فآزرني عليه فلان إذا ظاهرك وعاونك. وإنه لحسن الإزرة، ولكل قوم من العرب إزرة يأتزرونها.
canonical_definition.english: The root of al-azr is the izār, which is a garment; it is said izār, izārah, and miʾzar, and the izār is used as a euphemism for the wife. One says 'he girded his back with it,' and 'with him is one who consults him and supports him.' 'I wanted such-and-such, and so-and-so supported me against it' means he backed and aided me. 'He is excellent in his izrah' refers to the manner of wearing the waist-wrapper, and every Arab tribe has an izrah by which they gird themselves.

one who supports, backs, or aids another

mufradat.text: أصل الأزر: الإزار الذي هو اللباس، يقال: إزار وإزارة ومئزر، ويكنى بالإزار عن المرأة. قال الشاعر: 13- ألا أبلغ أبا حفص رسولا فدى لك من أخي ثقة إزاري (3) وتسميتها بذلك لما قال تعالى: هن لباس لكم وأنتم لباس لهن [البقرة/ 187]. وقوله تعالى: اشدد به أزري [طه/ 31]، أي: أتقوى به، والأزر: القوة الشديدة، وآزره: أعانه وقواه، وأصله من شد الإزار، قال تعالى: كزرع أخرج شطأه فآزره [الفتح/ 29]. يقال: آزرته فتأزر، أي: شددت أزره، وهو حسن الإزرة، وأزرت البناء وآزرته: قويت أسافله، وتأزر النبت: طال وقوي، وآزرته ووازرته: صرت وزيره، وأصله الواو، وفرس آزر: انتهى بياض قوائمه إلى موضع شد الإزار. قال تعالى: وإذ قال إبراهيم لأبيه آزر [الأنعام/ 74]، قيل: كان اسم أبيه تارخ فعرب فجعل آزر، وقيل: آزر معناه الضال في كلامهم (1).

entries.text: الزرع يؤازره بعضه بعضا إذا تلاحق والتف، وتأزر النبت تأزرا. وأنشد ثعلب: تأزر فيه النبت حتى تخايلت ... رباه وحتى ما ترى الشاء نوما وشد للأمر مئزره إذا تشمر له. قال في صفة الحمار: شد على أمر الورود مئزره وقال الفرزدق: فقلت لها ألما تعرفيني ... إذا شدت محافظتي الإزارا وعم الحيا فتعمم
شد به أزره، ومعه من يؤامره ويؤازره. وأردت كذا فآزرني عليه فلان إذا ظاهرك وعاونك. وإنه لحسن الإزرة، ولكل قوم من العرب إزرة يأتزرونها.

شد به أزره، ومعه من يؤامره ويؤازره. وأردت كذا فآزرني عليه فلان إذا ظاهرك وعاونك. وإنه لحسن الإزرة، ولكل قوم من العرب إزرة يأتزرونها. Metaphorical (Majaz): الزرع يؤازره بعضه بعضا إذا تلاحق والتف، وتأزر النبت تأزرا. وأنشد ثعلب: تأزر فيه النبت حتى تخايلت ... رباه وحتى ما ترى الشاء نوما وشد للأمر م

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root أزم is the act of biting down hard and holding fast with the teeth, specifically the clamping of the horse's mouth onto the bit of the bridle, and by extension any firm, tenacious grip or constriction.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the biting and holding fast of a horse upon the iron bit of the bridle (فأس اللجام), such that it clenches it firmly; hence a horse so described is أزوم. It also denotes the seizing and holding of property or wealth, as in أخذ مالي فأزم عليه.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root is applied to the concept of self-restraint in diet and the suppression of appetite, termed الحمية الأزم, and one who practices such abstinence is called آزِم. It further extends to a person who eats little and causes scant loss to food, described as رجل أزوم. In a proverbial and medical-philosophical register, the Arabs say: 'The origin of every disease is cold, and the origin of every remedy is أزم (restraint/abstinence).' The root thus carries the scholastic nuance of firm constriction, whether of the jaws upon the bit, the hand upon wealth, or the self upon desires.

canonical_definition.arabic: أزم الفرس على فأس اللجام: عض عليه وأمسكه، وفرس أزوم. وأخذ مالي فأزم عليه. ومنه قيل للحمية الأزم. ورجل أزوم: قليل الرزء من الطعام.
canonical_definition.english: The horse bit down on the iron bit of the bridle and held it fast; hence a horse is أزوم. He seized my wealth and held it firmly. From this, self-restraint in diet is called الأزم. A man who is أزوم eats little and causes scant loss to food.

derivations.english_translation: to bite and hold fast, to clench (as a horse on the bit); to seize and withhold (wealth)
a horse that bites and holds the bit firmly; a person who eats little, causing scant loss to food
one who practices self-restraint in diet, an abstainer
firm restraint, abstinence, especially in diet; constriction

entries.text: أزم الفرس على فأس اللجام: عض عليه وأمسكه، وفرس أزوم، وأخذ مالي فأزم عليه، ومنه قيل للحمية الأزم. وتقول العرب: أصل كل داء البردة، وأصل كل دواء الأزم. ويقال للمحتمي الآزم. ورجل أزوم: قليل الرزء من الطعام.

أزم الدهر علينا، وأزمتنا أزمة، وسنة آزمة وأزوم، وسنون أوازم، وأصابتهم أزمة، وتتابعت عليهم الأزمات. وأزم بالضيعة وعليها إذا حافظ. وقال: جذام سيوف الله في كل موطن ... إذا أزمت يوم اللقاء أزام وإن قصرت يوما أكف قبيلة ... على المجد نالته أكف جذام أي إذا عضت كريهة عضوض. والتقينا في مأ

أزم الفرس على فأس اللجام: عض عليه وأمسكه، وفرس أزوم، وأخذ مالي فأزم عليه، ومنه قيل للحمية الأزم. وتقول العرب: أصل كل داء البردة، وأصل كل دوا Metaphorical (Majaz): أزم الدهر علينا، وأزمتنا أزمة، وسنة آزمة وأزوم، وسنون أوازم، وأصابتهم أزمة، وتتابعت عليهم الأزمات. وأزم بالضيعة وعليها إذا حافظ. وقال: جذام

record.ontological_core: The root افح is not attested as an independent lexical root in the classical Arabic lexicographical tradition; its apparent presence in some sources reflects either a scribal variant, a dialectal form, or a mis-segmentation of a larger root such as فوح (diffusion of scent) or أفح (a rare verbal noun). No foundational physical origin (aṣl al-waḍʿ) can be established for it as a standalone root.
record.haqiqah_literal: No literal physical meaning is recorded for افح in Asās al-Balāghah or in the classical lexicons; the sequence is not recognized as a ḥaqīqah-bearing root.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested for افح as an independent root; any occurrence in later texts is either a variant of a known root or a nonce form without established majāz extension.

canonical_definition.arabic: افح: لم يثبت في لسان العرب ولا في المفردات كجذر مستقل؛ إنما هو صورة مهملة أو تحريف عن أصل معروف.
canonical_definition.english: Afḥ: Not established in Lisān al-ʿArab or Al-Mufradāt as an independent root; it is either an unused form or a corruption of a known root.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a state of intense, burdensome hardship or constriction, with a secondary physical sense of bending or curving under pressure.
record.haqiqah_literal: Literal physical meaning: to be in a state of hardship, distress, or constriction; also to bend or curve.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and theological usages: hardship as a trial (fitnah) that bends the soul toward humility; constriction as a metaphor for spiritual or moral difficulty.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأَنْكُ: الشِّدَّةُ وَالضِّيقُ، وَأَنِكَ الرَّجُلُ إِذَا وَقَعَ فِي شِدَّةٍ، وَأَنَكَ الشَّيْءَ إِذَا عَطَفَهُ وَحَنَاهُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ank: hardship and constriction; a man is in hardship when he falls into distress; to bend something is to curve and flex it.

derivations.english_translation: to be in hardship, to be distressed
hardship, distress
to bend, to curve
bending, curvature

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the involuntary or deliberate utterance of the interjection 'āwh/awwāh' (أوه), a vocalization expressing pain, grief, or intense emotional distress, rooted in the primal human sound of lamentation.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the act of saying 'āwh āwh' (أوه أوه) — a repeated sigh or groan — and any speech that signifies grief or sorrow; this is termed taʾawwuh.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, al-awwāh denotes one who frequently sighs out of fear of God, or the believing supplicant (al-muʾmin al-dāʿī), as in Qurʾān 11:75 'awwāhun munīb' (a compassionate, oft-sighing one, turning in repentance). It is also applied to one who displays piety and constant remembrance, and by extension to the devout person (mutāʾawwih) who is God-fearing.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأَوَّاهُ: الَّذِي يَكْثُرُ تَأَوُّهُهُ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَقُولَ: أَوْه أَوْه، وَكُلُّ كَلَامٍ يَدُلُّ عَلَى حُزْنٍ يُقَالُ لَهُ التَّأَوُّهُ، وَيُعَبَّرُ بِالأَوَّاهِ عَمَّنْ يُظْهِرُ خَشْيَةَ اللهِ تَعَالَى.
canonical_definition.english: Al-awwāh: one who sighs frequently, that is, who says 'āwh āwh'; and any speech that indicates grief is called taʾawwuh; and al-awwāh is used to express one who displays fear of God.

derivations.english_translation: one who sighs frequently; a devout, God-fearing supplicant
to sigh, to groan, to lament
sighing, groaning, lamentation
to say 'āwh' (interjection of pain or grief)

mufradat.text: الأواه: الذي يكثر التأوه، وهو أن يقول: أوه أوه، وكل كلام يدل على حزن يقال له: التأوه، ويعبر بالأواه عمن يظهر خشية الله تعالى، وقيل في قوله تعالى: أواه منيب [هود/ 75] أي: المؤمن الداعي، وأصله راجع إلى ما تقدم. قال أبو العباس (3)(رحمه الله): يقال: إيها: إذا كففته، وويها: إذا أغريته، وواها: إذا تعجبت منه.

entries.text: تأوه من خشية الله تعالى. وفلان متأله متأوه.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is a dense, tangled, interwoven thicket of trees—a grove so closely interlaced that its branches form an impenetrable canopy.
record.haqiqah_literal: A tangled grove or thicket of closely interlaced trees; a dense arborous mass.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically applied to a person of noble lineage as a 'branch of the thicket of glory' (i.e., deeply rooted in honor). Theologically, 'Aṣḥāb al-Aykah' (Companions of the Thicket) designates the people of the prophet Shuʿayb, either because they inhabited a dense grove or because al-Aykah was the name of their town; their story serves as a Quranic exemplum of rejecting prophetic warning.

canonical_definition.arabic: الأَيْك: شجر ملتف، وأصحاب الأيكة قيل: نسبوا إلى غيضة كانوا يسكنونها، وقيل: هي اسم بلد.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ayk: a tangled, densely interwoven grove of trees. The 'Companions of the Thicket' are said to have been named after a dense grove they inhabited; alternatively, it is said to be the name of a town.

derivations.english_translation: A single dense thicket or grove; also the proper name of the town or grove of the people of Shuʿayb.
A tangled grove; a dense, interwoven stand of trees.
Thickets; groves (plural).
Companion of the Thicket; one of the people of Shuʿayb.

mufradat.text: الأيك: شجر ملتف، وأصحاب الأيكة قيل: نسبوا إلى غيضة كانوا يسكنونها، وقيل: هي اسم بلد.

entries.text: فلان فرع من أيكة المجد. وتقول: كذب صاحب مليكه، كما كذب أصحاب الأيكه.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes physical bulk and largeness of bodily frame; its foundational sense is the concrete, observable quality of being corpulent and heavy-set.
record.haqiqah_literal: A man of large, bulky, corpulent frame; a physically massive and heavy-set person.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to the literal physical description of bodily bulk, and Ibn Manẓūr explicitly notes that its transmission is not firmly established (ليس بثبت).

canonical_definition.arabic: رجل بُرْزُل: وهو الضَّخْم، وليس بثَبَتٍ.
canonical_definition.english: A man who is بُرْزُل: namely, corpulent and large-bodied; and this report is not firmly established.

derivations.english_translation: a corpulent, large-bodied man; a person of massive physical frame

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the compact, clustered bud of a tree or plant — the dense node where leaves, blossoms, and fruit are gathered together in a single tight formation before unfolding.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the tree's bud (بَرْهَمَة / بُرْعُمَة): the concentrated locus in which its leaves, flowers, and fruit are collectively assembled.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension from the notion of a tightly gathered, fixed cluster, the derived verb بَرْهَمَ denotes the sustained fixing of the gaze upon an object — a prolonged, unbroken act of looking, as in the poetic line of al-ʿAjjāj. The semantic transfer moves from the physical coalescence of plant parts to the concentrated, unwavering fixation of the faculty of sight.

canonical_definition.arabic: بَرْهَمَةُ الشَّجَرِ: بُرْعُمَتُهُ، وَهُوَ مُجْتَمَعُ وَرَقِهِ وَثَمَرِهِ وَنَوْرِهِ. وَبَرْهَمَ: أَدَامَ النَّظَرَ.
canonical_definition.english: The barhama of a tree is its burʿuma: the locus in which its leaves, fruit, and blossoms are gathered together. And barhama means: to sustain and prolong the gaze.

derivations.english_translation: the bud of a tree; the compact cluster of its leaves, blossoms, and fruit
bud; the gathered node of foliage and fruit (variant form)
to fix or sustain the gaze; to look intently and continuously

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the forceful expulsion of saliva or spittle from the mouth, a physiological act of ejection. This root is a phonetic variant of ب ز ق (b-z-q) and ب س ق (b-s-q), all sharing the core sense of emitting moisture or matter outward.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to spit or expectorate saliva from the mouth. In Asās al-Balāghah, it is used literally in the phrase 'بصق في وجهه' (he spat in his face) as an act of contempt. It also denotes a white, glistening stone, termed 'بُصَاقَة القمر' (the moon's spittle), due to its resemblance to expelled saliva in whiteness and luminosity.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root extends to expressions of contempt and insult, as in 'بصق في وجهه' (he spat in his face), signifying extreme disrespect. The term 'بُصَاقَة مني أفضل منك' (a spittle from me is better than you) is a proverbial metaphor for self-elevation over another. In scholastic and poetic usage, 'بُصَاقُ القمر' (the moon's spittle) refers to a white, radiant stone, metaphorically linking the moon's luminous essence to the act of spitting. Additionally, 'بُصَاقُ الإبل' (the spittle of camels) may denote a plant or substance associated with camels, extending the root to botanical or descriptive domains.

canonical_definition.arabic: البُصاقُ: لغة في البُزاق، بَصَق يَبْصُق بَصْقاً. وبُصاقةُ القمر وبُصاقُه: حجر أبيض مُتَلأْلئٌ. وبُصاقُ الإبل: نبت.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Buṣāq: a variant of al-buzāq (spittle); baṣaqa yabṣuqu baṣqan (he spat, spitting). And the moon's spittle (buṣāqat al-qamar / buṣāquhu): a white, glistening stone. And the spittle of camels (buṣāq al-ibil): a plant.

derivations.english_translation: to spit, to expectorate
spittle, saliva
a spit, a spittle; also a white glistening stone (as in بُصَاقَة القمر)
the act of spitting, expectoration

entries.text: بصق في وجهه إذا استخف به. وهو أبيض كأنه بصاقة القمر وهي حجر أبيض يتلألأ. وبصقة مني أفضل منك.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical referent is the edible bulb of the onion plant (Allium cepa), a layered, subterranean vegetable whose concentric sheaths constitute its primary concrete reality.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the well-known onion bulb, and by concrete extension, any object resembling its layered, ovoid form — most notably the iron boss or pointed cap of a helmet (bayḍat al-ḥadīd) and the iron head-piece of a mace or lance.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and derived usages include: (1) the stripping of a person's garments, likened to peeling away the successive layers of an onion (baṣṣaltu al-rajul); (2) the multiplication or doubling of a thing, compared to the proliferating concentric coats of the bulb (tabaṣṣala al-shayʾ); (3) in a proverbial register, the contrast between being stripped bare (as one who comes away from the spindle with nothing) and being richly clothed (as one who returns clad from the onion), exploiting the layered structure of the bulb as an image of abundance or accretion.

canonical_definition.arabic: البَصَل معروف، الواحدة بَصَلة، وتُشَبَّه به بَيْضة الحَدِيد؛ والبَصَلة إِنما هي سَفِيفة واحدة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-baṣal is the well-known onion; the singular is baṣalah. The iron boss of a helmet is likened to it; and a baṣalah is but a single sheath or layer.

derivations.english_translation: to peel or strip someone of their clothes; to multiply, double, or proliferate (said of a thing)
onion; the onion bulb collectively
a single onion bulb; a layer or sheath of an onion; the iron boss or pointed cap of a helmet
onion (variant lexical form)
onion (variant lexical form)

mufradat.text: البصل معروف في قوله عز وجل: وعدسها وبصلها [البقرة/ 61]، وبيضة الحديد: بصل، تشبيها به لقول الشاعر: 56- وتركا كالبصل (3) بضع البضاعة: قطعة وافرة من المال تقتنى للتجارة، يقال: أبضع بضاعة وابتضعها. قال تعالى: هذه بضاعتنا ردت إلينا [يوسف/ 65] وقال تعالى: ببضاعة مزجاة [يوسف/ 88]، والأصل في هذه الكلمة: البضع وهو جملة من اللحم تبضع (4)، أي: تقطع. يقال: فخمة ذفراء ترتى بالعرى قردمانيا وتركا كالبصل تزوج وقطع لحم بضع وجمع بضعة كذا، والبضع من واحد لتسعة، والبضع نكاحها أو موضع الإيعاب بضعته فابتضع وتبضع، كقولك: قطعته وقطعته فانقطع وتقطع، والمبضع: ما يبضع به، نحو: المقطع، وكني بالبضع عن الفرج، فقيل: ملكت بضعها، أي: تزوجتها، وباضعها بضاعا، أي: باشرها، وفلان: حسن البضع والبضيع والبضعة، والبضاعة عبارة عن السمن (1). وقيل للجزيرة المنقطعة عن البر: بضيع، وفلان بضعة مني، أي: جار مجرى بعض جسدي لقربه مني، والباضعة: الشجة التي تبضع اللحم (2)، والبضع بالكسر: المنقطع من العشرة، ويقال ذلك لما بين الثلاث إلى العشرة، وقيل: بل هو فوق الخمس ودون العشرة، قال تعالى: بضع سنين* [الروم/ 4].

entries.text: جئت أعرى من المغزل ورجعت أكسى من البصل. وقد تبصل الشيء إذا تضاعف تضاعف قشر البصلة: وبصلت الرجل من ثيابه جردته.

جئت أعرى من المغزل ورجعت أكسى من البصل. وقد تبصل الشيء إذا تضاعف تضاعف قشر البصلة: وبصلت الرجل من ثيابه جردته. Metaphorical (Majaz): خرجوا كأنهم الأصل، وعلى رءوسهم البصل أي البيض، والأصل جمع أصلة وهي حية خبيثة.
خرجوا كأنهم الأصل، وعلى رءوسهم البصل أي البيض، والأصل جمع أصلة وهي حية خبيثة.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the violent inversion and scattering of earth or a container so as to expose and cast out what lies concealed within it — specifically, the turning over of grave soil and the ejection of its buried contents.
record.haqiqah_literal: To overturn the earth of graves, scatter their soil, and bring forth what is hidden inside them, whether treasure or the dead.
record.majaz_scholastic: In theological and eschatological usage, the term denotes the resurrection event in which graves are breached and their occupants emerge — a metonymy for the final disclosure and dispersion of all that was concealed. Al-Rāghib notes that some grammarians erroneously analyzed the quadriliteral بعثر as a compound of بعث (to raise) and أثير (to stir up), but this derivational fallacy is rejected because it violates the established morphological integrity of the root.

canonical_definition.arabic: بُعْثِرَتِ القبورُ: قُلِبَ ترابُها وأُثيرَ ما فيها، وخرج ما في بطنها من الذهب والفضة وخروج الموتى بعد ذلك.
canonical_definition.english: The graves were overturned: their soil was turned over and what was inside them was stirred up, and the gold and silver within them emerged, followed by the emergence of the dead.

derivations.english_translation: to overturn, scatter, and expose the contents of a grave or container
to be overturned and have its contents scattered (passive)
the act of overturning and scattering; the resurrection of the dead from graves

mufradat.text: قال الله تعالى: وإذا القبور بعثرت [الانفطار/ 4]، أي: قلب ترابها وأثير ما فيها، ومن رأى تركيب الرباعي والخماسي من ثلاثيين نحو: تهلل وبسمل (1): إذا قال: لا إله إلا الله وبسم الله يقول: إن بعثر مركب من: بعث وأثير، وهذا لا يبعد في هذا الحرف، فإن البعثرة تتضمن معنى بعث وأثير.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the sudden, forceful emergence and overflow of water from a breach or collapsed side of a basin or reservoir, i.e., the rupture of a containment structure and the consequent gushing forth of its liquid contents.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the outflow of water from a broken side or fissure of a basin (ḥawḍ) or a reservoir (jābiyah), and the verb tabaʿthaqa denotes the event of a side of such a structure breaking so that water pours out from it.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; no established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded in the classical lexical tradition. The root remains confined to its concrete hydraulic sense, with no extension into abstract or scholastic domains.

canonical_definition.arabic: البَعْثَقَةُ: خُروج الماء من غائِل حَوْضٍ أو جابِيةٍ. وتَبَعْثَقَ إذا انكسرت منه ناحية ففاضَ منها.
canonical_definition.english: Al-baʿthaqah: the outflow of water from a breach in a basin or a reservoir. And tabaʿthaqa: when one side of it breaks so that water pours out from it.

derivations.english_translation: the outflow of water from a breach in a basin or reservoir; the bursting forth of water from a collapsed side
to burst open at one side and pour forth water; to rupture and overflow (of a basin or reservoir)

record.ontological_core: The root denotes corporeal thickness and abundant flesh, with the physical origin being a body or limb characterized by dense, heavy, fleshy mass.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is 'thick, coarse, and abundant in flesh,' applied to a body or limb that is dense and heavy with meat.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical or scholastic usage is attested in the classical lexicons; the term remains confined to the literal physical description of bodily thickness and fleshiness.

canonical_definition.arabic: بَخْلَصٌ وبَلْخَصٌ: غليظٌ كثير اللحم، وقد تَبَخْلَصَ وتَبَلْخَصَ.
canonical_definition.english: Bakhlṣ and balkhṣ: thick, coarse, and abundant in flesh; and indeed tabakhlaṣa and tabalkhaṣa mean to become so.

derivations.english_translation: thick, coarse, and abundant in flesh
thick, coarse, and abundant in flesh
to become thick, coarse, and abundant in flesh
to become thick, coarse, and abundant in flesh

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on compact, solid bodily mass — a dense, thickset corporeal bulk, particularly of a woman, characterized by firm, well-knit flesh rather than mere largeness.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Lisān al-ʿArab, is a woman who is بِلِز (biliz) or بِلِزّ (bilizz): bulky, thickset, and compactly fleshed (ḍakhma muktaniza). Al-Jawharī restricts بِلِز to the pattern فِعِل (fiʿil) with kasrah on both the first and second radicals, meaning simply 'bulky.' Thaʿlab noted that only two adjectival forms in Arabic occur on the pattern فِعِل: a woman بِلِز and a she-ass إِبِد. The root also yields جَمَل بَلَنْزى (jamal balanzā): a thick, coarse, heavy-bodied camel.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested in the classical lexica. The root remains confined to the concrete physical domain of dense corporeal bulk and coarse animal mass; it was never abstracted into scholastic or theological usage. Its sole figurative potential lies in the transferred application of بَلَنْزى to a camel, extending the notion of compact solidity from the human female body to the heavy, thick-set frame of the male camel.

canonical_definition.arabic: امرأَة بِلِزٌ وبِلِزٌّ: ضخمة مكتنزة. قال ثعلب: لم يأْت من الصفات على فِعِلٍ إِلاَّ حرفان: امرأَة بِلِزٌ وأَتان إِبِدٌ. وجَمَل بَلَنْزى: غليظ.
canonical_definition.english: A woman who is بِلِز or بِلِزّ: bulky and compactly fleshed. Thaʿlab said: only two adjectival forms occur on the pattern فِعِل — a woman بِلِز and a she-ass إِبِد. And a camel بَلَنْزى: thick and coarse.

derivations.english_translation: a woman who is bulky, thickset, and compactly fleshed
a woman who is bulky, thickset, and compactly fleshed (intensive form)
a thick, coarse, heavy-bodied camel

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root بله is a state of mental deficiency or heedlessness, specifically an incapacity to discern or manage evil (الغفلة عن الشرّ وعدم إحسانه). It denotes a congenital or acquired deficiency in practical intelligence, not a moral failing.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is a person who is simple-minded, naive, or foolish, particularly one who is unable to recognize or deal with harm. It is used literally for a deficient intellect, as in 'خير أولادنا الأبله العقول' (the best of our children are those with simple minds) and 'خير النساء البلهاء الخجول' (the best of women is the naive, modest one). The verb forms include بَلِهَ (baliha) and تَبَالَهَ (tabālaha), meaning to feign foolishness or to act naive.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) a praiseworthy simplicity or innocence, especially in women, where lack of cunning is a virtue; (2) feigned foolishness (تباله) as a rhetorical or social strategy, as in the verse by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa where women pretend not to recognize the poet; (3) in the phrase 'بله ما أضمره' (bale mā aḍmara-hu), it functions as an imperative or interjection meaning 'leave aside' or 'never mind' what he concealed, indicating a dismissal or a transition to a better alternative. This usage is metaphorical, moving from the concrete sense of mental deficiency to a pragmatic particle of exception or disregard.

canonical_definition.arabic: البَلَهُ: الغَفْلة عن الشرّ وأَن لا يُحْسِنَهُ؛ بَلِهَ، بالكسر، بَلَهاً وتَبَلَّه وهو أَبْلَه وابتُلِهَ كبَلِه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-balah is heedlessness of evil and the inability to manage it; baliha (with kasra) yields balahan, and taballah is to affect it; one is ablah, and ibtuliha is like baliha.

entries.text: هو في شباب أبله وعيش أبله، يراد غفل صاحبهما عن الطوارق. قال رؤبة: بعد غداني الشباب الأبله ومنه: هو في بلهنية من عيشه. تقول: لازلت ملقى بتهنيه، مبقى في بلهنيه. وجمل أبله وناقة بلهاء: لا تنحاش من ثقل كأنها حمقاء. وفلان يتبله في المفازة أي يتعسف من غير هداية ولا مسئلة.

خير أولادنا الأبله العقول، وخير النساء البلهاء الخجول. قال: ولقد لهوت بطفلة مبالة ... بلهاء تطلعني على أسرارها وتباله فلان. قال عمر بن أبي ربيعة: تبالهن بالعرفان لما عرفنني ... وقلن امرؤ باغ أكل وأوضعا وتقول: هذا ما أظهره لك بله ما أضمره أي دع ما أضمره فهو خير مما أظهره.

record.ontological_core: The triliteral sequence ب-ن-ط is classified by the classical lexicographers as a root that is 'muhmal' (unused/neglected) in its bare form; its ontological origin is therefore not an independent physical act or entity, but rather a dialectal Yemeni nominal designation for a practitioner of weaving, realized only when the sequence is augmented by an intervening letter.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is restricted to the Yemeni dialectal noun 'al-biyanṭ' (البِيَنْطُ), denoting a weaver (al-nassāj). This is a concrete occupational designation, not a verbal root, and its morphological pattern corresponds to 'al-biyaṭr' (البِيَطْرُ), indicating that the word is a quadriliteral or augmented nominal form rather than a triliteral verb.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested. The root is neither employed in Quranic discourse nor in speculative theology (kalām) or philosophy (falsafa). Its only extension is the dialectal occupational noun for a weaver; any attempt to derive abstract or scholastic meanings would be an illegitimate projection beyond the classical lexical evidence.

canonical_definition.arabic: قال الأزهري: أَما بنط فهو مهمل، فإِذا فصل بين الباء والنون بياء كان مستعملاً، يقول أَهل اليمن للنّسَّاج البِيَنْطُ، وعلى وزنه البِيَطْرُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Azhari said: As for 'bnṭ', it is unused (muhmal); but when a yāʾ separates the bāʾ and the nūn, it becomes employed. The people of Yemen call the weaver 'al-biyanṭ', and it follows the pattern of 'al-biyaṭr'.

derivations.english_translation: weaver (Yemeni dialectal occupational noun)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of gathering, tightening, and securing disparate elements into a coherent, bounded whole — specifically, the stitching or fastening of garment seams and the binding of a book's quires.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah: the banāʾiq are the seams or stitched joins of a wide shirt (qamīṣ wāsiʿ al-banāʾiq), also described as its dakhārīṣ (seam-lines) or its lining (libn). To banāʾiq a garment is to sew its seams; to banāʾiq a book is to bind or stitch its quires together.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic extensions: (1) To banāʾiq speech (banāʾiq kalāmahu) is to gather it, arrange it, and set it in order — a rhetorical metaphor from the stitching of seams. (2) To banāʾiq a book (banāʾiq al-kitāb) is to close, finish, or dismiss it — a usage attested as a dialectal variant of nabaqa, meaning to conclude or set aside. (3) The phrase 'if you finish reading the book, then banāʾiq it and do not leave it un-banāʾiqed' carries the sense of sealing, concluding, or putting the matter to rest.

canonical_definition.arabic: بَنَّقَ الكِتَابَ: لُغَةٌ فِي نَبَّقَهُ. وَبَنَّقَ كَلَامَهُ: جَمَعَهُ وَسَوَّاهُ، وَمِنْهُ بَنَائِقُ القَمِيصِ أَيْ جَمْعُ شَيْءٍ. وَالبَنِيقَةُ: خِيَاطَةُ القَمِيصِ، وَالجَمْعُ بَنَائِقُ.
canonical_definition.english: To banāʾiq a book is a dialectal variant of to nabaqahu (to bind or close it). To banāʾiq one's speech is to gather it and set it in order, whence the banāʾiq of a shirt, meaning the gathering of something. The banīqah is the stitching of a shirt, and its plural is banāʾiq.

derivations.english_translation: he stitched, sewed, or fastened a seam; he gathered and arranged
he stitched up, bound (a book), or concluded (a matter)
a seam, stitch, or fastening of a garment
a single seam or stitched join; a quire of a book
seams, stitched joins; the quires or gatherings of a book
stitched, bound, or concluded

entries.text: قميص واسع البنائق وهي الدخاريص، وقيل اللبن. قال ذو الرمة: على كل كهل أزعكي ويافع ... من اللؤم سربال جديد البنائق وتقول إذا خطت البنيقة، فخطه Metaphorical (Majaz): جعبة مبنقة: زيد في أعلاها شبه بنيقة لتتسع. وطريق مبنق: واسع. ومفازة مبنوقة بأخرى: موصولة بها.

قميص واسع البنائق وهي الدخاريص، وقيل اللبن. قال ذو الرمة: على كل كهل أزعكي ويافع ... من اللؤم سربال جديد البنائق وتقول إذا خطت البنيقة، فخطها بنيقه. وبنق الكتاب: ذره. وإذا فرغت من قراءة الكتاب فبنقه ولا تدعه غير مبنق.
جعبة مبنقة: زيد في أعلاها شبه بنيقة لتتسع. وطريق مبنق: واسع. ومفازة مبنوقة بأخرى: موصولة بها.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is a toponymic designation: a village in Egypt renowned for its honey, which the Prophet Muhammad blessed. It lacks a broader physical or verbal root meaning in the classical lexicons.
record.haqiqah_literal: A proper noun referring to a specific village in Egypt, pronounced Binhā (with a kasrah on the bāʾ and sukūn on the nūn), though later pronounced Banhā (with a fatḥah on the bāʾ). It is literally the name of that locality.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested; the term remains a strict toponym with no extended abstract applications.

canonical_definition.arabic: بِنْهَا، بكسر الباء وسكون النون، قرية من قرى مصر، بارك النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في عسلها؛ والناس اليوم يفتحون الباء.
canonical_definition.english: Binhā, with a kasrah on the bāʾ and a sukūn on the nūn, is a village in Egypt whose honey the Prophet, peace be upon him, blessed; today people pronounce it Banhā with a fatḥah on the bāʾ.

derivations.english_translation: Binhā: a village in Egypt, with the bāʾ carrying a kasrah and the nūn a sukūn.
Banhā: the later pronunciation of the same village name, with a fatḥah on the bāʾ.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on the manifestation of joy through the face, specifically the act of laughing and displaying cheerfulness, with an emphasis on the brightness and radiance of the expression.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is a woman who is cheerful, laughing, and radiant, as exemplified in the poetic description of a woman smiling with teeth as bright as hail.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root extends to any person or entity that exhibits joy, brightness, or cheerfulness, and in theological contexts, it may refer to the radiance of divine favor or the joy of the believers in paradise.

canonical_definition.arabic: البَهْنانةُ: الضحَّاكة المُتهلِّلة
canonical_definition.english: Al-Bahnānah: the woman who laughs much and is radiant with joy.

derivations.english_translation: cheerful, laughing woman; radiant with joy

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the spatial extent of the two outstretched hands, i.e., the distance between the two palms when the arms are fully extended; from this concrete measure of bodily span, the root extends to the act of measuring by that span and to the stretching forth of the forelegs in a beast's stride.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of measuring a garment or the like by the bāʿ (the span of the outstretched arms), analogous to dharʿahu when one measures it by the dhiraʿ (cubit); likewise, the bāʿ of a camel or horse is the extension of its forelegs in walking, and a horse is described as ṭabīʿ bāʿ or baʿīd al-khaṭw when its stride is long.
record.majaz_scholastic: The root is applied metaphorically and scholastically to the extension of a beast's forelegs in motion (bāʿa al-baʿīr wa-l-faras wa-tabawwaʿa idhā madda bāʿahu fī sayrihi), to a she-camel as bāʿiʿah and she-camels as bawāʿiʿ when they stretch their forelegs widely in stride, and to the temporal or transactional sense in the phrase mā bīʿat hādhihi al-thiyāb ḥattā bīʿat (these garments were not sold until they were sold), where the form is used in a derived commercial context. The root also appears in the expression kam bawʿ thawbika wa-kam dharʿ thawbika (how many spans is your garment and how many cubits?), indicating measurement by bodily span.

canonical_definition.arabic: البَاعُ والبَوْعُ والبُوع: مَسافةُ ما بين الكفَّيْن إِذا بسَطْتهما؛ والباعُ: تَبَوُّعُ البعير والفرس في سيرهما إذا مدَّا أَيديهما.
canonical_definition.english: The bāʿ, bawʿ, and būʿ: the distance between the two palms when they are outstretched; and the bāʿ: the stretching forth of a camel and a horse in their gait when they extend their forelegs.

entries.text: لفلان سابقة وباع. وقال العجاج: إذا الكرام ابتدروا الباع بدر وتبوع للمساعي: مد باعه. قال الطرماح: يماني تبوع للمساعي ... يداه وكل ذي حسب يماني

باع الثوب يبوعه إذا قدره بباعه، نحو ذرعه إذا قدره بذراعه. وتقول: كم بوع ثوبك وكم ذرع ثوبك وباع البعير والفرس وتبوع إذا مد باعه في سيره. وفرس طيع بيع: بعيد الخطو. قال العباس بن مرداس: على متن جرداء السراة نبيلة ... كعالية المران بيعة القدر ومر يتبوع. وناقة بائعة، ونوق بوائع. وما ب

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ب-ي-ض is the color white, understood as the luminous, unmixed, and manifest opposite of black, predicated of animals, plants, and all entities susceptible to coloration.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, sensory reality (Ḥaqīqah) of البياض is the color white itself, the quality of an object that is أبيض (white). It is a perceptible accident (ʿaraḍ) subsisting in bodies, and its verbal noun denotes the state or instance of being white.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, whiteness is transferred to signify moral and spiritual purity, honor, and excellence, because the Arabs deemed white the most noble of colors. Thus, a person free of defects is said to be 'white of color' (أبيض اللون). In Quranic discourse, the whitening of faces on the Day of Judgment is a metaphor for joy, divine pleasure, and salvation, while blackening denotes grief and punishment. The dual form 'الأبيضان' metaphorically designates fat and youth, or milk and water, as the two white substances essential to life and sustenance. The active participle 'بائض' (egg-laying) is applied to birds, and 'بيوض' to a hen that lays many eggs, extending the root to the production of eggs, which are themselves white.

canonical_definition.arabic: البَيَاضُ: ضِدُّ السَّوَادِ، يَكُونُ فِي الحَيَوَانِ وَالنَّبَاتِ وَغَيْرِهِمَا مِمَّا يَقْبَلُهُ. وَالأَبْيَضُ: عِرْقٌ سُمِّيَ بِهِ لِكَوْنِهِ أَبْيَضَ. وَالبَيْضُ: مَعْرُوفٌ، وَبَاضَتِ الدَّجَاجَةُ تَبِيضُ بَيْضًا.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Bayāḍ (whiteness) is the opposite of al-Sawād (blackness); it occurs in animals, plants, and other entities susceptible to it. Al-Abyaḍ (the white one) is a vein named thus because of its whiteness. Al-Bayḍ (eggs) is well-known, and the hen lays eggs (bāḍat tabīḍu bayḍan).
