the process of becoming white
becoming white; that which is turning white

mufradat.text: البياض في الألوان: ضد السواد، يقال: ابيض يبيض ابيضاضا وبياضا، فهو مبيض وأبيض. قال عز وجل: يوم تبيض وجوه وتسود وجوه فأما الذين اسودت وجوههم أكفرتم بعد إيمانكم فذوقوا العذاب بما كنتم تكفرون* وأما الذين ابيضت وجوههم ففي رحمت الله [آل عمران/ 106- 107]. والأبيض: عرق سمي به لكونه أبيض، ولما كان البياض أفضل لون عندهم كما قيل: البياض أفضل، والسواد أهول، والحمرة أجمل، والصفرة أشكل، عبر به عن الفضل والكرم بالبياض، حتى قيل لمن لم يتدنس بمعاب: هو أبيض اللون. وقوله تعالى: يوم تبيض وجوه [آل عمران/ 106]، فابيضاض الوجوه عبارة عن المسرة، واسودادها عن الغم، وعلى ذلك وإذا بشر أحدهم بالأنثى ظل وجهه مسودا [النحل/ 58]، وعلى نحو الابيضاض قوله تعالى: وجوه يومئذ ناضرة [القيامة/ 22]، وقوله: وجوه يومئذ مسفرة* ضاحكة مستبشرة [عبس/ 38- 39]. وقيل: أمك بيضاء من قضاعة (1) وعلى ذلك قوله تعالى: بيضاء لذة للشاربين [الصافات/ 46]، وسمي البيض لبياضه، الواحدة: بيضة، وكني عن المرأة بالبيضة تشبيها بها في اللون، وكونها مصونة تحت الجناح. وبيضة البلد يقال في المدح والذم، أما المدح فلمن كان مصونا من بين أهل البلد ورئيسا فيهم، وعلى ذلك قول الشاعر: 73- كانت قريش بيضة فتفلقت فالمح خالصه لعبد مناف (2) أمك بيضاء من قضاعة في ال بيت الذي يستظل في طنبه وأما الذم فلمن كان ذليلا معرضا لمن يتناوله كبيضة متروكة بالبلد، أي: العراء والمفازة. وبيضتا الرجل سميتا بذلك تشبيها بها في الهيئة والبياض، يقال: باضت الدجاجة، وباض كذا، أي: تمكن. قال الشاعر: 74- بداء من ذوات الضغن يأوي صدورهم فعشش ثم باض (1) وباض الحر: تمكن، وباضت يد المرأة: إذا ورمت ورما على هيئة البيض، ويقال: دجاجة بيوض، ودجاج بيض (2).

entries.text: اجتمع للمرأة الأبيضان الشحم والشباب، وهو لا يشرب إلا الأبيضين. قال: ولكنه يأتي لي الحول كاملا ... وما لي إلا الأبيضين شراب يريد بالأبيضين اللبن والماء. وما رأيته مد أبيضان أي يومان. ودجاجة بيوض ودجاج بيض وغراب بائض.

فلان يحوط بيضة الإسلام وبيضة قومه. وباض بني فلان وابتاضهم: دخل في بيضتهم. وأوقعوا بهم فابتاضوهم أي استأصلوا بيضتهم. وباضت الأرض: أنبتت الكمأة وهي بيض الأرض وبه فسر المثل: " هو أذل من بيضة البلد " وباض الحر. اشتد. وأتيته في بيضة القيظ وبيضاء القيظ، وهي صميمه بين طلوع سهيل والدبران

اجتمع للمرأة الأبيضان الشحم والشباب، وهو لا يشرب إلا الأبيضين. قال: ولكنه يأتي لي الحول كاملا ... وما لي إلا الأبيضين شراب يريد بالأبيضين ال Metaphorical (Majaz): فلان يحوط بيضة الإسلام وبيضة قومه. وباض بني فلان وابتاضهم: دخل في بيضتهم. وأوقعوا بهم فابتاضوهم أي استأصلوا بيضتهم. وباضت الأرض: أنبتت الكمأ

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of returning, reverting, or turning back from a state or course to another; it denotes a movement of reversal and reorientation, whether physical or moral.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of a servant returning to God from his sin, and God's acceptance of that return; it also includes the judge offering repentance to an apostate, and the time of Islam being called the 'time of repentance' because people turn back from polytheism.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, it signifies the abandonment of sin in the most excellent manner, comprising four conditions: leaving the sin because of its vileness, regret for having committed it, resolve not to return to it, and restitution of possible missed obligations. It also denotes God's acceptance of repentance, and the concept of 'returning to God' implies seeking refuge and turning back to obedience. In scholastic usage, it is the act of contrition and amendment, and the root is used for both human repentance and divine forgiveness.

canonical_definition.arabic: التَّوْبَةُ: الرُّجُوعُ مِنَ الذَّنْبِ، وَتَابَ إِلَى اللَّهِ يَتُوبُ تَوْبًا وَتَوْبَةً وَمَتَابًا: أَنَابَ وَرَجَعَ عَنِ الْمَعْصِيَةِ إِلَى الطَّاعَةِ.
canonical_definition.english: Repentance is the return from sin; one repents to God, returning and turning back from disobedience to obedience.

derivations.english_translation: he repented, returned (to God)
repentance (as a collective or verbal noun)
a single act of repentance
return, place or time of return (to God)
Oft-Returning (one who accepts repentance repeatedly), an attribute of God
asking someone to repent, offering repentance

mufradat.text: التوب: ترك الذنب على أجمل الوجوه (1)، وهو أبلغ وجوه الاعتذار، فإن الاعتذار على ثلاثة أوجه: إما أن يقول المعتذر: لم أفعل، أو يقول: فعلت لأجل كذا، أو فعلت وأسأت وقد أقلعت، ولا رابع لذلك، وهذا الأخير هو التوبة، والتوبة في الشرع: ترك الذنب لقبحه والندم على ما فرط منه، والعزيمة على ترك المعاودة، وتدارك ما أمكنه أن يتدارك من الأعمال بالأعمال بالإعادة، فمتى اجتمعت هذه الأربع فقد كملت شرائط التوبة. وتاب إلى الله، فذكر «إلى الله» يقتضي الإنابة، نحو: فتوبوا إلى بارئكم [البقرة/ 54]، وتوبوا إلى الله جميعا [النور/ 31]، أفلا يتوبون إلى الله [المائدة/ 74]، وتاب الله عليه، أي: قبل توبته، منه: لقد تاب الله على النبي والمهاجرين [التوبة/ 117]، ثم تاب عليهم ليتوبوا [التوبة/ 118]، فتاب عليكم وعفا عنكم [البقرة/ 187]. والتائب يقال لباذل التوبة ولقابل التوبة، فالعبد تائب إلى الله، والله تائب على عبده. والتواب: العبد الكثير التوبة، وذلك بتركه كل وقت بعض الذنوب على الترتيب حتى يصير تاركا لجميعه، وقد يقال ذلك لله تعالى لكثرة قبوله توبة العباد (2) حالا بعد حال. وقوله: ومن تاب وعمل صالحا فإنه يتوب إلى الله متابا [الفرقان/ 71]، أي: التوبة التامة، وهو الجمع بين ترك القبيح وتحري الجميل. عليه توكلت وإليه متاب [الرعد/ 30]، إنه هو التواب الرحيم* [البقرة/ 54].

entries.text: تاب العبد إلى الله من ذنبه، وتاب الله على عبده، والله تواب، وإلى الله المتاب. واستتاب الحاكم فلانا: عرض عليه التوبة، والمرتد يستتاب. وأدرك فلان زمن التوبة أي الإسلام، لأنه يتاب فيه من الشرك. قال الجعدي: دار حي كانت لهم زمن التو ... بة لا عزل ولا أكفال

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the red, juicy, mulberry-like fruit known as al-firṣād; the root denotes this specific fruit as a concrete, tangible entity, with no attested abstract or verbal primitive underlying it.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the firṣād fruit (mulberry), a red, edible berry; its singular unit is tuwtha (one mulberry).
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical lexicons; the root remains confined to its concrete botanical reference. The only extended usage is the toponym Kafrtūthā, a place name derived from the root, which is a proper noun and not a semantic extension.

canonical_definition.arabic: التُّوثُ: الفِرْصادُ، واحدتُه تُوثةٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-tūth is the firṣād (mulberry); its singular unit is tuwtha.

derivations.english_translation: the firṣād fruit (mulberry), collective noun
a single mulberry (unit noun)
Kafrtūthā, a place name

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a thin, watery, diluted substance—specifically a broth or gruel reduced to a fluid, runny consistency, typically prepared with milk. Its foundational physical image is that of a liquid so thin it lacks body or cohesion, cooked down to a near-watery state.
record.haqiqah_literal: الثُّرْعُطَةُ: a thin, watery broth or gruel (حَسا رقيق); الثُّرُعْطُطُ: a thin broth cooked with milk (حَساً رقيق طبخ باللبن). The literal referent is a culinary preparation of extreme fluidity and minimal viscosity.
record.majaz_scholastic: No attested metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is recorded in the classical lexica. The root remains confined to its literal culinary domain; any figurative application (e.g., to speech or thought lacking substance) would be an ad hoc extension not sanctioned by the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: الثُّرْعُطَةُ: الحَسا الرَّقِيقُ. الثُّرُعْطُطُ: حَساً رقيق طبخ باللبن.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Thurʿuṭah: a thin, watery broth or gruel. Al-Thuruʿṭuṭ: a thin broth cooked with milk.

derivations.english_translation: a thin, watery broth or gruel
a thin broth cooked with milk

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the eruptive dispersal and surging agitation of a substance — dust, cloud, or the like — rising and spreading outward in a visible, turbulent motion.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the surging, eruption, and dispersal of dust, clouds, or similar substances, rising and spreading visibly; also the agitating of the earth to bring forth its contents, and the bull (ثور) as the animal by which the earth is agitated for plowing.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically: the eruption of anger (ثائر الغضب), the outbreak of evil (ثور شرا), the onset of a rash or disease (ثارت الحصبة) by analogy to the dispersal of dust; the rising of the dawn light (ثور الشفق) as the dispersing one; and the act of assaulting or leaping upon someone (ثاوره). The term ثأر (blood revenge) is excluded from this root as it belongs to the hamzated root ثأر, not the hollow root ثور.

canonical_definition.arabic: ثَارَ الشيءُ ثَوْراً وثُؤُوراً وثَوَرَاناً وتَثَوَّرَ: هاج وانتشر ساطعاً؛ وأَثَارَهُ غيره. والثَّوْرُ: البقر الذي يُثار به الأرض، وأصله مصدر جُعل في موضع الفاعل.
canonical_definition.english: The thing surged, erupted, and spread visibly (thawran, thu'uran, thawaran, tathawwara): it became agitated and dispersed; another caused it to rise (athara). The thawr is the bovine by which the earth is agitated for ploughing; its form is originally a verbal noun placed in the position of the active participle.

derivations.english_translation: to surge, erupt, rise and spread (as dust or cloud); to be agitated
eruption, surging, agitation, turbulence
the act of surging or erupting
to agitate, to stir up, to incite
to raise (dust), to stir up, to agitate, to plough (the earth)
to become agitated, to erupt, to surge forth
to assault, to leap upon, to attack suddenly
bull; the animal used for ploughing; (as a source noun) the act of surging

mufradat.text: ثار الغبار والسحاب ونحوهما، يثور ثورا وثورانا: انتشر ساطعا، وقد أثرته، قال تعالى: فتثير سحابا* [الروم/ 48]، يقال: أثرت الأرض، كقوله تعالى: وأثاروا الأرض وعمروها [الروم/ 9]، وثارت الحصبة ثورا تشبيها بانتشار الغبار، وثور شرا كذلك، وثار ثائره كناية عن انتشار غضبه، وثاوره: واثبه، والثور: البقر الذي يثار به الأرض، فكأنه في الأصل مصدر جعل في موضع الفاعل (1)، نحو: ضيف وطيف في معنى: ضائف وطائف، وقولهم: سقط ثور الشفق (2) أي: الثائر المنتثر، والثأر هو طلب الدم، وأصله الهمز، وليس من هذا الباب.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root جاز is the act of traversing, passing through, or crossing over a boundary, barrier, or medium—whether a road, a valley, a river, or a choking obstruction in the throat—such that the traverser moves from one side, state, or condition to another.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to pass or cross over something, as in crossing a road (جاز الطريق), traversing a valley (جاز الوادي), or passing through water (جاز الماء). It also denotes the physical act of a choking morsel or obstruction passing down the throat, as in the expression 'يا ماء إن أجأزت فكم أجزت من غصة' (O water, if you pass, how many a choking morsel have you passed!).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) the permissibility or validity of a thing (جواز), as in a legally or rationally permissible act (جائز), meaning it is not obstructed by prohibition or impossibility; (2) the granting of permission or authorization (إجازة), as in licensing a narrator, a physician, or a student, i.e., allowing them to pass beyond a boundary of qualification; (3) the execution or carrying out of a command or contract (إجازة العقد), meaning its effective passage into validity; (4) in theology and philosophy, the contingent or possible (جائز) in contrast to the necessary (واجب) and the impossible (ممتنع), denoting that whose existence or non-existence is not intrinsically obstructed; (5) the penetration of an idea or meaning through the mind (جاز المعنى في ذهنه), i.e., it passed through and was apprehended.

canonical_definition.arabic: جاز: أصلٌ يدلُّ على النُّفُوذ والمُضِيِّ في الشيء، يقال: جاز الطريقَ، وجاز الماءَ، وجازت الغُصَّةُ في الحلق. ثم استُعير للجواز بمعنى الإباحة والإمضاء، وللجائز في المنطق والكلام بمعنى الممكن الذي لا يمتنع وجوده ولا عدمه.
canonical_definition.english: Jāza: The root signifies penetration and passage through a thing. One says: he crossed the road, he passed through the water, and the choking morsel passed down the throat. It is then metaphorically extended to permissibility in the sense of allowance and execution, and to the 'contingent' in logic and theology, meaning the possible whose existence and non-existence are not intrinsically impossible.

derivations.english_translation: to pass, cross, traverse; to be permissible or valid
passing, crossing; the act of traversing
one who passes or crosses; a traverser
permissibility, validity, license
permissible, valid, allowable; contingent (in logic/theology)
authorization, license, permission; the act of granting passage or validity
one who authorizes, licenses, or permits passage
authorized, licensed, permitted; that which has been passed or validated

entries.text: فلان جئز شئز أي شرق قلق. وتقول: يا ماء إن أجأزت، فكم أجزت، من أجاز الغصة.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on compact, low-set corporeal form and the act of bringing a body down to the ground — a stocky, short-statured physique and the forcible casting of an opponent to the earth.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a man who is short and compact (jaʿd qaṣīr), with the feminine form جَحْدَرَةٌ; the verbal noun الجَحْدَرَةُ denotes this quality of shortness and compactness. The verb جَحْدَرَ صَاحِبَهُ means he threw his companion down to the ground, prostrated him.
record.majaz_scholastic: Beyond the physical sense, the root is applied metaphorically to the act of overpowering and casting down an adversary, i.e., to defeat and humiliate him by bringing him low. It is also used as a proper name (جَحْدَرٌ), a personal designation without descriptive force. No attested philosophical or theological technical usage is recorded in the classical lexica.

canonical_definition.arabic: الجَحْدَرُ: الرجل الجَعْدُ القَصِيرُ، والأُنثى جَحْدَرَةٌ، والاسم الجَحْدَرَةُ. ويقال: جَحْدَرَ صاحبَه وجَحْدَلَهُ إِذا صرعه. وجَحْدَرٌ: اسم رجل.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Jaḥdar: a short, compact man; the feminine is jaḥdarah, and the abstract noun is al-jaḥdarah. It is said: jaḥdara ṣāḥibahu wa-jaḥdalahu, meaning he threw his companion down to the ground. And Jaḥdar is a man's name.

derivations.english_translation: he threw him down to the ground; he prostrated him
the act of throwing down; shortness and compactness of build
a short, compact man; also a proper name
a short, compact woman

record.ontological_core: The root denotes massive, coarse, and rugged corporeal bulk — a thick, heavy, and solid physical constitution, whether of a camel, a person, or a valley.
record.haqiqah_literal: A huge, thick, and coarse she-camel; a bulky, thick-bodied man; a rugged, broad valley.
record.majaz_scholastic: Extended by Ibn Manẓūr to topographical and human referents: the rugged valley (al-wādī) and the corpulent, thick-set man (al-rajul al-ghalīẓ al-ḍakhm). Al-Azharī transmits from Shimr the application to a man of coarse, massive build, and to a woman of the same description. The term remains within the domain of physical magnitude and coarse solidity; no abstract or theological metaphorization is attested.

canonical_definition.arabic: الجِرْدَحْل من الإِبل: الضَّخْم. ناقة جِرْدَحْل: ضَخْمة غليظة. ورَجُل جِرْدَحْل: الغليظ الضَّخْم. والجِرْدَحْل: الوادي.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Jirdaḥl among camels: the massive one. A she-camel that is jirdaḥl: huge and coarse. A man who is jirdaḥl: thick and massive. And al-jirdaḥl: the valley.

derivations.english_translation: A huge, thick, coarse she-camel; a bulky, thick-bodied man; a rugged, broad valley
A woman of massive, coarse, and thick build

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is the act of taking livestock out to graze in the fresh spring pasture (al-jashar) near the dwellings, without returning them to the household for the night.
record.haqiqah_literal: To send horses or livestock out to graze in the spring herbage (al-jashar) in front of the tents or houses, and to remain with them overnight in the pasture rather than returning to the family dwellings.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, the root is employed metaphorically to denote spiritual negligence or distraction from prayer, as in the prophetic tradition of Ibn Masʿūd: 'Let not your grazing (jasharukum) deceive you from your prayer, for it is merely from your encampment.' Here, the literal act of grazing livestock near the camp is transposed to signify worldly preoccupations that keep one from devotional obligations. Additionally, the phrase 'they became jashar' is used to describe a group spending the night with their livestock, a metonymy for pastoral vigilance and separation from domestic comfort.

canonical_definition.arabic: الجَشَر: بَقْلُ الربيع. وجَشَرُوا الخَيْلَ وجَشَّروها: أَرْسَلُوها في الجَشْرِ. والجَشْرُ: أَن يخرجوا بخيلهم فَيَرْعَوْها أَمام بيوتهم. وأَصبحوا جَشْراً وجَشَراً.
canonical_definition.english: Al-jashar: the spring herbage. They sent out the horses and livestock to graze: they released them into the spring pasture. Al-jashr: the act of taking out their horses and grazing them in front of their dwellings. They became jashr or jashar: they spent the night with their livestock in the pasture, not returning to their homes.

derivations.english_translation: to send livestock to graze in the spring pasture; to graze livestock near the dwellings
to send out livestock to graze in the spring herbage (intensive form)
the act of taking livestock out to graze in the spring pasture; the spring herbage itself
spring herbage; fresh pasture
a group that spends the night with their livestock in the pasture, not returning to their homes
livestock sent out to graze; grazing animals

entries.text: جشر الرجل عن أهله إذا سافر. وجشر الصبح: خرج، ولاح أبلق جاشر. واصطبحوا الجاشرية وهي الشربة مع جشور الصبح نسيت إلى الصبح الجاشر. قال: إذا ما شربنا الجاشرية لم نبل ... أميرا وإن كان الأمير من الأزد

جشروا دوابهم، وجشروها: رعوها قريبا من البيوت. ومنه حديث ابن مسعود " لا يغرنكم جشركم من صلاتكم فإنما هي من كوفتكم " ونعم جشر، وهو جشار أنعامنا. وأصبح بنو فلان جشرا إذا باتوا مع النعم لا يروحون إلى بيوتهم. وجشر المال عن أهله: خرج إلى الرعي.

جشروا دوابهم، وجشروها: رعوها قريبا من البيوت. ومنه حديث ابن مسعود " لا يغرنكم جشركم من صلاتكم فإنما هي من كوفتكم " ونعم جشر، وهو جشار أنعامن Metaphorical (Majaz): جشر الرجل عن أهله إذا سافر. وجشر الصبح: خرج، ولاح أبلق جاشر. واصطبحوا الجاشرية وهي الشربة مع جشور الصبح نسيت إلى الصبح الجاشر. قال: إذا ما ش

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the substance of clay or mud (ṭīn), and by extension any moist, agglutinated mass such as dung collected and kneaded together; from this concrete sense of a cohesive, earthy lump the root extends to the posterior (the buttocks) as a bodily mass, and to the act of pelting someone with such a lump.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is clay or mud (al-ṭīn); it also denotes the posterior (al-ist), and a quantity of dung or similar matter gathered and formed into a mass. The verb jaʿʿa (جَعَّ) means: he threw clay or mud at someone.
record.majaz_scholastic: No attested metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded in the classical lexica; the root remains confined to its concrete physical and anatomical senses, with no extension into abstract, scholastic, or metaphysical domains.

canonical_definition.arabic: الجَعْوُ: الطين. يقال: جَعَّ فلانٌ فلاناً إِذا رماه بالجَعْوِ وهو الطين. والجَعْوُ: الاسْتُ. والجَعْوُ: ما جُمِعَ من بَعَرٍ أَو غيره فجُعِلَ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-jaʿw is clay. It is said: so-and-so jaʿʿa (pelting with clay) so-and-so, when he threw clay at him. Al-jaʿw is the posterior. And al-jaʿw is what is gathered from dung or other matter and formed into a mass.

derivations.english_translation: clay, mud; the posterior; a gathered mass of dung or similar matter
to throw clay or mud at someone

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of a body casting itself down and stretching out at full length upon the ground, whether lying on the side or flat on the back, in a state of complete extension and surrender of posture.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Asās al-Balāghah's strict ḥaqīqah, is the concrete posture of a person or animal that has thrown itself down and lies stretched out on the ground, either reclining on the side (muḍṭajiʿ) or lying supine (mustalqī) with limbs extended.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic extensions are limited in the classical lexica: the term may be applied figuratively to any entity or condition characterized by total prostration, abject abasement, or the abandonment of active resistance, as when one is said to be 'cast down' before another. In theological and ethical discourse, it can denote the soul's utter submission or the intellect's passive receptivity, though such usage remains an extension of the literal corporeal image rather than a distinct technical term.

canonical_definition.arabic: المُجْلَخِدُّ: المُضْطَجِعُ، وقيل: المُسْتَلْقِي الذي قد رَمَى بِنَفْسِهِ وامْتَدَّ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Mujlakhidd: the one lying down on his side; also said to be the one lying supine who has thrown himself down and stretched out at full length.

derivations.english_translation: One who has cast himself down and lies stretched out on the ground, either on his side or on his back.
He cast himself down and stretched out on the ground.
He threw himself down and lay at full length.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the removal of a covering or barrier, specifically the abandonment of modesty and restraint, manifesting as shamelessness and indecent speech or behavior.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (though not attested, derived from Lisān) is a woman's discarding of shame and speaking obscenely, or displaying herself provocatively.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root extends to any shameless or immodest act, including public indecency, brazenness, and the violation of social or moral boundaries. In theological contexts, it may denote a departure from virtuous conduct.

canonical_definition.arabic: جَلِعَت المرأَةُ، بالكسر، جَلَعاً، فهي جَلِعةٌ وجالِعةٌ، وجَلَعَت وهي جالع وجالَعَت وهي مُجالِعٌ كله إذا ترَكت الحَياء وتكلمت بالقبيح، وقيل إِذا كانت متَبرِّجةً.
canonical_definition.english: The woman became shameless (jalʿa), with a kasra, showing shamelessness (jalaʿan); she is shameless (jaliʿah) and shameless (jāliʿah). And she acted shamelessly (jalaʿat) while being shameless (jāliʿ), and she engaged in shameless behavior (jālaʿat) while being one who engages in shameless behavior (mujāliʿ) — all of this when she abandoned modesty and spoke obscenely, or it was said when she was displaying herself provocatively.

derivations.english_translation: to be shameless, to discard modesty (of a woman)
shameless woman, one who has abandoned modesty
shameless woman, one who speaks obscenely
to be shameless, to act immodestly
shameless man, one who acts immodestly
to act shamelessly with someone, to engage in immodest behavior
one who engages in shameless behavior with another

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the concrete image of a she-camel that is simultaneously fat and firm—an animal whose body combines abundant adipose tissue with a hard, compact, unyielding frame. This dual physical quality of corporeal density and solidity constitutes the root's primary sensory substrate, from which any further usage must be metaphorically derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in the classical lexical tradition, is a she-camel characterized by stoutness and hardness: ناقة جَلَنْباةٌ, i.e., a fat, firm she-camel. The term denotes a concrete, zoological referent and carries no abstract or figurative sense in its foundational usage.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological application is attested in the classical sources for this root. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī does not record it in Al-Mufradāt, and Al-Zamakhsharī does not treat it in Asās al-Balāghah. The root remains confined to its literal, concrete zoological domain; any extension beyond this would be an unsupported scholastic projection rather than an established majāz.

canonical_definition.arabic: ناقة جَلَنْباةٌ: سَمِينةٌ صُلْبةٌ
canonical_definition.english: A she-camel that is fat and firm.

derivations.english_translation: a fat and firm she-camel; a stout, solid-bodied she-camel
the root consonantal cluster denoting fatness combined with firmness in a she-camel

record.ontological_core: The root ج-م-ع-ل designates a bulky, aged, and physically coarsened entity — a creature or beast whose body has become thick, gnarled, and worn by time. Its foundational physical image is that of a heavy, hoary mass, whether a hyena (a stocky, coarse-haired predator) or an aged she-camel (a large, decrepit beast). The quadriliteral form جُمَعْلِيلَة carries an intensive diminutive-augmentative force, signaling a creature marked by both corpulence and senescence.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical referent is twofold: (1) the hyena (al-ḍabʿ), so named for its bulky, coarse, and ungainly body; and (2) an aged, decrepit she-camel (al-nāqa al-harima), whose frame has grown heavy and whose strength has decayed with advanced age. In both cases, the term denotes a concrete, observable animal whose physical constitution is characterized by mass, coarseness, and the ravages of time.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexicographical tradition. The term remains confined to its zoological and pastoral-literal domain. Any extended application — e.g., to a person of gross and aged constitution — would be a secondary, colloquial extension rather than a recognized majāz in the scholastic or rhetorical canon. Al-Zamakhsharī's Asās al-Balāghah does not record it, and Al-Rāghib's Al-Mufradāt does not treat it, confirming its status as a rare, concrete quadriliteral noun rather than a root with abstract or figurative derivations.

canonical_definition.arabic: الجُمَعْلِيلة: الضَّبُع، وقيل: الناقة الهَرِمة. قال ابن سيده: الجُمَعْلِيلة الضَّبُع. وقال الأزهري: الجُمَعْليلة الناقة الهَرِمة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-jumaʿlīlah: the hyena; or, it is said, the aged and decrepit she-camel. Ibn Sīdah stated: al-jumaʿlīlah is the hyena. Al-Azharī stated: al-jumaʿlīlah is the aged, decrepit she-camel.

derivations.english_translation: A hyena; or an aged, decrepit she-camel — a bulky, time-worn beast
A bulky, aged creature (hypothetical masculine form implied by the feminine)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a raised, rounded protuberance of a thing or of the earth, shaped like a dome or hemispherical mound.
record.haqiqah_literal: A raised, circular elevation of a thing or of the ground, resembling a dome; a domed mound or rounded protuberance.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, any domed or hemispherical structure or swelling; a place characterized by such rounded elevations (makān mujanbadh). The root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, so no philosophical or theological metaphorical usages are classically established; the term remains within the domain of physical topography and shape.

canonical_definition.arabic: الجُنْبُذَةُ، بالضم: ما ارتفع من الشيء واستدار كالقبة. والجُنْبُذَة: ما علا من الأَرض واستدار. ومكان مُجَنْبَذ: ذو جنابذ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Junbudhah, with ḍammah: that which is raised from a thing and is round like a dome. And al-junbudhah: that which is elevated from the ground and is round. And a place mujanbadh: possessing junbudhah-like elevations.

derivations.english_translation: a raised, rounded protuberance or domed mound (the standard classical form, with ḍammah on the bāʾ)
a raised, rounded protuberance or domed mound (colloquial variant, with fatḥah on the bāʾ)
a place abounding in rounded elevations or domed mounds

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is the act of covering, concealing, or shrouding an object — a concrete operation of overlaying something so as to hide it from view.
record.haqiqah_literal: To cover or conceal a thing; to shroud it. The verb جَنَزَ الشيءَ يَجْنِزُه جَنْزاً denotes the literal physical act of draping or wrapping an entity so that it is hidden.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, the root extends metaphorically to the shrouding of the dead — the ritual wrapping of a corpse in a burial shroud (تكفين) and the accompanying funeral prayer. The imperative form in the narration 'إِذا جَنَزْتُموها فآذِنُوني' ('when you have shrouded her, inform me') illustrates this transferred sense: the literal act of covering becomes the ritual preparation of the deceased for burial, and by further extension, the funeral procession itself. The root thus bridges the physical act of concealment and the theological domain of death, ritual purity, and eschatological transition.

canonical_definition.arabic: جَنَزَ الشيءَ يَجْنِزُه جَنْزاً: ستره. وذكروا أَن النَّوَار لما احْتُضِرَت أَوْصَت أَن يصلي عليها الحسن، فقيل له في ذلك، فقال: إِذا جَنَزْتُموها فآذِنُوني.
canonical_definition.english: He covered or concealed the thing, covering it with a janz. It is related that when al-Nawār was on her deathbed, she stipulated that al-Ḥasan should pray over her; when this was mentioned to him, he said: 'When you have shrouded her, inform me.'

derivations.english_translation: he covered, concealed, or shrouded (something)
the act of covering, concealment, or shrouding
one who covers or shrouds; a shrouder
covered, concealed, or shrouded (one)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is a particle of affirmation and assent, functioning as a vocal gesture of confirmation equivalent to 'yes' or 'indeed'. It is not derived from a concrete physical object but from a primitive linguistic utterance of agreement.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal meaning is the affirmative particle جَيْرِ, used to express assent, confirmation, or agreement, synonymous with أَجَلْ (yes/indeed).
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical or scholastic extensions are attested in the classical sources; the root remains confined to its literal affirmative function.

canonical_definition.arabic: جَيْرِ: بمعنى أَجَلْ
canonical_definition.english: Jayri: meaning 'yes' or 'indeed'.

derivations.english_translation: yes, indeed (affirmative particle)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root ج-ي-ش is the turbulent, surging motion of a liquid boiling and overflowing its vessel, from which the sense of a churning, agitated mass—whether of the self or of armed men—is derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the boiling and overflowing of a pot (جاشت القدر واستجاشت: غلت), and the consequent agitation of the soul (جاشت النفس: فاظت or غثت).
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension, the root denotes the mustering of an army (جيش فلان: جمع جيشا) and the solicitation of troops from a place (استجاش الأمير من مكان كذا: طلب الجيوش). The image of a boiling pot (صدره مرجل جياش) is applied to a person whose chest is seething with emotion or thought.

canonical_definition.arabic: جاشت القدر واستجاشت: غلت. وجاشَت النفسُ تَجِيش جَيْشاً وجُيوشاً وجَيَشاناً: فاظَتْ. وجيش فلان: جمع جيشا.
canonical_definition.english: The pot boiled and overflowed. The soul surged with a boiling, overflowing, and agitation. A person mustered an army.

derivations.english_translation: to boil, to surge, to overflow; to be agitated
army, troops; a surging multitude
turbulence, agitation, boiling over
armies, troops (plural of جَيْش)
to seek troops, to summon an army; to cause to boil

جاشت القدر واستجاشت: غلت. وكأن صدره مرجل جياش. وجيش فلان: جمع جيشا. واستجاش الأمير من مكان كذا: طلب الجيوش.

جاش البحر بالأمواج. وإن صدره ليجيش علي بالغل. وجاشت إليه نفسه. قال ذو الرمة: تجيش إلي النفس في كل دمنة ... لمى ويرتاح الفؤاد المشوق وجاشت الحرب بينهم. قال: تجيش علينا قدرهم فنديمها ... ونهنؤها عنا إذا حميها غلا وفرس جياش العنان. قال حسان: تعادى بنا أفراسنا كل شطبة ... عنود وجياش

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ح-ث-ر is a granular, rough, or crusted condition affecting a surface, specifically the eye, arising from accreted discharge or eruptive pustules.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a roughness or granulation experienced in the eye due to rheum (ramas), or the emergence of a red pustule or blister (bathr) on the eyelids, accompanied by a scaly or crusted texture.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in the classical philological sources as a metaphorical or scholastic term; the root remains confined to its literal medical-physical domain.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَثَرُ: خُشُونَةٌ يَجِدُهَا الرَّجُلُ فِي عَيْنِهِ مِنَ الرَّمَصِ، وَقِيلَ: هُوَ أَنْ يَخْرُجَ فِيهَا حَبٌّ أَحْمَرُ، وَهُوَ بَثْرٌ يَخْرُجُ فِي الأَجْفَانِ، وَقَدْ حَثِرَتْ عَيْنُهُ. وَالحَثَرَةُ: انْسِلاقُ العَيْنِ، وَتَصْغِيرُهَا حُثَيْرَةٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ḥathar: a roughness that a person experiences in his eye due to rheum; it is also said to be the emergence of a red grain-like eruption, which is a pustule that appears on the eyelids, and his eye has become affected. Al-Ḥatharah: a scaly condition of the eye, and its diminutive is ḥuthayrah.

derivations.english_translation: to become rough or granulated (said of the eye), to develop pustules on the eyelids
a single instance of ocular roughness or pustule formation
a scaly or crusted condition of the eye; ocular granulation
diminutive form of حَثَرَة, denoting a slight or small ocular roughness
roughness or granulation in the eye caused by rheum; a red pustule on the eyelids

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is the act of recoiling or pulling back from a forward advance—a sudden retreat or withdrawal from an initiated movement, particularly in the context of battle or confrontation.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to recoil, retreat, or pull back from a charge or advance; to desist from an attack after having engaged.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, it denotes a failure of resolve or courage—to be incapacitated by weakness or inability, to shrink back from a task or confrontation out of impotence or fear. In scholastic usage, it can signify the soul's retreat from intellectual or moral exertion.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَجْحَجَة: النُّكُوصُ. يقال: حملوا على القوم حملةً ثم حَجْحَجُوا. وحَجْحَجَ الرجلُ: نَكَصَ، وقيل: عجز.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ḥajḥajah: recoiling. It is said: they charged upon the people with a single charge, then they recoiled. And a man ḥajḥaja: he retreated, or it is said: he was incapacitated by weakness.

derivations.english_translation: recoiling, retreating, desisting from an advance
he recoiled, he retreated, he desisted
he withdrew repeatedly, he hesitated and pulled back

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the convergence or meeting-point of two things, from which the notion of constriction or narrowness between them is derived; hence the root denotes tightness, confinement, and the resultant moral or psychological constriction.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the narrowing or constriction of a space or the chest, as in 'ḥaraja ṣadruhu ḥarajan' (his chest became constricted), and the act of driving or forcing someone into a narrow place, as in 'aḥrajahu ilā kadhā' (he forced him into such a situation) and 'aḥraja al-sabʿ ilā maḍīq' (he drove the beast of prey into a narrow passage).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, the root signifies sin or moral impediment (al-ithm), as in 'al-ḥaraj' and 'al-ḥirj'; it also denotes the state of being constrained or inhibited from sin (al-mutaḥarrij), and in Qurʾānic usage it expresses the absence of constriction in religion (mā jaʿala ʿalaykum fī al-dīn min ḥaraj), the constriction of the heart due to disbelief (ḍayyiqan ḥarajan), and the psychological unease or doubt regarding revelation (ḥaraj minhu).

canonical_definition.arabic: الحِرْجُ والحَرَجُ: الإِثمُ. والحَرَجُ والحَرِجُ والمُتَحَرِّجُ: الكافُّ عن الإِثم. وأصل الحرج مجتمع الشيئين، وتصور منه ضيق ما بينهما، فقيل للضيق: حرج، وللإثم حرج.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥirj and al-ḥaraj mean sin. Al-ḥaraj, al-ḥarij, and al-mutaḥarrij denote one who refrains from sin. The root origin of ḥaraj is the convergence of two things, from which the narrowness between them is conceptualized; thus constriction is called ḥaraj, and sin is called ḥaraj.

derivations.english_translation: to be or become constricted, narrow, or distressed
sin, moral impediment
constriction, narrowness, sin
constricted, narrow, distressed
one who refrains from sin, scrupulous
to force into a narrow place, to constrain, to drive into a tight spot
a narrow place, a trap or snare (as in the verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ)

mufradat.text: أصل الحرج والحراج مجتمع الشيئين، وتصور منه ضيق ما بينهما، فقيل للضيق: حرج، وللإثم حرج، قال تعالى: ثم لا يجدوا في أنفسهم حرجا [النساء/ 65]، وقال عز وجل: وما جعل عليكم في الدين من حرج [الحج/ 78]، وقد حرج صدره، قال تعالى: يجعل صدره ضيقا حرجا [الأنعام/ 125]، وقرئ حرجا (1)، أي: ضيقا بكفره، لأن الكفر لا يكاد تسكن إليه النفس لكونه اعتقادا عن ظن، وقيل: ضيق بالإسلام كما قال تعالى: ختم الله على قلوبهم [البقرة/ 7]، وقوله تعالى: فلا يكن في صدرك حرج منه [الأعراف/ 2]، قيل: هو نهي، وقيل: هو دعاء، وقيل: هو حكم منه، نحو: ألم نشرح لك صدرك [الشرح/ 1]، والمتحرج والمتحوب: المتجنب من الحرج والحوب.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a small, low-creeping creature — a lizard (ʿaẓāʾah) — and, by extension, a beast of burden ridden to the point of total exhaustion, i.e., a quadruped reduced to its last remnant of strength.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (as delineated from Lisān al-ʿArab) is: a small lizard (ʿaẓāʾah), specifically the ḥirzaw n, a creeping reptile; and, in the domain of camels, a riding camel that is mounted continuously until no strength remains in it.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical, philosophical, and theological usages: The term is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah as a technical philosophical or theological concept. Its majāz potential lies in the extended image of the ridden camel: a being or faculty worn down to its last remainder (baqiyyah), i.e., reduced to utter exhaustion or depletion. In scholastic Arabic, it could be applied figuratively to a person or faculty that has been overworked until no residual capacity (baqiyyah) remains, but this is an analogical extension, not a canonical technical usage.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحِرْذَوْنُ: العَظَاءَةُ، مَثَّلَ به سيبويه وفسره السيرافي عن ثعلب. والحِرْذَوْنُ من الإبل: الذي يُرْكَبُ حتى لا تَبقى فيه بقيَّة. الجوهري: الحِرْذَوْنُ دُوَيْبَّة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥirzaw n: the lizard (ʿaẓāʾah), cited as an example by Sībawayh and explained by al-Sīrāfī on the authority of Thaʿlab. And al-ḥirzaw n among camels: the one that is ridden until no remnant of strength remains in it. Al-Jawharī: al-ḥirzaw n is a small creature.

derivations.english_translation: a small lizard; a creeping reptile (ʿaẓāʾah); a riding camel ridden until no strength remains
a female lizard; a small creeping creature (diminutive/unit form)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in Al-Mufradāt; based on classical lexical evidence, it denotes a specific physical condition of she-camels, either noble, high-bred (karīmah) or emaciated, lean (mahāzīl ḍawāmir), with the quadriliteral form suggesting a descriptive, onomatopoeic or intensifying function rather than a primary verbal root.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is not attested; based on Lisān al-ʿArab, the ḥaqīqah is a she-camel that is either noble and high-bred (al-nāqah al-karīmah) or emaciated and lean (al-ibil al-mahāzīl al-ḍawāmir), with the plural form ḥarāfiḍ.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical sources; the term remains confined to the concrete zoological domain of camel description, with no extension into abstract or scholastic registers.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحِرْفِضةُ: الناقة الكريمة، عن ابن دريد؛ وقيل: إِبل حَرافِضُ مهازِيلُ ضوامر.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥirfiḍah: the noble, high-bred she-camel, according to Ibn Durayd; it is also said: emaciated, lean she-camels.

derivations.english_translation: a noble, high-bred she-camel
noble, high-bred she-camels; or emaciated, lean she-camels

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of restraining, hindering, or preventing a being from acting or moving — a privative condition imposed upon a subject, conceived as a blockage or confinement of its capacity for free disposal and locomotion.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the prevention or hindrance of a person or animal from acting, moving, or disposing of affairs freely; it denotes a state of being held back, confined, or rendered incapable of motion or independent action.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root extends to any impediment — whether physical, moral, or circumstantial — that obstructs the actualization of a faculty or the execution of an intention. It may denote the inhibition of the soul's appetitive or irascible powers, the blockage of a process, or the privation of a perfection due to an external or internal obstacle. Theologically, it can signify the withholding of divine assistance or the imposition of a trial that restricts the servant's capacity, though such usage remains analogical and must not be conflated with the literal root sense of physical restraint.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَظْل: المَنْع من التصرّف والحركةِ، حَظَل يَحْظِل ويَحْظُل حَظْلاً وحِظْلاناً وحَظَلاناً.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ḥaẓl: prevention from free disposal and movement; ḥaẓala (yaḥẓil, yaḥẓul) — ḥaẓlan, ḥiẓlān, and ḥaẓalān.

derivations.english_translation: he prevented, hindered, or restrained (someone) from acting or moving
he was prevented, hindered, or restrained from acting or moving
prevention, hindrance, restraint from disposal or movement
the state or act of being prevented, hindered, or restrained
the state or act of being prevented, hindered, or restrained

record.ontological_core: A rare quadriliteral nominal root denoting a small, hard, granular substance — specifically the seed or kernel of a precious stone (ḥabb al-jawhar) and, by extension, a certain plant or herb.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical referent is a concrete, tangible object: the seed-like kernel or grain associated with a gemstone, and a specific herbaceous plant (nabt).
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extensions are attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to its concrete nominal sense.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحِفْرِدُ: حب الجوهر؛ عن كراع. والحِفْرِدُ: نبت.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥifrid: the seed of a gemstone, according to Kurāʿ; and al-ḥifrid: a plant.

derivations.english_translation: the seed or kernel of a gemstone; a certain plant

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of gathering, collecting, or bringing together a thing into a compact mass; a secondary, less authoritative strand denotes casting or throwing something from the hand, though the classical lexicographers explicitly judge the cognate root with ḍād (حفض) as the superior form for that latter sense.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the gathering and collecting of a thing (حَفَصَ الشيءَ: جَمَعَه), and the resulting substance so gathered is termed الحُفَاصة. A marginal literal usage denotes casting a thing away (حَفَصَ الشيءَ: أَلْقَاه), but Ibn Sīdah and Ibn Barrī both affirm that the variant with ḍād (حفض) is the higher and more correct form for the sense of throwing down.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological application is attested in the classical philological corpus. The root remains confined to its concrete physical signification of gathering/collecting, with the throwing sense treated as a dialectal or orthographic variant subordinate to the ḍād form. Consequently, no majāz extension into abstract, scholastic, or theological domains is warranted by the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: حَفَصَ الشيءَ يَحْفِصُه حَفْصاً: جَمَعَه. والحُفَاصةُ: اسمُ ما حُفِصَ. وحَفَصَ الشيءَ: أَلْقَاه، قال ابن سيده: والضاد أَعْلى.
canonical_definition.english: Ḥafaṣa al-shayʾa yaḥfiṣuhu ḥafṣan: he gathered it together. Al-ḥufāṣah: the noun denoting that which has been gathered. And ḥafaṣa al-shayʾa: he cast it away; Ibn Sīdah said: the ḍād variant is the higher and more correct form.

derivations.english_translation: he gathered, collected, or brought a thing together
he cast or threw a thing from his hand (a marginal usage; the ḍād variant is judged superior)
that which has been gathered or collected; the collected substance
the act of gathering or collecting; also a proper name (e.g., Ḥafṣ)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root حكر is the act of withholding, confining, or hoarding a commodity—specifically foodstuffs—by collecting and retaining it in expectation of scarcity and price inflation. It denotes a deliberate, self-serving retention that restricts circulation and access.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal meaning is the hoarding of food (احتكار الطعام), i.e., its retention and confinement for the purpose of selling at a higher price during times of scarcity. It also literally denotes a person who monopolizes something and acts exclusively with it (المحتجن للشيء المستبد به), and can describe difficulty, crookedness, or harshness in social interaction (عسر والتواء وسوء معاشرة).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and in scholastic usage, the root extends to any monopolistic or exclusive appropriation (استبداد) by which an individual controls a good or resource to the exclusion of others. It can also denote contentious disputation (مماراة) and hostile argumentation (مناكرة ومحاكرة). In economic and ethical theology, it signifies the sin of hoarding (احتكار) as a violation of communal welfare and trust.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَكْرُ: ادِّخارُ الطعام للتَّرَبُّصِ، وصاحبُه مُحْتَكِرٌ. والاحْتِكارُ: جمع الطعام ونحوه مما يؤكل واحتباسُه انتظارَ وقتِ الغَلاءِ به.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥakr is the storing of food in anticipation [of scarcity]; one who does so is a muḥtakir. Al-iḥtikār is the gathering of food and similar edible goods and retaining them in expectation of a time of high prices.

derivations.english_translation: to hoard, to withhold foodstuffs for profit
hoarding, monopolistic retention
the practice or trade of hoarding
one who hoards, a monopolist
the act of hoarding, monopolistic accumulation

entries.text: فلان حصر حكر وهو المحتجن للشيء المستبد به. وفيه حكر أي عسر والتواء وسوء معاشرة. وفيه مناكرة ومحاكرة أي مماراة. واحتكر الطعام: احتبسه للغلاء. وفلان حرفته الحكرة وهي الاحتكار.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in Al-Mufradāt; classical lexicography derives it from the semantic field of clinging, tenacious adherence and unyielding persistence, from which the meaning of courage and steadfastness is extrapolated.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is not attested; based on Lisān al-ʿArab, the ḥaqīqah is a person who clings firmly to something and does not let go, and by extension a brave, steadfast individual.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic usage applies the root to denote moral courage and resoluteness, where the physical act of clinging is transferred to the soul's firm adherence to valor and endurance; the term may also be used for a persistent, inseparable companion or quality.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَلْبَسُ والحَبَلْبَسُ والحُلابِسُ: الشجاع. والحَلْبَسُ: الحريض الملازم للشيء لا يفارقه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥalbas, al-ḥabalbās, and al-ḥulābis: the brave one. And al-ḥalbas: the eager one who clings to something and does not leave it.

derivations.english_translation: brave, courageous; one who clings tenaciously to something and does not leave it
brave, courageous; tenacious
brave, courageous; steadfast

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a succulent, fleshy herbaceous plant of the class of soft-stemmed pot-herbs (baql), specifically a variety resembling fresh, tender leek or rush (al-fathth al-ratb), of Nabataean (Aramaic) provenance subsequently Arabicized.
record.haqiqah_literal: A literal, concrete botanical referent: a green, edible herb or pasture-plant (baqlah aw ḥashīshah) characterized by softness and succulence, akin to fresh leek, known in Arabic as al-dhuraq.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested in the classical lexicographical tradition; the term remains confined to its concrete botanical designation, with the sole lexical note being its status as a Nabataean loanword (muʿarrab) naturalized into Arabic.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَنْدَقوقَى والحَنْدَقُوقُ والحِنْدَقُوقُ: بقلة أَو حَشِيشة كالفَثِّ الرَّطْب، نَبَطِيَّة مُعرَّبة، ويقال لها بالعربية الذُّرَقُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḥandaqūqā, al-ḥandaqūq, and al-ḥindaqūq: a pot-herb or pasture-plant resembling fresh leek, of Nabataean origin and Arabicized; in Arabic it is called al-dhuraq.

derivations.english_translation: a succulent herb resembling fresh leek; al-dhuraq
a succulent herb resembling fresh leek; al-dhuraq
a succulent herb resembling fresh leek; al-dhuraq

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the constriction and compression of the belly against the spine, as seen in a lean, emaciated horse; from this concrete image of tight inward contraction, the root extends to the psychological constriction of intense inward rage.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the adhesion of the belly to the back in a horse or other animal due to emaciation and leanness, as in the verse of Labīd: 'by a travel-worn steed, whose belly clung to its spine and hump.' It also denotes the compact, gathered head of grain before its awns and kernels emerge.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and theological usage denotes intense anger and wrath (shiddat al-ightiyāẓ), conceived as a constriction of the self analogous to the physical contraction of the belly to the spine. The verb forms ḥaniqa (to be enraged), aḥnaqa (to enrage), and the intensive ḥanīq and muḥnaq (one filled with rage) are used for the psychological state. In scholastic contexts, it signifies the soul's violent inward compression caused by perceived injury, without implying any corporeal change in God; when attributed to God, it is understood as His just displeasure and punitive will, not as an emotion or accident.

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَنَقُ: شِدَّةُ الاغْتِيَاظِ. وأَحْنَقَ الفرسُ وغيرهُ إذا التصقَ بطنهُ بصلبهِ ضُمْرًا.
canonical_definition.english: Ḥanaq is intense wrath. Aḥnaqa al-faras or other animal means its belly adhered to its spine due to emaciation.

derivations.english_translation: to be intensely angry, to be enraged
to enrage someone; (of a horse) to become lean so that its belly clings to its spine
intensely angry, enraged
one filled with rage, intensely angry
enraged, made angry
intense anger, wrath
lean horses whose bellies cling to their spines
lean horses whose bellies cling to their spines

entries.text: حنق على أخيه حنقا وأحنقته عليه فهو حنق وحنيق ومحنق، ومالك مغيظا محنقا. وأحنق الفرس وغيره إذا التصق بطنه بصلبه ضمرا. قال لبيد: بطليح أسفار تركن بقية ... منها فأحنق صلبها وسنامها وقال أبو النجم: قد قالت الأنساع للبطن الحقي ... قدما فآضت كالفنيق المحنق وخيل محانق ومحانيق. وعن ابن ال

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the sharp cry or call used to restrain and drive back camels (ḥawb as a deterrent cry), from which the root's semantic nucleus of restraint, prohibition, and consequent moral liability is derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the act of crying out to camels to restrain them (ḥāba ḥawban), and by extension, the state of being restrained or held back from something; also, the concrete kinship obligation or right (ḥawbah) that binds one to protect and provide for weak dependents, and the physical need or destitution (ḥawbah) that drives one to transgression.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, it denotes sin, moral offense, and the burden of guilt (ithm); the act of scrupulously avoiding sin (taḥawwub); the sacred inviolable right or sanctity (ḥurmah) of a person that, if neglected, incurs sin; and the soul (ḥawbāʾ) as the locus of moral accountability, specifically the soul that incites to evil (al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ).

canonical_definition.arabic: الحَوْبُ: الإِثْمُ. والحَوْبَةُ: الحاجَةُ والمَسْكَنَةُ، والحُرْمَةُ والحَقُّ، والقَرابَةُ من قِبَلِ الأُمِّ. والحَوْباءُ: النَّفْسُ. والأَصْلُ فيه حَوْبٌ لِزَجْرِ الإِبِلِ.
canonical_definition.english: Ḥawb is sin. Ḥawbah is need and destitution, an inviolable right and obligation, and maternal kinship. Ḥawbāʾ is the soul. Its origin is the cry 'ḥawb' used to restrain camels.

derivations.english_translation: to cry out to camels to restrain them; to commit a sin
sin, offense; a cry to restrain camels
a single act of sin; a need or destitution; a kinship obligation or right
a kinship obligation or right (variant of ḥawbah)
the soul; the self that incites to evil
to scrupulously avoid sin; to be burdened with guilt
the act of crying out to camels to restrain them

mufradat.text: الحوب: الإثم، قال عز وجل: إنه كان حوبا كبيرا [النساء/ 2]، والحوب المصدر منه، وروي: (طلاق أم أيوب حوب) (4) ، وتسميته بذلك لكونه مزجورا عنه، من قولهم: حاب حوبا وحوبا وحيابة، والأصل فيه حوب لزجر الإبل، وفلان يتحوب من كذا، أي: يتأثم، وقولهم: ألحق الله به الحوبة (5)، أي: المسكنة والحاجة. وحقيقتها: هي الحاجة التي تحمل صاحبها على ارتكاب الإثم، وقيل: بات فلان بحيبة سوء (6). والحوباء قيل هي النفس (7)، وحقيقتها هي النفس المرتكبة للحوب، وهي الموصوفة بقوله تعالى: إن النفس لأمارة بالسوء [يوسف/ 53].

entries.text: فيه حوب كبير، واللهم اغفر لي حوبتي. وهو يتحوب من القبيح: يتحرج منه. وحرس الله حوباك. وفعلت كذا لحوبة فلان أي لحرمته وحقه وما يأثم الرجل إن لم يراعه. قال الفرزدق: فهب لي خنيسا واتخذ فيه منة ... لحوبة أم ما يسوغ شرابها

record.ontological_core: An indeterminate locative particle (ẓarf mubham) denoting an unspecified place, whose precise reference is disambiguated only by the clause that follows it.
record.haqiqah_literal: A literal, indeterminate adverb of place (ẓarf makān mubham) governing the spatial sense of 'where' or 'in the place that', whose referent is specified by the subsequent clause.
record.majaz_scholastic: Extended in scholastic and philosophical usage to denote an indeterminate locus of condition, state, or logical circumstance (e.g., 'in the respect that', 'insofar as'), functioning as a conjunctive particle introducing causal, conditional, or circumstantial clauses rather than strictly spatial ones.

canonical_definition.arabic: حَيْثُ: ظَرْفٌ مُبْهَمٌ مِنَ الأَمْكِنَةِ، مَضْمُومٌ، وَبَعْضُ العَرَبِ يَفْتَحُهُ، وَزَعَمُوا أَنَّ أَصْلَهَا الوَاوُ؛ وَإِنَّمَا قُلِبَتِ الوَاوُ يَاءً طَلَبَ الخِفَّةِ.
canonical_definition.english: Ḥaythu is an indeterminate locative adverb of place, pronounced with a ḍammah, though some Arab speakers pronounce it with a fatḥah; it is claimed that its original root was wāw, which was changed to yāʾ for the sake of phonetic lightness.

derivations.english_translation: where; in the place that (indeterminate locative particle)
wherever; in whatever place (indeterminate locative with conditional force)
spatiality; the quality of being situated in a place (philosophical abstraction)

mufradat.text: حيث عبارة عن مكان مبهم يشرح بالجملة التي بعده، نحو قوله تعالى: وحيث ما كنتم* [البقرة/ 144]، ومن حيث خرجت* [البقرة/ 149].

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on concealment, hiding, and the act of rendering something invisible or sheltered from view. It encompasses both the physical act of covering or storing something away and the structural notion of a shelter (خِباء) that veils its occupants.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of hiding, concealing, or storing something away (خبأ), and the physical structure of a tent made of wool or hair (خِباء) that provides concealment. It also includes the literal sense of a young woman kept secluded (مخبأة) and the vessel for storing vinegar (خابية).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to the theological domain: 'God brings forth the hidden' (والله يخرج الخبء), referring to His bringing forth rain from the sky and vegetation from the earth as hidden treasures. It also encompasses the psychological act of concealing one's thoughts or intentions (اختبأت له خبيأ), and the strategic concealment of one's opinion (خابأتك أي حاجبتك). The term خِباء is used metaphorically for any sheltering structure, and خبأة describes a woman who conceals herself after being seen.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخِباءُ من الأَبنية: واحد الأَخْبية، وهو ما كان من وَبَر أَو صوف ولا يكون من شَعَر، وهو على عمودين أَو ثلاثة، وما فوقَ ذلك فهو بَيْت. والخبء: ما خفي، ومنه: والله يخرج الخبء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Khibāʾ is a type of structure: the singular of al-akhbiya (tents), and it is made of camel hair or wool, not of hair, and it is supported by two or three poles; anything larger is called a bayt (house). Al-Khabʾ means that which is hidden, and from it comes the phrase: 'And God brings forth the hidden.'

derivations.english_translation: to hide, to conceal, to store away
hidden thing, secret, concealed matter
hidden, concealed; a hidden thing
a hidden thing, a secret; a stored provision
tent (made of wool or hair), shelter
hiding place, place of concealment
hiding places, secret stores
large jar or vessel (for storing liquids like vinegar)
to hide oneself, to conceal oneself
a woman who conceals herself after being seen

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root خبب is rapid, oscillating locomotion—specifically, a gait in which a mount moves its right limbs together and then its left limbs together, or alternately swings forelegs and hindlegs, producing a swift, rocking, uneven motion. From this kinetic core radiate secondary physical senses: a long strip or fold of cloth (خُبَّة/خَبِيبة), and a cutaneous disease or mange (خَبَب/جَرَب) that spreads irregularly over the body.
record.haqiqah_literal: In its strict literal sense, خَبَب denotes a specific mode of running: the horse's simultaneous movement of all right limbs then all left limbs, or the alternating swing of forelegs and hindlegs; it is also used for the camel. Hence خَبَّت الدَّابَّةُ تَخُبُّ خَبّاً وخَبَباً وخَبِيباً: the mount moved with this gait. Literally, خُبَّة and خَبِيبة denote a long, extended strip or fold of cloth, and a garment described as خَبائب is one with such strips. Literally, خَبّ as a noun denotes mange or scabies (الجَرَب), and a man or woman afflicted is described as خَبٌّ or خَبَّة.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, خبب extends from physical gait to moral and social domains. In the ḥadīth of ʿUmar, 'no one spoke Persian except he خَبَّ'—i.e., became corrupt or afflicted with a moral disease—and 'he did not خَبَّ except that his manliness departed.' Thus خَبَّ عليه عبده وأمته وامرأته means he corrupted or ruined them (أفسد). The verbal form أَخَبَّ فَرَسَهُ means he urged his horse into a swift gait; مَرُّوا مُخِبِّينَ describes travelers moving rapidly with their mounts. The root also yields خَبْخَبَة (a rustling or confused sound) and تَخَبْخَبَ (to become agitated or mixed), extending the oscillatory core to acoustic and psychological perturbation.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخَبَبُ: ضَرْبٌ من العَدْوِ، وقيل: هو مِثْلُ الرَّمَلِ، وقيل: هو أَن يَنْقُل الفَرَسُ أَيامِنَه جميعاً وأَياسِرَه جميعاً، وقيل: هو أَن يُراوِحَ بين يديهِ ورجليهِ، وكذلك البعير؛ وقيل: الخَبَب السُّرْعَة. والخُبَّةُ والخَبِيبةُ: شِبْهُ طِيَّةٍ من الثوب مستطيلة. والخَبُّ: الجَرَبُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Khabab is a mode of running; it is said to resemble the ramal; it is said to be the horse's simultaneous movement of all its right limbs and then all its left limbs; it is said to be the alternating swing between its forelegs and hindlegs, and likewise for the camel; it is also said that al-khabab is speed. Al-khubba and al-khabība denote a long, extended fold or strip of cloth. Al-khabb denotes mange.

derivations.english_translation: to move with a swift, rocking gait; to become mangy or corrupt
to corrupt, ruin, or spoil (someone)
to urge a mount into a swift gait
mange, scabies; a mangy or corrupt person
a swift, rocking gait; mange

garments with long strips or folds

entries.text: خب البحر. وأصابهم الخب إذا التوت عليهم الرياح واضطربت الأمواج، فلجؤوا إلى الشط، وألقوا الأنجر. وخب النبات: طال وارتفع. واعترضتنا خبة من الرمل وخبيبة أي طريقة. وقطع لي خبة من اللحم وخبيبة.

اعصب يدك بالخبة والخبيبة وهي شبه طية من الثوب مستطيلة، وثوب خبائب مثل شبارق. ورجل خب بين الخب وهو الجربزة، وامرأة خبة، وقد خب يخب. وفي حديث Metaphorical (Majaz): خب البحر. وأصابهم الخب إذا التوت عليهم الرياح واضطربت الأمواج، فلجؤوا إلى الشط، وألقوا الأنجر. وخب النبات: طال وارتفع. واعترضتنا خبة من الرم

اعصب يدك بالخبة والخبيبة وهي شبه طية من الثوب مستطيلة، وثوب خبائب مثل شبارق. ورجل خب بين الخب وهو الجربزة، وامرأة خبة، وقد خب يخب. وفي حديث عمر رضي الله عنه: ما تكلم أحد بالفارسية إلا خب، وما خب إلا ذهبت مروءته. وخبب عليه عبده وأمته وامرأته: أفسد. وخب الفرس خببا وخبيبا، وجاؤا تخب

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of piercing or thrusting with spears in rapid, successive, overlapping strikes — a concentrated, repeated penetration that overwhelms the target.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is: thrusting or piercing with spears in a rapid, successive manner (al-ṭaʿn bi-l-rimāḥ mudārakan).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and derived usages include: (1) a feeling of languor, weakness, or slackness that a person experiences in the body (al-khataṭ: futūr yajiduhu al-insān fī badanihi); (2) a man's becoming shy and silent (akhatta al-rajul: istaḥyā wa-sakata), denoting a retreat into reticence and bashfulness.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخَتُّ: الطَّعْنُ بالرماح مُدارَكاً. والخَتَتُ: فُتُور يَجِدُه الإِنسان في بدنه. وأَخَتَّ الرجلُ: اسْتَحْيا وسَكَتَ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-khatt: thrusting with spears in rapid succession. Al-khatat: a languor or weakness that a person feels in his body. Akhatta al-rajul: he became shy and silent.

derivations.english_translation: to pierce or thrust with spears in rapid succession
languor, weakness, or slackness felt in the body
to become shy and silent

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on the notion of a fresh, supple, and elevated offshoot—specifically a tender, sap-rich branch or shoot that rises prominently from a tree, and by extension, a freshly cut slice or segment of a moist, fleshy vegetable or fat.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to the classical lexicographers is: a piece or slice of a gourd, cucumber, or fat; and a tender, succulent, elevated branch or twig of a tree, especially one of the current year's growth.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, its metaphorical and scholastic extensions are implicit in the classical material: the term may be applied to a young, slender, and graceful person (likened to a tender branch), or to any fresh, moist, and easily broken substance. In theological or philosophical discourse, it could serve as a concrete image for accidental qualities that are ephemeral and rooted in material substance, though no formal scholastic usage is recorded.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخُرْعُوبةُ: القِطْعةُ من القَرْعةِ والقِثَّاءِ والشَّحْمِ. والخَرْعَبُ والخُرْعُوبُ والخُرْعُوبةُ: الغُصْنُ لسَنَتِه، وقيل: هو القَضِيبُ السامِقُ الغَضُّ، وقيل: هو القَضِيبُ الناعِمُ الحديثُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Khurʿūbah: a piece of gourd, cucumber, or fat. Al-Kharʿab, al-Khurʿūb, and al-Khurʿūbah: a branch of the current year's growth; it is also said to be a tall, fresh twig; and it is said to be a tender, new branch.

derivations.english_translation: a piece or slice of gourd, cucumber, or fat; a tender branch
a tender, succulent branch or twig of the current year's growth
a tender, succulent branch or twig; a fresh shoot

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a marked, delimited tract of ground — a place-name or topographical locus set apart within the landscape.
record.haqiqah_literal: A named locality or place (خِرْفاشٌ: موضع); the literal sense is purely toponymic, referring to a specific site on the ground.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested; the root remains confined to toponymic reference, with no abstract or scholastic usage recorded in the classical lexica.

canonical_definition.arabic: خِرْفاشٌ: موضع.
canonical_definition.english: Khirfāsh: a place; a named locality.

derivations.english_translation: a place; a named locality

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the weaving of a coarse garment or tent-structure from the ṭalīf (the thick, tough hide of a sheep's neck), a material prized for its extreme durability and resistance to wear.
record.haqiqah_literal: A cloak (kisāʾ) or tent (khibāʾ) woven specifically from the neck-hide of a sheep, which, according to traditional report, scarcely ever wears out.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical or scholastic extensions are attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to its literal material and textile reference. The variant khasiyy is a phonological substitution (badal) of khisīj, not a semantic transfer.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخَسِيجُ والخَسِيُّ، على البدل: كِساءٌ أَو خِباءٌ ينسج من ظَلِيفِ عُنُقِ الشاةِ فلا يكادُ، زَعَمُوا، يَبْلى.
canonical_definition.english: Al-khisīj and al-khasiyy (the latter by consonantal substitution): a cloak or tent woven from the neck-hide of a sheep, which, it is asserted, scarcely ever wears out.

derivations.english_translation: A cloak or tent woven from sheep-neck hide, noted for its durability
Variant of khisīj (by consonantal substitution), same referent

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root خ ش م centers on the nasal cavity and its internal structures—specifically the bony and cartilaginous passages, vessels, and membranes situated between the nostrils and the brain. This anatomical locus is the seat of olfactory perception and the point at which the sense of smell is either enabled or obstructed. From this concrete physical referent, the root's primary semantic charge is the obstruction, alteration, or loss of olfactory function, and by extension, the alteration of odors themselves.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the nasal passage and its internal anatomy (al-khayāshīm), and the condition of a man who is akhsham—one who cannot detect odors due to a blockage or defect in his nasal passages. The wind or odor is said to penetrate (tasawwara) into the khayāshīm, i.e., the olfactory recesses of the nose.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and extended usages include: (1) the alteration or putrefaction of meat (khashima al-laḥm / akhshama), where the change in odor is conceptualized as a kind of nasal obstruction or corruption affecting the meat itself; (2) the theological and philosophical notion of olfactory privation (khasham) as a defect in the faculty of smell, analogous to blindness in the eye or deafness in the ear—a privation of a natural power, not merely a negation; (3) in scholastic physiology, the khayāshīm are described as the fine vessels or membranes at the extremity of the nose, connecting to the brain, serving as the instrument of the olfactory spirit (rūḥ al-shamm); (4) by extension, any blockage or obstruction in a channel of perception or communication may be termed khasham, though this remains a secondary, analogical usage.

canonical_definition.arabic: خَشِمَ اللحمُ خَشَماً وأَخْشَمَ: تغيرت رائحته. والخَيْشُوم من الأَنف: ما فوق نُخْرَتِهِ من القَصَبة وما تحتها من خَشارِمِ رأْسه، وقيل: الخَياشِيمُ غَراضيف في أَقصى الأَنف بينه وبين الدماغ، وقيل: هي عُروق.
canonical_definition.english: Khashima al-laḥm khashaman wa-akhshama: its odor became altered. Al-khayshūm of the nose: that which is above the nostril from the bridge and below it from the cartilaginous parts of its head. It is said: al-khayāshīm are the fine membranes at the extremity of the nose between it and the brain; and it is said: they are veins.

derivations.english_translation: to be or become obstructed in the nose; to lose the sense of smell; (of meat) to become altered in odor, to stink
to cause to become obstructed in the nose; (of meat) to become altered in odor, to putrefy
obstruction of the nasal passages; loss of the sense of smell; anosmia
a man whose nasal passages are obstructed; one who cannot smell; anosmic
the nasal cavity; the bony and cartilaginous structure of the nose above and below the nostril; the bridge of the nose
the internal nasal passages; the olfactory recesses; the fine vessels or membranes at the extremity of the nose connecting to the brain

entries.text: أشرفت خياشيم الجبال وهي أنوفها.
إن ريحه تسور في الخياشيم. ورجل أخشم، وبه خشم وهو الذي لا يجد الروائح لسدة في خياشيمه.
إن ريحه تسور في الخياشيم. ورجل أخشم، وبه خشم وهو الذي لا يجد الروائح لسدة في خياشيمه. Metaphorical (Majaz): أشرفت خياشيم الجبال وهي أنوفها.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root خ-ض-ب is the act of dyeing or staining a surface—specifically human hair or skin—with a coloring substance such as henna (ḥinnāʾ) or katam, thereby altering its visible hue toward red, yellow, or another color. The root's primary semantic nucleus is the material application of pigment to a corporeal substrate, producing a perceptible chromatic change.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal (ḥaqīqah) meaning is the direct, physical application of dye (khiḍāb) to hair or hand, as in 'khaḍaba shaʿrahu wa yadahu bi-l-khiḍāb' (he dyed his hair and hand with dye), yielding 'kaffin khaḍīb' (a dyed palm) and 'banānun mukhaḍḍab' (dyed fingertips). It also denotes the vessel used for dyeing, 'al-mikhḍab' (the dyeing tub or basin), and the cloths employed in the process, 'makhāḍib' (dye rags). The verb forms include 'khaḍaba' (he dyed), 'ikhtaḍaba' (he dyed himself), and 'takhaḍḍaba' (he applied dye repeatedly or intensively).
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root extends beyond literal dyeing to signify any alteration of color or appearance, even by non-dye substances, as when Lisān al-ʿArab notes 'ghayyara lawnahu bi-ḥumratin aw ṣufratin aw ghayrihimā' (he changed its color to red, yellow, or otherwise). The active participle 'khaḍīb' is applied metaphorically to a star or celestial body, as in 'ṭalaʿat al-kaff al-khaḍīb wa hiya najm' (the dyed palm rose, which is a star), where the reddish hue of the star is likened to a henna-dyed hand. The intensive nominal form 'khaḍiba' describes a woman who dyes herself frequently, indicating habitual action. The root thus acquires a secondary semantic layer of transformative coloration, whether literal or analogical, without losing its concrete material basis.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخِضابُ: ما يُخْضَبُ به مِن حِنَّاءٍ وكَتَمٍ ونحوه؛ وخَضَبَ الشيءَ يَخْضِبُهُ خَضْباً وخَضَّبَهُ: غيَّرَ لَوْنَه بحُمْرَةٍ أو صُفْرَةٍ أو غيرِهما.
canonical_definition.english: Al-khiḍāb is that with which one dyes, such as henna, katam, and the like; khaḍaba al-shayʾa yakḥḍibuhu khaḍban and khaḍḍabahu mean he changed its color to red, yellow, or another hue.

derivations.english_translation: he dyed, stained, or colored (something)
he dyed intensively or repeatedly; he colored thoroughly
he dyed himself, applied dye to his own person
he applied dye to himself repeatedly or with effort
dye, coloring substance (e.g., henna, katam)

entries.text: ظليم خاضب: أكل الربيع فاحمرت ساقاه وقوادمه: وخضبت العضاه: ا

خضب شعره ويده بالخضاب، وكف خضيب، وبنان مخضب. وطلعت الكف الخضيب وهي نجم. واختضب الرجل وتخضب. وامرأة خضبة: كثيرة الاختضاب، وقد خضبت تخضب. وأعط Metaphorical (Majaz): ظليم خاضب: أكل الربيع فاحمرت ساقاه وقوادمه: وخضبت العضاه: ا

خضب شعره ويده بالخضاب، وكف خضيب، وبنان مخضب. وطلعت الكف الخضيب وهي نجم. واختضب الرجل وتخضب. وامرأة خضبة: كثيرة الاختضاب، وقد خضبت تخضب. وأعطني من مخاضب حنائك وهي خرق الخضاب. وغسلت ثيابها في المخضب وهي الإجانة.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root خ ف ش is a congenital or acquired defect in the eye characterized by smallness, narrowness, and weakness of vision, without pain or ulceration.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal meaning is the smallness of the eyes and weakness of sight; a man is described as أَخْفَش (akhfash) and the condition is خَفَش (khafash). The verb خَفِشَتْ عَيْنُهُ (khafishat ʿaynu-hu) means his eye became weak or small.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt, later lexicographers and scholars extended its use metaphorically to denote any diminution or impairment of perceptive faculties, including intellectual or spiritual insight. The term أَخْفَش was also used as a nickname for several grammarians, possibly indicating a physical trait or a metaphorical reference to a subtle defect in their analytical vision. In theological contexts, it may symbolize a deficiency in apprehension (idrāk) of divine realities, though this is not a primary Quranic usage.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخَفَشُ: ضعف في البصر وضيق في العين، وقيل: صغرٌ في العين خلقةً، وقيل: هو فساد في جفن العين واحمرار تضيق له العيون من غير وجع ولا قُرْحٍ، خَفِش خَفَشاً، فهو خَفِشٌ وأَخْفَشُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Khafash: weakness of vision and narrowness of the eye; it is said to be a congenital smallness of the eye; or it is a corruption in the eyelid and a redness that causes the eyes to narrow, without pain or ulceration. One says khafisha khafashan, so he is khafish or akhfish.

derivations.english_translation: to have weak or small eyes; to become dim-sighted
weakness of sight; smallness or narrowness of the eye
one having weak or small eyes
one with small, weak eyes; a person with impaired vision
a woman with small, weak eyes

entries.text: رجل أخفش، وبه خفش وهو صغر العينين وضعف البصر، وقد خفشت عينه. خ قال: ض خفض الشيء ورفعه فانخفض. وهو في حال رفعة وحال خفضة. وختن الغلام، وخفضت Metaphorical (Majaz): خفض صوته ورفعه. وكلام مخفوض و
خفض صوته ورفعه. وكلام مخفوض و

رجل أخفش، وبه خفش وهو صغر العينين وضعف البصر، وقد خفشت عينه. خ قال: ض خفض الشيء ورفعه فانخفض. وهو في حال رفعة وحال خفضة. وختن الغلام، وخفضت الجارية. وفلانة خافضة. ونعمت الخافضة! وخفض رأس البعير إلى الأرض. قال: يكاد يستعصي على مخفضه

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is spatial and temporal emptiness: a place or thing devoid of any occupant, structure, or content, hence 'to be empty, vacant, unoccupied.'
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the state of a place or thing being empty and devoid of any being or object, as in 'خلا المكان' (the place became empty) and 'الخلاء' (the open, unsheltered void).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic applications extend to temporal passage (خلا الزمان: time elapsed and departed), to the absence of precedent or peer (خلت من قبله الرسل: messengers have passed away before him), and to moral or communal vacancy (خلت من قبلهم المثلات: exemplary punishments occurred before them). The root also yields the theological notion of divine solitude (الخلوة) and the philosophical concept of privation (الخلاء) as the absence of substance in a locus.

canonical_definition.arabic: خَلا المكانُ والشيءُ يَخْلُو خُلُوّاً وخَلاءً وأَخْلَى إِذا لم يكن فيه أَحد ولا شيء فيه، وهو خالٍ. والخَلاءُ من الأَرض: قَرارٌ خالٍ. واسْتَخْلَى: كخَلا.
canonical_definition.english: A place or thing becomes empty (خلا) with the verbal noun خُلُوّ and خَلاء, and one may say أَخْلَى when there is no one and nothing in it; it is then خالٍ (empty). الخَلاء from the earth is a vacant, level tract. اِسْتَخْلَى is synonymous with خلا.

derivations.english_translation: to be empty, vacant, or unoccupied; to pass away, elapse (of time)
emptiness, vacancy; solitude, privacy
open, unsheltered space; void, vacuum; emptiness
the state of being empty or free (of something); vacancy
empty, vacant, unoccupied; free from
to empty, vacate, clear out
