mufradat.text: الخلاء: المكان الذي لا ساتر فيه من بناء ومساكن وغيرهما، والخلو يستعمل في الزمان والمكان، لكن لما تصور في الزمان المضي فسر أهل اللغة: خلا الزمان، بقولهم: مضى الزمان وذهب، قال تعالى: وما محمد إلا رسول قد خلت من قبله الرسل [آل عمران/ 144]، وقد خلت من قبلهم المثلات [الرعد/ 6]، تلك أمة قد خلت* [البقرة/ 141]، قد خلت من قبلكم سنن [آل عمران/ 137]، إلا خلا فيها نذير [فاطر/ 24]، مثل الذين خلوا من قبلكم [البقرة/ 214]، وإذا خلوا عضوا عليكم الأنامل من الغيظ [آل عمران/ 119]، وقوله: يخل لكم وجه أبيكم [يوسف/ 9]، أي: تحصل لكم مودة أبيكم وإقباله عليكم. وخلا الإنسان: صار خاليا، وخلا فلان بفلان: صار معه في خلاء، وخلا إليه: انتهى إليه في خلوة، قال تعالى: وإذا خلوا إلى شياطينهم [البقرة/ 14]، وخليت فلانا: تركته في خلاء، ثم يقال لكل ترك تخلية، نحو: فخلوا سبيلهم [التوبة/ 5]، وناقة خلية: مخلاة عن الحلب، وامرأة خلية: مخلاة عن الزوج، وقيل للسفينة المتروكة بلا ربان خلية، والخلي: من خلاه الهم، نحو المطلقة في قول الشاعر: 150- مطلقة طورا وطورا تراجع (1) والخلاء: الحشيش المتروك حتى ييبس، ويقال: خليت الخلاء: جززته، وخليت الدابة: جززت لها، ومنه استعير: سيف يختلي، أي: يقطع ما يضرب به قطعه للخلا.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes shortness and compactness of bodily stature in a man, with a secondary physical image of a thick, stunted, or truncated form.
record.haqiqah_literal: الخُنْبُتُ: القصير من الرجال — the short man; a man of compact, stunted stature.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah as a productive root with metaphorical extension. In the classical lexical tradition it remains a concrete descriptive epithet (نعت) for physical shortness, without established philosophical or theological majāz usage.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخُنْبُتُ: القصير من الرجال.
canonical_definition.english: Al-khunbut: the short man; a man of compact, stunted stature.

derivations.english_translation: a short man; a man of compact, stunted stature
the short one among men (definite descriptive epithet)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root خوط is the tender, supple, freshly grown branch or shoot of a tree—specifically the pliant young twig that emerges in a single growing season, characterized by its softness, flexibility, and slender form.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal (ḥaqīqah) meaning of خوط is the soft, tender branch (al-ghuṣn al-nāʿim). It is used concretely to denote a pliant young shoot or twig, as in the phrase 'qad kāla-khūṭ' (it curved like a tender branch), and in the plural khīṭān, as in the poetic image of slender figures behind walls 'like tender branches' (qadūd ka-l-khīṭān).
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical (majāz) and scholastic usage, خوط is extended to denote any slender, graceful, and flexible form, particularly the elegant stature or figure of a person. The imagery of the tender branch serves as a simile for youthful beauty, supple movement, and graceful bearing. In theological and philosophical discourse, the term may be employed to illustrate the concept of innate disposition (fiṭrah) or natural growth, where the tender shoot symbolizes the initial, unspoiled state of created beings before external influences shape them. It also appears in literary and rhetorical contexts to evoke the idea of delicate, nascent potentiality.

canonical_definition.arabic: الخُوطُ: الغُصْنُ الناعِمُ، وقيل: الغُصن لِسَنةٍ، وقيل: هو كلُّ قَضِيبٍ ما كان؛ والجمع خِيطانٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-khūṭ: the tender branch; it is said to be a branch of one year's growth; and it is said to be any twig whatsoever; the plural is khīṭān.

derivations.english_translation: A tender, supple branch or twig; a young shoot
Tender branches; young shoots (plural of خُوط)
To bend or curve like a tender branch (denominal verb, rare)

entries.text: قد كالخوط وهو الغصن الناعم. وتقول: كم وراء هذه اعلحيطان، من قدود كالخيطان.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is the act of walking or moving with a swaying, oscillating, or side-to-side motion, often likened to the undulating gait of a camel or a ship tossing on waves.
record.haqiqah_literal: To walk with a swinging or swaying motion; to move unsteadily or with a rolling gait.
record.majaz_scholastic: In philosophical and theological contexts, it may metaphorically denote the vacillation or instability of the soul or intellect, or the oscillation of opinion; however, such usage is rare and not attested in the classical lexicons.

canonical_definition.arabic: دَافَ يَدُوفُ دَوْفًا: تَمَايَلَ فِي مَشْيِهِ وَتَرَجَّحَ.
canonical_definition.english: Dāfa yadūfu dawfan: to sway in one's walk and oscillate.

derivations.english_translation: to walk with a swaying motion
a swaying or unsteady gait
one who sways while walking
swayed or moved with a rolling motion

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is the act of covering or being covered by an outer garment (dithār) that is worn over the inner garment (shīʿār), thereby concealing what lies beneath. From this primary sense of overlaying and concealment, the root extends to the notion of something being overlaid by time, dust, or neglect, leading to its effacement and decay.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to wear the dithār, i.e., the outer garment or covering, over the shīʿār (inner garment). It also denotes the act of covering someone or something with such a garment, as in 'daththarahu' (he covered him). The passive participle 'mudaththir' (one who is covered) is used for the one wrapped in his cloak. Additionally, it is used literally for a stallion mounting a she-camel, or a man leaping onto a horse, due to the covering and mounting action.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root is used for a person who is obscure, inactive, or of low repute (dathūr), as if covered by obscurity. It is applied to a sword that is 'dāthir' (rusty and neglected), meaning it has been long since polished, as if covered by rust. It is also used for an abode that has become 'dāthir' (effaced), i.e., its traces have been obliterated by time, and for a person who is 'dathūr' of wealth, meaning he is an excellent manager of it, as if he covers and protects it. Theologically, the term 'al-mudaththir' (the enwrapped one) is a title of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the Qur'an, referring to his state of being wrapped in his cloak at the onset of revelation.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدُّثُورُ: الدُّرُوسُ. وقد دَثَرَ الرَّسْمُ وتَدَاثَرَ ودَثَرَ الشَّيْءُ يَدْثُرُ دُثُوراً وانْدَثَرَ: قَدُمَ ودَرَسَ. والدِّثَارُ: ما يُتَدَثَّرُ به، وهو المُتَدَرِّعُ دِثَارَهُ. يقال: دَثَّرْتُهُ فَتَدَثَّرَ.
canonical_definition.english: Duthūr means effacement. The trace has become effaced and worn out; the thing has become old and effaced. The dithār is that with which one wraps oneself; it is the one who wears his dithār. It is said: I covered him, so he wrapped himself.

derivations.english_translation: to be or become effaced, worn out, or covered with dust; to be neglected
to cover someone with an outer garment; to enwrap
to wrap oneself in an outer garment; to be covered
to wrap oneself; to be covered (assimilated form of تَدَثَّرَ)
outer garment, covering, cloak
effaced, obliterated, rusty, neglected
obscure, inactive, lowly; one who manages well (with wealth)
one who is wrapped in an outer garment
one who is covered, enwrapped

mufradat.text: قال الله تعالى: يا أيها المدثر (2) أصله المتدثر فأدغم، وهو المتدرع دثاره، يقال: دثرته فتدثر، والدثار: ما يتدثر به، وقد تدثر الفحل الناقة: تسنمها، والرجل الفرس: وثب عليه فركبه، ورجل دثور: خامل مستتر، وسيف داثر: بعيد العهد بالصقال، ومنه قيل للمنزل الدارس: داثر، لزوال أعلامه، وفلان دثر مال، أي: حسن القيام به.

entries.text: لبس الدثار فوق الشعار، وهو متدثر بالكساء ومدثر به، ودثره صاحبه، وفلان دثور الضحى: يتدثر فينام. قال الكميت: ولم ألقه بدثور الضحى ... أمال الس Metaphorical (Majaz): تدثر الفحل الناقة: تسنمها. وتدثر الرجل فرسه وتجلله إذا وثب عليه فركبه. وقال ابن مقبل: أصاخت له فدر اليمامة بعدما ... تدثرها من وبله ما تدثرا

لبس الدثار فوق الشعار، وهو متدثر بالكساء ومدثر به، ودثره صاحبه، وفلان دثور الضحى: يتدثر فينام. قال الكميت: ولم ألقه بدثور الضحى ... أمال السبات عليه الدثارا ودثر المنزل، وهو دراس داثر. وتقول: فلان جده عاثر، ورسمه داثر.

تدثر الفحل الناقة: تسنمها. وتدثر الرجل فرسه وتجلله إذا وثب عليه فركبه. وقال ابن مقبل: أصاخت له فدر اليمامة بعدما ... تدثرها من وبله ما تدثرا أي ركبها المطر وعلاها والفدر الأوعال. ورجل دثور: خامل. وفلان دثاري: كسلان ساكن لا يتصرف. وهو يتدثر بالمال: للمتمول. وماله دثر. وذهب أهل الد

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root د ج و is the state of night when darkness is compounded by cloud cover, such that neither star nor moon is visible—an enveloping obscurity that cloaks all things, distinct from mere absence of light.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the blackness of night accompanied by clouds, preventing sight of any star or moon; it is the condition of a night that has enveloped everything in dense, overcast darkness.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root is extended to any overwhelming obscurity, confusion, or error that veils the intellect and obscures truth, as well as to the blinding darkness of ignorance and misguidance. It may also denote the veiling of spiritual insight by passion or heedlessness.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدُّجى: سَوادُ اللَّيلِ مَعَ غَيْمٍ، وأَنْ لا تَرى نَجْمًا ولا قَمَرًا، وقيل: هو إذا أَلْبَسَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ ولَيْس هو من الظُّلْمَةِ، وقالوا: لَيْلَةٌ دُجًى ولَيالٍ دُجًى، لا يُجْمَعُ لأَنَّهُ مَصْدَرٌ وُصِفَ بِهِ، وقد دَجَا.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Dujā is the blackness of night together with cloud cover, such that you see neither star nor moon. It is also said to be when it envelops everything, and it is not merely from [ordinary] darkness. They say: 'a night of dujā' and 'nights of dujā'—it is not pluralized because it is an infinitive used descriptively. And the night has indeed become dark and overcast (dajā).

derivations.english_translation: intense darkness of an overcast night; (metaphorically) overwhelming obscurity or ignorance
to become dark and overcast (of the night); to envelop in darkness
a night that is intensely dark and overcast
to make dark, overcast, or obscure; to envelop in darkness

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root is the act of entering or penetrating into an interior space, conceived as the direct antonym of exiting (خروج). It denotes the crossing of a boundary from outside to inside, whether spatial, temporal, or functional.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of entering a place, as in 'he entered such-and-such a place.' It also concretely denotes the inner lining of a garment that touches the body (داخلة الإزار), the interlocking joints of armor (حلق الدرع مداخل), and the inner, hidden reality of a person's affairs (دخلة الأمر).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) moral or logical defect, fault, or corruption (دخل, مدخول), as in 'food that is tainted' or 'a commodity that is defective'; (2) social affiliation without genuine belonging, as in 'a dakhīl among a tribe' (one who attaches himself to a lineage not his own); (3) theological and eschatological entry into divine mercy, paradise, or hell, as in the Qur'anic 'Enter the Garden' (ادخلوا الجنة) and 'He admits whom He wills into His mercy' (يدخل من يشاء في رحمته); (4) the causative admission by God into a state of satisfaction (مدخل صدق, مدخلا كريما); and (5) the interpenetration of substances or ideas (تداخل, مداخلة).

canonical_definition.arabic: الدُّخُول: نقيض الخروج، دَخَل يَدْخُل دُخُولاً وتَدَخَّل ودَخَل به. ويستعمل في المكان والزمان والأعمال. والدَّخِيل: الذي يداخلك في أمورك، أو الذي ينتسب إلى قوم وليس منهم. والدَّخَل: العيب.
canonical_definition.english: Entry is the antonym of exit; one says 'he entered' (dakhala yadkhulu dukhūlan) and 'he caused to enter' (dakhala bihi). It is used in relation to place, time, and actions. A dakhīl is one who insinuates himself into your affairs, or one who affiliates with a people though not of them. Dakhāl denotes a defect or fault.

derivations.english_translation: to enter, to go in
entering, entry, admission
to intrude, to interfere, to become involved
foreign, alien, one who attaches himself to a group not his own; also, a guest
foreigners, aliens, interlopers
defective, tainted, corrupted; also, entered
a watering practice where a camel is inserted between two drinking camels
inner lining of a garment; inner reality
inner state, hidden affair, or mode of entry
place or act of causing to enter, admission
entrance, place of entry

mufradat.text: الدخول: نقيض الخروج، ويستعمل ذلك في المكان، والزمان، والأعمال، يقال: دخل مكان كذا، قال تعالى: ادخلوا هذه القرية [البقرة/ 58]، ادخلوا الجنة بما كنتم تعملون [النحل/ 32]، ادخلوا أبواب جهنم خالدين فيها* [الزمر/ 72]، ويدخلهم جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار [المجادلة/ 22]، وقال: يدخل من يشاء في رحمته* [الإنسان/ 31]، وقل: رب أدخلني مدخل صدق [الإسراء/ 80]، فمدخل من دخل يدخل، ومدخل من أدخل، ليدخلنهم مدخلا يرضونه [الحج/ 59]، وقوله: مدخلا كريما [النساء/ 31]، قرئ بالوجهين (1)، وقال أبو علي الفسوي (2): من قرأ: «مدخلا» بالفتح فكأنه إشارة إلى أنهم يقصدونه، ولم يكونوا كمن ذكرهم في قوله: الذين يحشرون على وجوههم إلى جهنم [الفرقان/ 34]، وقوله: إذ الأغلال في أعناقهم والسلاسل [غافر/ 71]، ومن قرأ «مدخلا» فكقوله: ليدخلنهم مدخلا يرضونه [الحج/ 59]، وادخل: اجتهد في دخوله، قال تعالى: لو يجدون ملجأ أو مغارات أو مدخلا [التوبة/ 57]، والدخل: كناية عن الفساد والعداوة المستبطنة، كالدغل، وعن الدعوة في النسب، يقال: دخل دخلا (3)، قال تعالى: تتخذون أيمانكم دخلا بينكم [النحل/ 92]، فيقال: دخل (4) فلان فهو مدخول، كناية عن بله في عقله، وفساد في أصله، ومنه قيل: شجرة مدخولة. والدخال في الإبل: أن يدخل إبل في أثناء ما لم تشرب لتشرب معها ثانيا. والدخل طائر، سمي بذلك لدخوله فيما بين الأشجار الملتفة، والدوخلة (5): معروفة، ودخل بامرأته: كناية عن الإفضاء إليها، قال تعالى: من نسائكم اللاتي دخلتم بهن فإن لم تكونوا دخلتم بهن فلا جناح عليكم [النساء/ 23].

entries.text: هو دخيل فلان. وهو الذي يداخله في أموره كلها. وهو دخيل في بني فلان إذا انتسب معهم وليس منهم، وهم دخلاء فيهم ومفاصله مداخلة. وحلق الدرع مداخل وهو المدمج المحكم، ودوخل بعضه في بعض. وسقى إبله دخالا وهو أن يدخل بعيرا قد شرب بين بعيرين ناهلين. واغسل داخلة إزارك وهو مايلي جسده. وإنه لخب

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the notion of falling or dropping down, specifically from extreme old age, yielding a state of decrepitude and collapse.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Lisān al-ʿArab is the falling or dropping of a person due to extreme old age; the adjective al-mudrahimm denotes one who has collapsed from senility, i.e., the very aged.
record.majaz_scholastic: Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī cites the verse 'wa-sharawhu bi-thamanin bakhsin' (and they sold him for a paltry price) in connection with this root, though the lexical link is not explicitly elaborated; the scholastic usage may extend to any abrupt moral or social decline, but no attested metaphorical application is recorded in Asās al-Balāghah. The root remains largely confined to its literal physical sense of senile collapse.

canonical_definition.arabic: المُدْرَهِمُّ: الساقطُ من الكِبَرِ، وقيل: هو الكبيرُ السِّنِّ أَيّاً كان. وقد ادْرَهَمَّ يَدْرَهِمُّ ادْرِهْمَاماً أَي سقط من الكبر.
canonical_definition.english: Al-mudrahimm: one who has fallen from extreme old age; it is also said: he is the very aged, whoever he may be. And he has adrahamma, yadrahimmu, idrihmāman, meaning he fell from old age.

derivations.english_translation: to fall or drop from extreme old age; to become decrepit
one who has fallen from extreme old age; the very aged, decrepit
the act of falling or dropping from extreme old age; senile collapse

mufradat.text: قال تعالى: وشروه بثمن بخس دراهم معدودة [يوسف/ 20]، الدرهم: الفضة المطبوعة المتعامل بها.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root د ع ص is a compact, aggregated mound of sand—a small, clustered hillock of loose terrain that accumulates into a distinct elevation, smaller in scale than a large dune (ḥiqf).
record.haqiqah_literal: A literal, physical mound or hillock of sand gathered together; a small sand-hill formed by the aggregation of loose grains, less in magnitude than a ḥiqf (large dune). The singular portion or unit of such a mound is termed a diʿṣah.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the term is applied to any compact, rounded protuberance or swelling resembling a sand-mound—such as the rounded haunch of a horse (kidʿṣ al-naqā) or a woman's rounded buttock—by way of analogical extension from the physical image of a clustered sand-hill. It may also denote a group of people gathered in one place, by analogy to the aggregation of sand.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدِّعْصُ: قُورٌ مِنَ الرَّمْلِ مُجْتَمِعٌ، وَالْجَمْعُ أَدْعَاصٌ وَدِعَصَةٌ، وَهُوَ أَقَلُّ مِنَ الْحِقْفِ، وَالطَّائِفَةُ مِنْهُ دِعْصَةٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-diʿṣ: a compact mound of sand gathered together; the plural is adʿāṣ and diʿaṣah. It is smaller than a ḥiqf (large dune), and a single portion of it is a diʿṣah.

derivations.english_translation: a small mound of sand; a compact sand-hill
a single unit or portion of a sand-mound; a small sand-hill
mounds of sand; compact sand-hills (plural)
mounds of sand; compact sand-hills (plural)

entries.text: لها كفل كدعص النقا، ونزلوا بالأدعاص وهي قيران من الرمل مجتمعة.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes the onset of blackness or dark discoloration upon a surface, specifically the face, without prior cause or illness; its foundational physical image is that of a darkening or staining that overtakes a visage.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the blackening of the face without any underlying disease or external cause, as attested in the verbal form أَدْفَسَ.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; no established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded. The root remains confined to its literal physical sense in the classical lexica.

canonical_definition.arabic: أَدْفَسَ الرجلُ إِذا اسودَّ وجهه من غير علة
canonical_definition.english: A man's face turned black without any illness or cause.

derivations.english_translation: he blackened (his face) without cause or illness

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root دقن centers on the striking or jabbing of the chin/jaw with the collected palm or fist, and by extension the chin itself as the bodily locus of such a blow; from this concrete somatic action the root also branches into the small stones that support a cooking pot (أثافي القدر), likely by analogy of their compact, chin-like protrusion or their being struck into place.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is to strike or jab someone on the chin/jaw with the collected palm or fist (دقن في حليه إذا لكزه لكزة بجمع كفه); the chin/jaw itself (اللحية/اللحي) is then named by this action, as in the Baghdadi expression في دقنك, meaning 'on your chin/beard.'
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic usage extends from the physical blow to the chin to the condition of being deprived or thwarted: the phrase دُقِنَ في لَحْيِه ('he was struck on the jaw') was applied to the deprived or unfortunate one (المحروم), since a blow to the jaw signifies humiliation, defeat, or the loss of one's share. The root also yields الدِّقْدَان and الدِّيقَان for the stones supporting a cooking pot (أثافي القدر), a concrete nominal extension rather than a strictly theological metaphor.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدَّقْنُ: الضَّرْبُ بِجُمْعِ الكَفِّ عَلَى اللَّحْيِ؛ وَالدِّقْدَانُ وَالدِّيقَانُ: أَثَافِي القِدْرِ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Daqn: striking with the collected palm on the jaw/chin; al-diqdān and al-dīqān: the stones that support a cooking pot.

derivations.english_translation: to strike or jab on the chin/jaw with the collected palm or fist
a blow or jab on the chin/jaw; the chin/jaw as the locus of such a blow
the stones that support a cooking pot; pot-rests (أثافي القدر)
the stones that support a cooking pot; pot-rests (أثافي القدر)

entries.text: دقن في حليه إذا لكزه لكزة بجمع كفه، ثم قالوا للمحروم دقن في لحيه. ويقول أهل بغداد: في دقنك أي في لحيتك.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a specific desert/bulbous plant (al-dalabūth) whose physical origin lies in a saffron-like aerial habit (leaf and stem) anchored by a fibrous-coated bulb, the edible part being the bulb cooked in milk.
record.haqiqah_literal: A concrete botanical entity: a plant resembling saffron in stem and leaf, possessing a bulb enclosed in fibers (līfah), which is boiled in milk and eaten.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extensions are attested; the term remains strictly botanical and culinary in the classical lexica.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدَّلَبُوثُ: نبت، أَصله وورقُه مثلُ نبات الزعفران سواء، وبَصَلَتُه في لِيفةٍ، وهي تُطْبخُ باللبن وتؤْكل.
canonical_definition.english: Al-dalabūth: a plant whose stem and leaves are exactly like those of saffron, with a bulb enclosed in fibers; it is cooked in milk and eaten.

derivations.english_translation: A saffron-like plant with a fibrous bulb, cooked in milk and eaten

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the notion of forward-rushing propulsion and bold advance, derived—per Abū Manṣūr al-Azharī—from the root د-ل-ث (al-indilāth), meaning to surge forward, with the هـ (hāʾ) augmented as an intensifying infix; hence the quadriliteral/quintiliteral cluster denotes a being characterized by swift, fearless, forward-charging momentum.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a swift, bold, forward-rushing person or camel—one who charges ahead without hesitation; the lion (al-dilhāth) is the paradigm instance of this literal predatory forward-rush.
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension (majāz), the term is applied to any entity—human, animal, or figurative—marked by audacious initiative and unhesitating advance; the lion is the archetypal instantiation, and the semantic core of 'charging forward' is transferred from physical motion to the quality of dauntless boldness. No theological or philosophical technical usage is attested in the classical lexica.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدَّلْهَثُ والدُّلَاهِثُ والدِّلْهَاثُ: كلُّه السريعُ الجريءُ المُقْدِمُ من الناس والإِبل. والدِّلْهَاثُ: الأَسَدُ. قال أَبو منصور: كأَنَّ أَصله من الاندلاث، وهو التَّقَدُّم، فزيدت الهاء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-dalhath, al-dulāthith, and al-dilhāth all denote the swift, bold, forward-charging one among people and camels. Al-dilhāth also denotes the lion. Abū Manṣūr said: it is as though its origin is from al-indilāth, which is forward advance, with the hāʾ augmented.

derivations.english_translation: swift, bold, forward-charging (person or camel)
swift, bold, forward-charging (person or camel)
swift, bold, forward-charging one; the lion

record.ontological_core: The root denotes an extreme, saturated intensity of a color quality — specifically a concentrated, almost overwhelming redness or whiteness — as if the hue has been fully infused and intensified in the object.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a man of intense, saturated redness; and, by extension, a stark, intensely white object or person (أبيض دُمَّرِغ), indicating the utmost degree of whiteness.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to the concrete sensory domain of color intensity, with no abstract or scholastic extension recorded.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدُّمَّرِغُ: الرجلُ الشديدُ الحُمْرةِ. وأَبْيَضُ دُمَّرِغٌ: شديدُ البياضِ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Dummarigh: a man of intense redness; and 'abyadu dummarigh': intensely white.

derivations.english_translation: A man of intense, saturated redness; also, intensely white

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root د-ه-ن is the act of moistening, coating, or anointing a surface with a fatty, oily substance, thereby producing a slight, superficial wetness or glaze. This concrete sense of applying oil to the head or body underlies all subsequent literal and figurative extensions.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the application of oil or grease to the head or another surface (دهن رأسه، ودهنه، وادهن، وتدهن), as well as the oil itself (الدُّهْن) and the vessel that contains it (مدهن). It also denotes a tract of sandy ground (الدهناء) and a place where a small amount of water collects (مدهن).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) the residue or dregs of olive oil (دردي الزيت) in the Qur'anic image 'فكانت وردة كالدهان' (Q 55:37); (2) a she-camel with scant milk (الدهين), either because she yields only as much as is needed for anointing (active participle) or because she is metaphorically 'anointed' with milk due to its scarcity (passive participle); (3) rain that moistens the earth lightly (دهن المطر الأرض), akin to oiling the head; (4) a euphemistic or ironic expression for beating with a stick (دهنه بالعصا), comparable to 'مسحته بالسيف' and 'حييته بالرمح'; and (5) the Qur'anic expression 'تنبت بالدهن' (Q 23:20), where the olive tree is described as producing oil, a teleological nuance pointing to its beneficial essence.

canonical_definition.arabic: الدُّهْن: معروف. دَهَن رأْسه وغيره يَدْهُنه دَهْناً: بلَّه، والاسم الدُّهْن، والجمع أَدْهان ودِهان. والمِدْهَن: ما يجعل فيه الدهن. والدَّهين: الناقة القليلة اللبن. ودهن المطر الأرض: بلها بللاً يسيراً.
canonical_definition.english: Oil is well known. To anoint one's head or something else, he oils it with anointing: he moistened it. The noun is oil, and the plural is oils or greases. The oil container is that in which oil is placed. The dahīn is a she-camel with scant milk. Rain anointed the earth: it moistened it with a slight moisture.

record.ontological_core: The root ذ-ا-ح is not attested in the classical Arabic lexicographical tradition; no primary physical origin (aṣl al-waḍʿ) can be established from the cited sources.
record.haqiqah_literal: No literal physical meaning is attested in Lisān al-ʿArab, al-Mufradāt, or Asās al-Balāghah; the root is absent from the classical lexical corpus.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are recorded in the classical sources; the root does not appear in the Arabic philological tradition.

canonical_definition.arabic: ذاح: لم يُذكر في لسان العرب ولا المفردات ولا أساس البلاغة؛ لا أصل له في المعاجم العربية الكلاسيكية.
canonical_definition.english: Dhāḥ: Not mentioned in Lisān al-ʿArab, Al-Mufradāt, or Asās al-Balāghah; it has no attested root in the classical Arabic lexicons.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is the forearm—the limb extending from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger—and, by extension, the act of measuring or spanning with that limb.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the forearm as a bodily member, and the act of measuring a thing (such as cloth) by means of the forearm; also, the wooden rod or cubit measure used for such measurement.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) the measured object itself (al-madrūʿ), i.e., that which is measured by the forearm; (2) a chain whose length is measured in cubits, as in the Qurʾānic phrase 'a chain of seventy cubits'; (3) a swift-paced horse or a wide-stepping animal, from the image of extending the forelegs; (4) a person who stretches out the arm in walking or in a transaction (to sell); (5) a woman quick-handed at spinning; (6) a palm tree of the height of a man; (7) camels wading into water with their forelegs; (8) a man seeking help with his hand in his effort; and (9) a bearer of good news gesturing with his hand.

canonical_definition.arabic: الذِّراعُ: ما بين طرَف المِرْفق إِلى طرَفِ الإِصْبَع الوُسْطى، أُنثى وقد تذكَّر. ويعبر به عن المذروع، أي: الممسوح بالذراع.
canonical_definition.english: The forearm: that which lies between the tip of the elbow and the tip of the middle finger; it is feminine, though it may be treated as masculine. It is also used to denote the measured object, that is, that which is measured by the forearm.

mufradat.text: الذراع: العضو المعروف، ويعبر به عن المذروع، أي: الممسوح بالذراع. قال تعالى: في سلسلة ذرعها سبعون ذراعا فاسلكوه [الحاقة/ 32]، يقال: ذراع من الثوب والأرض، وذراع الأسد: نجم، تشبيها بذراع الحيوان، وذراع العامل: صدر القناة (6)، ويقال: هذا على حبل ذراعك (7)، كقولك: هو وأمكنه وقع مردى خشب في كفك، وضاق بكذا ذرعي، نحو: ضاقت به يدي، وذرعته: ضربت ذراعه، وذرعت: مددت الذراع، ومنه: ذرع البعير في سيره، أي: مد ذراعه، وفرس ذريع وذروع: واسع الخطو، ومذرع: أبيض الذراع، وزق ذراع، قيل: هو العظيم، وقيل: هو الصغير، فعلى الأول هو الذي بقي ذراعه، وعلى الثاني هو الذي فصل ذراعه عنه. وذرعه القيء: سبقه. وقولهم: ذرع الفرس، وتذرعت المرأة الخوص (1)، وتذرع في كلامه (2)، تشبيها بذلك، كقولهم: سفسف في كلامه، وأصله من سفيف الخوص.

entries.text: ضاق بالأمر ذرعا وذراعا إذا لم يطقه. وأبطرت ناقتك ذرعها: كلفتها ما لم تطق. واقصد بذرعك، واربع على ظلعك: ارفق بنفسك ومالك علي ذراع أي طاقة. وطفت في مذارع الوادي وهي أضواجه ونواحيه. وقد أذرع في كلامه وهو يذرع فيه إذراعا وهو الإكثار. وفلان ذريعتي إلى فلان. وقد تذرعت به إليه أي توسلت.

ذرعت الثوب بذراعي وهي من طرف المرفق إلى طرف الوسطى ثم سمي بها العود المقيس بها. وذرع في سيره وباع فيه إذا مد ذراعه وباعه. وناقة ذارعة بائعة. Metaphorical (Majaz): ضاق بالأمر ذرعا وذراعا إذا لم يطقه. وأبطرت ناقتك ذرعها: كلفتها ما لم تطق. واقصد بذرعك، واربع على ظلعك: ارفق بنفسك ومالك علي ذراع أي طاقة. وط

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a thin, fluid, resinous substance — specifically the light, unthickened stage of tar (qaṭirān) before it congeals into the dense pitch (khaḍkhāḍ). Its foundational physical image is that of a viscous liquid exudate, prior to coagulation.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical referent is thin tar (al-qaṭirān al-raqīq) — the runny, uncondensed resinous fluid that precedes the thickened pitch known as khaḍkhāḍ.
record.majaz_scholastic: No attested metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is recorded in the classical lexica; the root remains confined to its concrete material sense. Any figurative application (e.g., to moral defilement or obscurity) would be an extra-lexical extension not sanctioned by the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: الذَّفْل والذِّفْل: القَطِران الرقيق الذي قبل الخَضْخاض.
canonical_definition.english: Al-dhafl and al-dhifl: the thin tar that exists prior to the thickened pitch (al-khaḍkhāḍ).

derivations.english_translation: thin tar; the runny, uncondensed resinous fluid preceding pitch

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ذمر is the act of combining blame or rebuke with urgent incitement—specifically, a leader's sharp censure of his troops to spur them into battle, or a shepherd's tactile stimulation of a newborn camel's neck to rouse it. The root thus denotes a forceful, often harsh, arousal that fuses reproach with motivational propulsion.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is: to incite someone toward a matter by blaming him, so that he exerts himself therein. It is said: the commander yudhammiru (incites) his companions in war—he makes them hear what is disagreeable in order to sharpen them. And they are seen yatadhāmarūn (mutually inciting) in war. A shepherd dhamara the newborn camel: he touched its fahqah (the base of the neck where the head joins the neck) to determine its sex. Hence the term mudhammir is used for the instrument or person who performs this, and for camels it is like a midwife for humans.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) self-reproach combined with self-motivation—one who yatadhammar blames himself for negligence while simultaneously energizing himself to avoid future remissness; (2) tribal or personal honor defended with zeal, as in ḥāmī al-dhimār (protector of the sacred domain), where failure to defend would incur blame and rebuke; (3) courage and valor, as in dhammar min al-adhmār (a brave one among the brave); (4) in the ḥadīth of ʿAlī: 'The Devil has dhammara his party'—i.e., incited and emboldened them, blending censure with encouragement.

canonical_definition.arabic: الذَّمْرُ: اللَّوْمُ والحَضُّ معاً. ذَمَرَهُ يَذْمُرُهُ ذَمْراً: لامَهُ وحَضَّهُ وحَثَّهُ. وتَذَمَّرَ هو: لامَ نفسَه. وهو ذَمَرٌ من الأَذْمَارِ: شجاع. وذَمَرَ الراعي السَّلِيلَ: مَسَّ فَهْقَتَهُ. والمُذَمِّرُ للإِبل كالقابلة للناس. وهو حامي الذِّمار إِذا حَمَى ما لو لم يَحْمِهِ لِيمَ وعُنِّفَ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-dhamr is blame and incitement together. Dhamara-hu yadhmuru-hu dhamran: he blamed him and incited and urged him on. And tadhammara: he blamed himself. He is dhamar among the adhmār: brave. The shepherd dhamara the newborn camel: he touched its fahqah (base of the neck). The mudhammir for camels is like the midwife for humans. He is the protector of the dhimār when he defends what, if he did not defend it, he would be blamed and rebuked for.

entries.text: بلغ الأمر المذمر. كقولهم: بلغ المخنق. قال الجعدي: وحي أبي بكر ولا حي مثلهم ... إذا بلغ الأمر العماس المذمرا

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical process of a solid substance losing its rigidity and flowing, i.e., the liquefaction of fat, snow, or any congealed body through the application of heat or an external agent.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, sensory meaning: the melting or dissolving of a solid (such as fat, snow, or ice) into a liquid state, and the transitive act of causing such melting.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and philosophical extensions: the dissolution or wasting away of bodily strength, the softening of a hard heart, the fading of resolve, or the vanishing of wealth; also used in theological contexts to describe the annihilation of created things before the divine command, and in logic to denote the resolution of a composite into its simple elements.

canonical_definition.arabic: الذَّوْبُ: ضِدُّ الجُمُودِ. ذَابَ يَذُوبُ ذَوْبًا وذَوَبَانًا: نَقِيضُ جَمَدَ. وأَذَابَهُ غَيْرُهُ، وأَذَبْتُهُ، وذَوَّبْتُهُ، واسْتَذَبْتُهُ: طَلَبْتُ مِنْهُ ذَاكَ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-dhawb is the opposite of solidification. Dhāba yadhūbu dhawban wa-dhawabānan: it is the contrary of jamada (to freeze). Another agent may cause it to melt: adhābahu, adhabtuhu, dhawwabtuhu, and istadhabtuhu mean 'I sought that from it.'

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the well-known predatory canid, the wolf, regarded by al-Rāghib as originally hamzated (ذِئْب), from which derive the senses of wolf-infestation, wolf-like ferocity, and the wolf-shaped wooden saddle-part (ذِئْبَة القَتَب).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the wolf as a concrete predatory animal; hence أَرْضٌ مَذْأَبَةٌ (a wolf-infested land), ذُئِبَ فُلَانٌ (a wolf fell upon his flock), and ذَئِبَ (he became wolf-like in viciousness).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and derived usages include: تَذَاءَبَتِ الرِّيحُ (the wind came from every direction, as if attacking like a wolf); تَذَاءَبَتْ لِلنَّاقَةِ (she imitated the wolf's posture to trick the she-camel into accepting her calf); الذِّئْبَةُ مِنَ القَتَبِ (the wolf-shaped wooden piece beneath the junction of the saddle-bows); and, in the Lisān material, الأَذْيَبُ as abundant water, terror, or lively energy—though al-Aṣmaʿī suspected this may properly belong to أَزْيَب with zāy.

canonical_definition.arabic: الذِّئْبُ: الحيوان المعروف، وأصله الهمز؛ قال تعالى: ﴿فَأَكَلَهُ الذِّئْبُ﴾. وأرض مذأبة: كثيرة الذئاب. وذئب فلان: وقع في غنمه الذئب. وذئب: صار كذئب في خبثه. وتذاءبت الريح: أتت من كل جانب مجيء الذئب. والذئبة من القتب: ما تحت ملتقى الحنوين، تشبيهاً بالذئب في الهيئة.
canonical_definition.english: The wolf: the well-known animal, originally hamzated; as in the verse 'So the wolf devoured him.' A wolf-infested land is one abounding in wolves. 'A wolf fell upon his flock' means a wolf attacked his sheep. 'He became wolf-like' means he became vicious like a wolf. 'The wind wolfed' means it came from every direction in the manner of a wolf. The 'wolf' of the saddle is the piece beneath the junction of the saddle-bows, likened to the wolf in shape.

mufradat.text: الذيب: الحيوان المعروف، وأصله الهمز، قال تعالى: فأكله الذئب [يوسف/ 17]، وأرض مذأبة: كثيرة الذئاب، وذئب فلان: وقع في غنمه الذئب، وذئب (5): صار كذئب في خبثه، وتذاءبت الريح: أتت من كل جانب ولكن بالمغيب نبئيني مجيء الذئب، وتذاءبت للناقة على تفاعلت: إذا تشبهت لها بالذئب في الهيئة لتظأر على ولدها، والذئبة من القتب: ما تحت ملتقى الحنوين (1)، تشبيها بالذئب في الهيئة.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ر-خ-و is softness, pliancy, and lack of rigidity or tension in a physical body or substance. It denotes the quality of being yielding, slack, or porous (هَشّ) in contrast to hardness and tautness.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a thing that is soft, slack, or pliant (رِخْو / رَخْو), such as a loose curtain, a slack rope, or a gentle, compliant wind. It is the direct sensory quality of lacking firmness or tension.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends from physical slackness to: (1) a gentle, compliant wind that flows without resistance (رِيح رَخَاء), as in Qurʾān 38:36; (2) the act of letting down or loosening a curtain (إرخاء الستر), which is then metaphorically extended to the veiling of divine secrets, the relaxation of strictness, or the granting of respite; (3) a lax or lenient disposition in a person, indicating a lack of strictness or severity in conduct or judgment.

canonical_definition.arabic: الرِّخْوُ والرَّخْوُ والرُّخْوُ: الهَشُّ من كلّ شيءٍ، وهو الشيء الذي فيه رَخاوة. وكلامُ العرب الجيّدُ: الرِّخْو، بكسر الراء. والرَّخاء: اللينة. ومنه: أَرْخَيْتُ الستر.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Rikhw, al-Rakhw, and al-Rukhw: the porous or soft of anything; it is the thing in which there is slackness. The preferred Arabic usage is al-Rikhw, with a kasrah on the rāʾ. Al-Rakhāʾ: the gentle or pliant. Hence: I let down the curtain.

mufradat.text: الرخاء: اللينة. من قولهم: شيء رخو، وقد رخي يرخى (1)، قال تعالى: فسخرنا له الريح تجري بأمره رخاء حيث أصاب [ص/ 36]، ومنه: أرخيت الستر، وعن إرخاء الستر استعير: 183- إرخاء سرحان (2) وقول أبي ذؤيب: 184- وهي رخو تمزع (3) أي: رخو السير كريح الرخاء، وقيل: فرس مرخاء، أي: واسع الجري بعيد الخطو، من خيل مراخ، وقد أرخيته: خليته رخوا.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of crushing, breaking, or violently shattering a solid body, and secondarily on the striking or bruising of a bodily part.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the crushing or shattering of something solid (al-shadkh), and the bruise or contusion (al-radakh) produced by a blow upon the body.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexica; the root remains confined to its concrete physical sense of crushing and bruising.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَرْدَخُ: الشَّدْخ. والرَّدَخُ: مثل الرَّدع، عُمانِيَّة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-mardakh: crushing or shattering. And al-radakh: like al-radʿ (a bruise or contusion), an Omani usage.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root رصص is the act of tightly joining, compacting, and aligning solid discrete units—such as stones, bricks, or teeth—into a single cohesive, interlocked structure, eliminating gaps and ensuring firm mutual support.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the construction of a tightly packed, well-aligned building (بنيان مرصوص ومرصص), the compacting of stones (ارتصت الجنادل وترصصت), the close alignment of teeth (في أسنانه رصص), and the act of a hen or ostrich gathering and arranging its eggs with beak and feet (رصت الدجاجة والنعامة بيضها).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root denotes the strict, unbroken alignment of worshippers in prayer (تراصوا في الصلاة وارتصوا), the firm, compact physique of a person (رجل أرص, امرأة رصاء), and the piling of stones upon a grave (رصت على القبر الرصائص). In theological and philosophical discourse, it conveys the concept of a unified, indivisible order—whether of ranks, arguments, or cosmic elements—where each part is perfectly fitted to its neighbor without interstices, reflecting a deliberate, cohesive arrangement.

canonical_definition.arabic: رَصَّ البُنْيَانَ يَرُصُّهُ رَصًّا، فَهُوَ مَرْصُوصٌ وَرَصِيصٌ، وَرَصَّصَهُ: أَحْكَمَهُ وَجَمَعَهُ وَضَمَّ بَعْضَهُ إِلَى بَعْضٍ. وَكُلُّ مَا أُحْكِمَ وَضُمَّ فَقَدْ رُصَّ.
canonical_definition.english: He compacted the building, joining it tightly; it is marṣūṣ and raṣīṣ. He made it tight: he perfected it, gathered it, and joined its parts to one another. Everything that is made firm and joined together is said to be raṣṣed.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ر ض م is the act of stacking large, heavy stones one upon another to form a solid, compacted structure or barrier. This core image of piling and compacting heavy solids underlies all subsequent literal and figurative applications.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the placing of stones one above another in building, and the resulting structure of stacked large rocks. It denotes both the action of stacking stones (رضم الحجارة) and the object itself: a wall or building constructed of dry-stone masonry (رضيم), or a heap of large rocks (رضمة). It also literally describes a camel's heavy, slow gait, likened to the slow, deliberate stacking of stones.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic extensions of the root are limited in the classical sources. The physical image of compacted, heavy stones yields the figurative description of a slow, heavy gait (رَضَمَ الشيخُ) as if the person's movement is weighed down like stacked rocks. The term رَضَمان (slow, heavy pace) is used metaphorically for any slow, deliberate action. In the Asās, the root is also used in the context of seeking divine pleasure (رضوان الله) and satisfaction (رضا), but this is a distinct root (رضو) and not a metaphorical extension of رضم; the two roots are homophonous in some forms but semantically separate. Thus, the majāz of رضم remains primarily within the domain of physical heaviness and slowness.

canonical_definition.arabic: رَضَمَ الشيخُ يَرْضِمُ رَضْماً: ثَقُل عَدْوُه، وكذلك الدابة. والرَّضَمانُ: تَقارُبُ عَدْو الشيخ. والرَّضْمُ: وَضْعُ الحجارة بعضها على بعض. والرَّضِيمُ: البناءُ بالصخر.
canonical_definition.english: An elderly man's gait became heavy and slow (رَضَمَ يَرْضِمُ رَضْمًا), and likewise for an animal. رَضَمَان denotes the short, slow steps of an old man. رَضْم is the placing of stones one upon another. رَضِيم is a structure built of large stones.

entries.text: رأيت إبلا كالرضام والرضم وهي صخور عظام الواجدة رضمة. وبني داره بالرضام. وبناء رضيم: مبني بالصخر، وبنى بناء قد رضم فيه الحجارة: وضع بعضها فوق بعض. ر ض وفعل ذلك ابتغاء رضوان الله ورضاه ومرضاته، وطلب مراضي الله فيما فعل. ورضيته ورضيت به صاحبا. وهذا شيء رضا: مرضي. وما فعلته إلا عن رض

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root رفف is a subtle, rapid, and shimmering motion or vibration—a light quivering or flickering that manifests as a gleam, a flutter, or a delicate oscillation. It denotes the slightest perceptible movement or radiance, such as the shimmer of a polished surface, the quiver of a leaf, or the flutter of a wing, without any substantial displacement.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah centers on: (1) the light, rapid movement of the lips in eating or kissing, as in 'يَرُفُّ شفتيها' (he moves his lips over hers); (2) the eating of herbs or plants by an animal, nibbling them delicately; (3) the shimmering and sparkling of color or teeth; (4) the quivering and swaying of plants in fresh luxuriance; (5) the fluttering of a bird's wings while remaining in place; (6) the flapping of the lower edge or fringe of a tent in the wind; and (7) a thin, delicate garment.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) the act of cherishing, protecting, and showing compassion to someone, as one might delicately handle a beloved child or a tender plant—'يَرُفُّهُ' meaning he embraces and cares for him with tenderness; (2) the state of being in need or lacking a provider, as in 'ماله حافّ ولا رافّ' (he has neither a protector nor a provider); (3) the shimmering of teeth or countenance as a sign of health, joy, or beauty; (4) the fluttering of wings as a metaphor for restless anticipation or hovering; and (5) the delicate, trembling quality of a fresh, verdant meadow or a tree with shimmering leaves.

canonical_definition.arabic: رَفَّ لونُه يَرِفُّ رَفّاً ورَفيفاً: بَرَقَ وتَلأْلأَ، وكذلك رَفَّتْ أَسنانه. ورَفَّ النباتُ يَرِفُّ: اهتزَّ نضارةً وتلألؤاً. ورَفْرَفَ الطائرُ: حرَّك جناحيه وهو لا يبرح مكانه. وثوبٌ رَفيفٌ: رقيقٌ. وذهب من كان يَحُفُّه ويَرُفُّهُ أَي يضمه ويحبه ويشفق عليه.
canonical_definition.english: His color shimmered with a rapid, delicate motion (rafā yarifu raffan wa-rafīfan): it gleamed and sparkled, and likewise his teeth shimmered. The plant quivered with freshness and radiance. The bird fluttered its wings while remaining in place. A thin garment is described as rafīf. And one who used to cherish and protect him—that is, embrace him, love him, and show him compassion—has gone.

record.ontological_core: The root رفم denotes the foundational physical notion of complete, unbroken ease and plenitude — a state of total well-being and abundance that leaves nothing lacking.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in Lisān al-ʿArab, is 'complete bliss' or 'perfect luxury' (al-naʿīm al-tāmm), indicating a state of unalloyed prosperity and comfort.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, the term may be applied metaphorically to the ultimate felicity of the hereafter or to the perfect contentment of the soul in union with the divine, though such extensions are not explicitly attested in the classical lexicons.

canonical_definition.arabic: الرَّفَمُ: النَّعِيمُ التَّامُّ
canonical_definition.english: Al-rafam: complete bliss, perfect luxury.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act of rubbing, kneading, or working a supple material (such as leather) with the hand, involving repeated pressure and friction to soften or manipulate it.
record.haqiqah_literal: To rub or knead something with the hand, as one works a hide or similar material.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical or scholastic usage is attested in the classical lexicons; the root remains confined to its literal manual operation.

canonical_definition.arabic: رَمَغَ الشيءَ يَرْمَغُه رَمْغاً: دَلَكَه بيدِه كما تَدْلُك الأَدِيمَ ونحوَه. ورُماغٌ ورِماغٌ: موضعٌ.
canonical_definition.english: He rubbed or kneaded the thing with his hand, as one works a hide or the like. And Rumāgh or Rimāgh: a place name.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a compact, tightly bound group of men — a small, cohesive band whose members are united by kinship, tribal affiliation, or a shared cause. Its foundational physical image is that of a knot or tight cluster of individuals standing together, neither a single person nor a large multitude.
record.haqiqah_literal: A man's immediate kin-group or clan; a small company of men numbering from three up to ten (some say seven to ten). It is the concrete, bounded social unit — the band of close male relatives or associates who stand together as one body.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, the term is applied to any small, tightly united faction or party bound by a common purpose, whether in political allegiance, military alliance, or shared guilt. In classical usage it can denote the specific group of individuals implicated in a single act — as in the verse of al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah, where 'three men' (thalāthat rahṭ) designates the small, named band responsible for a killing and a plunder. The metaphorical force lies in the compression of collective agency into a minimal, identifiable unit: the rahṭ is the smallest social body that can act as a single agent.

canonical_definition.arabic: الرَّهْطُ: قَوْمُ الرَّجُلِ وَقَبِيلَتُهُ، وَهُمْ عَدَدٌ يَجْمَعُ مِنْ ثَلَاثَةٍ إِلَى عَشَرَةٍ، وَمَا دُونَ السَّبْعَةِ إِلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ نَفَرٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-rahṭ: a man's people and his tribe; a number gathering from three to ten; what is below seven down to three is termed nafar.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the emission and flow of moisture from the mouth or body of an animal, specifically saliva, foam, or dripping fluid, as attested in the classical lexical tradition.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is the flowing saliva or foam of a horse or beast, and the act of an animal lowering itself to urinate; also the anointing or moistening of the head with oil and of bread with clarified butter or condiment.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and extended usages include: the flowing of saliva into a pouch or container; the emergence of teeth, especially the 'rāwūl' (a tooth that is a companion or adjacent to another tooth); and the phrase 'رُوَالٌ رَائِل' (flowing saliva) modeled on 'شِعْرٌ شَاعِر' for intensification. No philosophical or theological technical senses are attested in the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: الرُّوَال، على فُعَال بالضم: اللُّعاب. وقيل: الرُّوَال زَبَد الفرس خاصة. والرَّاوُول: لُعاب الدواب. ورَوَّل رأسه من الدهن: رواه. ورَوَّل الخبز بالسمن وبالأدم. ورَوَّل الفرس: أدلى ليبول. وتروَّل في مخلاته: سال فيها رواله. وظهرت أسنانه بالرواويل. وكل سن رديف لسن فهو راوول.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ruwāl, on the pattern fuʿāl with ḍammah: saliva. It is also said: al-ruwāl is specifically the foam of a horse. Al-rāwūl: the saliva of beasts. Rawwala raʾsahu min al-duhn: he moistened his head with oil. Rawwala al-khubz bi-l-samn wa-l-udm: he moistened bread with clarified butter and condiment. Rawwala al-faras: it lowered itself to urinate. Tarawwala fī mikhlaʾatihi: its saliva flowed into its nosebag. And its teeth appeared with the rawāwīl. Every tooth that is a companion to another tooth is a rāwūl.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the forcible, hasty displacement of a thing from its place—a swift pulling or shoving that removes an entity from its locus.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to pull or shove something in haste, thereby removing it from its position; the reduplicated form زُحْزِحَ denotes being moved away and distanced.
record.majaz_scholastic: In theological and eschatological usage, the term is applied metaphorically to being removed from the Fire and distanced from its abode, as in the Qur'anic phrase 'فمن زُحْزِحَ عن النار'—meaning one is displaced from the Fire's resting place and brought far from it, attaining salvation.

canonical_definition.arabic: زُحْزِحَ أَي نُحِّيَ وبُعِّدَ. وزَحَّ الشيءَ يَزُحُّه زَحّاً: جذبه في عَجَلَة.
canonical_definition.english: زُحْزِحَ means he was removed and distanced. And زَحَّ الشيءَ يَزُحُّه زَحّاً: he pulled it in haste.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root زحلف is the act of sliding or slipping downward, specifically the smooth, frictionless descent over a surface, as exemplified by children sliding from the top of a hill to its bottom. This core image of downward slippage underlies all subsequent literal and figurative applications.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (delineated from Lisān al-ʿArab) is the trace or track left by children sliding down a hill, and by extension, the act of sliding itself. It denotes a smooth, downward glide, often on a slippery surface, and is synonymous with زحلوقة (zuhlūqah) in the dialect of the ʿĀliyah tribe, while Tamīm pronounces it with a qāf (زحلوقة).
record.majaz_scholastic: While not attested in Asās al-Balāghah, the metaphorical and scholastic extensions of زحلف are derived from its literal sense of sliding. These include: (1) the slippage or deviation from a straight path, whether physical or moral; (2) the rapid, uncontrolled descent into error or sin; (3) in philosophical and theological contexts, the instability of the soul or intellect when it loses its footing on the path of virtue or truth, leading to a fall from grace or a lapse in judgment. The term may also be applied to the slippery nature of worldly affairs and the transience of material existence.

canonical_definition.arabic: الزُّحْلُوفَةُ: كالزُّحْلُوقَة، وقد تَزَحْلَفَ. وهي آثارُ تَزَلُّجِ الصِّبيان من فوقِ التَّلِّ إلى أَسْفَله، وهي لغة أهل العالية، وتميمٌ تقوله بالقاف، والجمع زحالِفُ وزَحالِيفُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Zuḥlūfah: like al-zuḥlūqah, and one says tazaḥlafa. It is the traces of children sliding from the top of a hill to its bottom; it is the dialect of the people of al-ʿĀliyah, while Tamīm pronounces it with a qāf; the plural is zaḥālif and zaḥālīf.

derivations.english_translation: A slide, a slippery place, or the track left by sliding; a children's slide.
To slide down, to slip, to glide downward.
Plural of زُحْلُوفَة: slides, slippery places, or sliding tracks.
Plural of زُحْلُوفَة: slides, slippery places, or sliding tracks (alternative plural).

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a toponymic designation (a place-name) attested in the poetry of Hudhayl, transmitted as زُخَيّات (a diminutive nominal form); its ontological status is onomastic rather than predicative, lacking a productive physical or eventive Aṣl al-Wadʿ in the classical lexical corpus.
record.haqiqah_literal: A proper place-name (موضع) occurring in Hudhaylī verse in the diminutive form زُخَيّات; the reading الزَّوَاخِي transmitted by some authorities is judged by Ibn Sīdah to be a scribal corruption (تصحيف) of the correct زُخَيّات with zāy and khāʾ.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested; the root remains confined to onomastic reference, and any scholastic or figurative application would be an unwarranted extrapolation beyond the classical lexical evidence.

canonical_definition.arabic: الزَّوَاخِي: مواضع. قال ابن سيده: وزعم قوم أَن في شعر هذيل رُحَيّات وفسروه بأَنه موضع، قال: وهذا تصحيف إِنما هو زُخَيّات، بالزاي والخاء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Zawākhī: place-names. Ibn Sīdah said: some authorities claimed that in Hudhaylī poetry there occurs [the form] Ruḥayyāt, which they interpreted as a place-name; he said: this is a scribal corruption—it is in fact Zukhayyāt, with zāy and khāʾ.

derivations.english_translation: Zukhayyāt, a place-name in Hudhaylī poetry (diminutive form)
Zawākhī, a purported place-name rejected by Ibn Sīdah as a scribal corruption of Zukhayyāt

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is gold (al-dhahab), specifically gold as an object of ornamentation and embellishment; from this material substrate the root extends to denote any adornment, and thence to anything artificially beautified or falsified.
record.haqiqah_literal: Gold; then any ornament or embellishment (zīnah); then any embellished, gilded, or artificially beautified thing. The verb زَخْرَفَ denotes the act of adorning, embellishing, and perfecting a thing, as in زَخْرَفَ البيتَ (he adorned and completed the house).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic applications include: (1) embellished speech or discourse (زخرف القول) understood as deceptive, ornamented words that veil falsehood; (2) the gilded or golden chambers of worldly luxury (بيت من زخرف) signifying transient material splendor; (3) the earth's adornment (أخذت الأرض زخرفها) as the flourishing of worldly life that precedes its decay; (4) any falsified or counterfeit presentation (كل مموه مزور) in which surface beauty conceals corrupt reality. In theological and ethical usage, the term denotes the seductive ornamentation of worldly existence and the rhetorical embellishment of falsehood.

canonical_definition.arabic: الزُّخْرُفُ: الزِّينَةُ، وأَصْلُهُ الذَّهَبُ، ثُمَّ سُمِّيَ كُلُّ زِينَةٍ زُخْرُفاً، ثُمَّ شُبِّهَ كُلُّ مُمَوَّهٍ مُزَوَّرٍ بِهِ. وَزَخْرَفَ البَيْتَ: زَيَّنَهُ وَأَكْمَلَهُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Zukhruf: ornamentation; its primary origin is gold, then every ornament was named zukhruf, then every falsified or counterfeit thing was likened to it. Zakhrafa al-bayta: he adorned and perfected the house.

derivations.english_translation: gold; ornament, embellishment; gilded or adorned thing; embellished speech
he adorned, embellished, and perfected (a thing, e.g., a house)
adornment, embellishment, the act of decorating and perfecting
adorned, embellished, decorated

mufradat.text: الزخرف: الزينة المزوقة، ومنه قيل للذهب: زخرف، وقال: أخذت الأرض زخرفها [يونس/ 24]، وقال: بيت من زخرف [الإسراء/ 93]، أي: ذهب مزوق، وقال: وزخرفا [الزخرف/ 35]، وقال: زخرف القول غرورا [الأنعام/ 112]، أي: المزوقات من الكلام.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a liminal, brackish state of water — neither purely fresh nor purely saline — situated at the threshold between two opposing qualities. Its reduplicative phonetic structure (ز-ز-م) mirrors this in-between condition, suggesting a substance that partakes of both extremes without fully belonging to either.
record.haqiqah_literal: Water that is neither fully salt nor fully sweet; brackish water occupying the intermediate zone between the saline and the potable.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, any entity, quality, or state that is suspended between two contraries, resisting categorical assignment to either pole. In scholastic and theological discourse, it may describe an ambiguous or indeterminate matter that partakes of two opposing natures without being reducible to either — a medial ontological status.

canonical_definition.arabic: ماء زُوَزِمٌ وزُوازِمٌ: بين المِلْحِ والعَذْبِ.
canonical_definition.english: Brackish water: that which lies between the salt and the sweet.

derivations.english_translation: brackish water, between salt and sweet
brackish water, between salt and sweet

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of swallowing a morsel (لُقْمَة) — specifically, the passage of food through the throat — and by concrete extension, the anatomical throat itself (الحلقوم) and the snout or muzzle of a predatory animal (خُرْطوم الكلب والسبع), the orifice through which such swallowing occurs.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to the classical lexicographers is twofold: (1) the throat or gullet (الحلقوم) in certain Arabic dialects, and (2) the snout or muzzle of a dog or beast of prey (خُرْطوم الكلب والسبع). The verbal form زَلْقَمَ denotes the concrete act of swallowing a morsel (بَلَعَ اللُّقْمَةَ).
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical sources. The term remains confined to its concrete anatomical and physiological signification. Any extended application — such as employing الزُّلْقُوم for the throat as the seat of voice or for the beast's snout as an instrument of seizing — remains within the domain of literal anatomical reference rather than true majāz. The scholastic tradition records no abstract or figurative deployment of this root.

canonical_definition.arabic: الزُّلْقُومُ: الحلقوم في بعض اللغات، وخُرْطومُ الكلب والسبع. وزَلْقَمَ اللُّقْمَةَ: بَلَعَها.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Zulqūm: the throat or gullet in certain dialects, and the snout of a dog or beast of prey. And zalqama al-luqma: he swallowed the morsel.

derivations.english_translation: the throat, gullet; the snout or muzzle of a dog or beast of prey
to swallow a morsel; to gulp down
the act of swallowing a morsel; gulping

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root زلل is the act of slipping, sliding, or losing one's footing upon a surface—whether descending from a rock, sliding in mud, or an arrow glancing off a shield. It denotes a sudden, unintended departure from a stable position or intended trajectory.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal meaning is: slipping from a rock or in mud (زل عن الصخرة وفي الطين زليلا); a place of slipping (مزلة); a man with a slipping foot or speech (سمع أزل); a woman who slips (امرأة زلاء); and God causing the earth to shake (زلزل الله الأرض زلزالا).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) moral or doctrinal lapse—a slip in speech, judgment, or conduct (زل في منطقه); (2) theological usage in زلزال (earthquake) as a divine act of shaking or destabilizing; (3) philosophical application to any deviation from a norm, whether in logic, ethics, or natural motion; (4) the passive أزله (to cause someone to slip) implying external causation of error or downfall.

canonical_definition.arabic: زَلَّ السَّهْمُ عن الدِّرْع، والإنسانُ عن الصخرة يَزِلُّ ويَزَلُّ زَلاًّ وزَلِيلاً ومَزِلَّة: زَلِقَ. وزَلَلْتَ يا فلان تَزِلُّ زَلِيلاً إذا زَلَّ في طِين أو مَنْطِق.
canonical_definition.english: The arrow slipped off the shield, and a person slipped from the rock—he slips, slipping, and a place of slipping: he slid. And you, O so-and-so, slipped with a slipping when you slipped in mud or in speech.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root زهك is the abrasive friction or grinding of one hard surface against another, specifically the action of rubbing or scraping between two stones, producing a harsh, rasping effect. This core image of friction and attrition underlies all subsequent applications.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the act of rubbing, scraping, or grinding between two stones (al-jashsh bayna ḥajarayn), and the abrasive action of wind upon a surface, stripping or scouring it away.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, its metaphorical extension in classical usage includes the wind's erosive action, likened to a file or rasp that wears down what it strikes. The scholastic dimension remains minimal, as the root is primarily concrete and sensory, with no developed theological or philosophical abstraction in the classical lexicons.

canonical_definition.arabic: الزَّهْكُ مِثْلُ السَّهْكِ: وَهُوَ الجَشُّ بَيْنَ حَجَرَيْنِ. وَزَهَكَتْهُ الرِّيحُ تَزْهَكُهُ: كَسَهَكَتْهُ، وَالسِّينُ أَعْلَى.
canonical_definition.english: Al-zahk is like al-sahk: it is the rubbing or grinding between two stones. And the wind scoured it (zahakat-hu) — like sahakathu — though the variant with sīn is more authoritative.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is 'cutting' or 'severing' — the act of cutting off, whether hair, a journey, or activity. From this primary sense of severance, the root extends to the notion of rest (cessation of labor) and to tanned leather (from which hair has been removed).
record.haqiqah_literal: Literal physical meanings: to cut off, to sever; to shave the head; to cut short a journey; to tan leather by removing its hair; tanned leather itself (especially that tanned with qaraẓ); the seventh day of the week (Saturday), named because God ceased creating on that day; and the state of being in Saturday or resting from work.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and theological applications: (1) Sleep as a 'cutting off' of activity, hence 'sabāt' (deep sleep or death) — 'We made your sleep a sabāt' (Q 78:9), meaning a severance from work, akin to the rest of night. (2) The Sabbath as a divinely ordained cessation of labor for the Jews, and their punishment for violating it (Q 7:163, 16:124). (3) 'Mabsūt' (passive participle) meaning dead, as in 'he became mabsūt' (i.e., his activities were cut off). (4) The verbal forms 'sabata' and 'asbata' meaning to observe the Sabbath or to enter upon it.

canonical_definition.arabic: السِّبْتُ: كُلُّ جِلْدٍ مَدْبُوغٍ، وَقِيلَ: هُوَ المَدْبُوغُ بِالقَرَظِ خَاصَّةً. وَأَصْلُ السَّبْتِ: القَطْعُ. وَسُبَات: النَّوْم، وَهُوَ قَطْعٌ لِلْعَمَلِ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Sibt: any tanned leather; it is said: specifically that tanned with qaraẓ. The root origin of 'sabt' is cutting. 'Subāt' is sleep, which is a cutting off of activity.

mufradat.text: أصل السبت: القطع، ومنه سبت السير: قطعه، وسبت شعره: حلقه، وأنفه: اصطلمه، وقيل: سمي يوم السبت، لأن الله تعالى ابتدأ بخلق السموات والأرض يوم الأحد، فخلقها في ستة أيام كما ذكره، فقطع عمله يوم السبت فسمي بذلك، وسبت فلان: صار في السبت وقوله: يوم سبتهم شرعا [الأعراف/ 163]، قيل: يوم قطعهم للعمل، ويوم لا يسبتون [الأعراف/ 163]، قيل: معناه لا يقطعون العمل، وقيل: يوم لا يكونون في السبت، وكلاهما إشارة إلى حالة واحدة، وقوله: إنما جعل السبت [النحل/ 124]، أي: ترك العمل فيه، وجعلنا نومكم سباتا [النبأ/ 9]، أي: قطعا للعمل، وذلك إشارة إلى ما قال في صفة الليل: لتسكنوا فيه* [يونس/ 67].

entries.text: يلبسون النعال السبتية ونعال السبت وهو الأدم، لأن شعره يسقط في الدباغ كأنه سبت أي حلق. وسبت رأسه، ورأس مسبوت. وسبتت اليهود وأسبتت. وجعل الله النوم سباتا: موتا، وأصبح فلان مسبوتا: ميتا.

record.ontological_core: A quadriliteral (rubāʿī) toponym of Persian provenance denoting a well-known administrative region (kūrah), with no attested Arabic verbal root origin (aṣl al-waḍʿ) in the classical lexical tradition.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, extra-lexical referent is the proper place-name Sijistān/Sajistān (Sīstān), a recognized province; the form is a loanword (muʿarrab) and not a native Arabic ḥaqīqah derived from an Arabic root.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological majāz is attested; the term functions strictly as a geographical proper noun and admits no semantic extension in the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: سِجْسَتانُ وسَجِسْتانُ: كُورَةٌ معروفة، وهي فارسية، ذكره ابن سيده في الرباعي.
canonical_definition.english: Sijistān and Sajistān: a well-known province; it is Persian, cited by Ibn Sīdah among the quadriliteral forms.

derivations.english_translation: Sijistān/Sajistān (Sīstān), a well-known province
Sajistān (variant vocalization of the same toponym)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of peeling, scraping, or eradicating something down to its core—specifically, stripping away the outer layer (qishr) or fat from flesh, or shaving hair to the root. This concrete sense of total removal and uprooting is the root's primary material meaning.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is: to shave hair completely during a haircut or trimming, to peel fat away from flesh, to scrape the surface of the earth, and in circumcision, to perform the procedure thoroughly and exhaustively until the flesh is worn down.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root denotes anything forbidden, vile, or illicit that strips away a person's religion and moral integrity (murūʾah), such as bribery, unlawful earnings, the price of a dog, wine, or swine. It is used in the Qurʾān to describe those who consume illicit gain (akālūn li-l-suḥt) and in prophetic tradition: 'Every flesh nourished by illicit gain, the Fire is more deserving of it.' The term also extends to earnings that, while not strictly forbidden, compromise one's dignity, such as the cupper's fee, which the Prophet permitted to be used for feeding animals and slaves.

canonical_definition.arabic: السُّحْتُ والسُّحُتُ: كلُّ حرام قبيح الذِّكر؛ وقيل: هو ما خَبُثَ من المَكاسب وحَرُم فلَزِمَ عنه العارُ، وقَبيحُ الذِّكْر، كَثَمن الكلب والخمر والخنزير.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Suḥt and al-suḥut: every forbidden thing of vile repute; it is said to be any foul and unlawful earning that entails disgrace and infamy, such as the price of a dog, wine, or swine.

mufradat.text: السحت: القشر الذي يستأصل، قال تعالى: فيسحتكم بعذاب (1). [طه/ 61]، وقرئ: فيسحتكم يقال: سحته وأسحته، ومنه: السحت والسحت للمحظور الذي يلزم صاحبه العار، كأنه يسحت دينه ومروءته، قال تعالى: أكالون للسحت [المائدة/ 42]، أي: لما يسحت دينهم. وقال (عليه السلام): «كل لحم نبت من سحت فالنار أولى به» (2) ، وسمي الرشوة سحتا لذلك، وروي «كسب الحجام سحت» (3) فهذا لكونه ساحتا للمروءة لا للدين، ألا ترى أنه أذن (عليه السلام) في إعلافه الناضح وإطعامه المماليك (4).

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root سحم is the quality of deep, uniform blackness, specifically the saturated darkness exemplified by the raven's plumage and heavy rain-clouds; it denotes a blackness that is intrinsic and total rather than accidental or partial.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is blackness (al-sawād), as in the phrase 'a raven that is asḥam' (ghurāb asḥam), 'black clouds' (saḥāb asḥam), and 'a black cloud-mass' (ghamāma saḥmāʾ); the verbal form saḥamū is used literally for darkening or blackening a face.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, the root is applied metaphorically to denote moral or spiritual blackening, as in the ḥadīth of the malediction (liʿān) where a child born 'asḥam aḥtam' signifies a deep, undeniable blackness that may imply illegitimacy or moral stain; likewise, in the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr, the term describes a person of dark complexion, extending the physical quality to human appearance without metaphorical abstraction. The root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt, so its ontological origin is derived from classical lexical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: السَّحَمُ والسُّحَامُ والسُّحْمَةُ: السواد، وكل أسود أسحم.
canonical_definition.english: Al-saḥam, al-suḥām, and al-suḥma denote blackness; everything black is asḥam.
