record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the notion of a surface being stripped bare or denuded, specifically of hair, yielding a state of smooth, hairless exposure.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is an eyebrow (ḥājib) that is completely devoid of hair, i.e., a hairless or bald eyebrow.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; no established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are recorded in the classical lexica. The term remains confined to its literal anatomical description.

canonical_definition.arabic: حاجب مُسَرْبَدٌ: لا شعر عليه؛ عن كراع.
canonical_definition.english: A hairless eyebrow: one upon which there is no hair; reported from Kurāʿ.

derivations.english_translation: A hairless, bald (eyebrow); devoid of hair

record.ontological_core: The root سرهج is a rare quadriliteral (rubāʿī) formation denoting a crafted, ornamental artifact — specifically a manufactured object of variegated inlay or mosaic workmanship (comparable to faysafisāʾ, Byzantine-style tessellated ornament). Its foundational physical origin is the concrete act of fabricating a decorated, multi-colored surface or object through artisanal technique (ṣanʿah).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical sense is a crafted ornamental object — a thing of artifice resembling mosaic or inlaid work (shayʾ min al-ṣanʿah ka-l-faysafisāʾ). The noun السرنج (al-saranj, on the pattern of samand) designates such an inlaid or tessellated artifact.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested in the classical lexica. The term remains confined to the concrete domain of craft and ornamentation; any figurative application would be an ad hoc extension and is not sanctioned by the philological tradition. Al-Zamakhsharī's Asās records no majāz for this root, and Al-Rāghib's Al-Mufradāt does not treat it — indicating the root never entered the abstract or scholastic register.

canonical_definition.arabic: السَّرْهَجَةُ: ضَرْبٌ مِنَ الصَّنْعَةِ كَالْفَسِيفَسَاءِ؛ وَالسَّرَنْجُ كَسَمَنْدٍ: شَيْءٌ مِنَ الصِّنَاعَةِ الْمُزَخْرَفَةِ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-sarhajah: a mode of craftsmanship akin to mosaic (faysafisāʾ); and al-saranj (on the pattern samand): an artifact of ornamental, variegated workmanship.

derivations.english_translation: the act or craft of producing ornamental inlay/mosaic work
an ornamental inlaid artifact; mosaic-like crafted object
a thing of artifice resembling mosaic or variegated inlay (pattern: samand)

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a rare, non-productive nominal pattern (fuʿlūl) attested only in the proper name Banū Saʿfūq, a clan or tribal group in al-Yamāma; its foundational origin is onomastic rather than lexical, with no attested verbal or abstract nominal derivation.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, concrete referent is the tribal designation Banū Saʿfūq (also vocalized Banū Suʿfūq), a kinship group or client clan (khawal) settled in al-Yamāma; the word functions strictly as a proper noun and carries no physical or sensory meaning beyond this referential use.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested. The term remains confined to onomastic and genealogical usage; any figurative application would be extra-lexical and unsupported by the classical authorities.

canonical_definition.arabic: بنو سَعْفوق: خَوَلٌ باليمامة، وبعضهم يقول سُعْفوق بالضم؛ وهو الحرف النادر الذي جاء على فُعْلول بفتح أوله، خلافاً لاطّراد الضم في زُنْبور وبُهْلول وعُمْروس.
canonical_definition.english: Banū Saʿfūq: a client clan (khawal) in al-Yamāma; some vocalize it Suʿfūq with ḍammah. It is the anomalous instance of the fuʿlūl pattern with an initial fatḥah, contrary to the regular ḍamm-initial formation seen in zunbūr, buhlūl, and ʿumrūs.

derivations.english_translation: Saʿfūq: a tribal name of a clan in al-Yamāma; anomalous in retaining initial fatḥah on a fuʿlūl pattern otherwise uniformly ḍamm-initial.
Suʿfūq: variant vocalization of the same tribal name, conforming to the regular ḍamm-initial fuʿlūl pattern.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes elongation and extension in bodily stature, with the quadrilateral structure (س-ق-ع-ب) suggesting an emphatic, intensive quality of tallness in the human frame.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a tall man, specifically one of pronounced height and extended frame; the root is attested with both س (sīn) and ص (ṣād) as the initial radical.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; no established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extensions are recorded in the classical lexical tradition. The term remains confined to its literal physical denotation of human stature.

canonical_definition.arabic: السَّقْعَبُ: الطَّوِيلُ مِنَ الرِّجَالِ، بِالسِّينِ وَالصَّادِ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-saqʿab: the tall one among men, attested with both sīn and ṣād.

derivations.english_translation: a tall man; one of pronounced height
a tall man (variant with ṣād as initial radical)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the emission of excrement by a bird, specifically the act of voiding droppings; it denotes a concrete, low-register physical event before any figurative extension.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (as delineated from Lisān al-ʿArab) is: a bird's defecation, i.e., the act of a sparrow or bird excreting its droppings.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic usages: The root is extended to human behavior in the form السُّقُق (al-suquq), meaning 'backbiters' or 'slanderers'—those who emit verbal filth analogous to a bird's droppings. This is a majāz based on the resemblance between noxious speech and physical excrement. Theologically, the root is not used for divine attributes; it remains confined to creaturely, base actions.

canonical_definition.arabic: سَقَّ العصفورُ وسَقْسَقَ الطائرُ: ذَرَقَ. والسُّقُق: المغتابون.
canonical_definition.english: The sparrow defecated and the bird voided droppings. And al-suquq: the backbiters.

derivations.english_translation: he defecated (of a bird); he voided excrement
he defecated (of a bird); he voided droppings
backbiters, slanderers (those who emit verbal filth)

record.ontological_core: The root denotes the physical state of a body reduced to skin and bone through emaciation, and by extension the deliberate act of subjecting an animal to such wasting in order to condition and slim it.
record.haqiqah_literal: The quadriliteral noun السِّلْقِد designates a person or animal that is lean, wasted, and emaciated; the verb أَسْلْقَدَ denotes the transitive act of rendering a horse lean and thin, i.e. putting it through a conditioning regimen of deliberate emaciation.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to its concrete physiological sense of emaciation and deliberate slimming. Any extended application to moral or spiritual attenuation would be an idiosyncratic modern extension, not a classical majāz.

canonical_definition.arabic: السِّلْقِدُ: الضَّاوِي المَهْزُولُ؛ ومنه: خَرَجْتُ أُسَلْقِدُ فَرَسِي، أَيْ أُضَمِّرُهُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Silqid: the lean, emaciated one; hence the expression 'I went out to slim my horse,' that is, to put it through a conditioning regimen of deliberate emaciation.

derivations.english_translation: a lean, emaciated person or animal; one reduced to skin and bone
to render lean, to emaciate; to condition a horse by deliberate slimming
he renders lean, he emaciates; he conditions by slimming
rendered lean, emaciated; subjected to a slimming regimen

record.ontological_core: The root denotes extension in length and elongation of bodily frame; its foundational physical origin is the quality of being drawn out or stretched in stature.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is 'tall' or 'long' with respect to bodily stature; it is used of a person or creature whose frame is elongated.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; no established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded in the classical lexical tradition. The term remains confined to the literal physical description of height.

canonical_definition.arabic: السَّلْهَجُ: الطويل.
canonical_definition.english: Al-salhaj: the tall one.

derivations.english_translation: tall, elongated in stature

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a legendary creature—avian or reptilian—endowed with the property of self-renewal through fire: when its generative capacity ceases and it succumbs to senescence, it casts itself into live embers and is restored to youthful vigor, remaining incombustible.
record.haqiqah_literal: A bird (ṭāʾir) that, upon the cessation of its progeny and the onset of decrepitude, throws itself into burning coals and thereby returns to its youthful state; alternatively, a creature (dābba) that enters fire without being consumed by it.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, the term is applied to any entity or process characterized by cyclical regeneration through destructive transformation—philosophically, the self-renewing intellect or soul that passes through the fire of material dissolution and emerges rejuvenated; in theological and mystical discourse, it figures the resurrection of the body and the purgative trial by fire that precedes renewal. The creature's incombustibility serves as a topos for essential incorruptibility amid accidental corruption.

canonical_definition.arabic: السَّمَنْدَلُ: طائرٌ إِذا انقطع نَسْلُهُ وهَرِمَ أَلْقى نفسه في الجَمْر فيعود إِلى شَبابه، وقيل: دابَّةٌ يدخل النار فلا تُحْرِقه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-samandal: a bird that, when its progeny ceases and it becomes decrepit, casts itself into live embers and returns to its youth; alternatively, a creature that enters fire and is not burned by it.

derivations.english_translation: the fire-renewing bird or creature; the salamander-like being that regenerates in fire

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root س-ن-ب-ل is the emergence of the ear or spike of grain (the seed-bearing head) from the stalk of a cereal plant, marking the plant's transition from vegetative growth to reproductive fruiting.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the ear or spike of grain (سُنْبُل), the compact, seed-bearing head of cereals such as wheat, barley, and maize; its singular unit is سُنْبُلَة (one ear/spike). The verb سَنْبَلَ denotes the plant's act of producing or putting forth its ear.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, later scholastic and poetic usage extends the term metaphorically to any clustered, grain-like arrangement—such as the ear-like clusters of a beard, the beaded tip of a sword, or the ornamental spike of a lamp—by analogy to the compact, aligned, seed-bearing structure of a cereal ear. In theological and philosophical discourse, the term remains strictly botanical and is not employed as a technical concept.

canonical_definition.arabic: السُّنْبُلُ من الزَّرْعِ واحدته سُنْبُلَةٌ، وقد سَنْبَلَ الزَّرْعُ إِذا خرج سُنْبُلُهُ.
canonical_definition.english: The ear of grain (سُنْبُل) is a unit of cereal crops, its singular being سُنْبُلَة; the verb سَنْبَلَ means the crop has produced its ear.

derivations.english_translation: to put forth ears (of grain); to ear
ear of grain; spike (collective)
a single ear of grain; one spike
ears of grain (plural)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root سنن is the tooth (al-sinn) as a hard, projecting, pointed structure—an instrument of cutting, grinding, and piercing—from which derive the senses of sharpening, pointing, flowing smoothly, and establishing a continuous, well-trodden path or normative practice.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah centers on the tooth (al-sinn) and its concrete derivatives: the sharpening of iron (sanna al-ḥadīda), the easy pouring of water (sanna al-māʾa ʿalā wajhihi), the smooth, swift movement of a horse (istanna al-faras), and the clear, beaten track of a road (sunan al-ṭarīq).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic usages include: (1) the establishment of a normative practice or precedent (sanna sunnatan ḥasanatan), (2) following a prophetic or authoritative model (istanna bi-sunnatihi), (3) the pursuit of a course or direction (iltazama sunana al-ṭarīq), (4) the agitated, energetic charging of a horse (istanna al-faras), and (5) the theological and legal concept of Sunna as the divinely guided way, encompassing both prophetic practice and the normative tradition of the community.

canonical_definition.arabic: السِّنُّ: واحدة الأَسنان، وهي الضِّرْسُ، أُنْثَى. والسُّنَّةُ: الطريقةُ والسيرةُ، حسنةً كانت أو قبيحةً. وسَنَّ الماءَ على وجهه: صبَّه صبًّا سهلاً. وسَنَّ الحديدةَ: حدَّدها.
canonical_definition.english: Al-sinn: the singular of teeth, namely a molar tooth, feminine. Al-sunna: a path or mode of conduct, whether good or evil. Sanna al-māʾa ʿalā wajhihi: he poured the water out smoothly. Sanna al-ḥadīda: he sharpened the iron.

derivations.english_translation: to sharpen, to point, to establish or institute (a practice), to pour out smoothly
tooth; age (as measured by teeth); a sharp point or edge
a normative practice, a precedent, a way of acting; the Sunna (prophetic tradition)
a path, a course, a way; a continuous flow
to prescribe, to legislate, to make into a norm
to follow a precedent, to adopt a practice; to move briskly (as a horse)
one who follows the Sunna, a practitioner of the normative way
spearhead, point of a weapon

mufradat.text: السن معروف، وجمعه أسنان. قال: والسن بالسن [المائدة/ 45]، وسان البعير الناقة: عاضها حتى أبركها، والسنون: دواء يعالج به الأسنان، وسن الحديد: إسالته وتحديده، والمسن: ما يسن به، أي: يحدد به، والسنان يختص بما يركب في رأس الرمح، وسننت البعير: صقلته، وضمرته تشبيها بسن الحديد، وباعتبار الإسالة قيل: سننت الماء، أي: أسلته. وتنح عن سنن الطريق، وسننه وسننه، فالسنن: جمع سنة، وسنة الوجه: طريقته، وسنة النبي: طريقته التي كان يتحراها، وسنة الله تعالى: قد تقال لطريقة حكمته، وطريقة طاعته، نحو: سنة الله التي قد خلت من قبل ولن تجد لسنة الله تبديلا [الفتح/ 23]، ولن تجد لسنت الله تحويلا [فاطر/ 43]، فتنبيه أن فروع الشرائع- وإن اختلفت صورها- فالغرض المقصود منها لا يختلف ولا يتبدل، وهو تطهير النفس، وترشيحها للوصول إلى ثواب الله تعالى وجواره، وقوله: من حمإ مسنون* [الحجر/ 26]، قيل: متغير، وقوله: لم يتسنه [البقرة/ 259]، معناه: لم يتغير، والهاء للاستراحة (1).

entries.text: سن سنة حسنة: طرق طريقة حسنة، واستن بسنته، وفلان متسنن: عامل. بالسنة. والزم سنن الطريق: قصده، وتنح عن سنن الخيل، واكتن عن سنن الريح. وجاء من الخيل سنن ما يرد. ورأيت سنن بني فلان: إبلهم المستنة نشاطا. قال: ومنا عصبة أخرى سراع ... زفتها الريح كالسنن الطراب واستن الفرس وهو عدوه إقبال

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is not attested as an independent verbal root in the classical lexica; its primary lexical datum is the toponym سُوَان (Suwān), a place-name. A secondary, dialectal usage is التَّسَوُّن (tasuwwun), denoting a slackening or relaxation of the belly, which Ibn Manẓūr and Abū Manṣūr relate to the root س و ل (s-w-l) through the substitution of the final lām with nūn.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is twofold: (1) سُوَان, a specific place-name; (2) التَّسَوُّن, the slackening or relaxation of the belly, as transmitted from Ibn al-Aʿrābī.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical sources. The term remains confined to toponymy and a dialectal physiological description; any extended application would be extra-lexical and unsupported by the philological tradition.

canonical_definition.arabic: سُوَانُ: موضع. والتَّسَوُّنُ: استرخاء البطن، كأَنه من التَّسَوُّل من سَوِلَ يَسْوَلُ إذا استرخى، فأُبدلت اللام نوناً.
canonical_definition.english: Suwān: a place-name. Al-tasuwwun: the slackening of the belly, as if derived from al-tasawwul from sawila yaswalu, meaning 'to become slack,' with the lām substituted by nūn.

derivations.english_translation: Suwān: a place-name
the slackening or relaxation of the belly

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ش-ب-ث is the act of clinging, adhering, or becoming physically attached to an object, such that it is seized and held fast. The root denotes a concrete, tactile grasping or entanglement—a thing becoming caught upon or fastened to another.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is: to cling to something, to hold fast to it, and to become attached to it. The phrase تشبث به (tashabbatha bihi) denotes direct, physical clinging or adherence. The related form شابثه (shābathahu) indicates mutual clinging or grappling. The noun شبث (shabath) and its plural شبثان (shubthān) refer to a thing that clings or is clung to, with the image of فرنده مدارج شبثان (faranduhu madārij shubthān)—its edge or fringe being like the winding paths of clinging things—evoking a concrete, physical entanglement.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root extends from physical clinging to intellectual and psychological attachment. Ibn al-Aʿrābī's statement ما أَدْري مِن أَين شَبِثْتُها (I do not know from where I seized it) employs the root to denote the grasping of a poetic verse or idea—an intellectual apprehension and retention. Similarly, التَّشَبُّثُ بالشيء (al-tashabbuthu bi-l-shayʾ) is used for emotional or conceptual attachment to a thing, and التَّثَبُّتُ (al-tathabbuth) is glossed as التَعَلُّق (al-taʿalluq), i.e., attachment or dependence. The root thus moves from the physical clinging of bodies to the mental clinging of concepts, memories, and affections, and further to the theological notion of the soul's attachment to worldly things or to the divine.

canonical_definition.arabic: شَبِثَ الشيءَ: عَلِقَه وأَخذه. والتَّشَبُّثُ بالشيء: التَّعَلُّق به. والتَّثَبُّتُ: التَّعَلُّق.
canonical_definition.english: He clung to the thing: he became attached to it and took hold of it. Clinging to a thing is attachment to it. And attachment is clinging.

derivations.english_translation: He clung to it, held fast to it, seized it
He caused to cling, made to adhere
He clung, adhered, attached himself
He clung to mutually, grappled with
Clinging, adherence, attachment
A thing that clings or is clung to
Clinging things, entangled matters (plural of شَبَث)

entries.text: تشبث به، وشابثه. وكأن فرنده مدارج شبثان وهو جمع شبث.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) denotes coarse, thick, and densely compacted bodily tissue — specifically the flesh of the fingers, hands, and feet — characterized by roughness of texture and a knotted, interlocking mass. The primary sensory image is that of a limb whose flesh is not smooth or supple but hard, rough, and closely packed.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in Lisān al-ʿArab, is a man whose fingers are thick and rough (شَثْل الأَصابع: غليظُها خَشِنُها), and a foot that is thick-fleshed and densely compacted (قَدَمٌ شَثْلةٌ: غليظةُ اللحم مُتَراكِبةٌ). The verb شَثِلَتْ يَدُهُ ورِجْلُهُ describes the hand or foot becoming thus thick, rough, and densely fleshed.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested in the classical lexicographical tradition. The root remains confined to the concrete, sensory domain of bodily texture. Ibn Manẓūr records the view of Yaʿqūb and Abū ʿUbayd that the final radical lām is a substitute (badal) for the nūn of شَثْن, making شَثْل a dialectal variant (lughah) of شَثْن, as explicitly stated by Ibn al-Sikkīt. This substitution is phonological, not semantic; it does not generate a distinct majāz. The root therefore possesses no scholastic or abstract application in the classical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: رجل شَثْل الأَصابع: غليظُها خَشِنُها. وقَدَمٌ شَثْلةٌ: غليظةُ اللحم مُتَراكِبةٌ. والشَّثْل لغة في الشَّثْن.
canonical_definition.english: A man with thick and rough fingers. And a foot that is thick-fleshed and densely compacted. And shathl is a dialectal variant of shathn.

derivations.english_translation: to become thick, rough, and densely fleshed (said of the hand or foot)
thick and rough (said of fingers); a dialectal variant of شَثْن
a foot that is thick-fleshed and densely compacted (qualifying a feminine noun such as قَدَم)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the concrete bodily constitution of a camel: bulk, mass, and elongation of the neck, i.e., a large-bodied, long-necked animal.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a bulky, long-necked camel; the plural شَرانِيصُ denotes camels of this description.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexical tradition; the term remains confined to the concrete zoological/physical description of camels.

canonical_definition.arabic: الليث: جمل شِرْناصٌ ضَخْم طويل العنق، وجمعه شَرانِيصُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Layth said: a shirnāṣ camel is bulky and long-necked; its plural is sharānīṣ.

derivations.english_translation: a bulky, long-necked camel
bulky, long-necked camels (plural)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the reciprocal transaction of exchange: the transfer of a commodity against a price, such that one party surrenders the object and receives the price while the other surrenders the price and receives the object. The root's primary semantic nucleus is the act of exchanging one entity for another, whether by sale or purchase.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the act of buying and selling, i.e., the exchange of a commodity for a price. In this literal sense, the buyer (al-mushtarī) pays the price and takes the commodity, while the seller (al-bāʾiʿ) delivers the commodity and takes the price. When the exchange is barter (commodity for commodity), each party can simultaneously be characterized as buyer and seller. The verb sharanī can mean either 'he bought from me' or 'he sold to me' depending on context, though shara (شَرَى) is more commonly used for 'he sold' and ibtāʿa (اِبْتَاعَ) for 'he bought'.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and theological usages extend the exchange paradigm to non-commercial domains: (1) In the Qurʾān, 'purchasing' (ishtarā) is used for the exchange of one's life, faith, or covenant for divine pleasure or worldly gain, e.g., 'Who sells his life seeking the pleasure of God' (Q 2:207), 'They sell the life of this world for the Hereafter' (Q 4:74), 'Those who purchase a small gain at the cost of God's covenant' (Q 3:77). (2) The root is applied to any acquisition or exchange of intangible goods, such as guidance for error, or punishment for forgiveness. (3) In scholastic theology, the metaphor conveys the deliberate transaction of one's ultimate allegiance, whether to God or to worldly interests, emphasizing volitional exchange and moral accountability.

canonical_definition.arabic: شَرَى الشيءَ يَشْرِيه شِرًى وشِرَاءً واشْتَرَاهُ سَوَاءٌ، وشَرَاهُ واشْتَرَاهُ: بَاعَهُ. والشراء والبيع يتلازمان، فالمشتري دافع الثمن وآخذ المثمن، والبائع دافع المثمن وآخذ الثمن.
canonical_definition.english: Shara al-shayʾa yashrīhi shiran wa-shirāʾan wa-ishtarāhu are equivalent; and sharāhu wa-ishtarāhu means 'he sold it.' Buying and selling are correlative: the buyer pays the price and takes the commodity, while the seller delivers the commodity and takes the price.

mufradat.text: الشراء والبيع يتلازمان، فالمشتري دافع الثمن، وآخذ المثمن، والبائع دافع المثمن، وآخذ الثمن. هذا إذا كانت المبايعة والمشاراة بناض وسلعة، فأما إذا كانت بيع سلعة بسلعة صح أن يتصور كل واحد منهما مشتريا وبائعا، ومن هذا الوجه صار لفظ البيع والشراء يستعمل كل واحد منهما في موضع الآخر. وشريت بمعنى بعت أكثر، وابتعت بمعنى اشتريت أكثر، قال الله تعالى: وشروه بثمن بخس [يوسف/ 20]، أي: باعوه، وكذلك قوله: يشرون الحياة الدنيا بالآخرة [النساء/ 74]، وتجوز بالشراء والاشتراء في كل ما يحصل به شيء، نحو: إن الذين يشترون بعهد الله [آل عمران/ 77]، لا يشترون بآيات الله [آل عمران/ 199]، اشتروا الحياة الدنيا [البقرة/ 86]، أولئك الذين اشتروا الضلالة بالهدى* [البقرة/ 16]، وقوله: إن الله اشترى من المؤمنين [التوبة/ 111]، فقد ذكر ما اشتري به، وهو قوله: يقاتلون في سبيل الله فيقتلون [التوبة/ 111]. ويسمى الخوارج بالشراة متأولين فيه قوله تعالى: ومن الناس من يشري نفسه ابتغاء مرضات الله [البقرة/ 207]، فمعنى «يشري»: يبيع، فصار ذلك كقوله: إن الله اشترى ... الآية [التوبة/ 111].

record.ontological_core: A marginal, quasi-nominal root attested only through the lexicographical report of Thaʿlab from Ibn al-Aʿrābī; its foundational physical referent is the shīṣ, the dry, hard, unpalatable date that remains on the palm cluster after the choice fruit has been taken.
record.haqiqah_literal: The concrete, literal sense is the شِيص: the inferior, dried, inedible dates left behind on the raceme, i.e., the residual fruit of poor quality.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is classically attested. The root is confined to the concrete horticultural domain and carries no abstract or scholastic application in the major lexica.

canonical_definition.arabic: الشَّشا: الشِّيصُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-shashā: the shīṣ, i.e., the dry, inferior dates remaining on the raceme.

derivations.english_translation: the dry, inferior dates left on the cluster; the shīṣ

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is spatial and relational estrangement: to be far removed, distant, or remote. This is exemplified by the long, tightly twisted rope (شَطَن) used to draw water from a deep well or to tether a horse, and by the deep well (بئر شطون) whose bottom is far from its mouth. A secondary, disputed origin is combustion (شاط يشيط): to burn with rage, from which the Satanic being is said to be created from fire.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the long, strong, tightly twisted rope used for drawing water or tethering an animal; a deep well (بئر شطون); a distant house (شطنت الدار); and a far-reaching journey or estrangement (غربة شطون). It also denotes the physical act of a horse resisting and being bound with two ropes from opposite sides (لينزو بين شطنين).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical, philosophical, and theological usages: (1) The being known as al-Shayṭān, whether from the root meaning 'to be distant' (from divine mercy) or from 'to burn' (with rage), created from fire, characterized by extreme irascible power and blameworthy zeal, who refused to prostrate to Adam. (2) Any rebellious, insolent being among jinn, humans, or animals (as per Abū ʿUbayda). (3) The human associates or leaders of evil (شياطين الإنس والجن). (4) The act of behaving in a devilish, rebellious, or insolent manner (تشيطن، فيه شيطنة). (5) The intense, uncontrollable restlessness of a horse compared to a devil (كأنه شيطان).

canonical_definition.arabic: الشَّطَنُ: الحَبْلُ الطَّوِيلُ الشَّدِيدُ الفَتْلِ يُسْتَقى به وتُشَدُّ به الخَيْلُ، والجمع أَشْطان. وشَطَنَتِ الدارُ: بَعُدَتْ. والشَّيْطانُ: اسمٌ لكلِّ عارِمٍ من الجِنِّ والإِنْسِ والحيواناتِ، وقيل: هو من شَطَنَ أَي تَباعَدَ، وقيل: من شاطَ يَشيطُ احْتَرَقَ غَضَباً.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Shāṭan: the long, tightly twisted rope used for drawing water and tethering horses; plural: ashṭān. The house shāṭanat: it became distant. Al-Shayṭān: a name for every rebellious, insolent being among jinn, humans, and animals. It is said to derive from shaṭana, meaning 'to be distant,' or from shāṭa yashīṭu, meaning 'to burn with rage.'

mufradat.text: الشيطان النون فيه أصلية (3)، وهو من: شطن أي: تباعد، ومنه: بئر شطون، وشطنت الدار، وغربة شطون، وقيل: بل النون فيه زائدة، من: شاط يشيط: احترق غضبا، فالشيطان مخلوق من النار كما دل عليه قوله تعالى: وخلق الجان من مارج من نار [الرحمن/ 15]، ولكونه من ذلك اختص بفرط القوة الغضبية والحمية الذميمة، وامتنع من السجود لآدم، قال أبو عبيدة (4): الشيطان اسم لكل عارم من الجن والإنس والحيوانات. قال تعالى: شياطين الإنس والجن [الأنعام/ 112]، وقال: وإن الشياطين ليوحون إلى أوليائهم [الأنعام/ 121]، وإذا خلوا إلى شياطينهم [البقرة/ 14]، أي: أصحابهم من الجن والإنس، وقوله: كأنه رؤس الشياطين [الصافات/ 65]، قيل: هي حية خفيفة الجسم، وقيل: أراد به عارم الجن، فتشبه به لقبح تصورها، وقوله: واتبعوا ما تتلوا الشياطين [البقرة/ 102]، فهم مردة الجن، ويصح أن يكونوا هم مردة الإنس أيضا، وقال الشاعر: 268- لو أن شيطان الذئاب العسل (5) جمع العاسل، وهو الذي يضطرب في وفيمن أقام من الحي هر وفي من أقام من الحي هر أم الظاعنون بها في الشطر عدوه، واختص به عسلان الذئب. وقال آخر: 269- ما ليلة الفقير إلا شيطان (1) وسمي كل خلق ذميم للإنسان شيطانا، فقال (عليه السلام): «الحسد شيطان والغضب شيطان» (2)

entries.text: بئر شطون: بعيدة القعر. وركبه شيطانه إذا غضب. وعن أبي الوجيه العكلي: كان ذلك حين ركبني شيطاني، قيل: وأي الشياطين تعني؟ قال: الغضب. قال منظور ابن رواحة: ولما أتاني ما يقول ترقصت ... شياطين رأسي وانتشين من الخمر وقال ابن ميادة: فلما أتاني ما تقول محارب ... بعثت شياطيني وجن جنونها ون

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the opening of a small water-skin (shakwah) to expose its contents; this concrete image of revealing what is contained within a vessel underlies all subsequent usage.
record.haqiqah_literal: To disclose or expose one's inner distress or grievance; literally, to open a small water-skin and reveal what it holds.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and theological applications: (1) To complain or lament before God, as in 'I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah' (Q 12:86) and 'She complains to Allah' (Q 58:1); (2) To cause someone to complain, i.e., to give them reason for complaint (ashkāhu); (3) To remove someone's complaint or grievance (ashkāhu); (4) The niche (mishkāt) as a non-piercing lamp recess, symbolizing the heart that contains the light of God (Q 24:35).

canonical_definition.arabic: الشَّكْوُ والشَّكَايَةُ والشَّكَاةُ والشَّكْوَى: إظهارُ البَثِّ. وأصلُ الشَّكْوِ: فَتْحُ الشَّكْوَةِ وإظهارُ ما فيها، وهي سِقاءٌ صغيرٌ يُجعل فيه الماءُ. والمِشْكَاةُ: كُوَّةٌ غيرُ نافذةٍ.
canonical_definition.english: Complaint, grievance, and lamentation: the disclosure of inner distress. The root origin of complaint is the opening of a small water-skin and the exposure of its contents; it is a small vessel used for water. The mishkāt is a non-piercing niche.

mufradat.text: الشكو والشكاية والشكاة والشكوى: إظهار البث، يقال: شكوت واشتكيت (3)، قال تعالى: إنما أشكوا بثي وحزني إلى الله [يوسف/ 86]، وقال: وتشتكي إلى الله [المجادلة/ 1]، وأشكاه أي: يجعل له شكوى، نحو: أمرضه، ويقال: أشكاه أي: أزال شكايته، وروي: «شكونا إلى رسول الله (صلى الله عليه وسلم آله) حر الرمضاء في جباهنا وأكفنا فلم يشكنا» (4) . وأصل الشكو فتح الشكوة وإظهار ما فيه، وهي: سقاء صغير يجعل فيه الماء، وكأنه في الأصل استعارة، كقولهم: بثثت له ما في وعائي، ونفضت ما في جرابي (5): إذا أظهرت ما في قلبك. والمشكاة: كوة غير نافذة. قال تعالى: كمشكاة فيها مصباح [النور/ 35]، وذلك مثل القلب، والمصباح مثل نور الله فيه.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the soul's innate inclination and appetitive pull toward what it desires, rooted in the body's need for what sustains it.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the soul's appetitive inclination toward an object of desire, specifically the bodily need for what is indispensable to health, such as the craving for food when hungry.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, it denotes the appetitive faculty itself; it is divided into true desire (what the body requires) and false desire (what is superfluous). It is applied to the eschatological reward of the Garden, where believers obtain whatever their souls desire, and to blameworthy worldly cravings that lead to transgression.

canonical_definition.arabic: أصل الشهوة: نزوع النفس إلى ما تريده، وذلك في الدنيا ضربان: صادقة، وكاذبة، فالصادقة: ما يختل البدن من دونه كشهوة الطعام عند الجوع، والكاذبة: ما لا يختل من دونه.
canonical_definition.english: The root of shahwa is the soul's appetitive inclination toward what it desires. In this world it is of two kinds: true and false. The true is what the body would be impaired without, such as the craving for food when hungry; the false is what the body would not be impaired without.

mufradat.text: أصل الشهوة: نزوع النفس إلى ما تريده، وذلك في الدنيا ضربان: صادقة، وكاذبة، فالصادقة: ما يختل البدن من دونه كشهوة الطعام عند الجوع، والكاذبة: ما لا يختل من دونه، وقد يسمى المشتهى شهوة، وقد يقال للقوة التي تشتهي الشيء: شهوة، وقوله تعالى: زين للناس حب الشهوات [آل عمران/ 14]، يحتمل الشهوتين، وقوله: اتبعوا الشهوات [مريم/ 59]، فهذا من الشهوات الكاذبة، ومن المشتهيات المستغنى عنها، وقوله في صفة الجنة: ولكم فيها ما تشتهي أنفسكم [فصلت/ 31]، وقوله: في ما اشتهت أنفسهم [الأنبياء/ 102]، وقيل: رجل شهوان، وشهواني، وشيء شهي.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root شور is the act of extracting, exposing, or bringing something hidden into plain view — most concretely, the extraction of honey from its hive (شَارَ العَسَلَ) and the exposure of goods or a beast for inspection and sale. From this primary sense of 'bringing forth what was concealed' radiate the derivative meanings of consultation (استشارة, as the eliciting of hidden opinion), the exposure of the body's private parts (شَوَار), and the display of a horse in a show-ring (مِشْوَار).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Asās al-Balāghah, is the extraction of honey from the hive (شَارَ العَسَلَ وَاشْتَارَهُ), and the leading forth of a riding beast or horse to be displayed and inspected for sale (شَرْتُ الدَّابَّةَ وَشَوَّرْتُهَا: عَرَضْتُهَا لِلْبَيْعِ). It also denotes the place or act of such display, the مِشْوَار (show-ring, parade ground), and the visible goods or wares (الشَّوَار: مَا يَبْدُو مِنَ الْمَتَاع).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to: (1) Consultation and counsel (شَاوَرَهُ، اسْتَشَارَهُ، تَشَاوَرُوا، اشتوروا) — the eliciting of a hidden opinion, as if extracting honey from its receptacle; the Quranic principle of شُورَى (mutual consultation) and the phrase وَأَمْرُهُمْ شُورَىٰ بَيْنَهُمْ derive from this. (2) The exposure of one's private parts (شَوَار, عَوْرَة) — as in the curse 'أَبْدَى اللهُ شَوَارَكَ' (May God expose your shame), and the proverbial 'أَشْوَارُ عَرُوسٍ تُرَى' (the bride's adornments are displayed to be seen). (3) The testing or probing of a horse's gait and character (شَوَّرَهَا يَنْظُرُ كَيْفَ مِشْوَارُهَا) — hence 'فَرَسٌ حَسَنُ الْمِشْوَارِ' (a horse of fine show and gait). (4) The indication or gesture (الإِشَارَة) — a pointing that reveals meaning without speech, and by extension 'رَجُلٌ حَسَنُ الشَّارَةِ' (a man of fine appearance and bearing). (5) In the Ḥadīth of al-Zabāʾ, the display of a bride's ornaments. The theological usage in 'أَبْدَى اللهُ شَوَارَكَ' is a curse invoking divine exposure of hidden shame, while the political-theological term شُورَى denotes the collective deliberation of the community in matters of governance, as when ʿUmar (رضي الله عنه) left the caliphate as a matter of شُورَى.

canonical_definition.arabic: شَارَ العَسَلَ يَشُورُهُ شَوْراً وَشِيَاراً وَشِيَارَةً وَمَشَاراً وَمَشَارَةً: اسْتَخْرَجَهُ مِنَ الوَقْبَةِ وَاحْتَنَاهُ. وَالشَّوَارُ: مَا يَبْدُو مِنَ الْمَتَاعِ، وَيُكْنَى بِهِ عَنِ الفَرْجِ. وَشَوَّرَ الدَّابَّةَ: عَرَضَهَا لِلْبَيْعِ. وَاسْتَشَارَهُ فَأَشَارَ عَلَيْهِ بِالصَّوَابِ، وَشَاوَرَهُ، وَتَشَاوَرُوا وَاشْتَوَرُوا. وَالشُّورَى: التَّشَاوُرُ.
canonical_definition.english: شَارَ العَسَلَ (he extracted the honey) — he drew it out from the hive and gathered it. الشَّوَار denotes visible goods or wares, and is used euphemistically for the private parts. شَوَّرَ الدَّابَّةَ means he displayed the beast for sale. اسْتَشَارَهُ فَأَشَارَ عَلَيْهِ بِالصَّوَابِ means he sought his counsel and he advised him correctly; likewise شَاوَرَهُ, and تَشَاوَرُوا / اشْتَوَرُوا (they consulted one another). الشُّورَى is the act of mutual consultation.

mufradat.text: الشوار: ما يبدو من المتاع، ويكنى به عن الفرج، كما يكنى به عن المتاع، وشورت به: فعلت به ما خجلته، كأنك أظهرت شوره، أي: فرجه، وشرت العسل وأشرته: أخرجته، قال الشاعر: 277- وحديث مثل ماذي مشار (3) وشرت الدابة: استخرجت عدوه تشبيها بسماع يأذن الشيخ له بذلك، وقيل: الخطب مشوار كثير العثار (1)، والتشاور والمشاورة والمشورة: استخراج الرأي بمراجعة البعض إلى البعض، من قولهم: شرت العسل: إذا اتخذته من موضعه، واستخرجته منه. قال الله تعالى: وشاورهم في الأمر [آل عمران/ 159]، والشورى: الأمر الذي يتشاور فيه. قال: وأمرهم شورى بينهم [الشورى/ 38].

Metaphorical (Majaz): الخطب مشوار، كثير العثار. واستشارت إبله: سمنت لأنه يشار إليها بالأصابع كأنها طلبت الإشارة. وفحل مستشير. قال ابن مقبل: غدت كالفنيق المستشير إ

شورت به فتشور، ومنه قيل: أبدى الله تعالى شوارك أي عورتك كما قيل: الحياء. وفي حديث الزباء: أشوار عروس ترى. وشرت الدابة وشورتها: عرضتها للبيع. ويقال: شورها تنظر كيف مشوارها أي اختبرها تعلم كيف سيرتها. وفرس حسن المشوار. قال جرير: طاح الفرزدق في الغبار وغمه ... غمر البديهة صادق المشو

الخطب مشوار، كثير العثار. واستشارت إبله: سمنت لأنه يشار إليها بالأصابع كأنها طلبت الإشارة. وفحل مستشير. قال ابن مقبل: غدت كالفنيق المستشير إذا غدا ... سما فثناها عن سنان فأرقلا من سان الناقة حتى نوخها أي تركها وجفر عنها.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root شوع is the dispersal, scattering, and unruly spreading of hair, such that individual strands separate and stand apart in a manner resembling thorns (شَوْك) — a condition of disheveled, bristling separation rather than smooth cohesion.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the spreading and dispersion of hair (انتشار الشعر وتفرقه), where the hair becomes disheveled and separates into distinct, thorn-like strands, particularly as manifest on the cheeks (خدّين) of a woman, producing a rough, unkempt texture.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, its literal sense of scattering and thorn-like separation may be extended metaphorically to any condition of disorderly dispersion or bristling irregularity, though no established scholastic or theological usage is recorded in the classical philological tradition.

canonical_definition.arabic: الشَّوَعُ: انْتِشارُ الشَّعر وتَفَرُّقُه كأَنَّه شَوْك
canonical_definition.english: Al-Shawaʿ: the spreading and dispersion of hair such that it resembles thorns.

derivations.english_translation: Disheveled spreading of hair; a scattering of hair resembling thorns
A woman whose hair is disheveled and spreading (as used in the poetic citation)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act denoted by the root is the excavation and turning over of earth—digging into the ground with a tool. The root's primary material instantiation is thus the manual labor of hollowing out soil, from which the instrumental noun for the digging implement is derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the act of digging or excavating the earth (ḥafr al-arḍ). The concrete instrument by which this action is performed is the مِصْخَفَة (miṣkhafah), a digging tool or hoe (misḥāh), a usage explicitly identified as Yemeni in provenance.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extensions are attested in the classical lexicographical tradition for this root. The root remains confined to its concrete, agricultural-artisanal semantic field; no abstract or scholastic applications (majāz) are recorded in Lisān al-ʿArab, al-Mufradāt, or Asās al-Balāghah.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصَّخْفُ: حَفْرُ الأَرْضِ. وَالمِصْخَفَةُ: المِسْحَاةُ، يَمَانِيَةٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṣakhf: the digging or excavation of the earth. And al-miṣkhafah: the hoe or digging tool, a Yemeni term.

derivations.english_translation: the act of digging or excavating the earth
a digging tool or hoe (misḥāh); a Yemeni term

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a traversed, extended path or roadway; its foundational physical image is a linear, beaten track that one follows toward a destination. Classical philologists note the phonological proximity of the voiceless alveolar sibilant /s/ and the emphatic alveolar sibilant /ṣ/, with the ṣād form being a dialectal or assimilated variant of the underlying sīn, owing to the adjacency of the emphatic ṭāʾ.
record.haqiqah_literal: A road, path, or way; specifically, a clear and straight thoroughfare that is physically traversed. The literal sense is attested in the paired forms al-ṣirāṭ and al-sirāṭ, both denoting a roadway.
record.majaz_scholastic: In theological and ethical discourse, the term is applied metaphorically to the straight path of truth, divine guidance, and prophetic law. The Qurʾānic phrase 'the straight path' (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) signifies the unswerving course of monotheism and righteous conduct, and the petition 'guide us to the straight path' is understood as a request for steadfastness in the apprehension and practice of revealed truth. The metaphor rests on the literal image of a road that leads reliably to its intended destination.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصراط: الطريق المستقيم. وقال الأزهري: وأصل صاده سين قلبت مع الطاء صاداً لقرب مخارجها. وقال الجوهري: الصراط والسراط.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṣirāṭ: the straight path. Al-Azharī said: the original of its ṣād is a sīn, which was changed to ṣād alongside the ṭāʾ due to the proximity of their points of articulation. Al-Jawharī said: al-ṣirāṭ and al-sirāṭ.

derivations.english_translation: a road, path, or way; the straight path (in Qurʾānic and theological usage)
a road, path, or way (dialectal variant with initial sīn)

mufradat.text: الصراط: الطريق المستقيم. قال تعالى: وأن هذا صراطي مستقيما [الأنعام/ 153]، ويقال له: سراط، وقد تقدم.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on firm adherence, cleaving, or persistent attachment to a thing, such that the subject remains bound or fastened to it.
record.haqiqah_literal: To cling to, adhere to, or persistently attach oneself to a thing; to remain fastened to it.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah. In scholastic or extended usage, the sense of adherence may be applied to moral or conceptual persistence, but no established philosophical or theological majāz is classically recorded for this root.

canonical_definition.arabic: صَكا إذا لزِمَ الشيءَ.
canonical_definition.english: He clung to the thing, adhered to it, or remained persistently attached to it.

derivations.english_translation: to cling to, adhere to, or persist in attachment to something

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the robust, mature, and powerful male camel, specifically denoting a stallion distinguished by advanced age, formidable strength, and imposing length; it is a quadriliteral root (rubāʿī) with no triliteral derivation, and its primary semantic nucleus is the concrete image of a mighty, seasoned beast of burden.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (inferred from Lisān al-ʿArab) is: a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a stallion of advanced age and great power; also used for a strong stallion, with the feminine form denoting a she-camel of similar qualities.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical, philosophical, and theological usages: Not attested in the classical lexicons for abstract or scholastic domains; the term remains confined to the concrete zoological sphere, with no extension to metaphysical, ethical, or theological concepts in the sources consulted.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصَّلْخَدُ والصِّلَخْدُ والصِّلْخَدُّ والصُّلَاخِدُ والصِّلْخَادُ والصَّلَخْدَى كله: الجمل المُسِنُّ الشَّديدُ الطَّويلُ، وقيل: هو الماضي من الإِبل، وقيل للفحْل الشديد صَلَخْدًى، بالتنوين، والأُنثى صَلَخْدَاةٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṣalkhad, al-ṣilakhd, al-ṣilkhadd, al-ṣulākhid, al-ṣilkhād, and al-ṣalakhdā all denote: a mature, strong, and tall male camel; it is also said to be a camel of advanced age and vigor; a strong stallion is called ṣalakhdā with tanwīn, and the feminine is ṣalakhdāh.

derivations.english_translation: a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a powerful stallion
a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a powerful stallion
a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a powerful stallion
a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a powerful stallion
a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a powerful stallion
a mature, strong, and tall male camel; a powerful stallion (also used with tanwīn for a strong stallion)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the she-camel as a lactational vessel, denoting an animal whose milk-yield is either scant or copious—an ontological polarity rooted in the concrete reality of pastoral husbandry and the biological economy of the herd.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah: a she-camel (nāqah) characterized by a specific quantity of milk, whether meager or abundant; by extension, the plural form denotes emaciated livestock, particularly sheep or goats, in their physical state of bodily wasting.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic application: the term is transposed from the domain of pastoral wealth to signify any entity or person reduced to a state of extreme leanness or depletion, functioning as a descriptor of physical attenuation and loss of substance. In philological usage, it may also serve as a morphological exemplar for the debate over the augmentative status of the medial mīm, a question of derivational economy rather than semantic extension.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصِّمْرِدُ، بالكسر، من الإِبل: الناقة القليلة اللبن؛ وقيل: الناقة الغَزيرة اللبن. والصَّمارِدُ: الغَنم المِهازِيل. والصَّمارِيدُ: الغنم.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ṣimrid, with the kasrah, among camels: a she-camel of scant milk; it is also said: a she-camel of abundant milk. Al-Ṣamārid: emaciated sheep. Al-Ṣamārīd: sheep.

derivations.english_translation: a she-camel with scant milk; (by extension) a lean, emaciated animal
emaciated sheep or goats; livestock reduced to leanness
emaciated livestock, especially sheep; a herd in a state of bodily wasting

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the melting and liquefying of fat (إذابة الشحم), from which flows the derived sense of a molten substance (صهارة) and, by extension, the dissolution of solidity through intense heat. From this concrete physical process, the root branches into the abstract domain of marital kinship, conceived as a bond that dissolves the boundaries between separate households and creates a new fused social entity.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of melting fat (صهر الشحم: أذابه), its liquefied product (صهارة: ذوبه), and the use of that molten fat as a condiment for bread (صهر الخبز: أدمه بها) or as an ointment for the head (صهر رأسه: دهنه بالصهارة). It also denotes the concrete kinship relation itself: a man's in-law (صهر) and the family into which one marries (أصهار).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root denotes the bond of marital kinship (حرمة الزواج) that unites families, as in the Qur'anic verse 'فجعله نسبا وصهرا' (Q 25:54), where 'صهر' signifies the affinal tie established by marriage. It extends to the state of being connected by marriage, lineage, or even neighborly protection (الإصهار: التحرم بجوار أو نسب أو تزوج). Theologically, the root is applied to the punishment of the damned in Q 22:20, 'يصهر به ما في بطونهم' — 'that which is in their bellies will be melted' — where the physical melting of fat becomes a metaphor for the dissolution of the body under divine chastisement. The phrase 'لأصهرنك بيمين مرة' (I will melt you with an oath once) further illustrates the metaphorical extension to the dissolution of a person's resolve or integrity through a solemn oath.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصَّهْرُ: القَرَابَةُ. والصِّهْرُ: حُرْمَةُ الخُتُونَةِ، وخَتَنُ الرَّجُلِ صِهْرُهُ، والمُتَزَوِّجُ فِيهِمْ أَصْهَارُ الخَتَنِ، والأَصْهَارُ أَهْلُ بَيْتِ المَرْأَةِ. والصَّهْرُ: إِذَابَةُ الشَّحْمِ. والصَّهَارَةُ: مَا ذَابَ مِنْهُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṣahr is kinship. Al-ṣihr is the sacred bond of affinal relation; a man's in-law is his ṣihr, and those who marry into a family are the aṣhār of the in-law. The aṣhār are the family of the wife. Al-ṣahr is the melting of fat, and al-ṣahārah is that which melts from it.

derivations.english_translation: to melt, to liquefy (fat); to render (fat)
affinal kinship; in-law; the bond of marriage
a molten substance; liquefied fat
the liquefied residue of melted fat; molten matter
bread seasoned with molten fat; melted
to establish an affinal bond; to marry into a family
to intermarry with; to become an in-law to
one who is bound by marriage, lineage, or neighborly protection
in-laws; the family of one's spouse
a stand or rack for copper and brass vessels

mufradat.text: الصهر: الختن، وأهل بيت المرأة يقال لهم الأصهار، كذا قال الخليل (2). قال ابن الأعرابي: الإصهار: التحرم بجوار، أو نسب، أو تزوج، يقال: رجل مصهر: إذا كان له تحرم من ذلك. قال تعالى: فجعله نسبا وصهرا [الفرقان/ 54]، والصهر: إذابة الشحم. قال تعالى: يصهر به ما في بطونهم [الحج/ 20]، والصهارة: ما ذاب منه، وقال أعرابي: لأصهرنك بيمين مرة (3)، أي: لأذيبنك.

entries.text: بينهم صهر وصهورة وهو حرمة الزواج. " فجعله نسبا وصهرا "، وفلان صهر فلان: لمن يتزوج إليه، وهم أصهار بني فلان: لأهل بيت من تزوج إليهم. وقد يقال Metaphorical (Majaz): أصهر الجيش للجيش إذا دنا له. وصهره الحر: اشتد عليه. وغط رأسك لا تصهره الشمس. واصطهر الحرباء. وصهرته الشمس. وما في البعير صهارة إذا لم يكن في

أصهر الجيش للجيش إذا دنا له. وصهره الحر: اشتد عليه. وغط رأسك لا تصهره الشمس. واصطهر الحرباء. وصهرته الشمس. وما في البعير صهارة إذا لم يكن فيه نقي ولا يستعمل إلا في النقي. وصهره باليمين صهرا إذا استحلفه على يمين شديدة، وهو مصهور باليمين، ولأصهرنك بيمين مرة.

بينهم صهر وصهورة وهو حرمة الزواج. " فجعله نسبا وصهرا "، وفلان صهر فلان: لمن يتزوج إليه، وهم أصهار بني فلان: لأهل بيت من تزوج إليهم. وقد يقال لأهل بيت الزوجين جميعا: هم أصهار. وقد يقال لأهل النسب والصهر جميعا: أصهار، وأصهرت إلى بني فلان وصاهرت إليهم إذا تزوجت إليهم، وأنا مصهر بهم.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes blackness or deep darkness, specifically the blackness of complexion; its foundational physical origin is the dark, lustrous hue of the female slaves (al-jawārī al-sūd) attested by Abū ʿAmr.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the black female slaves (al-jawārī al-sūd), i.e., women of dark complexion.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical or scholastic extension is attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to its literal physical reference to black female slaves.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصُّهْكُ: الجواري السُّودُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṣuhk: the black female slaves.

derivations.english_translation: black female slaves; women of dark complexion

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root ص-ي-ح is the emission of a loud, piercing sound, specifically a vocal cry that strains the utterer's maximum capacity. It denotes an intense auditory event, whether from a human, animal, or inanimate object, and by extension, the act of calling out to someone or something.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is to shout, cry out, or emit a loud sound with one's utmost effort. It also encompasses calling out to someone (صاح به) and the reciprocal act of shouting at one another (تصايحوا). Additionally, it is used literally for the splitting or cracking of objects like a garment or a stick (انصاح الثوب, انصاحت العصا).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root is applied to non-vocal entities, such as a palm tree or dates (صيحاني, صيحانية), which are named after a specific ram called صيحان, thus transferring the proper name to a botanical variety. The meaning of 'splitting' is extended to abstract disintegration or rupture. In theological and philosophical discourse, the term may be used to describe the 'crying out' of inanimate objects as a metaphor for their testimony or the manifestation of divine power, though such usage is rare and strictly metaphorical.

canonical_definition.arabic: الصِّيَاحُ: الصوتُ؛ صوتُ كل شيء إِذا اشتدّ. صاحَ يَصِيحُ صَيْحة وصِياحاً وصُياحاً، وصَيْحاً وصَيَحاناً، وصَيَّحَ: صَوَّتَ بأَقصى طاقته، يكون ذلك في الناس وغيرهم.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Ṣiyāḥ is sound; the sound of anything when it intensifies. Ṣāḥa yaṣīḥu (he shouted) yields the verbal noun ṣayḥah, ṣiyāḥ, ṣuyāḥ, ṣayḥ, and ṣayaḥān; and ṣayyaḥa means to vocalize with one's utmost capacity. This applies to humans and others.

derivations.english_translation: to shout, to cry out
a shout, a cry
a single shout, a cry
shouting, clamor
shouting, clamor
shouting, clamor
to shout vehemently
to shout at one another
