entries.text: صاح صيحة شديدة، وصاح به وصيح به وصايحه: ناداه، وضح لي بفلان: ادعه لي، وتصايحا: صاحوا، وتصايحوا: تداعوا. وتمر صيحاني، ونخلة صيحانية، قالوا: شد إلى نخلة كبش اسمه صيحان فنسبت إليه. وانصاح الثوب. وانصاحت العصا وتصيحت: تشققت.

صاح صيحة شديدة، وصاح به وصيح به وصايحه: ناداه، وضح لي بفلان: ادعه لي، وتصايحا: صاحوا، وتصايحوا: تداعوا. وتمر صيحاني، ونخلة صيحانية، قالوا: ش Metaphorical (Majaz): أتيته قبل كل صيح ونفر: قبل كل شيء. وغصب من غير صيح ونفر: من غير شيء. قال: كذوب محول يجعل الله عرضة ... لأيمانه من غير صيح ولا نفر وصاحت الشج

أتيته قبل كل صيح ونفر: قبل كل شيء. وغصب من غير صيح ونفر: من غير شيء. قال: كذوب محول يجعل الله عرضة ... لأيمانه من غير صيح ولا نفر وصاحت الشجرة: طالت، وبأرض بني فلان شجر قد صاح. وصاح الكافور إذا ظهر الطلع ونحوه كالكرم إذا نادى من الكافور. وقال الفرزدق: والشيب ينهض في الشباب كأنه .

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the notion of a hard, protective, or defensive structure — a fortified enclosure, a horn, a spur, or a hardened date-pit — that serves as a means of defense or resistance.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (as delineated via Lisān al-ʿArab) is: a fortress or stronghold; anything by which one fortifies oneself; specifically, the horn of a bull or the spur of a rooster; and in the dialect of Balḥārith ibn Kaʿb, the hardened, dry date-pit (ḥashaf).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical, philosophical, and theological usages: In the Qurʾānic verse 'and He brought down those of the People of the Book who supported them from their strongholds' (Q 33:26), 'ṣayāṣī' (pl. of ṣīṣah) denotes their fortresses and places of refuge. The term is extended to any means of self-protection or defense, including the horn of a bull and the spur of a rooster, as these are instruments of defense or combat. The root also appears in the context of date palms: 'aṣāṣat al-nakhlah' and 'ṣayyaṣat taṣyīṣan' mean the palm became 'shīṣ' (unripe or hardened dates), derived from ṣīṣ (hardened date-pit), not from ṣīṣāʾ (a different root).

canonical_definition.arabic: الصِّيصُ: الحَشَفُ من التمر، والصِّيصَةُ: الحصن، وكل ما يُتحصَّن به؛ وقيل لقرن البقر: صِيصَة، وللشوكة التي يقاتل بها الديك: صِيصَة.
canonical_definition.english: Ṣīṣ: the hardened, dry date-pit; ṣīṣah: a fortress, and anything by which one fortifies oneself; the horn of a bull is called ṣīṣah, and the spur with which a rooster fights is called ṣīṣah.

derivations.english_translation: to become hardened (as a date-pit); to fortify
to become shīṣ (hardened dates); to fortify
hardened date-pit; fortress
fortress, stronghold; horn; spur
fortresses, strongholds

mufradat.text: قوله تعالى: وأنزل الذين ظاهروهم من أهل الكتاب من صياصيهم [الأحزاب/ 26]، أي: حصونهم، وكل ما يتحصن به يقال له: صيصة، وبهذا النظر قيل لقرن البقر: صيصة، وللشوكة التي يقاتل بها الديك: صيصة، والله أعلم بمراده وأسرار كتابه. تم كتاب الصاد بتوفيق الله تعالى تحت العجاج وأخرى تعلك اللجما ||| كتاب الضاد بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم*، نستعين بالله تعالى، وهو خير معين، الحمد لله حق حمده، والصلاة على خير خلقه، ومظهر حقه محمد وآله وصحبه (1).

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root ضخخ is the forceful, extended emission of a liquid stream—specifically urine or water—from an orifice or conduit, characterized by propulsion and continuity rather than mere spillage.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the extension and projection of urine (امتداد البول), and by extension the forceful ejection of water through a tube or pipe; the instrument المضخة is a reed or tube containing a wooden rod used to expel water from the mouth.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is primarily concrete and hydraulic, it admits limited figurative extension to any forceful, directed emission or infusion of a substance, as in the phrase ضَخَّه ضَخّاً (he injected or infused it with water). No attested philosophical or theological abstraction is recorded in the classical lexica; the term remains rooted in physical propulsion and hydraulic mechanics.

canonical_definition.arabic: الضَّخُّ: امتداد البول. والمضخة: قصبة في جوفها خشبة يرمى بها الماء من الفم. والضخ مثل النضخ للماء؛ وقد ضَخَّه ضخّاً إِذا نضحه بالماء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḍakhkh: the extension and projection of urine. Al-miḍakhkhah: a reed or tube within which is a wooden rod, by means of which water is ejected from the mouth. Al-ḍakhkh is like al-naḍkh for water; one says ḍakhkhahu ḍakhkhan when he sprinkled or infused it with water.

derivations.english_translation: to eject or project a liquid forcefully; to spurt or gush
the act of forceful liquid emission; a spurt or gush
a tube or reed fitted with a wooden rod for expelling water; a primitive pump or syringe

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on a lush, verdant, well-watered meadow (rawḍah) that is fresh, tender, and free of blemish or decay—a self-contained, flourishing garden spot. The underlying sensory image is that of soft, moist, thriving herbage, from which the root's nominal form al-ḍaghīghah is derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Lisān al-ʿArab, is a fresh, blooming, unblemished meadow or garden (al-rawḍah al-nāḍirah al-mutakhalliyah), also called al-ḍaghīghah, al-marghadah, al-maghmaghah, al-makhjalah, al-marghah, and al-ḥadīqah. Abū Ḥanīfah reports the idiom: 'They are in a ḍaghīghah of the ḍaghāḍigh'—i.e., in a state of lush, abundant, and pleasant verdure.
record.majaz_scholastic: No attested metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded in the classical lexica for this root. The term remains confined to its concrete botanical and topographical sense. Any extended application—such as describing a person or community as being 'in a ḍaghīghah'—is idiomatic and rhetorical, signifying ease, prosperity, or luxuriant well-being, but it does not constitute a formal majāz in the scholastic or theological register.

canonical_definition.arabic: الضَّغِيغَةُ: الرَّوْضَةُ النَّاضِرَةُ المُتَخَلِّيَةُ. وَيُقَالُ: هُمْ فِي ضَغِيغَةٍ مِنَ الضَّغَاضِغِ إِذَا كَانُوا فِي رِيَاضٍ مُعْشِبَةٍ نَاعِمَةٍ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ḍaghīghah: a fresh, blooming, unblemished meadow. It is said: 'They are in a ḍaghīghah of the ḍaghāḍigh' when they are amid lush, tender, herbaceous gardens.

derivations.english_translation: A fresh, blooming, unblemished meadow or garden; a lush, well-watered herbage spot.
Plural of ḍaghīghah; lush meadows, verdant gardens (used in the idiom 'in a ḍaghīghah of the ḍaghāḍigh').

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ض-ف-ع is the emission of excrement or the act of defecation, specifically denoting the expulsion of waste from the body. It is a primary, concrete bodily function, with a variant root فضع carrying the same meaning.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of defecating or excreting, as in ضَفَعَ الرجلُ (the man defecated). It also extends to the emission of urine and dung, as in ضَفَعَ بِبَوْلِهِ وَسَلَحَ (he urinated and defecated).
record.majaz_scholastic: While the root is primarily literal and concrete, it may be used metaphorically in scholastic or theological contexts to denote the expulsion of waste or impurity, symbolizing moral or spiritual corruption. However, no attested majāz usage is recorded in the classical sources; the term remains within the domain of physical bodily functions.

canonical_definition.arabic: ضَفَعَ الرجلُ يَضْفَعُ ضَفْعاً: جَعَسَ وأَحْدَثَ، وقيل: أَبْدَى، وفَضَعَ لغة فيه. ويقال: ضَفَعَ وقَعَ بِبَوْلِه وسَلَحَ. وقال ابن الأَعرابي: نَجْوُ الفيل الضَّفْعُ.
canonical_definition.english: A man defecated, he excreted and produced waste; it is also said: he exposed [excrement]. فَضَعَ is a variant dialect form. It is said: he defecated, he urinated and defecated. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: The dung of the elephant is called al-ḍafʿ.

derivations.english_translation: he defecated, excreted
defecation, excrement (especially of an elephant)
he defecated (variant form)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is not attested in the classical lexical tradition as an independent primary root; it is identified by Ibn Manẓūr, on the authority of Thaʿlab from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, as a metathesized variant (maqlūb) of the root ضيم / ضام, whose concrete sense is to wrong, oppress, or diminish another's right.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is not established as an autonomous ḥaqīqah in Asās al-Balāghah; the form ضَمَى is recorded in Lisān al-ʿArab as a dialectal or transposed usage meaning 'he acted unjustly' (ظَلَمَ), standing in place of the standard ضَامَ.
record.majaz_scholastic: No distinct metaphorical or scholastic extension is attested for this root in the classical sources; its only recorded usage is the literal ethical-legal sense of wrongdoing, understood as a metathesis of ضامَ. The parallel cited by Abū Manṣūr, بَضَى as a transposition of بَاضَ, confirms that the phenomenon is phonological rearrangement rather than semantic figuration.

canonical_definition.arabic: ضَمَى إِذا ظَلَمَ، كأَنَّهُ مَقْلُوبٌ مِنْ ضَامَ.
canonical_definition.english: ḍamā means 'he acted unjustly'; it appears to be a metathesized form of ḍāma.

derivations.english_translation: he acted unjustly, he wronged (recorded as a metathesis of ضَامَ)
he stayed, he remained (cited as a metathesis of بَاضَ)

mufradat.text: الضم: الجمع بين الشيئين فصاعدا. قال تعالى: واضمم يدك إلى جناحك [طه/ 22]، واضمم إليك جناحك [القصص/ 32]، والإضمامة: جماعة من الناس أو من الكتب أو الريحان أو نحو ذلك (1)، وأسد ضمضم وضماضم: يضم الشيء إلى نفسه. وقيل: بل هو المجتمع الخلق، وفرس سباق الأضاميم: إذا سبق جماعة من الأفراس دفعة واحدة.

record.ontological_core: The root ضود is not attested as an independent lexical root in the classical philological tradition; the sequence ض و د appears in Lisān al-ʿArab only as an incidental collocation within the entry for the letter ḍād (ض), where the letter itself is treated as a phonological and orthographic primitive rather than as a semantic root. Its ontological core is therefore the consonantal letter ḍād as a majhūra (voiced) and mustaʿliya (elevated) Arabic phoneme, exclusive to Arabic speech.
record.haqiqah_literal: No literal physical meaning is established for ضود as a root in Asās al-Balāghah or in the classical lexical corpus; the only literal referent attested is the letter ḍād (ض) itself, described as a voiced, elevated Arabic consonant that functions as an aṣl (radical) and never as a badal (substitute) or zāʾid (augment).
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and philological usage, the discussion of ض is metaphorical or metalinguistic rather than semantic: the letter is said to be khāṣṣa li-l-ʿArab (peculiar to the Arabs), absent from non-Arab speech except rarely, and this exclusivity is cited in exegetical and rhetorical commentary, including on the verse of Abū al-Ṭayyib. No theological or philosophical majāz is attested for the sequence ضود as a root.

canonical_definition.arabic: الضاد حرف هجاء وهو حرف مَجْهُور، وهو أَحد الحروف المُسْتَعْلية، يكون أَصلاً لا بدلاً ولا زائداً، والضاد للعَرَب خاصة ولا توجد في كلام العجم إِلا في القليل.
canonical_definition.english: The ḍād is a letter of spelling; it is a voiced consonant and one of the elevated letters; it functions as a radical, not as a substitute or an augment; and the ḍād is peculiar to the Arabs, not occurring in non-Arab speech except rarely.

derivations.english_translation: not attested as a verbal root in the classical sources; the form is listed only as a hypothetical pattern
not attested as a nominal root in the classical sources; the form is listed only as a hypothetical pattern
not attested as a nominal root in the classical sources; the form is listed only as a hypothetical pattern

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in the classical lexicographical tradition as an independent radical cluster; Ibn Manẓūr records it only as a dialectal or orthographic variant of ضيم (ḍ-y-m), whose primary physical sense is the exertion of force or pressure upon a thing, resulting in injustice or wrong.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as recorded by Ibn Manẓūr, is the act of wronging or oppressing someone: ضُمْتُه, i.e., ظَلَمْتُه ('I wronged him'). This is treated as a variant of ضِمْتُه, with the same concrete sense of imposing an unjust burden or harm.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested for this root in the classical sources. Because the root is not an independent lexical entry in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, it carries no scholastic extension; any usage remains within the literal domain of injustice and oppression, and the form is best analyzed as a dialectal or orthographic reflex of ضيم.

canonical_definition.arabic: ضُمْتُه: كضِمْتُه، أَي ظَلَمْتُه.
canonical_definition.english: I wronged him: equivalent to ḍimtuhu, meaning I treated him unjustly.

derivations.english_translation: to wrong, to oppress, to treat unjustly
a wronging, an act of oppression (recorded as a variant of ضَيْم)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of overlaying, covering, or fitting one thing closely upon another, such that the two correspond and coincide — a concrete operation of physical matching and concealment.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is التَّطْبِيس (al-taṭbīs), the act of applying or fitting one thing over another (التَّطْبِيق), i.e., bringing two surfaces or entities into close correspondence and covering.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, the root is used in toponymic and geographic reference: الطَّبَسَان (al-Ṭabasān) designates two districts (kūratān) in Khurāsān, a usage that shifts from the concrete verbal sense of covering/fitting to a fixed proper name. No attested philosophical or theological metaphorical usage is recorded in the classical lexical sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: التَّطْبِيسُ: التَّطْبِيقُ. والطَّبَسَان: كُورَتَانِ بِخُرَاسَانَ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-taṭbīs is the act of fitting or overlaying (al-taṭbīq). And al-Ṭabasān refers to two districts in Khurāsān.

derivations.english_translation: The act of fitting, overlaying, or applying one thing upon another; correspondence
Al-Ṭabasān: two districts in Khurāsān (a dual proper name)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root طحا is the act of spreading something out flat and extending it outward, closely parallel to the root دحو; it denotes the expansive flattening and outward extension of a surface.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to spread out, flatten, and extend a thing outward upon a surface, as in the spreading of the earth.
record.majaz_scholastic: In theological and cosmological usage, the root is applied to God's act of spreading out the earth (وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا طَحَاهَا), signifying divine expansive creation and providential ordering of the terrestrial plane; the active participle الطَّاحِي denotes the one who spreads or extends, and by extension the overwhelming or dominant force that flattens opposition.

canonical_definition.arabic: الطَّحْوُ كالدَّحْوِ، وهو البَسْطُ، وفيه لغتان: طَحَا يَطْحُو وطَحَى يَطْحَى.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṭaḥw is like al-daḥw: it is the spreading out flat; it has two dialectal forms: ṭaḥā yaṭḥū and ṭaḥā yaṭḥā.

derivations.english_translation: he spread out, flattened, extended
he spread out, flattened (variant form)
spreading out, flattening, extension
spreading out, flattening, extension
one who spreads out, flattens, or extends; overwhelming force

mufradat.text: الطحو: كالدحو، وهو بسط الشيء والذهاب به. قال تعالى: والأرض وما طحاها [الشمس/ 6]، قال الشاعر: 298- طحا بك قلب في الحسان طروب (1) أي: ذهب.

record.ontological_core: A constructed basin or reservoir, wide like a cistern, positioned at the outlet of a water channel, in which water gathers before bursting forth to irrigate a cultivated field.
record.haqiqah_literal: The concrete, physical referent is a wide, basin-like reservoir (mājil) built at the mouth of a canal or qanāt, functioning as a collecting and discharge point for irrigation water before it flows into the farmland.
record.majaz_scholastic: The root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, and no established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extensions are recorded in the classical lexical tradition. Its usage remains confined to the concrete hydraulic-agricultural domain. Ibn Manẓūr explicitly notes that the word is a loanword (dakhīl), neither purely Persian nor purely Arabic, which further restricts any derivation of abstract or scholastic meanings from an indigenous Arabic root system.

canonical_definition.arabic: الطَّرْخَة: ماجِلٌ يُتَّخَذُ كالحوض الواسع عند مخرج القناة، يجتمع فيها الماء ثم يتفجر منها إلى المزرعة، وهو دخيل ليست فارسية محضة ولا عربية محضة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṭarkhah: a wide basin-like reservoir constructed at the outlet of a water channel, in which water gathers and then bursts forth to the cultivated field; it is a loanword, neither purely Persian nor purely Arabic.

derivations.english_translation: A wide basin or reservoir at the outlet of a water channel, where water collects and then bursts forth to irrigate a field; a loanword of non-pure Arabic origin.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root ط ل س is the act of effacing, obliterating, or wiping out written traces from a surface, and the resulting state of a document or hide whose markings have been erased or obscured. From this primary sense of erasure and obscuration, the root extends to denote a dusty, ash-grey, or dusky coloration that obscures the natural brightness of a thing, as in the grey wolf (ذئب أطلس).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the effacement of writing: طَلَسَ الكتابَ means to erase the book, and طَلَّسَهُ means to efface it thoroughly so as to corrupt its script. When the effacement is complete and the writing is reduced to a blank, superfluous surface, it becomes a طِرْس. The physical instrument of erasure is the طَلَاسَة, a rag or cloth used to wipe the tablet. Literally, it also denotes a dusty, greyish coloration, as in ذئب أطلس, a grey wolf, and ذئاب طلس, grey wolves.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root denotes the obliteration of intellectual or spiritual traces, the obscuring of clear evidence, and the effacement of identity or reputation. The phrase خرج القاضي متقلسا متطلسا describes a judge who goes out wearing a طيلسان (a type of cloak) and covering himself, deriving from the sense of concealment and overlaying. The term طَلْس is used as a variant of طِرْس for a erased or blank sheet, and by extension, for any surface or mind devoid of legible content. The greyness of the wolf (أطلس) metaphorically signifies a dusky, indistinct appearance that conceals the animal's form, paralleling the obscuration of writing.

canonical_definition.arabic: الطَّلْسُ: لغة في الطِّرْس، وهو المَحْوُ. طَلَسَ الكتابَ طَلْساً وطَلَّسَهُ فَتَطَلَّسَ: كَطَرَّسَهُ. ويقال للصحيفة إذا محيت: طِلْسٌ وطِرْسٌ. والذئب الأطلس: الأغبر.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṭals is a variant of al-ṭirs, and it means effacement. He erased the book with a single act of erasure (ṭalasa) or with intensive erasure (ṭallasa), so it became erased (taṭallasa), just as one says ṭarrasa. A sheet, when it is effaced, is called ṭils and ṭirs. The wolf that is aṭlas is the dusty, ash-grey one.

derivations.english_translation: he erased, effaced, or obliterated (writing)
he effaced thoroughly, corrupted the script by erasure
erasure, effacement; a blank or erased sheet (variant of طِرْس)
an erased or effaced sheet, a blank page
a rag or cloth used for erasing or wiping
dusty, ash-grey, dusky (especially of a wolf)
feminine of أطلس; a grey she-wolf
erasure, effacement (plural or verbal noun)
a cloak or mantle (a garment that covers and conceals)
it became erased or effaced; he covered himself

entries.text: ذئب أطلس: أغبر، وذئاب طلس، وذئبة طلساء. وطلست الكتاب طلسا، وطلسته تطليسا وهو أن تمحوه لتفسد خطه، فإذا أعمت محوه وصيرته من الفضول التي يستغنى Metaphorical (Majaz): طلس بصره وطمسه: ذهب به. وشققت طيالس الظلام. قال أبو النجم: كم في لجيم من أغر كأنه ... صبح يشق طيالس الظلماء وتقول العرب: يا ابن الطيلسان: ير
طلس بصره وطمسه: ذهب به. وشققت طيالس الظلام. قال أبو النجم: كم في لجيم من أغر كأنه ... صبح يشق طيالس الظلماء وتقول العرب: يا ابن الطيلسان: يريدون يا عجمي.

ذئب أطلس: أغبر، وذئاب طلس، وذئبة طلساء. وطلست الكتاب طلسا، وطلسته تطليسا وهو أن تمحوه لتفسد خطه، فإذا أعمت محوه وصيرته من الفضول التي يستغنى عنها وصيرته طرسا: فقد طرسته. ومحا اللوح بالطلاسة وهي الخرقة. وجاء البرد والطيالسة. وخرج القاضي متقلسا متطلسا.

record.ontological_core: The root ط-و-غ denotes transgression, overflow, and exceeding the proper bound — the foundational physical image being that of a torrent or flood that bursts its channel and overruns its limits, hence any entity that oversteps the measure of the created order.
record.haqiqah_literal: In its strict literal (ḥaqīqah) sense, طاغوت designates any object of worship set up alongside or instead of God — idols, the Devil, soothsayers, or human authorities who claim absolute obedience — insofar as each has transgressed (ṭaghā) the bound of creatureliness and usurped a prerogative belonging to the Divine alone.
record.majaz_scholastic: Scholastically and theologically, طاغوت is extended (majāz) to every 'head' or leader in error (raʾs fī al-ḍalāl), every false claimant to authority, and every system of thought or governance that commands allegiance contrary to divine law. The Qurʾānic pairing with al-jibt (يؤمنون بالجبت والطاغوت) marks it as the archetype of false transcendence — the metaphysical counterfeit of the Divine — and in later kalām and uṣūl al-fiqh it functions as a technical term for any authority whose command is obeyed in defiance of the Sharīʿah.

canonical_definition.arabic: الطَّاغُوتُ: ما عُبِدَ من دون الله عز وجل، وكلُّ رَأْسٍ في الضلالِ طاغوتٌ؛ وقيل: الأَصْنامُ، وقيل: الشيطانُ، وقيل: الكَهَنةُ، وقيل: مَرَدةُ أَهل الكتاب.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṭāghūt: that which is worshipped besides God — Mighty and Majestic — and every leader in error is a ṭāghūt; it is said to be idols, or the Devil, or soothsayers, or the rebellious ones among the People of the Book.

derivations.english_translation: to transgress, to overflow, to exceed the proper bound
transgression, overflow, tyrannical excess
false deity, idol, devil, soothsayer, or any authority usurping divine prerogative
one who transgresses, an overreacher, a tyrant
habitually or intensely transgressive, exceedingly tyrannical

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is spatial extension in a single dimension — the quality of a body, object, or duration being drawn out in length, standing in direct opposition (نقيض) to shortness (قِصَر). This primary corporeal sense of linear elongation is the root from which all temporal, quantitative, and moral extensions are derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the contrary of shortness (نقيض القِصَر) in people and other beings, whether animate or inanimate: the state of a thing being extended in length. It applies to concrete entities (aʿyān) such as a body, a rope, or a horse's tether, and to the act of lengthening or letting out (e.g., طَوِّلْ فَرَسَكَ, 'let out your horse's tether').
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension from spatial length, the root is applied metaphorically to temporal duration (الزمان), as in فَطَالَ عَلَيْهِمُ الأَمَدُ ('the term was prolonged for them') and سَبْحًا طَوِيلًا ('a long course of swimming'). It is further transferred to abstract and moral domains: الطَّوْل denotes superabundance, favor, and beneficence (الفضل والمن), as in ذِي الطَّوْلِ ('possessor of bounty'); it signifies wealth and capacity (سعة المال والقدرة), as in أُولُو الطُّولِ ('those of ample means') and مَنْ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ مِنْكُمْ طَوْلًا ('those who cannot afford'), a metonymy for what is spent on dower and maintenance. تَطَاوَلَ means to manifest length or to claim superiority, as in فَتَطَاوَلَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْعُمُرُ ('the age was prolonged over them'). طَوَالَ الدَّهْرِ denotes the duration of time.

canonical_definition.arabic: الطُّولُ: نقيض القِصَر في الناس وغيرهم من الحيوان والمَوات؛ ويقال للشيء الطويل: طالَ يَطُولُ طُولاً، فهو طَويلٌ وطُوالٌ. والطَّوْلُ: الفضل والمن والسعة والقدرة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ṭūl is the contrary of shortness (al-qiṣar) in people and other beings, whether animate or inanimate; a long thing is said to be ṭāla yaṭūlu ṭūlan, and it is ṭawīl or ṭuwāl. Al-ṭawl denotes favor, beneficence, ample means, and capacity.

derivations.english_translation: to be or become long; to extend in length or duration
long, extended, tall (masculine singular)
very long, elongated (intensive adjective)
long (plural of طَوِيل)
long (alternative plural of طَوِيل)
to lengthen, to extend, to let out (e.g., a tether)
to manifest length; to claim superiority, to domineer
length; bounty, favor, wealth, capacity
duration, extent (as in طَوَالَ الدَّهْرِ, 'throughout time')

mufradat.text: الطول والقصر من الأسماء المتضايفة كما تقدم، ويستعمل في الأعيان والأعراض كالزمان وغيره قال تعالى: فطال عليهم الأمد [الحديد/ 16]، سبحا طويلا [المزمل/ 7]، ويقال: طويل وطوال، وعريض وعراض، وللجمع: طوال، وقيل: طيال، وباعتبار الطول قيل للحبل المرخي على الدابة: طول (3)، وطول فرسك، أي: أرخ طوله، وقيل: طوال الدهر لمدته الطويلة، وتطاول فلان: إذا أظهر الطول، أو الطول. قال تعالى: فتطاول عليهم العمر [القصص/ 45]، والطول خص به الفضل والمن، قال: شديد العقاب ذي الطول [غافر/ 3]، وقوله تعالى: استأذنك أولوا الطول منهم [التوبة/ 86]، ومن لم يستطع منكم طولا [النساء/ 25]، كناية عما يصرف إلى المهر والنفقة. وطالوت اسم علم وهو أعجمي.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of innate formation and molding—God's original constitution of a creature's nature, as in clay shaped by a potter. This concrete sense of kneading and shaping underlies the abstract notion of inborn disposition.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is God's creation and formation of a being according to a fixed innate constitution, as expressed in the phrase طامَهُ اللهُ على الخَير (God molded him upon good). The noun الطِّيماء denotes the resulting innate nature or natural disposition, e.g., الشِّعْر مِنْ طِيمائِه (poetry is from his innate disposition).
record.majaz_scholastic: In philosophical and theological usage, the root is applied to the concept of innate disposition (طِيماء) as the God-given, pre-rational constitution of a soul, akin to the scholastic notion of natural inclination or fitrah. It is also used to describe the natural aptitude for poetry as an inborn quality rather than an acquired skill. The verb طامَ is not used metaphorically for human agency in this sense; it remains a divine act of creation.

canonical_definition.arabic: طامَهُ الله على الخَير يَطِيمُه طَيْماً: جَبَله. والطِّيماءُ: الجِبِلَّةُ والطبيعةُ.
canonical_definition.english: God molded him upon good, He forms him innately: He created him with an innate constitution. And الطِّيماء means innate nature and natural disposition.

derivations.english_translation: to mold, to form innately (said of God)
innate formation, molding
innate nature, natural disposition

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ع-د-س is twofold: (1) the well-known legume (lentil), a small, round, dark seed; and (2) the act of pressing heavily upon the earth, treading forcefully, and striving/laboring (al-kadḥ), from which derives the sense of journeying or departing into the land, and being carried away by fate.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Lisān al-ʿArab: العَدْس (al-ʿads) with a silent dāl (sukūn) denotes severity of treading upon the earth and also striving/laboring. The verb عَدَسَ يَعْدِسُ عَدْسًا وعَدَسَانًا وعُدُوسًا means he went forth into the land; it is said عَدَسَتْ بِهِ المَنِيَّةُ (fate carried him away). The noun العَدَس (al-ʿadas) is the well-known legume (lentil). The noun العَدَسَة (al-ʿadasa) is a pustule or blister resembling a lentil in shape. عَدَسْ is an onomatopoeic interjection used to urge on a mule or similar beast.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and extended usages: (1) The lentil (العَدَس) is used literally in the Qurʾānic verse 'and its lentils and its onions' (Q 2:61) as a reference to the Israelites' request for earthly produce. (2) The pustule (العَدَسَة) is a derived nominal metaphor based on resemblance to the lentil's shape. (3) The verb عَدَسَ in the sense of 'to go forth into the land' or 'to be carried away by fate' is a semantic extension from the physical act of treading heavily, implying departure and motion. (4) The interjection عَدَسْ is a conventionalized onomatopoeic imperative for driving beasts, not a lexical metaphor. No strictly scholastic or theological majāz is attested in the provided sources.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَدْسُ: شدة الوطء على الأرض والكدح. وعَدَسَ الرجلُ يَعْدِسُ عَدْسًا وعَدَسَانًا وعُدُوسًا: ذهب في الأرض. والعَدَسُ: الحب المعروف. والعَدَسَةُ: بثرة على هيئته. وعَدَسْ: زجر للبغل ونحوه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿads: severity of treading upon the earth and striving/laboring. ʿAdasa al-rajulu yaʿdisu ʿadsan wa-ʿadasānan wa-ʿudūsan: he went forth into the land. Al-ʿadas: the well-known legume (lentil). Al-ʿadasa: a pustule resembling it in shape. ʿAdas: an interjection to urge on a mule or similar beast.

derivations.english_translation: he trod heavily; he strove/labored; he went forth into the land
lentil (the legume)

severity of treading; striving/laboring

mufradat.text: العدس: الحب المعروف. قال تعالى: وعدسها وبصلها [البقرة/ 61]، والعدسة: بثرة على هيئته، وعدس: زجر للبغل ونحوه، ومنه: عدس في الأرض (3)، وهي عدوس (4).

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in Al-Mufradāt; classical lexicography derives it from the nominal form عَيْدَه, denoting an ingrained defect of temperament or constitution, specifically ill-nature or vicious disposition in humans and camels.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is not attested; based on Lisān al-ʿArab, the ḥaqīqah is the concrete quality of being ill-tempered or vicious, as predicated of a person or a camel.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical sources; the term remains confined to its literal ethological and ethical application.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَيْدَهُ: السَّيِّءُ الخُلُقِ من الناس والإِبل.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿaydah: the ill-natured one among people and camels.

derivations.english_translation: ill-natured, vicious (of a person or camel)

record.ontological_core: The root ع-ر-ج-ل denotes a collective body of beings or entities moving on foot or in a compact group, with an underlying physical image of a mass of walkers or a herd gathered together.
record.haqiqah_literal: A group or troop of horses; a group of people, specifically a group of foot-soldiers or pedestrians; a herd of goats.
record.majaz_scholastic: Extended to any collective movement on foot (e.g., 'the people went out as pedestrians'), and by further abstraction, any assembled group or band, without the strict requirement of walking.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَرْجَلة: القِطْعة من الخيل، وقيل: الجماعة منها. والعَرْجَلة: الجماعة من الناس، وقيل: جماعة الرَّجّالة. وخَرَجَ القومُ عَرَاجِلَةً أَي مُشاةً. والعَرْجَلة: الجماعةُ من المَعَز.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿarjalah: a troop of horses, or a group thereof. Al-ʿarjalah: a group of people, or a group of foot-soldiers. The people went out as ʿarājilah, i.e., on foot. Al-ʿarjalah: a herd of goats.

derivations.english_translation: a group of horses; a group of people; a group of foot-soldiers; a herd of goats
pedestrians, foot-soldiers (plural)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on hardness, rigidity, and firmness of a physical body or structure — the quality of being solid, unyielding, and resistant to pressure.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is: a solid, hard, and extremely strong entity; something rigid and unyielding in its physical constitution.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root is extended to describe a person of extreme firmness, resolve, or severity — one who is unyielding in character, opinion, or treatment. In theological and philosophical usage, it may denote an entity or argument that is rigorously established, indubitable, and resistant to refutation. The augmented form العَرَنْدَل (with additional nūn) carries the same semantic force of intensified hardness and strength.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَرْدَلُ: الصُّلْبُ الشَّدِيدُ، والعَرَنْدَلُ مِثْلُهُ، والنون زائدة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿardal: the solid, extremely strong; and al-ʿarandal is the same, with the nūn being augmentative.

derivations.english_translation: solid, hard, extremely strong; rigid, unyielding
very solid, extremely hard and strong; intensely rigid (nūn is augmentative)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the notion of a wedding celebration (ʿurs) and the bride (ʿarūs), from which derive associated meanings of adornment, intimacy, and habitation. A secondary, distinct root sense denotes bewilderment or stupefaction (dahash), as in ʿarisa al-rajul (the man was bewildered).
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is the wedding feast or celebration (ʿurs), and the bride (ʿarūs). It also literally denotes the act of a man endearing himself to his wife (tataʿarrasa li-mraʾatihi), and the lair or den of a lion (ʿirs al-asad) where it resides with its lioness (ʿarīs). Additionally, it refers to a brief stop or encampment (taʿrīsa) likened to a bird's sip.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to expressions of poverty or lack of good (e.g., 'purer than the good of the bride's basin' meaning he has no good), and to the notion of a place of dwelling or intimacy (maʿras). The secondary sense of bewilderment (dahash) is used to describe a person overwhelmed or stupefied, as in the poetry of Abū Dhuʾayb. The term ʿarūs is feminine, and the plural ʿarāʾis is used for camels likened to brides due to their beauty and value.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَرَسُ، بالتحريك: الدَّهَشُ. وعَرِسَ الرجل وعَرِشَ، بالكسر والسين والشين، عَرَساً، فهو عَرِسٌ: بَطِرَ، وقيل: أَعْيَا ودَهِشَ. والعرس: مؤنثة، وهي حفل الزفاف. والعروس: المرأة في عرسها. والعرس: مأوى الأسد. والتعريس: نزول القوم في آخر الليل للاستراحة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿaras (with a vowel on the second radical) means bewilderment. ʿArisa al-rajul (the man was bewildered) and ʿarisha, with kasra and either sīn or shīn, ʿarasan, so he is ʿaris: he was insolent, or it is said he was exhausted and bewildered. Al-ʿurs (wedding) is feminine, and it is the wedding celebration. Al-ʿarūs is the woman in her wedding. Al-ʿirs is the lion's lair. Al-taʿrīs is when people stop at the end of the night to rest.

derivations.english_translation: to celebrate a wedding; to dwell, to stay
lair, den (of a lion); wedding
bewilderment, stupefaction
bewildered, stupefied; insolent
bride, bridegroom
brides; beautiful camels
to endear oneself to one's wife; to dwell
brief stop, encampment; wedding celebration

entries.text: " هو أنقى من الخير من طست العروس " أي لا خير عنده، " ولا مخبأ لعطر بعد عروس ". وشهدنا عرس فلان فيا لها من عرس، ورأينا عرسه فيا لها من عرس، والعرس مؤنثة. قال: إنا وجدنا عرس الخياط ... مذمومة لئيمة الحواط وفلان يتعرس لامرأته أي يتحبب إليها. وهذه عرائس الإبل وعطراتها: لكرامها. وهو أ

record.ontological_core: A marginal, dialectally-attested root denoting the act of exposing or uncovering oneself during intimate congress; its foundational physical origin is the manifest disclosure of the body in the marital act.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the act of a man uncovering or exposing himself when he comes to his wife for intercourse.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested; the root remains confined to its concrete physical sense and is treated as a dialectal variant of عذط.

canonical_definition.arabic: قال الأَزهري في ترجمة عذط: ومنهم من يقول: عِظْيَوْطٌ، بالظاء، وهو الذي إِذا أَتَى أَهلَه أَبْدَى.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Azhari, in the entry for ʿadhṭ, reports: some say ʿiẓyawṭ, with ẓāʾ, meaning one who exposes himself when he comes to his wife.

derivations.english_translation: A man who exposes himself when he comes to his wife for intercourse.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of this root is the open, cleared tract of ground immediately surrounding a dwelling or settlement — the courtyard, precinct, or vacant lot abutting a house or quarter. The root denotes spatial periphery and open circumjacent ground, not the structure itself but the cleared space that encircles and belongs to it.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the courtyard (sāḥah) of a house and the open ground surrounding a dwelling, quarter, or locality; the plural forms are ʿiqāʾ. One says nazala bi-ʿaqwatihi, 'he alighted in its courtyard,' and mā bi-ʿaqwati hādhihi al-dāri mithlu fulān, 'there is no one in the precinct of this house like so-and-so.'
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension from the physical courtyard, the term is applied to the immediate vicinity, environs, or sphere of a place or person — the domain within which someone's presence or influence is felt. The phrase mā yaṭūru aḥadun bi-ʿaqwati hādhā, 'no one flutters about the precinct of this one,' is used figuratively to assert that no one approaches, rivals, or encroaches upon that person's domain. The scholastic usage thus shifts from the concrete cleared ground to the abstract notion of a protected perimeter or exclusive sphere of access.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَقْوةُ والعَقَاةُ: الساحة وما حَوْلَ الدارِ والمَحَلَّة، وجمعُهما عِقاءٌ. وعَقْوَةُ الدار: ساحَتُها.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿaqwah and al-ʿaqāh: the courtyard and the area surrounding a house or quarter; their plural is ʿiqāʾ. The ʿaqwah of a house is its courtyard.

derivations.english_translation: courtyard; precinct; open ground surrounding a dwelling
courtyard; precinct; environs of a house or locality
courtyards; precincts; plural of ʿaqwah and ʿaqāh

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is vertical elevation and height above a baseline, conceived as the spatial opposite of lowness (sifl). It denotes the act of rising, ascending, or being positioned above something, whether in physical space or in rank.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is height, elevation, or the upper part of a thing. It is used primarily for spatial and corporeal elevation, as in 'he rose above the place' or 'the upper part of the house' (ʿilw al-dār). The verb ʿalā (يَعْلُو) is used for both praiseworthy and blameworthy elevation, whereas ʿaliya (يَعْلَى) is reserved for praiseworthy elevation only.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, the root extends to elevation in rank, status, or power. It can denote arrogance and tyrannical self-exaltation, as in Pharaoh's 'exalting himself in the land' (Q 28:4) and the 'haughty' people (Q 23:46). It also signifies the transcendent elevation of God, and in scholastic contexts, the ontological superiority of causes over effects. The term ʿulw (height) is contrasted with sufl (lowness), and ʿulwī/ suflī designate the celestial and terrestrial realms respectively.

canonical_definition.arabic: العُلُوُّ: ضِدُّ السُّفْلِ، والارتفاعُ. عَلا يَعْلُو عُلُوًّا فهو عالٍ، وعَلِيَ يَعْلَى عَلَاءً فهو عَلِيٌّ. وعُلْوُ كلِّ شيءٍ وعِلْوُه وعَلْوُه وعُلاوَتُه وعالِيه وعالِيَتُه: أَرْفَعُه.
canonical_definition.english: Elevation is the opposite of lowness, and it is rising. He rose, rising, and is high; he was high, being high, and is exalted. The height of anything, its upper part, its summit, and its topmost portion: its highest part.

to be high, elevated (used only in praiseworthy contexts)

height, elevation
the highest part, summit
