mufradat.text: العلو: ضد السفل، والعلوي والسفلي المنسوب إليهما، والعلو: الارتفاع، وقد علا يعلو علوا وهو عال (5)، وعلي يعلى علاء فهو علي (6)، فعلا بالفتح في الأمكنة والأجسام أكثر. قال تعالى: عاليهم ثياب سندس [الإنسان/ 21]. وقيل: إن (علا) يقال في المحمود والمذموم، و(علي) لا يقال إلا في المحمود، قال: إن فرعون علا في الأرض [القصص/ 4]، لعال في الأرض وإنه لمن المسرفين [يونس/ 83]، وقال تعالى: فاستكبروا وكانوا قوما عالين [المؤمنون/ 46]، وقال لإبليس: أستكبرت أم كنت من العالين [ص/ 75]، لا يريدون علوا في الأرض [القصص/ 83]، ولعلا بعضهم على بعض [المؤمنون/ 91]، ولتعلن علوا كبيرا [الإسراء/ 4]، واستيقنتها أنفسهم ظلما وعلوا [النمل/ 14]. والعلي: هو الرفيع القدر من: علي، وإذا وصف الله تعالى به في قوله: أن الله هو العلي الكبير* [الحج/ 62]، إن الله كان عليا كبيرا [النساء/ 34]، فمعناه: يعلو أن يحيط به وصف الواصفين بل علم العارفين. وعلى ذلك يقال: تعالى، نحو: تعالى الله عما يشركون [النمل/ 63]، [وتخصيص لفظ التفاعل لمبالغة ذلك منه لا على سبيل التكلف كما يكون من البشر] (1)، وقال عز وجل: تعالى عما يقولون علوا كبيرا [الإسراء/ 43]، فقوله: (علوا) ليس بمصدر تعالى. كما أن قوله (نباتا) في قوله: أنبتكم من الأرض نباتا [نوح/ 17]، و(تبتيلا) في قوله: وتبتل إليه تبتيلا [المزمل/ 8]، كذلك (2). والأعلى: الأشرف. قال تعالى: أنا ربكم الأعلى [النازعات/ 24]، والاستعلاء: قد يكون طلب العلو المذموم، وقد يكون طلب العلاء، أي: الرفعة، وقوله: وقد أفلح اليوم من استعلى [طه/ 64]، يحتمل الأمرين جميعا. وأما قوله: سبح اسم ربك الأعلى [الأعلى/ 1]، فمعناه: أعلى من أن يقاس به، أو يعتبر بغيره، وقوله: والسماوات العلى [طه/ 4]، فجمع تأنيث الأعلى، والمعنى: هي الأشرف والأفضل بالإضافة إلى هذا العالم، كما قال: أأنتم أشد خلقا أم السماء بناها [النازعات/ 27]، وقوله: لفي عليين [المطففين/ 18]، فقد قيل هو اسم أشرف الجنان (3)، كما أن سجينا اسم شر النيران، وقيل: بل ذلك في الحقيقة اسم سكانها، وهذا أقرب في العربية، إذ كان هذا الجمع يختص بالناطقين، قال: والواحد علي نحو بطيخ. ومعناه: إن الأبرار في جملة هؤلاء فيكون ذلك كقوله: فأولئك مع الذين أنعم الله عليهم من النبيين [النساء/ 69]، الآية. وباعتبار العلو قيل للمكان المشرف وللشرف: العلياء، والعلية: تصغير عالية فصار في التعارف اسما للغرفة، وتعالى النهار: ارتفع، وعالية الرمح: ما دون السنان، جمعها عوال، وعالية المدينة، ومنه قيل: بعث إلى أهل العوالي (1)، ونسب إلى العالية فقيل: علوي (2). والعلاة: السندان حديدا كان أو حجرا. ويقال: العلية للغرفة، وجمعها علالي، وهي فعاليل، والعليان: البعير الضخم، وعلاوة الشيء: أعلاه. ولذلك قيل للرأس والعنق: علاوة، ولما يحمل فوق الأحمال: علاوة. وقيل: علاوة الريح وسفالته، والمعلى: أشرف القداح، وهو السابع، واعل عني، أي: ارتفع (3). و(تعال) قيل: أصله أن يدعى الإنسان إلى مكان مرتفع، ثم جعل للدعاء إلى كل مكان، قال بعضهم: أصله من العلو، وهو ارتفاع المنزلة، فكأنه دعا إلى ما فيه رفعة، كقولك: افعل كذا غير صاغر تشريفا للمقول له. وعلى ذلك قال: فقل تعالوا ندع أبناءنا [آل عمران/ 61]، تعالوا إلى كلمة [آل عمران/ 64]، تعالوا إلى ما أنزل الله* [النساء/ 61]، ألا تعلوا علي [النمل/ 31]، تعالوا أتل [الأنعام/ 151]. وتعلى: ذهب صعدا. يقال: عليته فتعلى، و(على): حرف جر، وقد يوضع موضع الاسم في قولهم: 331- غدت من عليه (4) عم العم: أخو الأب، والعمة أخته. قال تعالى: أو بيوت أعمامكم أو بيوت عماتكم [النور/ غدت من عليه بعد ما تم ظمؤها تصل وعن قيض بزيزاء مجهل وردت في النحو كلمات أتت تارة حرفا، وفعلا، وسما وهي: من والهاء والهمز وهل رب والنون وفي أعني فما عل لما وبلى حاشا ألا وعلى والكاف فيما نظما وخلا لات وها فيما رووا وإلى أن فرو الكلما 61]، ورجل معم مخول (1)، واستعم عما، وتعممه، أي: اتخذه عما، وأصل ذلك من العموم، وهو الشمول وذلك باعتبار الكثرة. ويقال: عمهم كذا، وعمهم بكذا. عما وعموما، والعامة سموا بذلك لكثرتهم وعمومهم في البلد، وباعتبار الشمول سمي المشوذ (2) العمامة، فقيل: تعمم نحو: تقنع، وتقمص، وعممته، وكني بذلك عن السيادة. وشاة معممة: مبيضة الرأس، كأن عليها عمامة نحو: مقنعة ومخمرة. قال الشاعر: 332- يا عامر بن مالك يا عما أفنيت عما وجبرت عما (3) أي: يا عماه سلبت قوما، وأعطيت قوما. وقوله: عم يتساءلون [عم/ 1]، أي: عن ما، وليس من هذا الباب.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical referent is the grape: the fruit of the vine (al-karm), and by extension the vine itself. The root's primary ontological anchor is the concrete, edible berry produced by the grapevine, from which the secondary sense of a small pustule or blister (ʿunbah) is derived by structural resemblance.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the grape: the well-known fruit of the vine, both individually as a single berry (ʿinabah) and collectively as grapes (ʿinab). It also denotes the grapevine itself (al-karm). The plural forms are aʿnāb and ʿinab. The diminutive/singulative ʿunbah denotes a single grape-berry, and by literal extension a pustule or blister on the body, due to its resemblance in shape to a grape.
record.majaz_scholastic: In the Qurʾānic and theological register, ʿinab appears strictly in its literal botanical sense within enumerations of divine bounty: 'And from the fruits of the date-palm and grapes' (al-Naḥl 16:67); 'a garden of date-palms and grapes' (al-Isrāʾ 17:91); 'gardens of grapes' (al-Raʿd 13:4); 'orchards and grapes' (al-Nabaʾ 78:32); 'and grapes and clover and olives' (ʿAbasa 80:28); 'two gardens of grapes' (al-Kahf 18:32). No metaphorical or scholastic technical usage is attested in the classical lexical sources. The only extended application is the concrete anatomical analogy: ʿunbah as a blister or pustule, which remains a literal resemblance-based usage rather than a philosophical metaphor.

canonical_definition.arabic: العِنَبُ: معروف، واحدتُه عِنَبة؛ ويُجْمَعُ العِنبُ أَيضاً على أَعناب. وهو العِنَباءُ، بالمدّ، أَيضاً. وقال الراغب: العنب يقال لثمرة الكرم، وللكرم نفسه، الواحدة: عنبة، وجمعه: أعناب. والعنبة: بثرة على هيئته.
canonical_definition.english: ʿInab is the well-known grape; its singular is ʿinabah, and it is also pluralized as aʿnāb. It is also called ʿinbāʾ, with madd. Al-Rāghib said: ʿInab denotes the fruit of the vine and the vine itself; the singular is ʿinabah, and its plural is aʿnāb. And the ʿunbah is a pustule or blister resembling it in shape.

derivations.english_translation: grapes (collective noun); the grape fruit collectively
a single grape; one grape-berry
grapes (plural)
a pustule, blister, or small swelling on the body (resembling a grape in shape)
grapes (dialectal variant, with madd)

mufradat.text: العنب يقال لثمرة الكرم، وللكرم نفسه، الواحدة: عنبة، وجمعه: أعناب. قال تعالى: ومن ثمرات النخيل والأعناب [النحل/ 67]، وقال تعالى: جنة من نخيل وعنب [الإسراء/ 91]، وجنات من أعناب* [الرعد/ 4]، حدائق وأعنابا [النبأ/ 32]، وعنبا وقضبا* وزيتونا [عبس/ 28- 29]، جنتين من أعناب [الكهف/ 32]، والعنبة: بثرة على هيئته.

record.ontological_core: The root ع ن ت ه (ʿ-n-t-h) is a quadriliteral (rubāʿī) formation, likely of onomatopoeic or dialectal origin, denoting intense, exaggerated immersion or exertion in an affair. Its foundational physical image is that of a person plunging headlong into a matter with excessive zeal, to the point of saturating or exhausting it.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in Lisān al-ʿArab, is a man who is عُنْتُهٌ or عُنْتُهِيٌّ — that is, one who goes to extremes and exerts himself excessively in an affair once he has entered into it.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah. In scholastic and theological usage, the root does not appear as a technical term; its metaphorical extension would denote excessive, immoderate commitment (ghuluw) in any matter, which classical ethics often censures as a deviation from the virtuous mean (iʿtidāl).

canonical_definition.arabic: رجل عُنْتُهٌ وعُنْتُهِيٌّ، وهو المُبالِغُ في الأمرِ إذا أَخذَ فيه.
canonical_definition.english: A man who is ʿuntuh or ʿuntuhiyy — one who goes to extremes in an affair once he has entered into it.

derivations.english_translation: one who is excessively zealous or extreme in an affair
one characterized by excessive zeal or extremism in an affair

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is rapid, forceful, and agile motion, specifically the swift, bounding, or trotting gait characteristic of a wolf (عَسَلان الذئب), from which the quadriliteral root is derived by the addition of the augmentative نون.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a strong, swift she-camel (الناقة القوية السريعة), characterized by speed and power in her movement.
record.majaz_scholastic: While the term is primarily a concrete zoological descriptor, it may be applied metaphorically to any entity or person possessing exceptional speed and strength, though classical sources do not record a distinct scholastic or theological majāz usage.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَنْسَل: الناقة القوية السريعة، والنون زائدة، مأخوذ من عَسَلان الذئب.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿansal: the strong, swift she-camel; the nūn is augmentative, derived from the wolf's swift, bounding gait.

derivations.english_translation: a strong, swift she-camel
swiftness, agility (as of a wolf)

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a nominal entity, likely a plant or natural object, with no attested verbal derivation in the classical lexicon; its foundational physical origin is obscure but points to a concrete, perhaps botanical, referent.
record.haqiqah_literal: A literal noun (ism) referring to a specific entity, possibly a plant or shrub, as recorded in Lisān al-ʿArab without metaphorical extension.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical sources; the term remains a hapax legomenon with no scholastic application.

canonical_definition.arabic: عَنْشَق: اسم.
canonical_definition.english: ʿAnshaq: a noun.

derivations.english_translation: a noun, possibly a plant name

record.ontological_core: The root denotes elongation and stretching, specifically a tall, slender, and extended bodily frame; its foundational physical image is that of something drawn out or extended in length.
record.haqiqah_literal: A tall, slender woman of extended stature; the literal physical meaning is a woman characterized by elongation and height.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical or scholastic usage is attested in the classical lexicons; the term remains confined to its literal physical description of stature.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَنْقَس من النساء: الطويلة المُعْرِقة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿAnqas, of women: the tall, slender one of extended stature.

derivations.english_translation: A tall, slender woman of extended stature

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a specific desert plant or shrub, characterized by its dense, tangled, matted growth and its desirability as forage for the spiny-tailed lizard (ḍabb).
record.haqiqah_literal: A type of desert vegetation or shrub that grows in a tangled, matted form; it is a plant craved by the ḍabb (spiny-tailed lizard), which scrapes it with its tail.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical or scholastic usages are attested in the classical sources; the term remains strictly botanical and zoological in its reference.

canonical_definition.arabic: العَنْكَثُ: ضَرْبٌ من النَّبْتِ، وقيل: هو شجر يَشْتَهيه الضَّبُّ فيَسْحَجُها بِذَنَبِه
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿankath: a type of vegetation; it is said to be a shrub that the spiny-tailed lizard (ḍabb) craves, scraping it with its tail.

derivations.english_translation: a tangled desert shrub; a plant sought by the spiny-tailed lizard

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a specific desert plant or herb, termed العِنْه, characterized by its growth in arid environments; this botanical entity serves as the concrete substrate from which all derived meanings emanate.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the plant known as العِنْه (al-ʿinh), a singular unit being عِنْهَة (ʿinhah), which is a type of herbage or vegetation.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical, philosophical, and theological usages are not attested in the classical sources for this root; the term remains confined to its literal botanical reference, with no extension into abstract or scholastic domains.

canonical_definition.arabic: العِنْهُ نَبْتٌ، واحدتُه عِنْهَةٌ
canonical_definition.english: Al-ʿinh is a plant; its singular unit is ʿinhah.

derivations.english_translation: A plant or herb of the desert
A single unit of the plant ʿinh

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is glue or adhesive substance (al-ghirāʾ), derived from fish, used to bind and attach one thing to another; hence the primary sense of sticking, adhering, and cleaving.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the act of gluing or pasting, as in غَرَوْتُ الجِلْدَ (I glued the hide), and the substance itself, الغِراء (glue), which causes one thing to adhere to another.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root denotes persistent attachment, devotion, or incitement: غَرِيَ بكذا (he became devoted to it, clung to it), أَغْرَيْتُ فلاناً بكذا (I made him cling to it, incited him to it), and in theology, God's incitement of enmity and hatred among people (فأغرينا بينهم العداوة والبغضاء) and His incitement of the believers against the hypocrites (لنغرينك بهم). The semantic extension moves from physical adhesion to psychological and social binding, including passionate attachment and provocation.

canonical_definition.arabic: الغِراءُ: الذي يُلْصَقُ به الشيءُ، يكونُ من السَّمَكِ. وغَرَا الجِلْدَ: أَلْصَقَهُ بالغِراءِ. وغَرِيَ بكذا: لَهِجَ به ولَصِقَ. وأَغْرَيْتُ فلاناً بكذا: أَلْهَجْتُهُ به.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ghirāʾ is that with which a thing is glued, made from fish. He glued the hide: he attached it with glue. He became devoted to something: he became passionately attached and clung to it. I incited someone to something: I made him cling to it.

derivations.english_translation: glue, adhesive substance
he glued, pasted, adhered
he became devoted, clung, adhered (to something)
he incited, made cling, provoked
adhesion, sticking; also a wonder or marvel (in idiomatic usage)

mufradat.text: غري بكذا (2)، أي: لهج به ولصق، وأصل ذلك من الغراء، وهو ما يلصق به، وقد أغريت فلانا بكذا، نحو: ألهجت به. قال تعالى: فأغرينا بينهم العداوة والبغضاء [المائدة/ 14]، لنغرينك بهم [الأحزاب/ 60].

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of enclosing, sheathing, or wrapping an object within a protective or containing cover (ghilāf), such as a sword in its scabbard, a flask in its case, or a bud within its calyx.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is a thing covered by a sheath or container, e.g., a sheathed sword (sayf aghlaf), a covered saddle (raḥl maghlūf), or a covered beard dyed with henna.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, it denotes hearts that are covered, sealed, or wrapped in a veil preventing them from receiving prophetic guidance, as in 'Our hearts are ghulf' (Q 2:88). It also expresses the heart as a receptacle (wiʿāʾ) for knowledge, or as being in a state of heedlessness (ghaflah) and blindness to revelation. The term also refers to the uncircumcised male (ghulām aghlaf) by extension of the covering of the foreskin (ghulfah).

canonical_definition.arabic: الغِلاف: الصِّوان وما اشتمل على الشيء كقَمِيص القَلْب وغِرْقِئِ البيض وكِمام الزَّهْر وساهُور القَمر، والجمع غُلُفٌ. وسيف أَغْلَف وقوس غَلْفاء، وكذلك كل شيء في غِلاف.
canonical_definition.english: Al-ghilāf: the protective container and that which encloses a thing, such as the pericardium of the heart, the membrane of an egg, the calyx of a flower, and the halo of the moon; the plural is ghuluf. A sheathed sword (sayf aghlaf) and a covered bow (qaws ghalfāʾ), and likewise anything within a cover.

derivations.english_translation: sheath, cover, envelope, integument
sheaths, covers (plural of ghilāf)
sheathed, covered, uncircumcised
sheathed (feminine), e.g., a covered bow
foreskin, prepuce
to sheathe, to cover, to wrap
to be sheathed, to be covered, to dye (the beard)

mufradat.text: قوله تعالى: قلوبنا غلف* [البقرة/ 88]، قيل: هو جمع أغلف، كقولهم: سيف أغلف. أي: هو في غلاف، ويكون ذلك كقوله: وقالوا قلوبنا في أكنة [فصلت/ 5]، في غفلة من هذا* [ق/ 22]. وقيل: معناه قلوبنا أوعية للعلم (2). وقيل: معناه قلوبنا مغطاة، وغلام أغلف كناية عن الأقلف، والغلفة كالقلفة، وغلفت السيف، والقارورة، والرحل، والسرج: جعلت لها غلافا، وغلفت لحيته بالحناء، وتغلف نحو تخضب، وقيل: قلوبنا غلف* [البقرة/ 88]، هي جمع غلاف، والأصل: غلف بضم اللام، وقد قرئ به (3)، نحو: كتب، أي: هي أوعية للعلم تنبيها أنا لا نحتاج أن نتعلم منك، فلنا غنية بما عندنا.

entries.text: السلطان من تجرد لخلافه، جرد له السيف من غلافه. ورحل مغلوف: له غلاف. قال ذو الرمة يصف ناقة: فمازلت أكسو كل يوم سراتها ... خصاصة م

record.ontological_core: The root غيذ denotes the act of forming a correct conjecture that subsequently proves true; its foundational physical origin is the hitting or striking of a target, from which the cognitive sense of 'hitting upon the truth' is derived.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is 'to strike or hit a target' (as in striking with a weapon or arrow), which then metaphorically extends to the mental act of forming an opinion that corresponds to reality.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, the root is employed to describe the faculty of conjecture (ẓann) that aligns with actuality, often discussed in epistemology and the philosophy of mind regarding the validity of probable knowledge and its correspondence to truth.

canonical_definition.arabic: الغَيْذان: الذي يظن فيصيب
canonical_definition.english: Al-ghaydhān: the one who conjectures and then hits upon the truth.

derivations.english_translation: one who conjectures and is correct; a person whose surmise hits the mark

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in Al-Mufradāt; however, the Lisān material points to a core sense of swelling, rising, and towering—a physical expansion upward that manifests as haughtiness and self-magnification.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is not explicitly attested; based on Lisān al-ʿArab, the ḥaqīqah is the act of swelling, rising, and towering physically, as in the swelling of a she-camel's hump or the rising of a structure.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic usage, as delineated by Al-Zamakhsharī's method, transfers the physical sense of swelling and towering to the domain of character and social behavior: haughtiness, arrogance, self-aggrandizement, and overweening pride. The Lisān citation of al-Layth explicitly states that al-fajs and al-tafajjus denote greatness, pride, and self-elevation, with the poetic image of a she-camel's prideful swelling serving as the concrete basis for the abstract moral quality.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفَجْسُ والتَفَجُّس: عَظَمة وتَكَبّر وتطاوُل.
canonical_definition.english: Al-fajs and al-tafajjus: greatness, pride, and self-elevation.

derivations.english_translation: swelling, towering; haughtiness, arrogance
self-magnification, arrogant swelling, haughty towering

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; classical lexicography records only a derived participial form denoting self-magnification and coarseness of conduct, without a recoverable concrete physical prototype.
record.haqiqah_literal: Not attested in Asās al-Balāghah; the sole classical datum is the participial adjective مُتَفَحِّز, meaning 'one who magnifies himself and behaves coarsely or obscenely' (mutaʿaẓẓim mutafaḥḥish), as transmitted by al-Jawharī from Ibn al-Sikkīt.
record.majaz_scholastic: No philosophical or theological majāz is recorded in the classical sources; the term remains confined to the ethical-psychological register of self-aggrandizement and vulgarity, with no attested extension into metaphysics, logic, or theology.

canonical_definition.arabic: رجل مُتَفَحِّز أَي متعظم متفحش؛ حكاه الجوهري عن ابن السكيت.
canonical_definition.english: A man who is مُتَفَحِّز, that is, self-magnifying and coarse or obscene in conduct; al-Jawharī transmitted it from Ibn al-Sikkīt.

derivations.english_translation: one who magnifies himself and behaves coarsely; self-aggrandizing and vulgar

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical referent is the anatomical segment of the limb situated between the hip and the knee—the thigh—conceived as a distinct, bounded bodily member whose primary ontological mode is that of a corporeal part susceptible to injury.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, strictly anatomical sense is the thigh: the bodily member extending from the hip joint to the knee. In its verbal derivation, the root denotes the infliction of injury upon this member, as in 'he struck his thigh, rendering it fractured' (كُسِرَتْ فَخِذُهُ فَهُوَ مَفْخُوذٌ), and 'I struck him so that I injured his thigh' (رَمَيْتُهُ فَفَخَذْتُهُ).
record.majaz_scholastic: Beyond the anatomical literal, the root admits extended and figurative applications. In genealogical and social discourse, the plural أَفْخَاذ designates the major sub-lineages or branches of a tribe, by analogy of the tribal body to a physical body whose limbs are its constituent clans. In juridical and lexical classification, the term may denote a portion or division of a larger whole, reflecting the part-whole relation inherent in the limb. The passive participle مَفْخُوذٌ is applied to one whose thigh has been injured, and by extension to any structure or entity metaphorically 'wounded' in its supporting member.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفَخِذُ: وصل ما بين الساق والورك، أُنثى، والجمع أَفخاذ. وفُخِذَ فَخْذاً، فهو مفخوذ: أُصيبت فخذه.
canonical_definition.english: The fakhidh is the anatomical segment connecting the lower leg and the hip; it is feminine, and its plural is afkhādh. One is said to have been fakhidha—sustaining a fakhdh—when their thigh has been injured, rendering them mafkhūdh.

derivations.english_translation: to sustain a thigh injury; to be wounded in the thigh
to strike or injure someone in the thigh
thigh (alternative vocalization with kasrah on the fāʾ)
thigh (primary nominal form)
to have one's thigh injured (passive)
one whose thigh has been injured; thigh-wounded
thighs; major tribal sub-lineages or branches

entries.text: فخذ الرجل: كسرت فخذه فهو مفخوذ.
فخذ الرجل: كسرت فخذه فهو مفخوذ. Metaphorical (Majaz): هذا فخذي بالتذكير أي أدنى عشيرتي. وفلان من فخذ من أفخاذ بني تميم، وفخذ قبيلته: جعلهم فخذا فخذا. وفخذت بني فلان فلم أر عندهم خيرا أي أتيتهم ف

هذا فخذي بالتذكير أي أدنى عشيرتي. وفلان من فخذ من أفخاذ بني تميم، وفخذ قبيلته: جعلهم فخذا فخذا. وفخذت بني فلان فلم أر عندهم خيرا أي أتيتهم فخذا فخذا فسألتهم في حمالة أو غيرها. ولما أنزل على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قوله تعالى: " وأنذر عشيرتك الأقربين " بات يفخذ عشيرته أي يدعو

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of a creature (human or camel) lowering and pressing its hindquarters or forelegs flat against the ground in a slack, spread-out posture, specifically during sitting or kneeling.
record.haqiqah_literal: Literal physical meaning: A man's pressing his buttocks to the ground and resting his legs (as a pillow); a camel's kneeling in a relaxed manner, pressing its forearms to the ground, or spreading out in the act of kneeling.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical sources; the root remains confined to its literal zoological and postural sense.

canonical_definition.arabic: فَرْشَط الرجلُ فَرْشَطة: أَلصق أَليتيه بالأَرض وتوسَّد ساقيه. وفَرْشَط البعيرُ فَرْشَطة وفِرْشاطاً: برَك بُروكاً مسترخياً فأَلصق أَعضاده بالأَرض، وقيل: هو أَن ينتشر بِرْكةَ البعير عند البُروك.
canonical_definition.english: A man performed farshata: he pressed his buttocks to the ground and used his legs as a pillow. A camel performed farshata and firshāṭ: it knelt in a relaxed manner, pressing its forearms to the ground; it is also said to be the spreading out of a camel's kneeling posture when it kneels.

derivations.english_translation: to press one's buttocks to the ground and rest one's legs; (of a camel) to kneel in a relaxed, spread-out manner
the act of pressing the buttocks to the ground and resting the legs; a camel's relaxed kneeling with forearms pressed to the ground
a camel's kneeling in a slack, spread-out posture

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a sharp, guttural vocalization directed at a dog—an onomatopoeic summons or command, rooted in the physical act of calling out to an animal with a distinctive, percussive sound.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the call or summons addressed to a dog (دعاء الكلب), i.e., the utterance used to invoke, command, or incite a dog.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical or scholastic extension is attested in the classical lexica; the term remains confined to its literal onomatopoeic function as an animal call. Ibn Manẓūr cross-references the root قرقس, indicating a parallel or variant form with the same semantic field.

canonical_definition.arabic: فِرْقِس وفُرْقُوس: دعاءُ الكلب.
canonical_definition.english: Firqis and furqūs: the call or summons addressed to a dog.

derivations.english_translation: a call or summons to a dog; an utterance used to invoke a dog
a call or summons to a dog; an utterance used to invoke a dog

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root فرم is the act of constricting, narrowing, or tightening an orifice—specifically the vagina—by means of a medicinal agent or physical obstruction, thereby inducing a state of constriction (taḍayyuq).
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is the use of a drug or medicinal substance (farām) to constrict the vagina, as in the phrase 'istaframat al-marʾah' (the woman used a constricting agent). The root also appears in the proverbial expression 'more abject than the faram of a slave-girl,' referring to the medicinal plug used for vaginal constriction.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root extends to any act of tightening, narrowing, or restricting, whether physical or abstract. The phrase 'ibn al-mustafrimah bi-ʿajam al-zabīb' (son of the woman who constricted herself with grape seeds) in the ḥadīth of ʿAbd al-Malik employs the root as a derogatory allusion to base origin, metaphorically linking physical constriction to moral or social degradation. The variant form 'tafrīm' (with mīm) is used interchangeably with 'tafrīb' (with bāʾ) in the sense of narrowing the woman's orifice.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفَرْمُ والفِرَامُ: ما تَتَضَيَّقُ به المرأَة من دواء. وامرأَةٌ فَرْماءُ ومُسْتَفْرِمة: وهي التي تجعل الدواء في فرجها ليضيق.
canonical_definition.english: Al-farm and al-firām: a medicinal substance by which a woman constricts [her vagina]. A woman who is farmāʾ or mustafrimah is one who places a drug in her vulva in order to narrow it.

derivations.english_translation: a constricting medicinal agent or plug used to narrow the vagina
a medicinal substance or plug employed for vaginal constriction
a woman who has constricted her vagina with a medicinal agent
a woman who uses a constricting agent on her vagina
the act of constricting or narrowing (especially of the vagina)

entries.text: استفرمت المرأة إذا تضيقت بالفرم، ويقال: أذل من فرم الأمة. وفي حديث عبد الملك: يا ابن المستفرمة بعجم الزبيب.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a small, lowly, or contemptible entity; its foundational physical origin appears to be the scorpion (العَقْرَب), a creature perceived as base, harmful, and of low status, from which the meaning of meanness and ignobility derives.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the scorpion (العَقْرَب), as stated by al-Azharī; it also literally denotes a person of low, ignoble, or base character (اللئيم).
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension, the term is applied to a person of vile or ignoble disposition, likening such a person to a scorpion in harmfulness and lowliness; it may also be used as an invective or term of abuse.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفُصْعُل والفِصْعِل: اللئيم. الأَزهري: الفُصْعُل العَقْرَب.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Fuṣʿul and al-Fiṣʿil: the ignoble one. Al-Azharī said: al-Fuṣʿul is the scorpion.

derivations.english_translation: scorpion; ignoble, base person
ignoble, base person

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on a sharp, penetrating cognitive grasp — an acute mental alertness that seizes upon a matter swiftly and thoroughly, as opposed to dullness or obtuseness (ghabāwah). It is the mind's capacity to apprehend subtle distinctions and respond with precision.
record.haqiqah_literal: To be acutely aware of, to grasp a matter with mental sharpness, to perceive something with alert intelligence; said of a person who is keenly attentive and quick to understand (فَطِنٌ), and of the act of making someone else attentive or sharpening their understanding (تفطين).
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, فِطْنَة denotes the faculty of intellectual apprehension (idrāk) by which the rational soul grasps intelligible meanings, distinguished from mere sensory perception. It is the cognitive virtue opposed to heedlessness (ghaflah) and stupidity (ghabāwah), and is closely allied to fiqh (deep understanding) and ḥikmah (wisdom). The verb فَطَّنَ (to make someone attentive) is used in pedagogical and ethical contexts to signify the cultivation of the rational faculty through instruction and discipline.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفِطْنَةُ: كالفهم، وهي ضد الغباوة. ورجل فَطِنٌ بَيِّنُ الفِطْنَة والفَطَن، وقد فَطَنَ لهذا الأمر يَفْطُنُ فِطْنَةً، وفَطُنَ.
canonical_definition.english: Fiṭnah is akin to understanding (fahm), and it is the opposite of dullness (ghabāwah). A man who is faṭin is one in whom acute intelligence and mental alertness are manifest; he has grasped this matter with keen perception, and he is sharp-witted.

derivations.english_translation: to be acutely aware, to be sharp-witted, to understand quickly
to be keenly intelligent, to possess mental acuity
acute intelligence, mental sharpness, quick apprehension; the opposite of dullness
keenness of mind, alertness (verbal noun)
acutely intelligent, sharp-witted, quick to understand
to make someone attentive, to sharpen someone's understanding, to instruct
to become attentive, to grasp something with alertness
to engage in mutual understanding, to be sharp-witted with someone
mutual sharp-wittedness, reciprocal alertness in understanding

entries.text: مررت به فما فطن لي، وإذا حدثتك بشيء فافطن له، وتفطن لما أقول لك، وفاطن صاحبه مفاطنة، وهو فطن، وقد فطن وفطن فطانة، وفطنته للأمر، وفطنه المعلم: رده فطنا بتأديبه وتثقيفه. قال رؤبة: وقد أعاصي في الشباب الميال ... موعظة الأدنى وتفطين الوال

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is not attested in Al-Mufradāt; however, the Lisān material points to a quadriradical (or quasi-quadriradical) cluster denoting meanness, lowliness, and mixed/base descent, with the physical origin likely rooted in the notion of paucity, stinginess, and social inferiority.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is not attested; based on Lisān, the literal sense is 'a stingy, base person' and 'a person of mixed descent, especially one whose father is a client (mawlā) and whose mother is a client (mawlā).'
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic usages: The term is applied to moral and social inferiority, including extreme miserliness and lowly lineage. In genealogical and legal discourse, it denotes a person of mixed parentage (hajīn) or one whose parents are of servile/client status (muqrif), extending to broader notions of baseness and ignobility.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفَلْقَسُ والفَلَنْقَس: البخيل اللئيم. والفَلَنْقَس: الهَجِين من قِبَل أَبَوَيْه الذي أَبُوه مَوْلًى وأُمّه مَوْلاة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-falqas and al-falanqas: the stingy, base person. And al-falanqas: the person of mixed descent on both parental sides, whose father is a client (mawlā) and whose mother is a client (mawlā).

derivations.english_translation: a stingy, base person
a stingy, base person; a person of mixed descent whose father and mother are both clients (mawlā)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a group of people in motion—specifically, a company or band that passes along swiftly and in successive waves, conceived as a moving collective rather than a static aggregate.
record.haqiqah_literal: A company or band of people passing by rapidly; a troop or crowd advancing in motion, such that the valley surges with them wave upon wave.
record.majaz_scholastic: In theological and eschatological usage, the term denotes successive multitudes or waves of humanity: the recurrent bands cast into the Fire (Q 67:8), the intruding faction thrust in alongside the damned (Q 38:59), and the peoples entering the religion of God in successive waves (Q 110:2). The plural أفواج conveys rhythmic, wave-like succession, whether of believers embracing the faith or of groups consigned to perdition.

canonical_definition.arabic: الفَوْجُ: الجماعة من الناس المارّة المسرعة، والجمع أَفْوَاجٌ وأَفَاوِجُ وأَفَاوِيجُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Fawj: a company of people passing by swiftly; its plurals are afwāj, afāwij, and afāwīj.

derivations.english_translation: a company, band, or troop of people passing swiftly; a wave of humanity
companies, bands, troops; successive waves or multitudes
companies, bands (rare plural form)
companies, bands (rare plural form)
a company or band of people; a passing troop

mufradat.text: الفوج: الجماعة المارة المسرعة، وجمعه أفواج. قال تعالى: كلما ألقي فيها فوج [الملك/ 8]، هذا فوج مقتحم معكم [ص/ 59]، في دين الله أفواجا [النصر/ 2].

entries.text: أقبلوا فوجا فوجا، يموج بهم الوادي موجا.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ف-و-خ is the emission and diffusion of a scent or odor, specifically the rising and spreading of a fragrant or malodorous exhalation through the air, akin to the root ف-و-ح. It denotes the effusion of a volatile substance that fills the surrounding atmosphere and may be perceived by the sense of smell, sometimes with a forceful or overpowering quality.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah (as inferred from Lisān al-ʿArab) is: the diffusion and rising of a smell or odor, whether pleasant (like musk) or foul, such that it spreads through the air; also, the emission of wind (flatulence) from a person, and the act of a smell taking away one's breath due to its intensity.
record.majaz_scholastic: While not attested in Asās al-Balāghah, the metaphorical and scholastic extensions may include: the diffusion of reputation or news (as a scent spreads), the emanation of spiritual or moral influence, and in theological contexts, the manifestation of divine attributes or the diffusion of sanctity. However, these are not classical attestations and remain speculative; the primary usage is literal sensory.

canonical_definition.arabic: فَاخَ المِسْكُ يَفُوخُ وَيَفِيخُ فَوْخًا وَفَوَخَانًا: سَطَعَ مِثْلَ فَاحَ. وَفَاخَ الرَّجُلُ يَفُوخُ فَوْخًا وَأَفَاخَ يُفِيخُ: خَرَجَتْ مِنْهُ رِيحٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Musk diffused and rose like fāḥa. A man emitted wind: he passed wind.

derivations.english_translation: to diffuse (a smell), to emit odor, to stink or smell sweet
to be diffused (of a smell), to spread
diffusion of odor, emission of wind
diffusion, spreading (of scent)
to emit odor, to cause a smell to spread
he/it diffuses (present tense)
he/it diffuses (variant present tense)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ق ب و is the act of gathering, collecting, or picking up a substance with the fingers or hand, specifically the harvesting of saffron and safflower. This concrete manual act of aggregation is the root's primary material sense, from which all subsequent applications derive by extension or restriction.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the direct, manual gathering of a substance—such as saffron (زعفران) or safflower (عصفر)—by the fingers, i.e., picking or harvesting it. It also denotes the physical convergence or closing of the lips (القَبْوة: انضمام ما بين الشفتين).
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic extensions include: (1) The term القابية (al-qābiya) for a woman who gathers saffron, a nominal derivation from the literal act; (2) The garment known as القَباء (al-qabāʾ), a long outer robe or cloak, which is a lexical extension from the root's sense of 'gathering' or 'enclosing' the body, though morphologically distinct (madd). In philosophical and theological usage, the root does not appear in classical scholastic texts for substance or accident; its majāz remains confined to concrete and social domains.

canonical_definition.arabic: قَبا الشيءَ قَبْواً: جمعه بأَصابعه. والقَبْوةُ: انضمام ما بين الشفتين. والقَباء، ممدود، من الثياب.
canonical_definition.english: He gathered the thing with his fingers. Al-qabwa is the closing of the lips. Al-qabāʾ, with madd, is a type of garment.

derivations.english_translation: He gathered or picked it up with his fingers (e.g., saffron).
The closing or convergence of the lips; a single act of gathering.
A woman who gathers or picks saffron.
A long outer robe or cloak (madd form).

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of taking or extracting a burning brand or flame from a larger fire—a portion of fire seized from its main mass.
record.haqiqah_literal: A burning brand, flame, or firebrand taken from a larger fire; the act of taking such a flame.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically extended to the seeking of knowledge, guidance, or illumination, as in the Quranic verse 'Look at us, that we may borrow from your light' (57:13). Also applied to a stallion swift in impregnation, likened to fire in its speed.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَبَس: الشُّعْلة من النار، واقْتِباسها الأَخذ منها.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Qabas: a burning brand from fire; its iqtibās is the taking from it.

derivations.english_translation: to take or extract a flame; to acquire knowledge
the act of taking a flame
a burning brand, flame, or firebrand
a stallion swift in impregnation
the seeking or taking of a flame; acquisition of knowledge
one who frequently takes flames or acquires knowledge

mufradat.text: القبس: المتناول من الشعلة، قال: أو آتيكم بشهاب قبس [النمل/ 7]، والقبس والاقتباس: طلب ذلك، ثم يستعار لطلب العلم والهداية. قال: انظرونا نقتبس من نوركم [الحديد/ 13]. وأقبسته نارا أو علما: أعطيته، والقبيس: فحل سريع الإلقاح تشبيها بالنار في السرعة.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on the act of falling headlong or collapsing downward, and by extension, entering a house or enclosed space. It denotes a sudden, forceful downward motion or penetration into an interior.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is: a man falling down prostrate or headlong; and entering a house. It also denotes the act of falling upon one's head.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, it may be used to describe a sudden downfall, a headlong plunge into a situation, or a forceful entry into a matter. In scholastic contexts, it could signify a precipitous decline or an abrupt incursion.

canonical_definition.arabic: تقَحْذَم الرجل: وقع مُنْصَرِعاً. وتقَحْذَم البيتَ: دخَله. والقَحْذَمةُ والتَّقَحْذُم: الهُوِيّ على الرأْس.
canonical_definition.english: A man fell prostrate. He entered the house. Al-Qaḥdhamah and al-Taqaḥdhum: falling upon the head.

derivations.english_translation: to fall headlong; to enter a house
a headlong fall; the act of falling upon the head
the act of falling headlong; entering

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a specific cultivar of date palm fruit (tamr), characterized by its black color and rapid detachment of its skin from its flesh upon ripening (irtibāb).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is a type of date (tamr) that is black, quick to have its skin peel away from its flesh when it ripens, and is considered the most delicious date in its unripe (busran) stage.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Asās al-Balāghah or Al-Mufradāt for metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages. The term remains within the domain of concrete botanical and culinary reference, with no evidence of abstract extension in the classical lexicographical tradition.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَرِيثاء: ضَرْبٌ من التمر، وهو أَسْودُ سريعُ النَقْضِ لقِشْرِه عن لِحائه إِذا أَرْطَبَ، وهو أَطيَبُ تمرٍ بُسْراً؛ يُضافُ ويوصَفُ به، ويُثنَّى ويُجْمع.
canonical_definition.english: Al-qarīthāʾ: a variety of date (tamr) that is black, rapidly detaches its skin from its flesh when it ripens (irtabā), and is the most delicious date when eaten unripe (busran); it may be used in construct (iḍāfa) and as an adjective, and may be dualized and pluralized.

derivations.english_translation: A specific variety of black date that peels easily when ripe; the most delicious date when eaten unripe (busran).
A date of the qarīthāʾ variety; used as an adjective to describe such dates.

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a specific, rugged, and remote topographical location—a place-name (موضع) characterized by harsh, broken terrain. Its foundational physical origin is the concrete designation of a desolate, stony ground or a rugged tract of land, from which the abstract sense of scattering and dispersal derives by analogy: to be cast into such broken country is to be dispersed beyond recovery.
record.haqiqah_literal: A proper noun (اسم علم) for a specific rugged, stony place or tract of land. In its strict literal usage, it is a toponym, indeclinable (غير مصروف) as a place-name, denoting a harsh, broken terrain. The phrase ذهبوا شَعالِيل بِقِرْدَحْمةٍ means 'they scattered in every direction at Qirdahma,' i.e., they dispersed across a rugged, remote location.
record.majaz_scholastic: By metonymic extension (مجاز مرسل), the toponym is used to signify total, irrecoverable dispersal. The scholastic usage is idiomatic: 'they went off to Qirdahma' (ذهبوا بقردحمة) signifies that a group has scattered in all directions, never to regroup. The underlying trope is spatial: a rugged, remote place serves as the emblem of utter dispersion. Al-Liḥyānī records the variant قِنْدَحْرة and قِدَّحْرة in the same idiomatic sense, confirming that the root's semantic core is the notion of scattering into a harsh, broken landscape.

canonical_definition.arabic: قِرْدَحْمة: موضع. الفراء: ذهبوا شَعالِيل بِقِرْدَحْمةٍ أَي تفرقوا. قال ابن بري: وفي الغريب المصنف بِقِرْدَحْمةَ غير مصروف. وحكى اللحياني في نوادره: ذهب القوم بِقِنْدَحْرةٍ وقِنْدَحْرةٍ وقِدَّحْرة
canonical_definition.english: Qirdahma: a place. Al-Farrāʾ said: 'They went off in every direction at Qirdahma,' i.e., they scattered. Ibn Barrī said: In al-Gharīb al-Muṣannaf it appears as 'bi-Qirdahmata' in the indeclinable form. Al-Liḥyānī related in his Nawādir: 'The people went off to Qindahra, Qindahra, and Qiddahra' [in the same sense of dispersal].

derivations.english_translation: Qirdahma: a rugged, stony place; a toponym used idiomatically to denote total dispersal
Qirdahm: a rugged, broken tract of land (hypothetical base form)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a thin, flat sheet of writing material — specifically papyrus (bardī) manufactured in Egypt — serving as a surface for inscription.
record.haqiqah_literal: A physical sheet or scroll of papyrus used for writing; also a type of Egyptian striped cloth (burd) and a stretched hide set up as a target for archery.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, any written document or scripture (as in Qurʾānic 'kitāb fī qirṭās'); the target-hide (qirṭās) metaphorically denotes the goal or aim (gharaḍ) in archery and, by further abstraction, any object of pursuit or intention.

canonical_definition.arabic: القِرْطاس: ما يُكتب فيه، معروف يُتَّخذ من بَرْدِيّ يكون بمصر. وكل أَديم يُنْصَب للنِّضال فاسمه قِرْطاس، ويسمَّى الغَرَض قِرْطاساً.
canonical_definition.english: Qirṭās: that upon which one writes; a well-known material made from papyrus (bardī) in Egypt. Every hide set up for archery is called a qirṭās, and the target itself is also called a qirṭās.

derivations.english_translation: sheet of papyrus; writing material; document; target-hide
a single sheet of papyrus; a small document
sheets of papyrus; documents (plural of qirṭās)
to write on papyrus; to set up a target-hide
papyrus-related; of papyrus

mufradat.text: القرطاس: ما يكتب فيه. قال الله تعالى: ولو نزلنا عليك كتابا في قرطاس [الأنعام/ 7]، قل من أنزل الكتاب الذي جاء به موسى نورا وهدى للناس تجعلونه قراطيس [الأنعام/ 91].

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of hooding and sealing a bird of prey — specifically, sewing shut the eyes of a falcon or hawk at the moment of its capture, and the consequent loss or molting of its feathers during the taming process. The quadrilaterals قَرْنَس / قَرْنَص denote this concrete falconry operation, with the س and ص variants reflecting an ancient dialectal alternation on the فَعْلَل pattern.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is: a falcon (البازي) was hooded and its eyes were stitched shut immediately upon capture, causing its plumage to drop; likewise said of a rooster (الديك) when its eyes are sealed or its feathers fall. The verb is intransitive (لازم) in this usage, describing the bird's condition rather than an agent's action.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical lexica. The term remains confined to the concrete domain of falconry and avian husbandry; any extended application (e.g., to a person whose sight or insight is forcibly obstructed) would be an ad hoc rhetorical extension rather than a recognized majāz of the root.

canonical_definition.arabic: قَرْنَسَ البازي: كُرِّزَ، أي سقط ريشه، وخِيطَتْ عيناه أول ما يُصاد؛ فعل لازم. وقَرْنَسَ الديكُ وقَرْنَصَ: إذا كُرِّزَ وسقط ريشه.
canonical_definition.english: Qarnasa al-bāzī: it was hooded — that is, its feathers dropped and its eyes were stitched shut at the moment of capture; the verb is intransitive. And qarnasa al-dīk / qarnaṣa: when it was hooded and its feathers fell.

derivations.english_translation: to hood a falcon and sew its eyes shut upon capture; (of the bird) to be hooded and lose its feathers
dialectal variant of قَرْنَسَ: to hood and seal the eyes of a falcon or rooster
the act of hooding and sealing a bird of prey's eyes; the state of being so hooded

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is the act of overpowering and subduing another by force, compelling them against their will.
record.haqiqah_literal: To overpower, subdue, or compel someone to do something against their will; to coerce or force.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, it denotes the exercise of absolute authority or political domination, as in a ruler who subjugates and coerces the populace. Theologically, it may refer to the divine compelling of souls or events, though classical lexicographers primarily emphasize human coercion. The term 'qaswara' (lion) is derived from this root, metaphorically representing the lion's overwhelming predatory force.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَسْرُ: القَهْرُ على الكُرْه. قَسَرَه يَقْسِرُه قَسْراً واقْتَسَرَه: غَلَبه وقَهَره، وقَسَرَه على الأَمر قَسْراً: أَكرهه عليه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-qasr is overpowering by force against one's will. Qasarahu yaqsiruhu qasran and iqtasarahu mean he overpowered and subdued him. Qasarahu 'ala al-amr qasran means he compelled him to do the matter.

derivations.english_translation: he overpowered, coerced, compelled
overpowering, coercion, compulsion

he overpowered, subdued, coerced

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act of stripping away an outer covering from a thing, thereby exposing what lies beneath; the root denotes the removal of a protective or concealing integument, whether by peeling, flaying, or husking.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical removal of an outer layer or rind from a thing, such as peeling a fruit or stripping bark from a tree; the integument itself, especially the rind or husk of fruit, the skin of a snake, or the outer covering of a garment.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and extended usages include: a thin garment likened to the sloughed skin of a serpent; a snake or tree described as 'qashrāʾ' (peeled/covered only by its integument); and the pistachio termed 'muqashshar' (the peeled one) as a dominant designation. In scholastic and theological contexts, the root may be applied to the stripping away of accidents or veils from a substance to reveal its essential nature, though such usage is analogical rather than primary.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَشْرُ: سَحْقُك الشيء عن دِيهِ. والقِشْرُ: واحد القُشُور، والقِشْرَة أَخص منه. قَشَرَ الشيءَ يَقْشِرُه ويَقْشُره قَشْراً فانْقَشَر وقَشَّرَهُ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Qashr is the stripping of a thing from its outer covering. Al-Qishr is the singular of al-qushūr (peels/rinds), and al-qishrah is more specific than it. One says: qashara al-shayʾa yaqshiruhu wa yaqshuruhu qashran (he peeled the thing), fa-inqashara (and it became peeled), wa qashsharahu (and he peeled it thoroughly).

he peeled or stripped thoroughly (intensive)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ق ط و is the notion of heaviness and slowness in gait — a ponderous, dragging mode of walking. This sensory kernel of weighted movement is the root's primitive semantic nucleus, from which the name of the well-known bird (al-qaṭā) is derived by reason of its sluggish, heavy tread.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is: to walk heavily and slowly (قَطَا يَقْطُو: ثَقُلَ مَشْيُهُ). The noun al-qaṭā denotes the well-known bird (sandgrouse), so named because of the heaviness of its walking; its singular is qaṭāh, and its plural forms are qaṭawāt and qaṭayāt. Its characteristic manner of walking is termed al-iqṭīṭāʾ, expressed in the verb iqṭawṭat al-qaṭāh (the sandgrouse walked in its heavy, dragging fashion).
record.majaz_scholastic: No securely attested metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded in the classical lexical tradition for this root. The semantic field remains confined to the literal domain of heavy, slow locomotion and the ornithonym derived from it. Any extended or figurative application would be secondary and non-canonical; the root exhibits no established majāz in the scholastic or theological register.

canonical_definition.arabic: قَطَا يَقْطُو: ثَقُلَ مَشْيُهُ. وَالقَطَا: طَائِرٌ مَعْرُوفٌ، سُمِّيَ بِذَلِكَ لِثِقَلِ مَشْيِهِ، وَاحِدَتُهُ قَطَاةٌ، وَالجَمْعُ قَطَوَاتٌ وَقَطَيَاتٌ، وَمَشْيُهَا الاقْطِيطَاءُ.
canonical_definition.english: Qaṭā yaqṭū: to walk heavily and slowly. Al-qaṭā is the well-known bird (sandgrouse), so named because of the heaviness of its walking; its singular is qaṭāh, its plurals are qaṭawāt and qaṭayāt, and its manner of walking is al-iqṭīṭāʾ.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a well or spring of abundant, copious water — a source that gushes forth and never runs dry, denoting plenitude and inexhaustible supply.
record.haqiqah_literal: A well (biʾr) that is abundant (ghazīrah) and copious in water (kathīrat al-māʾ); a gushing, overflowing wellspring.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, the term may be applied metaphorically to any person, source, or entity characterized by inexhaustible generosity, abundant knowledge, or overflowing beneficence — a 'fount' of giving. In scholastic and theological usage, it can denote the divine attribute of infinite provision (al-Razzāq) or the superabundant grace (fayḍ) that never ceases. The root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, so the literal-metaphorical boundary is drawn strictly from Lisān al-ʿArab: the ḥaqīqah is the physical well; the majāz is any analogous plenitude.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَلَيْذَمُ: البئر الغزيرة الكثيرة الماء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-qalaydham: the well that is abundant and copious in water.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root قلق is the agitated, unstable motion of a thing that is unsettled from its place—specifically, the restless shifting of a saddle or load upon a camel, or the trembling of a pivot in its socket, indicating a loss of firmness and equilibrium.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is the restlessness and instability of a person, animal, or object: a man is قلق (restless, agitated); a woman is قلقة or مقلاق (restless); a girl whose sash (وشاح) is unsettled; a she-camel whose saddle girth (وضين) is restless; the pivot of a pulley (محور البكرة) trembles; a sick person tosses on his bed; and a camel is made restless by its saddle and gear (أقلق البعير).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root denotes psychological and emotional disquiet: anxiety, unease, and perturbation of the self (الانزعاج). It is used for the agitation caused by grief, fear, or pain (أقلقني الحزن والخوف والرح), and for a state of apprehension and anxiety (به شفق وقلق). In theological and philosophical contexts, it signifies the soul's lack of tranquility and its unsettled movement away from its stable center, often contrasted with سكون (tranquility) and طمأنينة (composure).

canonical_definition.arabic: القَلَقُ: الانزعاج. يقال: بات قَلِقاً، وأقلَقَهُ غيره.
canonical_definition.english: Al-qalaq is agitation/restlessness. It is said: 'He spent the night restless,' and 'someone else made him restless.'

entries.text: رجل قلق: نزق. وامرأة قلقة ومقلاق، وجارية قلق وشاحها، وهي مقلاق الوشاح. وناقة مقلاق الوضين، وسيرتها حتى قلق وضينها، وأقلقت إليك وضن الركائب. وقلق محور البكرة. وقلق المريض على فراشه. وأقلقني الحزن والخوف والرح. وبه شفق وقلق. وأقلق البعير: قلق ما عليه من جهازه وهو قتبه وآلته.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root قمح is the emergence and maturation of wheat-grain within the ear of corn, specifically from the onset of ripening until the grain is fully formed and compacted. From this concrete agricultural image, the root extends to the physical act of raising the head, particularly in refusal or aversion, as when a camel lifts its head away from water.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is: to take roasted barley or other grain in the palm of the hand and raise it to the mouth; to eat a morsel of such grain; and, of a camel, to raise its head away from water, refusing to drink due to aversion, cold, satiety, or some ailment. A camel doing so is described as قَامِح or مُقَامِح, and the two coldest months of winter are called شَهْرَا قِمَاح because camels lift their heads from the cold water during them.
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and theological usage is built on the image of raising the head in refusal. In the Qurʾānic verse 'مُقْمَحُونَ' (Q 36:8), it is a simile for those who are stubbornly averse to submitting to the truth, to accepting guidance, and to spending in the way of God. It is also said to allude to their state on the Day of Resurrection, when iron collars and chains will be around their necks (Q 40:71), forcing their heads upward. The root thus signifies obstinate refusal and the inability to lower the head in submission.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَمْحُ: البُرُّ حين يجري الدقيقُ في السُّنْبُل، وقيل: من لَدُنِ الإِنضاج إِلى الاكتناز. والقَمْحُ: رفع الرأس لسف الشيء، ثم يقال لرفع الرأس كيفما كان: قمح. وقمح البعير: رفع رأسه عن الماء لا يشرب.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Qamḥ: wheat when the flour begins to form in the ear, or from the onset of ripening until full compaction. Al-Qamḥ: the raising of the head to take something; then any raising of the head is called qamḥ. A camel's qamḥ is its raising its head away from water, refusing to drink.

mufradat.text: قال الخليل (3): القمح: البر إذا جرى في السنبل من لدن الإنضاج إلى حين الاكتناز، ويسمى السويق المتخذ منه قميحة، والقمح: رفع الرأس لسف الشيء، ثم يقال لرفع الرأس كيفما كان: قمح، وقمح البعير: رفع رأسه، وأقمحت البعير: شددت رأسه إلى خلف. وقوله: مقمحون [يس/ 8] تشبيه بذلك، ومثل لهم، وقصد إلى وصفهم بالتأبي عن الانقياد للحق، وعن الإذعان لقبول الرشد، والتأبي عن الإنفاق في سبيل الله، وقيل: إشارة إلى حالهم في القيامة إذ الأغلال في أعناقهم والسلاسل [غافر/ 71].

record.ontological_core: The root denotes a man who tolerates or facilitates the illicit sexual conduct of his dependents, specifically a cuckold or procurer (dayyūth); its foundational origin is not pure Arabic but a Syriac loanword, with the variant قنذع (with dhāl) being the more attested form.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a man who is a cuckold or procurer (dayyūth), i.e., one who does not exhibit protective jealousy (ghīrah) over his wife or female relatives and permits their illicit sexual relations.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical or philosophical usage is attested in the classical lexica; the term remains a concrete social-ethical designation. Any extended application to moral laxity or failure of guardianship would be a later rhetorical extension, not a classical majāz.

canonical_definition.arabic: القُنْدُعُ والقُنْدُوعُ: الدَّيُّوثُ، سريانية ليست بعربية محضة، وقد يقال بالدال المهملة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-qunduʿ and al-qundūʿ: the cuckold or procurer (dayyūth); it is Syriac, not pure Arabic, and may also be pronounced with the unpointed dāl.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on elongated extension and unconstrained forward motion, specifically a man walking with loose, unhindered stride, and by extension any entity marked by length or bulk, particularly a large head.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a man walking in an unconstrained, extended manner (مَشى في استرسال); the root also literally denotes something long or tall (الطويل), and a large-headed, bulky creature among camels and mounts (الضخم الرأس من الإبل والدوابّ), comparable to عَنْدَل.
record.majaz_scholastic: No attested metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is recorded in the classical lexical sources; the term remains confined to its literal physical and descriptive applications.

canonical_definition.arabic: قَنْدَل الرجلُ: مَشى في استرسال. والقَنْدَل: الطويل. والقَنْدَل والقُنَادِل: الضخم الرأس من الإبل والدوابّ مثل العَنْدَل.
canonical_definition.english: A man qandala: he walked with an unconstrained, extended stride. Al-qandal: the long or tall one. Al-qandal and al-qunādil: the large-headed, bulky one among camels and mounts, like al-ʿandal.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is not attested in the classical lexical tradition as a productive root; the only recorded form is the nominal قُنْصُل, denoting shortness of stature or a short person, with no established verbal or derivational root family.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to the classical lexica is 'short, of short stature' (قَصِير), applied to a person or thing lacking height.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usages are attested in the classical sources; the term remains a restricted descriptive adjective with no scholastic extension.

canonical_definition.arabic: قُنْصُل: قَصِير.
canonical_definition.english: Qunṣul: short, of short stature.

derivations.english_translation: short, of short stature; a short person

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of inclining or bending toward something, specifically the lowering or turning of the head or hand toward an object, as when a camel lowers its head to drink or a person extends a hand in supplication. This concrete image of orientation toward a source underlies all subsequent semantic developments.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the act of bending or inclining the head, hand, or a vessel toward something, such as a camel lowering its head to a watering trough, a man extending his hands in prayer, or tilting a container to receive water from a stream. It also denotes the physical posture of a mouth with teeth inclined inward.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root signifies contentment and satisfaction with a modest portion of necessary provisions, as in the phrase 'contentment is a treasure' (al-qanāʿah kanz). It further denotes the act of asking or begging, particularly when done without importunity, as in the Quranic term 'al-qāniʿ' (the petitioner who does not persist). Theologically, it expresses the virtue of being satisfied with what God has apportioned, and the derived form 'aqnaʿa' means 'to cause someone to be content.' The root also extends to the notion of inclining toward people in need or supplication, and to the pastoral image of livestock inclining toward pasture.

canonical_definition.arabic: قَنِعَ بنفسه قَنَعاً وقَناعةً: رَضِيَ؛ ورجل قانِعٌ من قوم قُنَّعٍ، وقَنِعٌ من قوم قَنِيعِينَ، وقَنِيعٌ من قوم قَنِيعينَ وقُنَعاءَ. والقناعة: الاجتزاء باليسير من الأعراض المحتاج إليها. وقَنَعَ يقنَع قُنُوعاً: إذا سأل.
canonical_definition.english: Qaniʿa bi-nafsihi qanaʿan wa-qanāʿatan: he was content. A man is qāniʿ (content) from a people qunnaʿ, qaniʿ from a people qanīʿīn, qanīʿ from a people qanīʿīn and qunaʿāʾ. Al-qanāʿah is sufficiency with a little of the necessary provisions. Qanaʿa yaqnaʿu qunūʿan: he asked or begged.

causing contentment; inclining (as in a mouth with inward-slanting teeth)

mufradat.text: القناعة: الاجتزاء باليسير من الأعراض المحتاج إليها. يقال: قنع يقنع قناعة وقنعانا: إذا رضي، وقنع يقنع قنوعا: إذا سأل (4). قال تعالى: وأطعموا القانع والمعتر [الحج/ 36]. قال بعضهم (5): القانع هو السائل الذي لا يلح في السؤال، ويرضى بما يأتيه عفوا، قال الشاعر: العبد حر إن قنع والحر عبد إن قنع فاقنع ولا تقنع فما شيء يشين سوى الطمع 372- لمال المرء يصلحه فيغني مفاقره أعف من القنوع (1) وأقنع رأسه: رفعه. قال تعالى: مقنعي رؤسهم [إبراهيم/ 43] وقال بعضهم: أصل هذه الكلمة من القناع، وهو ما يغطى به الرأس، فقنع، أي: لبس القناع ساترا لفقره كقولهم: خفي، أي: لبس الخفاء، وقنع: إذا رفع قناعه كاشفا رأسه بالسؤال نحو خفى إذا رفع الخفاء، ومن القناعة قولهم: رجل مقنع يقنع به، وجمعه: مقانع. قال الشاعر: 373- شهودي على ليلى عدول مقانع (2) ومن القناع قيل: تقنعت المرأة، وتقنع الرجل: إذا لبس المغفر تشبيها بتقنع المرأة، وقنعت رأسه بالسيف والسوط.

entries.text: العز في القناعة والذل في القنوع وهو السؤال. وفلان قنع بالمعيشة وقنيع وقنوع وقانع. أنشد الكسائي: فإن ملكت كفاك قوطا فكن به ... قنيعا فإن المت Metaphorical (Majaz): أقنع صوته: رفعه. قال الراعي: زجل الحداء كأن في حيزومه ... قصبا ومقنعة الحنين عجولا وثكلى رافعة حنينها. وقنعت رأسه بالعصا وبالسوط. وكشف قناعه

العز في القناعة والذل في القنوع وهو السؤال. وفلان قنع بالمعيشة وقنيع وقنوع وقانع. أنشد الكسائي: فإن ملكت كفاك قوطا فكن به ... قنيعا فإن المتقي الله قانع وقنع بالشيء واقتنع وتقنع. وأقنعك الله بما أعطاك. وفلان حريص ما يقنعه شيء. وقنع إليه: سأله وهو من قنعت الماشية للمرتع: مالت إليه

أقنع صوته: رفعه. قال الراعي: زجل الحداء كأن في حيزومه ... قصبا ومقنعة الحنين عجولا وثكلى رافعة حنينها. وقنعت رأسه بالعصا وبالسوط. وكشف قناعه وألقى جلبابه. وقنعته خزية وعارا، وتقنع من الخزية. قال: وإني بحمد الله لا ثوب عاجز ... لبست ولا من خزية أقتنع وتقنعوا في الحديد، وهو مقنع با

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root قنفش is the act of contraction, shriveling, or drawing together into a compact, wrinkled mass, coupled with the rapid, forceful gathering of a thing. It denotes a sudden, tight coalescence—whether of a body shrinking upon itself or of objects being swept together swiftly.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is contraction (التقبض) and rapid gathering (الجمع السريع). It describes a person or animal that is shriveled, tightly drawn together, or a thing that has been snatched up and collected in haste. It also denotes a small creeping creature (دويبة), likely so named for its contracted, compact form.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, it is applied to an old woman (عجوز قنفشة) to describe her as hunched, shriveled, and contracted by age. It is also used in the phrase مُقَنْفِشاً لحيته (with his beard bristling or drawn together), indicating a posture of aggression, defiance, or intense concentration. In scholastic usage, it conveys the idea of a sudden, defensive, or avaricious withdrawal into oneself, or the hasty, disordered accumulation of something.

canonical_definition.arabic: القَنْفَشَةُ: التقبُّضُ. وعجوز قِنْفِشَةٌ: مُتَقبِّضةٌ. وقَنْفَشَ الشيءَ: جمعه سريعاً. والقِنْفِشَةُ: دُوَيْبّة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Qanfashah: contraction. An old woman who is qinfishah: shriveled/contracted. Qanfasha al-shayʾ: he gathered the thing quickly. Al-Qinfishah: a small creeping creature.

derivations.english_translation: contraction; shriveling; rapid gathering
a shriveled old woman; a small creeping creature
to contract; to gather quickly; to snatch up
one who is contracted, bristling, or drawn together (e.g., the beard)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the withdrawal or recession of appetite from food — a turning-away of the desiring faculty from nourishment, whether from satiety, distaste, or a constitutional diminution of hunger, without organic disease.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the cessation or retreat of the appetite for food, such that one turns away from eating; it is said of a man of little food-intake: qad aqhā wa-qad aqham.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and ethical usage, the root denotes the deliberate withholding of the appetitive faculty from what is present and desired — the case in which one is able to eat but refrains though still craving it. This is distinguished from the pathological loss of appetite and from the mere absence of hunger; it thus borders on the ethical discipline of restraining the concupiscible appetite (al-shahwah) and is compared to aqham, which carries the additional sense of aversion or loathing.

canonical_definition.arabic: أَقْهى عن الطعام واقْتَهى: ارتدَّت شهوتُه عنه من غير مرض، مثل أَقْهَمَ؛ يقال للرجل القليل الطُّعم: قد أَقْهَى وقد أَقْهَم، وقيل: هو أَن يقدر على الطعام فلا يأَكله وإِن كان مشتهياً له.
canonical_definition.english: Aqhā ʿan al-ṭaʿām and iqtahā: his appetite receded from it without disease, like aqham; it is said of a man of little food-intake: qad aqhā wa-qad aqham. It is also said to be that he is able to eat but does not eat it, even though he craves it.

derivations.english_translation: to turn away from food; to lose or withdraw the appetite for eating
to have one's appetite recede from food without illness
to be averse to food; to have little appetite
withdrawal of appetite; aversion to food

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on massive, engulfing bulk — specifically the image of a creature or beast of enormous size that swallows and devours everything, and by extension the towering, raging male camel (al-faḥl al-ḍakhm al-mughtalim). The quadriliteral reduplicative form (القَهْقَمّ) itself iconically reinforces the sense of heaving, repetitive engulfment.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Lisān al-ʿArab, is: a being or beast that swallows everything (al-ladhī yabtaliʿu kulla shayʾ); and a huge, raging stallion-camel (al-faḥl al-ḍakhm al-mughtalim). Abū ʿAmr records القَهْقَبّ and القَهْقَمّ as synonyms for the enormous camel (al-jamal al-ḍakhm).
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah. In scholastic and rhetorical usage, the term may be extended metaphorically (majāz) to denote any person or entity of insatiable, all-consuming appetite or overwhelming, destructive force — e.g., a tyrant, a devouring army, or an intellect that absorbs all knowledge. The reduplicative quadriliteral pattern (فَعْلَلّ) carries an intensifying, hyperbolic force (mubālaghah), making the majāz extension natural in classical Arabic rhetoric.

canonical_definition.arabic: القِهْقَمُّ: الذي يبتلع كل شيء. والقَهْقَمُ: الفحل الضخم المغتلم. وقال أبو عمرو: القَهْقَبُّ والقَهْقَمُّ: الجمل الضخم.
canonical_definition.english: Al-qihqamm: the one who swallows everything. Al-qahqam: the huge, raging stallion-camel. Abū ʿAmr said: al-qahqabb and al-qahqamm: the enormous camel.

derivations.english_translation: one who swallows everything; a huge, raging stallion-camel
a huge camel (synonym of قَهْقَمّ, per Abū ʿAmr)
to swallow up, to devour (denominal verb, inferred)
the act of swallowing up or devouring (verbal noun, inferred)

record.ontological_core: The root ك ب ه (k-b-h) is not attested in the classical lexical tradition as an independent root with a stable physical origin (aṣl al-wadʿ). Its sole documented occurrence is a dialectal phonetic variant in which the initial ج (jīm) of جَبْهة (forehead) is shifted toward the kāf's articulation point, yielding كَبْهة. The root therefore has no autonomous ontological core; it is a phonological reflex of ج ب ه (j-b-h), whose foundational physical referent is the broad, flat frontal surface of the face.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the forehead (al-jabha), specifically a broad, wide forehead (ʿarīḍ al-jabha). The form كَبْهة is not an independent lexical item but a dialectal pronunciation of جَبْهة, produced by fronting the jīm from its palatal articulation point toward the kāf's velar articulation point. This substitution is attested among certain Arab tribes and was recorded by Sībawayh alongside six other letters subject to analogous shifts.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical, philosophical, or theological extension is attested for this root in the classical sources. The only contextual usage is the Prophetic description of the Dajjāl as a man of broad forehead (ʿarīḍ al-kabha), where the dialectal form كَبْهة substitutes for جَبْهة. The term carries no abstract, ethical, or metaphysical signification; it remains strictly a physiognomic descriptor within an eschatological narrative.

canonical_definition.arabic: الكَبْهةُ: لغةٌ في الجَبْهةِ، وهي الجبهةُ العريضةُ؛ أَخرجَ الجيمَ بين مَخرجِها ومَخرجِ الكافِ، وهي لغةٌ لقومٍ من العرب، ذكرها سيبويه مع ستةِ أحرفٍ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-kabha: a dialectal variant of al-jabha (the forehead), denoting a broad forehead; the jīm is articulated between its own point of articulation and that of the kāf. It is a dialect of certain Arab tribes, recorded by Sībawayh alongside six other letters.

derivations.english_translation: forehead (dialectal variant of جَبْهة, with jīm fronted toward kāf)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act of joining one surface to another by stitching or sewing, as in sewing a waterskin or fastening the two lips of a beast with a ring; hence the primary image is that of bringing separate edges together into a single bounded unit.
record.haqiqah_literal: To sew or stitch one piece of leather to another; to join the two edges of a waterskin or the two lips of an animal by a ring; by extension, to join letters to one another in writing, and to set down words in a written line.
record.majaz_scholastic: By established usage, the joining of letters by script; then any joining of words by speech, even without writing. Thus the speech of God is called kitāb though it is not written, and the term kitāb is applied to the revealed scripture, to the sheet containing writing, and to the act of writing itself. The root also yields the sense of prescription, decree, and inscribing upon the self, as in the theological notion of God's writing deeds upon the servant.

canonical_definition.arabic: الكِتابُ: معروف، والجمع كُتُبٌ وكُتْبٌ. كَتَبَ الشيءَ يَكْتُبه كَتْباً وكِتاباً وكِتابةً، وكَتَّبَه: خَطَّه. وأصل الكتابة: ضم أديم إلى أديم بالخياطة، ثم استعير لضم الحروف بعضها إلى بعض بالخط.
canonical_definition.english: Kitāb is a well-known term; its plurals are kutub and kutb. He wrote the thing, writing it with a writing, a book, and a writing. He inscribed it: he traced it. The original sense of writing is the joining of one piece of leather to another by stitching; then it was metaphorically extended to the joining of letters to one another by script.

derivations.english_translation: he wrote; he joined by stitching
book, scripture, writing, letter
writing, act of writing, scribal craft
books, writings
books, writings
writer, scribe
written, inscribed, that which is written
he wrote out, he inscribed, he caused to write
writing, act of writing

mufradat.text: الكتب: ضم أديم إلى أديم بالخياطة، يقال: كتبت السقاء، وكتبت البغلة: جمعت بين شفريها بحلقة، وفي التعارف ضم الحروف بعضها إلى بعض بالخط، وقد يقال ذلك للمضموم بعضها إلى بعض باللفظ، فالأصل في الكتابة: النظم بالخط لكن يستعار كل واحد للآخر، ولهذا سمي كلام الله- وإن لم يكتب- كتابا كقوله: الم* ذلك الكتاب [البقرة/ 1- 2]، وقوله: قال إني عبد الله آتاني الكتاب [مريم/ 30]. والكتاب في الأصل مصدر، ثم سمي المكتوب فيه كتابا، والكتاب في الأصل اسم للصحيفة مع المكتوب فيه، وفي قوله: يسئلك أهل الكتاب أن تنزل عليهم كتابا من السماء [النساء/ 153] فإنه يعني صحيفة فيها كتابة، ولهذا قال: ولو نزلنا عليك كتابا في قرطاس الآية [الأنعام/ 7]. ويعبر عن الإثبات والتقدير والإيجاب والفرض والعزم بالكتابة، ووجه ذلك أن الشيء يراد، ثم يقال، ثم يكتب، فالإرادة مبدأ، والكتابة منتهى. ثم يعبر عن المراد الذي هو المبدأ إذا أريد توكيده بالكتابة التي هي المنتهى، قال: كتب الله لأغلبن أنا ورسلي [المجادلة/ 21]، وقال تعالى: قل لن يصيبنا إلا ما كتب الله لنا [التوبة/ 51]، لبرز الذين كتب عليهم القتل [آل عمران/ 154]، وقال: وأولوا الأرحام بعضهم أولى ببعض في كتاب الله* [الأنفال/ 75] أي: في حكمه، وقوله: وكتبنا عليهم فيها أن النفس بالنفس [المائدة/ 45] أي: أوجبنا وفرضنا، وكذلك قوله: كتب عليكم إذا حضر أحدكم الموت [البقرة/ 180]، وقوله: كتب عليكم الصيام [البقرة/ 183]، لم كتبت علينا القتال [النساء/ 77]، ما كتبناها عليهم [الحديد/ 27]، لو لا أن كتب الله عليهم الجلاء [الحشر/ 3] أي: لو لا أن أوجب الله عليهم الإخلاء لديارهم، ويعبر بالكتابة عن القضاء الممضى، وما يصير في حكم الممضى، وعلى هذا حمل قوله: بلى ورسلنا لديهم يكتبون [الزخرف/ 80] قيل: ذلك مثل قوله: يمحوا الله ما يشاء ويثبت [الرعد/ 39]، وقوله: أولئك كتب في قلوبهم الإيمان وأيدهم بروح منه [المجادلة/ 22] فإشارة منه إلى أنهم بخلاف من وصفهم بقوله: ولا تطع من أغفلنا قلبه عن ذكرنا [الكهف/ 28]، لأن معنى «أغفلنا» من قولهم: أغفلت الكتاب: إذا جعلته خاليا من الكتابة ومن الإعجام، وقوله: فلا كفران لسعيه وإنا له كاتبون [الأنبياء/ 94] فإشارة إلى أن ذلك مثبت له ومجازى به. وقوله: فاكتبنا مع الشاهدين* [آل عمران/ 53] أي: اجعلنا في زمرتهم إشارة إلى قوله: فأولئك مع الذين أنعم الله عليهم ... الآية [النساء/ 69] وقوله: ما لهذا الكتاب لا يغادر صغيرة ولا كبيرة إلا أحصاها [الكهف/ 49] فقيل إشارة إلى ما أثبت فيه أعمال العباد. وقوله: إلا في كتاب من قبل أن نبرأها [الحديد/ 22] قيل: إشارة إلى اللوح المحفوظ، وكذا قوله: إن ذلك في كتاب إن ذلك على الله يسير [الحج/ 70]، وقوله: ولا رطب ولا يابس إلا في كتاب مبين [الأنعام/ 59]، في الكتاب مسطورا* [الإسراء/ 58]، لو لا كتاب من الله سبق [الأنفال/ 68] يعني به ما قدره من الحكمة، وذلك إشارة إلى قوله: كتب ربكم على نفسه الرحمة [الأنعام/ 54] وقيل: إشارة إلى قوله: وما كان الله ليعذبهم وأنت فيهم [الأنفال/ 33]، وقوله: لن يصيبنا إلا ما كتب الله لنا [التوبة/ 51] يعني: ما قدره وقضاه، وذكر «لنا» ولم يقل «علينا» تنبيها أن كل ما يصيبنا نعده نعمة لنا، ولا نعده نقمة علينا، وقوله: ادخلوا الأرض المقدسة التي كتب الله لكم [المائدة/ 21] قيل: معنى ذلك وهبها الله لكم، ثم حرمها عليكم بامتناعكم من دخولها وقبولها، وقيل: كتب لكم بشرط أن تدخلوها، وقيل: أوجبها عليكم، وإنما قال: «لكم» ولم يقل: «عليكم» لأن دخولهم إياها يعود عليهم بنفع عاجل وآجل، فيكون ذلك لهم لا عليهم، وذلك كقولك لمن يرى تأذيا بشيء لا يعرف نفع مآله: هذا الكلام لك لا عليك، وقوله: وجعل كلمة الذين كفروا السفلى وكلمة الله هي العليا [التوبة/ 40] جعل حكمهم وتقديرهم ساقطا مضمحلا، وحكم الله عاليا لا دافع له ولا مانع، وقال تعالى: وقال الذين أوتوا العلم والإيمان لقد لبثتم في كتاب الله إلى يوم البعث [الروم/ 56] أي: في علمه وإيجابه وحكمه، وعلى ذلك قوله: لكل أجل كتاب [الرعد/ 38]، وقوله: إن عدة الشهور عند الله اثنا عشر شهرا في كتاب الله [التوبة/ 36] أي: في حكمه. ويعبر بالكتاب عن الحجة الثابتة من جهة الله نحو: ومن الناس من يجادل في الله بغير علم ولا هدى ولا كتاب منير* [الحج/ 8]، أم آتيناهم كتابا من قبله [الزخرف/ 21]، فأتوا بكتابكم [الصافات/ 157]، أوتوا الكتاب* [البقرة/ 144] (1)، كتاب الله* [النساء/ 24]، أم آتيناهم كتابا* [فاطر/ 40]، فهم يكتبون* [الطور/ 41] فذلك إشارة إلى العلم والتحقق والاعتقاد، وقوله: وابتغوا ما كتب الله لكم [البقرة/ 187] إشارة في تحري النكاح إلى لطيفة، وهي أن الله جعل لنا شهوة النكاح لنتحرى طلب النسل الذي يكون سببا لبقاء نوع الإنسان إلى غاية قدرها، فيجب للإنسان أن يتحرى بالنكاح ما جعل الله له على حسب مقتضى العقل والديانة، ومن تحرى بالنكاح حفظ النسل وحصانة النفس على الوجه المشروع فقد ابتغى ما كتب الله له، وإلى هذا أشار من قال: عنى بما كتب الله لكم الولد (1)، ويعبر عن الإيجاد بالكتابة، وعن الإزالة والإفناء بالمحو. قال: لكل أجل كتاب [الرعد/ 38]، يمحوا الله ما يشاء ويثبت [الرعد/ 39] نبه أن لكل وقت إيجادا، وهو يوجد ما تقتضي الحكمة إيجاده، ويزيل ما تقتضي الحكمة إزالته، ودل قوله: لكل أجل كتاب [الرعد/ 38] على نحو ما دل عليه قوله: كل يوم هو في شأن [الرحمن/ 29] وقوله: وعنده أم الكتاب [الرعد/ 39]، وقوله: وإن منهم لفريقا يلوون ألسنتهم بالكتاب لتحسبوه من الكتاب وما هو من الكتاب [آل عمران/ 78] فالكتاب الأول: ما كتبوه بأيديهم المذكور في قوله: فويل للذين يكتبون الكتاب بأيديهم [البقرة/ 79]. والكتاب الثاني: التوراة، والثالث: لجنس كتب الله، أي: ما هو من شيء من كتب الله سبحانه وتعالى [وكلامه] (2)، وقوله: وإذ آتينا موسى الكتاب والفرقان [البقرة/ 53] فقد قيل: هما عبارتان عن التوراة، وتسميتها كتابا اعتبارا بما أثبت فيها من الأحكام، وتسميتها فرقانا اعتبارا بما فيها من الفرق بين الحق والباطل. وقوله: وما كان لنفس أن تموت إلا بإذن الله كتابا مؤجلا [آل عمران/ 145] أي: حكما لو لا كتاب من الله سبق لمسكم [الأنفال/ 68]، وقوله: إن عدة الشهور عند الله اثنا عشر شهرا في كتاب الله [التوبة/ 36] كل ذلك حكم منه. وأما قوله: فويل للذين يكتبون الكتاب بأيديهم [البقرة/ 79] فتنبيه أنهم يختلقونه ويفتعلونه، وكما نسب الكتاب المختلق إلى أيديهم نسب المقال المختلق إلى أفواههم، فقال: ذلك قولهم بأفواههم [التوبة/ 30] والاكتتاب متعارف في المختلق نحو قوله: أساطير الأولين اكتتبها [الفرقان/ 5]. وحيثما ذكر الله تعالى أهل الكتاب فإنما أراد بالكتاب التوراة والإنجيل، أو إياهما جميعا، وقوله: وما كان هذا القرآن أن يفترى إلى قوله: وتفصيل الكتاب [يونس/ 37] (3)، فإنما أراد بالكتاب هاهنا ما تقدم من كتب الله دون القرآن، ألا ترى أنه جعل القرآن مصدقا له، وقوله: وهو الذي أنزل إليكم الكتاب مفصلا [الأنعام/ 114] فمنهم من قال: هو القرآن، ومنهم من قال: هو القرآن وغيره من الحجج والعلم والعقل (1)، وكذلك قوله: فالذين آتيناهم الكتاب يؤمنون به [العنكبوت/ 47]، وقوله: قال الذي عنده علم من الكتاب [النمل/ 40] فقد قيل: أريد به علم الكتاب، وقيل: علم من العلوم التي آتاها الله سليمان في كتابه المخصوص به، وبه سخر له كل شيء، وقوله: وتؤمنون بالكتاب كله [آل عمران/ 119] أي: بالكتب المنزلة، فوضع ذلك موضع الجمع، إما لكونه جنسا كقولك: كثر الدرهم في أيدي الناس، أو لكونه في الأصل مصدرا نحو: عدل، وذلك كقوله: يؤمنون بما أنزل إليك وما أنزل من قبلك* [البقرة/ 4] وقيل: يعني أنهم ليسوا كمن قيل فيهم: ويقولون نؤمن ببعض ونكفر ببعض [النساء/ 150]. وكتابة العبد: ابتياع نفسه من سيده بما يؤديه من كسبه، قال: والذين يبتغون الكتاب مما ملكت أيمانكم فكاتبوهم [النور/ 33] واشتقاقها يصح أن يكون من الكتابة التي هي الإيجاب، وأن
