يكون من الكتب الذي هو النظم والإنسان يفعل ذلك.

entries.text: كتب الكتاب يكتبه كتبة وكتابا وكتابة وكتبا، وا

record.ontological_core: A quadriliteral nominal stem denoting a specific plant or herb; its foundational physical origin is the concrete botanical referent designated by the name, without a productive verbal root in classical usage.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the plant or herb named كَحْلَب; it is a concrete botanical entity, not a derived verbal action or abstract quality.
record.majaz_scholastic: No established metaphorical, philosophical, or theological usage is attested in the classical philological tradition; the term remains a concrete nominal designation for a plant.

canonical_definition.arabic: كَحْلَبٌ: اسم.
canonical_definition.english: Kaḥlab: a noun (name of a plant).

derivations.english_translation: a plant or herb so named; a botanical name

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the retardation, delay, or sluggishness of a natural process — specifically, the tardiness of the earth in bringing forth its vegetation, such that the soil remains barren or slow to sprout despite its latent fertility.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Lisān al-ʿArab, is the delayed or sluggish emergence of vegetation from the earth: كَدَت الأَرض تَكْدو كَدْواً وكُدُوًّا, فهي كاديةٌ — 'The earth was slow to vegetate, hence it is kādiyah (sluggish/barren in sprouting).' The concrete referent is a tract of land whose herbage is late in appearing.
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension (majāz), the root's semantic nucleus of 'sluggishness in bringing forth' is transferred from the soil to any process, faculty, or agent whose productive or cognitive output is retarded. In scholastic and philosophical usage, it may describe the tardiness of a faculty (e.g., a sluggish intellect or a delayed apprehension), the inertia of a substance in actualizing its potential, or the reluctance of an agent to effect its proper operation. The majāz preserves the literal image of a fertile ground that withholds its yield, mapping it onto ontological or epistemological delay.

canonical_definition.arabic: كَدَت الأَرض تَكْدو كَدْواً وكُدُوًّا، فهي كاديةٌ إِذا أَبطأَ نباتها.
canonical_definition.english: The earth was slow to vegetate with a kadw or kudūw, so it is kādiyah when its vegetation is tardy.

derivations.english_translation: to be slow, tardy, or sluggish (said of the earth in producing vegetation)
slowness, tardiness (in the emergence of vegetation)
sluggishness, delayed productivity (of the soil)
slow to vegetate, barren or tardy in sprouting (said of land)

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the violent bringing-down of a body to the ground, i.e. throwing someone down prostrate, together with a rapid, jolting forward motion in walking; the two senses share the primitive image of abrupt downward or forward displacement of the body.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is: كَرْتَحَه 'he threw him down, prostrated him, cast him to the ground'; and كَرْتَح في مشيه 'he hastened, moved swiftly in his walking'.
record.majaz_scholastic: Not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah; no established philosophical or theological majāz is recorded. Any extended use would be secondary and non-canonical, since the root remains confined to the concrete physical senses of throwing down and rapid motion.

canonical_definition.arabic: كَرْتَحه: صَرَعَه. وكَرْتَح في مشيه: أَسرع.
canonical_definition.english: Kartaḥahu: he threw him down, prostrated him. And kartaḥa fī mashyihi: he hastened in his walking.

derivations.english_translation: to throw down, prostrate, cast to the ground; to hasten in walking
the act of throwing down or prostrating; swift, jolting movement
one who throws down or prostrates; one who hastens in walking

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act of striking the rear or hindquarters of a person or thing with the hand, foot, or an instrument, driving forward from behind.
record.haqiqah_literal: To strike with the hand or foot, specifically with the front of the foot, upon the posterior of a person or object; to smite the hindquarters.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and extended usages include: (1) to pursue and strike the rear of an enemy with a sword, i.e., to attack from behind; (2) to strike a she-camel's udder with cold water to drive milk back to her body, thereby strengthening her; (3) to retort to someone's speech with a painful word, i.e., to strike back verbally; (4) of horses: to tuck their tails between their legs (اكتسع), indicating retreat or submission; (5) proverbial: 'the regret of al-Kasʿī' (ندامة الكسعي), denoting belated and futile remorse.

canonical_definition.arabic: الكَسْعُ: أَنْ تَضْرِبَ بيدك أَو برجلك بصدر قدمك على دبر إِنسان أَو شيء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Kasʿ: to strike with your hand or foot, using the front of your foot, upon the posterior of a person or thing.

derivations.english_translation: he struck the rear, he smote the hindquarters
the act of striking the posterior with hand or foot
one who strikes the rear; (of a horse) one that tucks its tail between its legs
instrument for striking the rear, e.g., a stick or goad
to tuck one's tail between the legs (said of a horse); to be struck on the rear
horses that tuck their tails between their legs

entries.text: كسعه: ضربه بيده أو برجله على دبره. وكسع الغلام الدوامة بالمكسع. وكسع الناقة بغبرها: ضرب أخلافها بالماء البارد ليتراد اللبن في ظهرها فيكون أشد لها. واتبع آثارهم يكسعهم بالسيف، ويكسع أدبارهم، وكسعت الرجل بما ساءه إذا تكلم فرميته على أثر كلامه بكلمة تسوءه. وكسعت الخيل بأذنابها واكتس

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) denotes co-lying, the act of two bodies sharing a single resting-place or bed, and by extension the intimate companion who shares that bed.
record.haqiqah_literal: Literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah: كَامَعَ المرأَةَ signifies he lay with the woman as a bedfellow; الكِمْع and الكَمِيع denote the bedfellow or consort.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and extended usage: the term is applied to the husband as the wife's bedfellow (كَمِيعُها), and by further extension to any intimate companion or close associate. The poet ʿAntarah employs it figuratively for his sword as his constant companion in battle: وسَيْفِي كالعَقِيقة، فهْو كِمْعِي.

canonical_definition.arabic: كامَعَ المرأَةَ: ضَاجَعَها، والكِمْعُ والكَمِيعُ: الضَّجِيعُ؛ ومنه قيل للزوج: هو كَمِيعُها.
canonical_definition.english: He lay with the woman as a bedfellow; الكِمْع and الكَمِيع denote the bedfellow; hence the husband is called her كَمِيع (bedfellow).

derivations.english_translation: he lay with as a bedfellow, he cohabited with
bedfellow, consort, intimate companion
bedfellow, consort, spouse

entries.text: هو كمعها وكميعها: ضجيعها، وكامعها.
بات السيف كميعي.
هو كمعها وكميعها: ضجيعها، وكامعها. Metaphorical (Majaz): بات السيف كميعي.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the designation of a specific bird, the magpie (Pica pica), a corvid known for its harsh chattering call and its reputation in classical Arabic lore as a creature of ill omen and innate malevolence.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the magpie (العَقْعَق), a black-and-white bird of the crow family, characterized by its noisy, chattering cry and its association with mischief and bad luck.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic usages: The term is employed in proverbial expressions to denote extreme wickedness or malevolence, as in the phrase 'أَخْبَثُ مِنْ كُنْدُشٍ' (more malignant than a magpie). In theological and ethical discourse, it may serve as a parabolic figure for a person of corrupt nature or a harbinger of discord, though such extensions remain rooted in the literal avian referent and are not attested in the major lexicons as independent abstract concepts.

canonical_definition.arabic: الكُنْدُشُ: العَقْعَقُ. قال ابن الأَعرابي: أَخبرني المفضّل يقال هو أَخبَثُ من كُنْدُشٍ، وهو العَقْقعَق.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Kundush: the magpie. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: Al-Mufaḍḍal informed me that it is said, 'He is more malignant than a kundush,' which is the magpie.

derivations.english_translation: magpie (the bird)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root ل ح ص is the constriction and closure of a narrow aperture, specifically the eye of a needle, such that passage through it is blocked. The root thus denotes the state of being tightly closed, narrow, or impenetrable.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in Asās al-Balāghah, is the closing or sealing of the eye of a needle (خَرْتُ الإبرة), i.e., its becoming blocked and impassable.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension, the root is applied metaphorically to any confined, narrow, or straitened space, such as a cramped grave or a tight dwelling. In classical usage, the derived forms لَحْص, لَحَص, and لَحِيص all denote constriction and narrowness, whether physical or circumstantial. The theological or philosophical application is minimal; the term remains primarily descriptive of spatial and material confinement.

canonical_definition.arabic: اللَّحْصُ واللَّحَصُ واللَّحِيصُ: الضَّيِّقُ. والتحص خرت الإبرة: انسد.
canonical_definition.english: Al-laḥṣ, al-laḥaṣ, and al-laḥīṣ: the narrow. And the closing of the eye of a needle: it became blocked.

derivations.english_translation: narrowness, constriction; a tight or confined place
narrowness, constriction; a tight or confined place
very narrow, tightly confined; a cramped space (as in a grave)

entries.text: التحص خرت الإبرة: انسد.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ل-ح-ط is the act of sprinkling or scattering water upon a surface, specifically a door or wall, as a practical measure of dust suppression, cooling, or ritual cleansing.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is to sprinkle water on the door of one's house, as attested in the report that ʿAlī passed by a group who were sprinkling water on the door of their dwelling.
record.majaz_scholastic: No metaphorical or scholastic extensions are attested in the classical lexica; the root remains confined to its concrete physical application of sprinkling water.

canonical_definition.arabic: اللَّحْطُ: الرَّشُّ. يقال: لَحَطَ بابَ دارِه إِذا رَشَّه بالماء.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Laḥṭ is the sprinkling of water. It is said: he sprinkled water on the door of his house.

derivations.english_translation: he sprinkled (water) on the door of his house
the act of sprinkling water

record.ontological_core: The root لشش denotes lightness, agility, and rapid, unencumbered motion. Its foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the quality of being light in weight or movement, often applied to a person's constitution or gait. It is a rare root in Arabic, with the sequence of ش after ل being uncommon, as noted by classical philologists.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is 'lightness' or 'agility' in a person, as in رجل لَشْلاشٌ (a light, agile man). It also denotes the rapid, repeated movement or trembling associated with lightness, as in اللَّشْلَشَةُ (frequent, quick motion).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically, the root extends to describe intellectual quickness or fickleness, though such usage is not extensively attested in classical theological or philosophical texts. The primary metaphorical application is to denote a lack of seriousness or stability, derived from the physical sense of lightness.

canonical_definition.arabic: قال الخليل: ليس في كلام العرب شين بعد لام ولكن كلها قبل اللام. قال الأزهري: وقد وُجِد في كلامهم الشين بعد اللام. قال ابن الأعرابي وغيره: رجل لَشْلاشٌ إذا كان خفيفاً. قال الليث: اللَّشْلَشَةُ كثرةُ الحركة.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Khalīl said: There is no shīn after lām in Arabic speech; rather, they all occur before lām. Al-Azharī said: But shīn after lām has been found in their speech. Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: A man is lashlāsh when he is light. Al-Layth said: Al-lashlashah is frequent movement.

derivations.english_translation: light, agile, quick-moving (of a person)
lightness, agility; frequent, rapid motion

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ل-غ-ا is the emission of unstructured, non-referential sound — specifically the chirping of sparrows and similar birds — which carries no semantic weight, no deliberative intent, and no consequential effect. From this acoustic substrate, the root extends to any utterance or act that is discarded, unaccounted for, and yields no benefit.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is sound that is mere noise: the twittering of sparrows and other birds, and by extension any speech emitted without reflection or deliberation, falling outside the domain of intentional, meaningful discourse. It is the acoustic residue that carries no informational or practical payload.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root denotes: (1) speech that is vain, idle, or obscene — utterances that are not contracted upon (غير معقود عليه), i.e., not bound to any truth-claim, obligation, or benefit; (2) acts that are null, void, or legally inconsequential, such as an oath uttered without intent (لغو اليمين), which carries no expiation; (3) in theological and philosophical discourse, the accidental or non-essential in speech and action — that which is neither truth nor falsehood, neither virtue nor vice, but mere surplus. The majāz moves from the acoustic to the ethical and juridical: from birdsong to the voiding of moral and legal accountability.

canonical_definition.arabic: اللَّغْو واللَّغا: السَّقَط وما لا يُعتدّ به من كلام وغيره، ولا يُحصَل منه على فائدة ولا نفع. وقيل: هو ما كان من الكلام غير معقود عليه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-laghw and al-laghā: the discarded and the unaccounted-for in speech and otherwise, from which no benefit or utility is obtained. It is also said: that which is of speech not contracted upon.

derivations.english_translation: vain, idle, or obscene speech; that which is not contracted upon; unaccounted-for utterance
to speak vainly or idly; to utter nonsense; (of a bird) to chirp
vain or idle talk; speech not bound to any consequence
to speak falsely or vainly; to err in speech
language, dialect, or idiom (originally: a mode of speech, from the same root of utterance)

mufradat.text: اللغو من الكلام: ما لا يعتد به، وهو الذي يورد لا عن روية وفكر، فيجري مجرى اللغا، وهو صوت العصافير ونحوها من الطيور، قال أبو عبيدة: لغو ولغا، نحو: عيب وعاب وأنشدهم: 407- عن اللغا ورفث التكلم (5) يقال: لغيت تلغى. نحو: لقيت تلقى، وقد يسمى كل كلام قبيح لغوا. قال: لا يسمعون فيها لغوا ولا كذابا [النبأ/ 35]، وقال: وإذا سمعوا اللغو أعرضوا عنه [القصص/ 55]، لا يسمعون فيها لغوا ولا تأثيما [الواقعة/ 25]، وقال: والذين هم عن اللغو معرضون [المؤمنون/ 3]، وقوله: وإذا مروا باللغو مروا كراما [الفرقان/ 72]، أي: كنوا عن القبيح لم يصرحوا، وقيل: معناه: إذا صادفوا أهل اللغو لم يخوضوا معهم. ويستعمل اللغو فيما لا يعتد به، ومنه اللغو في الأيمان. أي: ما لا عقد عليه، وذلك ما يجري وصلا للكلام بضرب من العادة. قال: لا يؤاخذكم الله باللغو في أيمانكم* [البقرة/ 225] ومن هذا أخذ الشاعر ورب أسراب حجيج كظم فقال: 408- ولست بمأخوذ بلغو تقوله إذا لم تعمد عاقدات العزائم (1) وقوله: لا تسمع فيها لاغية [الغاشية/ 11] أي: لغوا، فجعل اسم الفاعل وصفا للكلام نحو: كاذبة، وقيل لما لا يعتد به في الدية من الإبل: لغو، وقال الشاعر: 409- كما ألغيت في الدية الحوارا (2) ولغي بكذا. أي: لهج به لهج العصفور بلغاه. أي: بصوته، ومنه قيل للكلام الذي يلهج به فرقة فرقة: لغة.

record.ontological_core: The root is not a trilateral lexical root but a primitive particle (ḥarf) whose foundational linguistic function is referential indeterminacy: it designates an unspecified entity, quantity, or proposition, and from this core radiate the functions of negation, interrogation, conditionality, relative connection, and generic predication.
record.haqiqah_literal: In its literal, non-metaphorical usage, ما is a particle of negation (ḥarf nafy), as in ما فعل (he did not do); it may also function as a relative pronoun equivalent to الذي (that which), as a conditional particle, as an expression covering all categories of the indefinite (ʿibārah ʿan jamīʿ anwāʿ al-nakirah), as a substitute for مَنْ (who), and as a particle of interrogation (istifhām). In certain dialectal or phonological contexts, the final alif may be replaced by hāʾ, yielding مَهْ.
record.majaz_scholastic: Scholastic and philosophical usage extends ما beyond simple negation or relativization into the domain of logical quantification and ontological predication. In kalām and falsafa, ما functions as a tool of definitional inquiry (mā al-ḥaqīqiyyah) and as a quantifier over quiddities, allowing the theologian or philosopher to ask what a thing is in its essence. In grammar and uṣūl al-fiqh, it is treated as a general particle (ḥarf ʿāmm) whose scope may encompass all indefinite categories, and its conditional usage generates universal propositions. Its interrogative force is also employed in dialectical theology to pose questions of essence and existence, while its negative force is used to deny attributes or propositions without implying a positive counterpart.

canonical_definition.arabic: ما: حَرْفُ نَفي، وتكون بمعنى الذي، وتكون بمعنى الشَّرط، وتكون عِبَارة عن جميع أَنواع النكرة، وتكون موضُوعة موضع مَنْ، وتكون بمعنى الاسْتِفهام، وتُبْدَل من الأَلف الهاء فيقال مَهْ.
canonical_definition.english: Mā: a particle of negation; it may also mean 'that which'; it may denote conditionality; it may express all categories of the indefinite; it may stand in the place of 'who'; it may function as a particle of interrogation; and the alif may be replaced by hāʾ, giving māh.

derivations.english_translation: not; that which; what; whatever
what? (dialectal variant of ما with hāʾ substitution)

mufradat.text: ما في كلامهم عشرة: خمسة أسماء، وخمسة حروف. فإذا كان اسما فيقال للواحد والجمع والمؤنث على حد واحد، ويصح أن يعتبر في الضمير لفظه مفردا، وأن يعتبر معناه للجمع. فالأول من الأسماء بمعنى الذي نحو: ويعبدون من دون الله ما لا يضرهم [يونس/ 18] (4) ثم قال: هؤلاء شفعاؤنا عند الله [يونس/ 18] لما أراد الجمع، وقوله: ويعبدون من دون الله ما لا يملك لهم رزقا ... الآية [النحل/ 73]، فجمع أيضا، وقوله: بئسما يأمركم به إيمانكم [البقرة/ 93]. الثاني: نكرة. نحو: نعما يعظكم به [النساء/ 58] أي: نعم شيئا يعظكم به، وقوله: فنعما هي [البقرة/ 271] فقد أجيز أن يكون ما نكرة في قوله: ما بعوضة فما فوقها [البقرة/ 26]، وقد أجيز أن يكون صلة، فما بعده يكون مفعولا. تقديره: أن يضرب مثلا بعوضة (1). الثالث: الاستفهام، ويسأل به عن جنس ذات الشيء، ونوعه، وعن جنس صفات الشيء، ونوعه، وقد يسأل به عن الأشخاص، والأعيان في غير الناطقين. وقال بعض النحويين: وقد يعبر به عن الأشخاص الناطقين (2)، كقوله تعالى: إلا على أزواجهم أو ما ملكت أيمانهم* [المؤمنون/ 6]، إن الله يعلم ما يدعون من دونه من شيء [العنكبوت/ 42] وقال الخليل: ما استفهام. أي: أي شيء تدعون من دون الله؟ وإنما جعله كذلك، لأن «ما» هذه لا تدخل إلا في المبتدإ والاستفهام الواقع آخرا. الرابع: الجزاء نحو: ما يفتح الله للناس من رحمة فلا ممسك لها، وما يمسك فلا مرسل له الآية [فاطر/ 2]. ونحو: ما تضرب أضرب. الخامس: التعجب نحو: فما أصبرهم على النار [البقرة/ 175]. وأما الحروف: فالأول: أن يكون ما بعده بمنزلة المصدر كأن الناصبة للفعل المستقبل. نحو: ومما رزقناهم ينفقون* [البقرة/ 3] فإن «ما» مع رزق في تقدير الرزق، والدلالة على أنه مثل «أن» أنه لا يعود إليه ضمير لا ملفوظ به ولا مقدر فيه، وعلى هذا حمل قوله: بما كانوا يكذبون* [البقرة/ 10]، وعلى هذا قولهم: أتاني القوم ما عدا زيدا، وعلى هذا إذا كان في تقدير ظرف نحو: كلما أضاء لهم مشوا فيه [البقرة/ 20]، كلما أوقدوا نارا للحرب أطفأها الله [المائدة/ 64]، كلما خبت زدناهم سعيرا [الإسراء/ 97]. وأما قوله: فاصدع بما تؤمر [الحجر/ 94] فيصح أن يكون مصدرا، وأن يكون بمعنى الذي (3). واعلم أن «ما» إذا كان مع ما بعدها في تقدير المصدر لم يكن إلا حرفا، لأنه لو كان اسما لعاد إليه ضمير، وكذلك قولك: أريد أن أخرج، فإنه لا عائد من الضمير إلى أن، ولا ضمير لها بعده. الثاني: للنفي وأهل الحجاز يعملونه بشرط نحو: ما هذا بشرا [يوسف/ 31] (1). الثالث: الكافة، وهي الداخلة على «أن» وأخواتها و«رب» ونحو ذلك، والفعل. نحو: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء [فاطر/ 28]، إنما نملي لهم ليزدادوا إثما [آل عمران/ 178]، كأنما يساقون إلى الموت [الأنفال/ 6] وعلى ذلك «ما» في قوله: ربما يود الذين كفروا [الحجر/ 2]، وعلى ذلك: قلما وطالما فيما حكي. الرابع: المسلطة، وهي التي تجعل اللفظ متسلطا بالعمل، بعد أن لم يكن عاملا. نحو: «ما» في إذما، وحيثما، لأنك تقول: إذما تفعل أفعل، وحيثما تقعد أقعد، فإذ وحيث لا يعملان بمجردهما في الشرط، ويعملان عند دخول «ما» عليهما. الخامس: الزائدة لتوكيد اللفظ في قولهم: إذا ما فعلت كذا، وقولهم: إما تخرج أخرج. قال: فإما ترين من البشر أحدا [مريم/ 26]، وقوله: إما يبلغن عندك الكبر أحدهما أو كلاهما [الإسراء/ 23]. تم كتاب الميم إعمال «ليس» أعملت «ما» دون «إن» مع بقا النفي، وترتيب زكن وسبق حرف جر أو ظرف ك ما بي أنت معنيا أجاز العلما ||| كتاب النون

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of settling and taking up residence in a place, from which the noun for a settlement or city derives. Ibn Manẓūr notes that the verb مَدَنَ بِالمَكَانِ (madana bi-l-makān) meaning 'to dwell in a place' is a dead verb (فِعْلٌ مُمَات), preserved chiefly in the derived noun المَدِينَة (al-madīnah).
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is a place of residence and settlement, i.e., a city or town. Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī reports that some hold المَدِينَة to be of the pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīlah), with its plural مَدَن (madan), while others treat the mīm as augmentative, making it مَفْعِلَة (mafʿilah) from دِنْتُ (dintu), meaning 'I was possessed or ruled.' Ibn Manẓūr records its plurals as مَدَائِن (madāʾin), مُدْن (mudn), and مُدُن (mudun).
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and theological usage, المَدِينَة denotes the polity or community settled in a city, not merely its physical structures. The Qurʾānic phrase وَمَنْ أَهْلِ المَدِينَةِ مَرَدُوا عَلَى النِّفَاقِ (Q 9:101) refers to the hypocrites among the city's inhabitants, while وَجَاءَ مِنْ أَقْصَا المَدِينَةِ رَجُلٌ يَسْعَى (Q 36:20) and وَدَخَلَ المَدِينَةَ عَلَى حِينِ غَفْلَةٍ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا (Q 28:15) employ the term for the urban settlement as a social and political entity. The etymological debate over whether the mīm is radical or augmentative reflects a broader lexical ambiguity: if from دِنْتُ, the city is conceptually that which is possessed and governed; if from مَدَنَ, it is that in which one settles.

canonical_definition.arabic: مَدَنَ بِالمَكَانِ: أَقَامَ بِهِ، فِعْلٌ مُمَات، وَمِنْهُ المَدِينَة، وَهِيَ فَعِيلَة، وَتُجْمَعُ عَلَى مَدَائِنَ وَمُدْنٍ وَمُدُنٍ.
canonical_definition.english: مَدَنَ بِالمَكَانِ: he dwelt in the place—a dead verb—and from it derives المَدِينَة (the city), which is of the pattern فَعِيلَة, and its plurals are مَدَائِن, مُدْن, and مُدُن.

derivations.english_translation: to dwell, to settle in a place (described as a dead verb)
city, town, settlement
cities, towns (plural)
cities, towns (plural, light form)
cities, towns (plural, heavy form)

mufradat.text: المدينة فعيلة عند قوم، وجمعها مدن، وقد مدنت مدينة، وناس يجعلون الميم زائدة، قال تعالى: ومن أهل المدينة مردوا على النفاق [التوبة/ 101] قال: وجاء من أقصا المدينة رجل يسعى [يس/ 20]، ودخل المدينة على حين غفلة من أهلها [القصص/ 15].

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root م س ط is the manual insertion of the hand into the reproductive cavity of a she-camel or mare to extract the accumulated seminal fluid (wathr) that has failed to result in conception after repeated copulation. The root thus denotes a concrete veterinary intervention: a tactile, evacuative act performed by the herdsman to cleanse the womb and restore fertility.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in Lisān al-ʿArab, is the act of a man inserting his hand into the vagina of a she-camel to extract the wathr—the retained water of the stallion that has coagulated in the womb due to excessive mounting without conception. The verb مَسَطَ النَّاقَةَ / الفَرَسَ يَمْسُطُهَا مَسْطًا signifies this direct manual extraction.
record.majaz_scholastic: Since the root is not attested in Al-Mufradāt or Asās al-Balāghah, no established metaphorical or scholastic extensions are recorded in the classical philological tradition. Any figurative usage would be an analogical projection from the literal veterinary act—such as the removal of an obstruction or the extraction of a hidden substance—but such extensions lack canonical attestation and remain outside the strict ḥaqīqah–majāz boundary delineated by Al-Zamakhsharī.

canonical_definition.arabic: المِسْطُ: أَن يُدخِل الرجُل يدَه في حَياء الناقة فيستَخْرِج وَثْرها، وهو ماء الفحل يجتمع في رحمها، وذلك إِذا كثر ضِرابُها ولم تَلْقَح. ومَسَطَ الناقَةَ والفَرَسَ يَمْسُطُها مَسْطاً: أَدخل يدَه في حَيائها فاستخرج وَثْرها.
canonical_definition.english: Al-misṭ is the act of a man inserting his hand into the vagina of a she-camel to extract the wathr—the stallion's fluid that accumulates in her womb when she has been repeatedly mounted without conceiving. He masata the she-camel or the mare, yamsuṭuhā masṭan: he inserted his hand into her vagina and extracted the wathr.

derivations.english_translation: He inserted his hand into the womb of a she-camel or mare to extract the retained seminal fluid.
The act of manual extraction of the wathr (retained stallion's fluid) from the womb.
The verbal noun denoting the act of extracting the wathr by hand.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root م-ض-ض is a sharp, penetrating burning or biting sensation—like the sting of collyrium in the eye or the smart of a wound—that causes acute pain and distress.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is: pain, grief, or words that cause a burning, piercing sensation; to be afflicted by a calamity or speech in a manner that stings and hurts; and the application of kohl to the eye, which causes a biting smart.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root is used to describe the intense, burning effect of anxiety, sorrow, or harsh words upon the heart or soul, signifying emotional or spiritual torment. It is applied to any agent that causes severe distress, whether internal (grief) or external (speech), and conveys the idea of being consumed or scorched by an affliction.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَضُّ: الحُرْقَةُ. مَضَّني الهَمُّ والحُزْنُ والقول يَمُضُّني مَضّاً ومَضِيضاً وأَمَضَّني: أَحْرَقَني وشقّ عليّ. والهمُّ يَمُضُّ القلبَ أَي يُحْرِقُه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Maḍḍ is burning. Anxiety, sorrow, or speech burns me with a burning and intense pain; and it caused me burning pain: it burned me and was severe upon me. Anxiety burns the heart, i.e., it scorches it.

derivations.english_translation: to burn, sting, cause acute pain
to feel a burning pain, be distressed
to cause intense burning pain
to burn, cause severe pain
burning pain, smart
intense burning pain, distress
acts of causing burning pain
state of being burned or distressed

entries.text: ما مضمضت عيني بالنوم أرقا وما تمضمضت. قال المروح السلمي: لما اتكأن على النمارق مضمضت ... بالنوم أعينهن غير غرار وتمضمض النوم في عينه. قال: يمسح بالكفين وجها أبيضا ... إذا الكرى في عينه تمضمضا
أمضني الوجع والهم ومضني، وضربه فأمضه ومضه، والكحل يمض عيني، ومضضت من المصيبة ومن كلامك مضيضا بكسر العين.

أمضني الوجع والهم ومضني، وضربه فأمضه ومضه، والكحل يمض عيني، ومضضت من المصيبة ومن كلامك مضيضا بكسر العين. Metaphorical (Majaz): ما مضمضت عيني بالنوم أرقا وما تمضمضت. قال المروح السلمي: لما اتكأن على النمارق مضمضت ... بالنوم أعينهن غير غرار وتمضمض النوم في عينه. قال: ي

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the intense, visceral aversion aroused by the perception of something ugly or morally repugnant; it denotes a hatred that is not merely emotional but is provoked by the apprehension of a blameworthy act or quality.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal meaning is to hate someone intensely because of a vile or repulsive matter; it is a loathing directed at a person due to an ugly deed, and it is used literally in expressions such as 'he hated him with intense hatred' and 'he became hateful to people'.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root is applied to the marriage of a man to his father's wife, termed 'nikāḥ al-maqt' (the marriage of hatred), because it was considered an abominable and detestable practice. Theologically, in the Qur'anic verse 'It was an indecency and a hateful thing and an evil way' (4:22), it denotes a divinely abhorred act. The term 'maqīt' (مقيت) is also used as a divine name meaning 'the Guardian' or 'the Preserver', but this is derived from the root قوت (q-w-t), not from مقت, as clarified by al-Rāghib and Ibn Manẓūr; thus it is a homonymic form, not a semantic extension of the root مقت.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَقْتُ: أَشَدُّ الإِبْغاضِ. مَقُتَ مَقاتَةً، ومَقَتَه مَقْتاً: أَبْغضه، فهو مَمْقُوتٌ ومَقِيتٌ. والمَقِيتُ: الحافِظُ، والميم فيه مضمومة وليست بأصلية، وهو من القوت.
canonical_definition.english: Al-maqt is the most intense form of hatred. He was hateful (maquta) with hatefulness (maqāta), and he hated him (maqatahu) with hatred (maqt), so he is hated (mamqūt) and hateful (maqīt). Al-maqīt means 'the Guardian', and the mīm in it is a prefixed letter, not a root letter, as it derives from al-qūt (sustenance).

derivations.english_translation: he hated intensely
he was hateful, he became an object of intense hatred
intense hatred, abhorrence
state of being intensely hated, hatefulness
hated, hateful (also, from قوت: guardian, preserver)
hated, detested
he became hateful to someone, he incurred hatred
he hated one another, he exchanged hatred
they hated one another

mufradat.text: المقت: البغض الشديد لمن تراه تعاطى القبيح. يقال: مقت مقاتة فهو مقيت، ومقته فهو مقيت وممقوت. قال تعالى: إنه كان فاحشة ومقتا وساء سبيلا [النساء/ 22] وكان يسمى تزوج الرجل امرأة أبيه نكاح المقت، وأما المقيت فمفعل من القوت، وقد تقدم (1).

entries.text: مقته مقتا وهو بغض عن أمر قبيح. ومنه قيل لنكاح الرجل رابته: نكاح المقت " إنه كان فاحشة ومقتا " ومقت إلى الناس مقاتة، نحو: بغض بغاضة، وهو ممقوت ومقيت، وتمقت إليه: نقيض تحبب إليه. وماقته. وتماقتوا، ومقته إلي: قبح فعله.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act of striking or crushing the neck (دَقُّ العُنُق) with a rod until the bone fractures while the skin remains intact; by extension, the steeping or soaking of salted fish in water or vinegar to draw out its brine.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical sense is the crushing or pounding of the neck with a stick, breaking the bone beneath unbroken skin. A secondary literal sense is the immersion of salted fish in water or vinegar (نَقْع السَّمَك المَالِح) to leach out its salt.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and derived usages include: (1) bitterness (مَرَارَة) predicated of a person or thing, as in the phrase 'مُمَقَّرٌ مُرٌّ' (intensely bitter), applied to a harsh individual toward his enemies yet sweet as honey to his intimates; (2) milk described as مُمَقَّر when it has nearly turned bitter due to the acidity of the stomach (لِقَرُوصِهِ); (3) fish termed مَمْقُور when its neck has been crushed; (4) the imperative form 'أَمْقِرْ' (from the root) denoting patience or endurance (الصَّبْر), as attested in the command 'مُقِرْ'.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَقْرُ: دَقُّ العُنُقِ. مَقَرَ عُنُقَهُ يَمْقُرُهَا مَقْراً إِذَا دَقَّهَا وَضَرَبَهَا بِالعَصَا حَتَّى تَكَسَّرَ العَظْمُ وَالجِلْدُ صَحِيحٌ. وَالمَقْرُ: إِنْقَاعُ السَّمَكِ المَالِحِ فِي المَاءِ. وَمَقَرَ السَّمَكَةَ المَالِحَةَ مَقْراً: أَنْقَعَهَا فِي الخَلِّ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Maqr: the crushing of the neck. One says maqara ʿunuqahu yamquruha maqran when he pounded and struck it with a rod until the bone fractured while the skin remained intact. Al-Maqr also denotes the steeping of salted fish in water. And maqara al-samakata al-māliḥata maqran: he steeped it in vinegar.

derivations.english_translation: He crushed or pounded (the neck), breaking the bone while leaving the skin intact.
The act of crushing the neck; the steeping of salted fish in water or vinegar.
He made (something) bitter; he caused to become bitter or acrid.
Having its neck crushed (said of fish); made bitter or acrid.
Intensely bitter; harsh or acrid in disposition.
He became bitter; (of milk) it became nearly bitter.
It (milk) became bitter or acrid.

entries.text: " أمر من المقر " وهو الصبر. ومر ممقر، وقد أمقر. قال لبيد: ممقر مر على أعدائه ... وعلى الأذنين حلو كالعسل ولبن ممقر: كاد يمر لقروصه. وسمك ممقور: من مقر عنقه إذا دقها.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is extreme elongation combined with extreme thinness — a stretched, attenuated bodily frame, and by extension the act of drawing out or extracting something entirely from its container.
record.haqiqah_literal: In its literal physical sense, مَقَق denotes excessive length conjoined with fineness or slenderness; a man is described as أَمَقّ and a woman as مَقَّاء, and a horse as أَشَقّ أَمَقّ. It also denotes the complete extraction of marrow from a bone (تَمَقَّقْتُ ما في العظم) and the draining of milk from the udder by a young camel (تَمَقَّقَ الفصيل ما في الضرع).
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension, the root is applied to a person who speaks from the deepest part of his throat (مُقَامِق), i.e., with an affected, strained, or hollow vocalization. It is also used in the idiomatic imprecation مَقَّ الله عيني, meaning 'May God pluck out my eye,' where the physical act of extraction is transferred to a curse of removal or deprivation. The elongation sense may further shade into a pejorative description of excessive, ungainly tallness.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَقَقُ: الطول عامة، وقيل: هو الطول الفاحش في دقة. ورجل أمق وامرأة مقاء. وتمققت ما في العظم: استخرجته كله. وفلان مقامق: يتكلم بأقصى حلقه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Maqaq denotes length in general; it is also said to be excessive length combined with slenderness. A man is described as amaqq and a woman as maqqā'. TamAqqaqtu mā fī al-'aẓm means 'I extracted everything within the bone.' Fulān muqāmiq means 'so-and-so speaks from the deepest part of his throat.'

derivations.english_translation: to draw out, extract entirely; to drain
to be or become excessively long and thin
excessive length, especially in conjunction with slenderness
excessively long and thin (masculine)
excessively long and thin (feminine)
one who speaks from the deepest part of the throat; affected in speech
to extract completely, to drain out

entries.text: بلد أمق، وأرض مقاء: بعيدة الأرجاء. قال الكميت يصف ظالما: تمقق أخلاف المعيشة منهم ... رضاعا وأخلاف المعيشة حفل

رج أمق، وامرأة مقاء، والمقق: طول في دقة، وفرس أشق أمق، ووصف أعرابي فرسا فقال: شقاء مقاء، طويلة الأنقاء. وتمققت ما في العظم: استخرجته كله. وتمقق الفصيل ما في الضرع. وفلان مقامق: يتهكلم بأقصى حلقه. وعن بعض العرب: مق الله عيني وإلا فلا بلغ الله بي ظلام الليل إن كنت جلست مجلسا إلا ذه

رج أمق، وامرأة مقاء، والمقق: طول في دقة، وفرس أشق أمق، ووصف أعرابي فرسا فقال: شقاء مقاء، طويلة الأنقاء. وتمققت ما في العظم: استخرجته كله. وت Metaphorical (Majaz): بلد أمق، وأرض مقاء: بعيدة الأرجاء. قال الكميت يصف ظالما: تمقق أخلاف المعيشة منهم ... رضاعا وأخلاف المعيشة حفل

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on fixedness and settled persistence in a place, with a secondary concrete sense of a boil or pustule reaching full maturation and becoming engorged with pus.
record.haqiqah_literal: To remain, stay, or abide in a place; to settle firmly. In the concrete medical sense: a boil or pustule (al-ʿudd) becoming fully engorged with pus, and its incision or rupture.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension from physical residence, the root denotes any state of persistent fixation or immovable adherence. The medical usage is extended metaphorically to describe any condition reaching a point of critical fullness or maturation requiring release, though classical lexicographers treat the boil-sense as a distinct concrete application rather than a purely figurative one.

canonical_definition.arabic: مَكَتَ بالمكان: أَقام، كمَكَدَ. واسْتَمْكَتَ العُدُّ: امتلأَ قيحاً.
canonical_definition.english: He remained in the place: he stayed, like makada. And the boil became fully engorged: it filled with pus.

derivations.english_translation: to remain, stay, abide in a place; to settle
to become fully engorged with pus (said of a boil); to reach maturation
residence, settled abode; fixedness

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the notion of fixed, unmoving persistence in a place or state — a thing that stays put and does not shift, flow away, or dissipate. From this concrete sense of stationary continuance, the root extends to denote anything enduring, perpetual, or unceasing, such as water that remains and does not dry up.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is: to remain, stay, abide, or dwell in a place (مَكَدَ بالمكان يَمْكُدُ مُكُوداً: أَقام به). It is synonymous with ثَكَمَ (to stay) and رَكَدَ (to be still, motionless). Applied to water, ماءٌ ماكِدٌ denotes water that is permanent, unfailing, and never ceasing — standing water that persists rather than draining or evaporating.
record.majaz_scholastic: By extension from the literal sense of stationary persistence, the root is applied metaphorically to anything characterized by uninterrupted continuance: enduring states, perpetual conditions, and unceasing phenomena. The participle ماكِد thus describes not merely what is physically still, but what is constant and everlasting — e.g., water that is دائم (perpetual), and by analogy any quality, blessing, or condition that abides without interruption. The scholastic usage preserves the core image of something that does not move away or come to an end.

canonical_definition.arabic: مَكَدَ بالمكان يَمْكُدُ مُكُوداً: أَقام به؛ وثَكَمَ يَثْكُم مثله، ورَكَدَ رُكوداً. وماءٌ ماكِدٌ: دائمٌ.
canonical_definition.english: مَكَدَ in a place, يَمْكُدُ مُكُوداً: he stayed or dwelt there; ثَكَمَ يَثْكُم is the same, and رَكَدَ رُكوداً [is likewise]. And ماءٌ ماكِدٌ means perpetual, unfailing water.

derivations.english_translation: to remain, stay, abide, or dwell in a place; to be stationary and persistent
the act or state of remaining, staying, or abiding; stationary persistence
remaining, staying, abiding; permanent, perpetual, unceasing (e.g., water that never dries up)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root م-ل-ز is the act of slipping away, escaping, or quietly departing from a place, grasp, or state. It denotes a subtle, often elusive motion of withdrawal or release, frequently paired with its phonetic sibling م-ل-س (malasa), which carries the same semantic field of slipping out or slipping away.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is: a thing slipped away from me, departed, or went off (مَلَزَ الشيءُ عَنِّي); and one escaped or got free from a matter (امَّلَزَ من الأمر), or extracted oneself from it (تَمَلَّزَ من الأمر). The transitive form مَلَّزْتُه means: I caused it to slip away or made it depart.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root is applied to the subtle evasion of an obligation, the quiet withdrawal from a commitment, or the eluding of a grasp—whether physical, legal, or moral. It conveys a stealthy disentanglement rather than a forceful escape, and in theological or ethical discourse it may describe the soul's slipping away from a virtuous state or the intellect's evasion of a conclusive proof. The paired root م-ل-س is used interchangeably in classical texts for the same range of literal and figurative slipping.

canonical_definition.arabic: مَلَزَ الشيءُ عَنِّي مَلْزاً وامَّلَزَ ومَلَّزَ: ذهب. وتَمَلَّزَ من الأَمر تَمَلُّزاً وتَمَلَّسَ تَمَلُّساً: خرج منه. وامَّلَزَ من الأَمر وامَّلَسَ إِذا انفلت. وقد مَلَّزْتُه ومَلَّسْتُه إِذا فعلت به ذلك.
canonical_definition.english: The thing slipped away from me (malaza), and it escaped (immallaza) and slipped away (mallaza): it departed. And he extracted himself from the matter (tamallaza) and slipped out (tamallasa): he exited from it. And he escaped from the matter (immallaza) and slipped free (immallasa) when he got loose. And I caused it to slip away (mallaztuhu) and made it slip free (mallastuhu) when I did that to it.

derivations.english_translation: he/it slipped away, departed, went off
he caused to slip away, made depart
he extracted himself, slipped out (from a matter)
he escaped, got free, slipped away
a slipping away, departure, escape
the act of extracting oneself, slipping out

record.ontological_core: Rapid, light-footed motion across the earth — the foundational physical image is that of swift, unencumbered travel or pursuit over terrain, with an emphasis on speed and levity of movement.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is swift, light movement or travel across the ground; it denotes a pace faster than walking but below the gallop (al-khabab), and is applied to a she-camel moving briskly in her gait.
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension, the root is applied to a swift bird of prey — specifically an eagle or falcon described as milāʿ (swift in flight) — and to a person of exceptional quickness or lightness of hand, as in the idiom 'you are lighter of hand than the wing of a swift eagle.' The term milāʿ is also attested as a proper name for a tract of land, likely named for the swiftness required to traverse it.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَلْعُ: الذَّهَابُ في الأَرض، وقيل الطَّلَبُ، وقيل السُّرْعَةُ والخِفَّةُ، وقيل شِدَّةُ السَّيْرِ، وقيل العَدْوُ الشَّدِيدُ، وقيل فوق المشي دون الخَبَبِ، وقيل هو السَّيْرُ السَّرِيعُ الخَفِيفُ، مَلَعَ يَمْلَعُ مَلْعاً ومَلَعَاناً.
canonical_definition.english: Al-malʿ: going forth across the earth; also pursuit; also speed and lightness; also intensity of travel; also vigorous running; also a pace above walking but below the gallop; also swift, light travel. The verb is malaʿa, yamlaʿu, malʿan and malaʿānan.

derivations.english_translation: he moved swiftly and lightly; he went forth rapidly across the earth
swift, light motion; rapid traversal
swiftness; lightness of movement (verbal noun)
a swift she-camel; one characterized by rapid, light gait
swift, light, quick (adjective)
swift (used of an eagle or falcon); a tract of land (proper noun)
very swift, exceedingly quick (intensive adjective)

entries.text: ناقة ميلع: تملع في سيرها ملعا أي تسرع. قال الكميت: عنتريس شملة ذات لوث ... هوجل ميلع كتوم البغام وتقول: طار إلى بعض القلاع، كأنه عقاب ملاع. قال أبو زيد: ملاع اسم أرض ويجوز أن يكون وصفا على تقدير: عقاب قادمة ملاع، أو خفقة ملاع بمعنى مالعة سريعة. قال المسيب: أنت الوفي فما تذم وبعضه

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the act of cutting or severing a rope or cord, and the consequent state of a rope that is worn, frayed, and weakened to the point of breaking. From this concrete sense of physical debilitation and severance, the root branches into two major semantic streams: (1) the bestowal of a heavy favor or benefit that 'cuts' or burdens the recipient with obligation, and (2) the notion of a weak, severed, or depleted thing, whether a rope, a person's strength, or a garment's fabric.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is a rope (ḥabl) that is weak, worn out, and severed (manīn), and the act of cutting (mann) a rope. It also denotes the physical act of a person being weakened or depleted, as in 'manat-hu al-manūn' (the fates cut him off) and 'manat-hu al-safar' (travel weakened him). The literal sense also includes the physical burden of a heavy favor, as in 'manna fulānun ʿalā fulān' (a person burdened another with a favor).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, the root is used to denote the bestowal of a favor or blessing (niʿmah), especially from God to His servants, as in 'God conferred a favor upon the believers' (Q 3:164). This usage is considered majāz because the favor is not a physical rope but is likened to a heavy burden that 'cuts' or obligates the recipient. The term 'mannān' (the Ever-Bestowing) is a divine attribute. It also metaphorically signifies the psychological burden of a favor that is reminded of repeatedly, which is condemned in Islamic ethics. Additionally, 'manīn' is used metaphorically for a weak person or a worn-out garment, and 'manūn' (fate) is personified as that which cuts off life.

canonical_definition.arabic: مَنَّهُ يَمُنُّهُ مَنّاً: قطعه. والمَنِينُ: الحبل الضعيف. وحبل مَنينٌ: مقطوع. والمنة: النعمة الثقيلة. والمنان: الكثير المنن. والمنون: القطع، والمنية: الموت.
canonical_definition.english: Mannahu yamunnuhu mannan: he cut it. Al-manīn: the weak rope. A rope that is manīn: severed. Al-minnah: the heavy favor. Al-mannān: the one who bestows many favors. Al-manūn: cutting, and al-maniyyah: death.

derivations.english_translation: to cut, to sever; to confer a favor, to burden with a favor
one who bestows many favors; the Ever-Bestowing (divine attribute)
weak, worn-out, severed (rope); a weak person; a worn-out garment
fate, destiny (that which cuts off life); a cutting or severing thing
a favor, a benefit; a burden of obligation
worn-out ropes (plural of manīn)
worn-out ropes (plural of manīn)
mutual conferring of favors; mutual burdening with obligations
gratitude, acknowledgment of a favor; the act of being grateful

mufradat.text: المن: ما يوزن به، يقال: من، ومنان، وأمنان، وربما أبدل من إحدى النونين ألف فقيل: منا وأمناء، ويقال لما يقدر: ممنون كما يقال: موزون، والمنة: النعمة الثقيلة، ويقال ذلك على وجهين: أحدهما: أن يكون ذلك بالفعل، فيقال: من فلان على فلان: إذا أثقله بالنعمة، وعلى ذلك قوله: لقد من الله على المؤمنين [آل عمران/ 164]، كذلك كنتم من قبل فمن الله عليكم [النساء/ 94]، ولقد مننا على موسى وهارون [الصافات/ 114]، يمن على من يشاء [إبراهيم/ 11]، ونريد أن نمن على الذين استضعفوا [القصص/ 5]، وذلك على الحقيقة لا يكون إلا لله تعالى. والثاني: أن يكون ذلك بالقول، وذلك مستقبح فيما بين الناس إلا عند كفران النعمة، ولقبح ذلك قيل: المنة تهدم الصنيعة (4)، ولحسن ذكرها عند الكفران قيل: إذا كفرت النعمة حسنت المنة. وقوله: يمنون عليك أن ألا يا دار الحي بالسبعان أمل عليها بالبلى الملوان أسلموا قل لا تمنوا علي إسلامكم [الحجرات/ 17] فالمنة منهم بالقول، ومنة الله عليهم بالفعل، وهو هدايته إياهم كما ذكر، وقوله: فإما منا بعد وإما فداء [محمد/ 4] فالمن إشارة إلى الإطلاق بلا عوض. وقوله: هذا عطاؤنا فامنن أو أمسك بغير حساب [ص/ 39] أي: أنفقه، وقوله: ولا تمنن تستكثر [المدثر/ 6] فقد قيل: هو المنة بالقول، وذلك أن يمتن به ويستكثره، وقيل معناه: لا تعط مبتغيا به أكثر منه، وقوله: لهم أجر غير ممنون* [الانشقاق/ 25] قيل: غير معدود كما قال: بغير حساب* (1) [الزمر/ 10] وقيل: غير مقطوع (2) ولا منقوص. ومنه قيل: المنون للمنية، لأنها تنقص العدد وتقطع المدد. وقيل: إن المنة التي بالقول هي من هذا، لأنها تقطع النعمة وتقتضي قطع الشكر، وأما المن في قوله: وأنزلنا عليكم المن والسلوى [البقرة/ 57] فقد قيل: المن شيء كالطل فيه حلاوة يسقط على الشجر، والسلوى: طائر، وقيل: المن والسلوى، كلاهما إشارة إلى ما أنعم الله به عليهم، وهما بالذات شيء واحد لكن سماه منا بحيث إنه امتن به عليهم، وسماه سلوى من حيث إنه كان لهم به التسلي. ومن عبارة عن الناطقين، ولا يعبر به عن غير الناطقين إلا إذا جمع بينهم وبين غيرهم، كقولك: رأيت من في الدار من الناس والبهائم، أو يكون تفصيلا لجملة يدخل فيهم الناطقون، كقوله تعالى: فمنهم من يمشي الآية [النور/ 45]. ولا يعبر به عن غير الناطقين إذا انفرد، ولهذا قال بعض المحدثين (3) في صفة أغتام نفى عنهم الإنسانية: تخطئ إذا جئت في استفهامه بمن تنبيها أنهم حيوان أو دون الحيوان. ويعبر به عن الواحد والجمع والمذكر والمؤنث. قال تعالى: ومنهم من يستمع* [الأنعام/ 25]، وفي أخرى: من يستمعون إليك [يونس/ 42] وقال: ومن يقنت منكن لله ورسوله وتعمل صالحا [الأحزاب/ 31]. و: من لابتداء الغاية، وللتبعيض، وللتبيين، وتكون لاستغراق الجنس في النفي والاستفهام. نحو: فما منكم من أحد [الحاقة/ 47]. وللبدل. نحو: خذ هذا من ذلك. أي: بدله، قال تعالى: ربنا إني أسكنت من ذريتي بواد [حولي بكل مكان منهم خلق] [إبراهيم/ 37]، (فمن) اقتضى التبعيض، فإنه كان نزل فيه بعض ذريته، وقوله: من السماء من جبال فيها من برد [النور/ 43] قال: تقديره أنه ينزل من السماء جبالا، فمن الأولى ظرف، والثانية في موضع المفعول، والثالثة للتبيين كقولك: عنده جبال من مال. وقيل: يحتمل أن يكون قوله: «من جبال» نصبا على الظرف على أنه ينزل منه، وقوله: من برد نصب. أي: ينزل من السماء من جبال فيها بردا، وقيل: يصح أن يكون موضع من في قوله: من برد رفعا، ومن جبال نصبا على أنه مفعول به، كأنه في التقدير: وينزل من السماء جبالا فيها برد، ويكون الجبال على هذا تعظيما وتكثيرا لما نزل من السماء. وقوله تعالى: فكلوا مما أمسكن عليكم [المائدة/ 4]، قال أبو الحسن: من زائدة (1)، والصحيح أن تلك ليست بزائدة، لأن بعض ما يمسكن لا يجوز أكله كالدم والغدد وما فيها من القاذورات المنهي عن تناولها.

entries.text: من الله تعالى على عباده، وهو المنان، وله علي منة ومنن، ومن علي بما صنع، وامتن، وإنه لمنونة، وامتننت منك بما فعلت منة جسيمة أي احتملت منة. وهو ضعيف المنة، وليس لقلبه منة أي قوة، وهم ضعاف المنن، ومنة السفر: أضعفه وذهب بمنته. قال ابن ميادة: منناهن بالإدلاج حتى ... كأن متونهن عصي ضال

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin centers on the act of giving or assigning a dower (ṣadāq) to a woman, and by extension, the notion of a contractual payment that seals a union; from this concrete transactional sense, the root branches into the idea of skill or mastery, conceived as a 'price' or 'acquisition' of proficiency, and into the concrete noun for a camel's nose-ring (mihār), a device that controls and directs.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is the dower given to a woman (mahr al-marʾah: to give her the dower), and the verbal noun denotes the act of assigning or paying that dower; it also literally denotes a nose-ring (mihār) placed in the nose of a camel, and a horse possessing such a ring (faras mumhar).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root is used for skill and mastery in a craft or activity: māhir means 'skilled, expert' (e.g., a skilled orator, a skilled swimmer), and tamahhara means 'to become proficient' or 'to swim well.' The dower is also metaphorically extended to any gift or compensation that seals a contract, and the nose-ring is metaphorically applied to any controlling or directing device. Theologically, the dower is a legal obligation in marriage, and the root's semantic shift to 'skill' is understood as a metaphorical 'price' paid for excellence.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَهْرُ: الصَّداق، والجمع مُهور؛ وقد مَهَرَ المرأَةَ يَمْهَرُها ويَمْهُرُها مَهْراً وأَمْهَرَها. والمَاهِرُ: الحاذق بالشيء، وقد مَهَرَ يَمْهَرُ مَهَارَةً. والمِهَارُ: عود في أنف البختي.
canonical_definition.english: The mahr is the dower; its plural is muhūr. One says mahara al-marʾah yamharuhā or yamhurhā mahran, and amharahā, meaning he gave her the dower. The māhir is one who is skilled in something; he became skilled (mahara) with skill (mahārah). The mihār is a stick placed in the nose of a camel.

derivations.english_translation: to give a dower to a woman; to marry by giving a dower
to be skilled, to be proficient
dower, bridal gift
dowers, bridal gifts (plural)
skilled, expert, proficient
skill, proficiency, mastery
nose-ring (for a camel)
a horse having a nose-ring; a woman given a dower
a woman who has received a dower; a free woman married by dower
free women married by dower (plural)

entries.text: مهر في الصناعة وتمهر فيها ومهرها ومهر بها، وهو ماهر بين المهارة، وخطيب ماهر، وسابح ماهر، وقوم مهرة، وتمهر فلان: سبح. ومهر المرأة: أعطاها المهر " كالممهورة إحدى خدمتيها " وأمهرها: سمي لها مهرا وتزوجها به. قال: أخذن اغتصابا خطبة عجرفية ... وأمهرن أرماحا من الخط ذبلا وله مهيرة وسرية

record.ontological_core: The root م و ا is a secondary, denominative formation from the primary root م و ه / م ي ه (water), denoting the substance of water and, by extension, anything that shares its defining property of limpid transparency and reflective clarity.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical referent of the derived noun مَاوِيَّة is a mirror (مِرْآة), so named because it is fashioned from, or functions as, a polished watery surface: images are seen in it exactly as they are seen in clear, still water. A second literal application is the crystal stone (حَجَر البِلَّوْر), i.e. rock crystal, on account of its water-like translucency.
record.majaz_scholastic: The scholastic and figurative extension rests on the transferred attribute of صَفَاء (limpidity) and انعكاس الصورة (image-reflection): any polished, transparent, or specular medium may be termed مَاوِيَّة by assimilation to the reflective surface of water. The lexicographers explicitly ground this majāz in the resemblance (تشبيه) of the mirror's function to that of still water, and they affirm that the medial mīm is radical (أصلية), not an augment, thereby anchoring the word in the water-root rather than treating it as a mere instrumental noun of رؤية.

canonical_definition.arabic: المَاوِيَّةُ: المِرْآةُ، كأَنَّها نُسِبَت إِلى الماءِ لصَفائها وأَنَّ الصُّورَ تُرى فيها كما تُرى في الماءِ الصافي، والميمُ أَصليةٌ فيها؛ وقيل: المَاوِيَّةُ حَجَرُ البِلَّوْرِ، وثلاثُ مَاوِيَّاتٍ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-māwiyyah: the mirror, as though it were attributed to water (al-māʾ) because of its limpidity and because images are seen in it just as they are seen in clear water; the mīm therein is radical. It is also said that al-māwiyyah is rock crystal; the plural is three māwiyyāt.

derivations.english_translation: mirror; also rock crystal (بِلَّوْر), by virtue of its water-like transparency and reflective surface
mirrors; crystal stones (plural of مَاوِيَّة)

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root م-ي-ث is the act of dissolving a solid substance—such as salt, bread, or clay—in water through kneading, rubbing, and maceration until it loses its solid form and becomes fully incorporated into the liquid medium.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning according to Asās al-Balāghah is twofold: (1) the softening and leveling of land, as in أرض ميثاء (soft, level ground) and أراض ميث (soft, level lands); and (2) the physical dissolution of a solid in water, as in ماث الخبز والملح والطين في الماء (he dissolved bread, salt, and clay in water) and انماث (it dissolved).
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic extensions of the root derive from the physical process of dissolution. In theological and philosophical discourse, the root is used to describe the annihilation of a thing's distinct essence or form through its complete absorption into another medium, akin to the dissolution of salt in water. This serves as a metaphor for the obliteration of individual identity, the merging of substances, or the total assimilation of one entity into another, often with connotations of loss of distinct existence or the subsuming of the particular into the universal.

canonical_definition.arabic: مَاثَ الشيءَ مَيْثاً: مَرَسَه. وماثَ المِلحَ في الماء: أَذابه؛ وكذلك الطين، وقد انماثَ. وكلُّ شيءٍ مَرَسته في الماء فذاب فيه، فقد مِثْته ومُثْته.
canonical_definition.english: He macerated the thing with a mays: he rubbed and kneaded it. And he dissolved salt in water: he made it dissolve; likewise clay, and it became dissolved. And anything you rub in water and it dissolves therein, you have macerated and dissolved it.

derivations.english_translation: he dissolved, macerated, or kneaded (a solid in water)
it dissolved, became soft or liquid
soft, level ground (feminine adjective)
soft, level lands (plural)
it dissolved, became dissolved
dissolution, the process of dissolving

entries.text: أرض ميثاء، وأراض ميث. وماث الخبز والملح والطين في الماء وانماث.
أرض ميثاء، وأراض ميث. وماث الخبز والملح والطين في الماء وانماث. Metaphorical (Majaz): لبني عذرة قلوب تنماث كما ينماث الملح في الماء، ورجل ميث القلب: لينه. وميث الرجل: ذلله، وتميث: ذل واسترخى.
لبني عذرة قلوب تنماث كما ينماث الملح في الماء، ورجل ميث القلب: لينه. وميث الرجل: ذلله، وتميث: ذل واسترخى.

record.ontological_core: The root ن-و-ث (n-w-th) denotes the fundamental act of agitating, shaking, or loosening a thing from its compacted or settled state, and by extension, the scattering or dispersing of its constituent parts.
record.haqiqah_literal: To shake or agitate something so as to loosen it, or to scatter and disperse it; said of a thing that is stirred up and broken apart.
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root appears in the form ناث (nātha) meaning to scatter or disperse, as in the dispersal of people or the scattering of leaves by the wind. It is also used in the sense of extracting or eliciting something, such as drawing out a secret or a hidden matter. Theologically, it may be applied to the dispersal of created beings on the Day of Judgment, though this is not a primary Qur'anic usage.

canonical_definition.arabic: نَاثَ الشَّيْءَ يَنِيثُهُ نَيْثًا: حَرَّكَهُ وَفَرَّقَهُ. وَالنَّيْثُ: التَّحْرِيكُ وَالتَّفْرِيقُ.
canonical_definition.english: He shook the thing and dispersed it; al-nayth is the act of shaking and dispersing.

derivations.english_translation: he scattered, dispersed, or shook loose
scattering, dispersal, agitation
one who scatters or disperses
scattered, dispersed

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the abrupt rousing of a dormant or heedless being into wakefulness and attentive presence — the transition from the inertia of sleep or negligence to active consciousness and alertness.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, per Asās al-Balāghah, is awakening from sleep: a person wakes from his sleep (انتبه من نومه), is roused (استنبه، تنبّه), and one rouses him (نبّهه). It also denotes a person of alert, discerning mind (رجل نبيه), and to raise someone's name in renown (نبّهت باسمه: I made his name prominent).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends from sensory waking to intellectual and moral awakening: to become mindful of what one had overlooked (أضلّوه نبهاً: they lost it without realizing when, until they became attentive to it); to be distinguished by nobility of intellect and character (نباهة, نبيه); and to elevate someone's reputation through public mention (تنبيه الاسم, tanwīh). In theological and philosophical usage, it denotes the rousing of the rational soul from heedlessness (ghaflah) to apprehension and intellection, and the divine or prophetic summons that awakens the intellect to its obligations.

canonical_definition.arabic: النُّبْهُ: القيامُ والانْتِباهُ من النوم، وقد نَبَّهَهُ وأَنْبَهَهُ من النوم فتَنَبَّهَ وانْتَبَهَ، وانْتَبَهَ من نومه: استَيقَظ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Nubh is rising and awakening from sleep; one rouses him (nabbahahu) or awakens him (anbahahu) from sleep, so he becomes roused (tanabbaha) and wakes (intabaha); he woke from his sleep: he became awake.

derivations.english_translation: to rouse, awaken, alert, or call someone's attention
to awaken or rouse someone from sleep
to become aware, attentive, or awakened
to wake up, become alert, or take heed
to be roused or to awaken
alert, discerning, noble-minded, renowned
alertness, discernment, nobility of mind, renown
waking, rising from sleep, alertness
rousing, awakening, admonition, notification

entries.text: انتبه من نومه واستنبه وتنبه ونبه نبها. قال: وتبذل لي سلمى إذا نمت حاجتي ... وتلقى خلال النبه وهي منوع وأضلوه نبها: لا يدرون متى ضل حتى انتبه Metaphorical (Majaz): سمعت كلاما فما نبهت له: فما فطنت له. ومالي به نبه ونبه. ونبهته من غفلته، وتنبهت على الأمر: تفطنت له.
انتبه من نومه واستنبه وتنبه ونبه نبها. قال: وتبذل لي سلمى إذا نمت حاجتي ... وتلقى خلال النبه وهي منوع وأضلوه نبها: لا يدرون متى ضل حتى انتبهوا له. ورجل نبيه، وقد نبه نباهة، ونبهت باسمه: نوهت به.
سمعت كلاما فما نبهت له: فما فطنت له. ومالي به نبه ونبه. ونبهته من غفلته، وتنبهت على الأمر: تفطنت له.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) of the root ن-ت-ش is the act of extracting or pulling out a foreign, embedded object—such as a thorn, splinter, or hair—from within a substance, typically flesh or skin, by means of a specialized grasping instrument. This core sense of forcible removal from a state of penetration or attachment is the root's primary ontological anchor.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning, as attested in Asās al-Balāghah, is the extraction of a thorn with a pair of extractors (مِنْتَاش), or the removal of a thorn with a pair of tweezers (مِنْقَاش). It also denotes the act of taking or seizing something from someone, as in the phrase 'I did not extract anything from him' (ما نتشت منه شيئا), meaning 'I did not take anything from him.'
record.majaz_scholastic: The metaphorical and scholastic applications of the root extend from the physical act of extraction to intellectual and epistemic domains. Al-Zamakhsharī notes the expression 'he extracts from every science and plucks from it' (ينتش من كل علم وينتف منه), signifying the acquisition of knowledge by selectively drawing out or extracting elements from various disciplines. In this majāz, the intellect is likened to a hand that plucks or extracts insights from the body of knowledge, mirroring the literal act of removing a thorn from flesh. Additionally, Ibn Manẓūr records a distinct nominal usage: النَّتَش (al-natash) refers to the whiteness that appears at the base of the fingernail, a physical phenomenon that may be considered a secondary literal or observational extension of the root's semantic field.

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّتْشُ: النَّتْفُ للحم ونحوه، وإخراجُ الشوك بالمِنْتَاش وهو المِنْقاش. والنَّتَشُ: البياضُ الذي يظهر في أصل الظفر.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Natsh: the plucking of flesh and the like, and the extraction of a thorn with the mintāsh, which is the minqāsh. Al-Natash: the whiteness that appears at the base of the fingernail.

derivations.english_translation: to extract, to pull out (e.g., a thorn), to pluck
extraction, plucking, removal (of a thorn or hair)
whiteness appearing at the base of the fingernail
instrument for extraction, tweezers, extractor

entries.text: نتش الشوكة بالمنتاش، ونقشها بالمنقاش. وما نتشت منه شيئا: ما أخذت، وهو ينتش من كل علم وينتف منه.

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin is not attested in Al-Mufradāt; classical lexicography derives it from the quadriliteral noun النَّيْرَب, denoting evil, slander, and malicious gossip, with an underlying sense of corrupt, divisive speech that severs social bonds.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal meaning is: 'So-and-so is possessed of nīrab' — that is, he is characterized by evil and slanderous speech; the phrase 'فلان ذو نيرب' is used to describe someone who is a tale-bearer and a source of corruption among people.
record.majaz_scholastic: In scholastic and ethical usage, النَّيْرَب is extended from the physical act of slander to denote the moral vice of calumny and the deliberate sowing of discord; it is applied to a person who habitually engages in malicious gossip (نميمة) and whose speech is a vehicle for evil, thereby corrupting friendships and social cohesion. The term is not used in philosophical or theological contexts for substance or accident, but remains within the domain of ethical censure.

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّيْرَبُ: الشَّرُّ والنَّمِيمَةُ؛ قال الشاعر عَدِيُّ ابن خُزاعِيّ: ولَسْتُ بذي نَيْرَبٍ في الصَّديقِ، ومَنَّاعَ خَيْرٍ، وسَبَّابَها
canonical_definition.english: Al-nayrab: evil and slander; the poet ʿAdī ibn Khuzāʿī said: 'I am not one who engages in malicious gossip among friends, nor one who withholds good, nor one who habitually reviles them.'

derivations.english_translation: evil, slander, malicious gossip; a tale-bearer, one who sows discord
a single act of slander or malicious gossip

entries.text: فلان ذو نيرب: تمام.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the exhaustive drawing-off of a well's water, ladle by ladle, until the source is completely depleted; hence the root denotes total evacuation of a contained substance, whether water, blood, tears, or, by extension, the rational faculties.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is to drain a well completely by drawing its water out gradually, or for a well to become so drained; it is used transitively (nazafa al-bīra) and intransitively (nazafat al-bīru), and in the passive (nuzifat). It also applies literally to the complete extraction of blood (nazafa damahu) or tears (nazafa damʿahu).
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic usages include: (1) the depletion of intellect or understanding by intoxication, hence 'sakrān nazīf' (a drunkard whose reason has been drained) and the Qurʾānic 'lā yuṣaddaʿūna ʿanhā wa-lā yunzafūn' (they will neither suffer headache from it nor lose their minds), with the variant 'yunzafūn' derived from 'anzafū' meaning their drink is exhausted or their minds are removed; (2) the exhaustion of one's argument in disputation, as in 'nazafa al-rajulu fī al-khuṣūmah' (the man's proof was cut off); (3) the proverbial 'ajbanu min al-manzūfi ḍarṭan' (more cowardly than one whose flatulence has been drained), referring to extreme fear.

canonical_definition.arabic: نَزَفْت ماء البئر نَزْفاً إذا نزحْته كله، ونزَفَت هي، يتعدّى ولا يتعدّى، ونُزِفت أَيضاً على ما لم يسم فاعله. ونزف دمه أو دمعه أي نزع كله. ومنه قيل: سكران نزيف: نزف فهمه بسكره.
canonical_definition.english: I drained the well's water completely (nazaftu māʾa al-biʾri nazfan) when I drew it all out; and the well itself became drained (nazafat), being both transitive and intransitive; and it may also be put in the passive (nuzifat). His blood or tears were drained, meaning they were entirely removed. Hence it is said: 'a drunkard is nazīf'—his understanding was drained by his intoxication.

mufradat.text: نزف الماء: نزحه كله من البئر شيئا بعد شيء، وبئر نزوف: نزف ماؤه، والنزفة: الغرفة، والجمع النزف، ونزف دمه، أو دمعه. أي: نزع كله، ومنه قيل: سكران نزيف: نزف فهمه بسكره. قال تعالى: لا يصدعون عنها ولا ينزفون [الواقعة/ 19] (1) وقرئ: ينزفون (2) من قولهم: أنزفوا: إذا نزف شرابهم، أو نزعت عقولهم. وأصله من قولهم: أنزفوا. أي: نزف ماء بئرهم، وأنزفت الشيء: أبلغ من نزفته، ونزف الرجل في الخصومة: انقطعت حجته، وفي مثل: هو أجبن من المنزوف ضرطا (3).

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root is the act of something separating, detaching, or falling away from a larger body or surface—such as hair, fur, or feathers shedding from an animal, or a garment slipping off a person. This core image of detachment and outward emission underlies all subsequent derivations.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal, physical meaning is the falling or shedding of hair, fur, or feathers from an animal, or the slipping off of a garment from a person. It denotes a concrete, observable separation of a part from its whole.
record.majaz_scholastic: By metaphorical extension, the root denotes progeny, offspring, and lineage—the 'shedding' of descendants from a progenitor, as if they were particles detached from the parent. It also encompasses the act of reproduction and multiplication of a family or tribe. In philosophical and theological usage, it can refer to the causal generation of one thing from another, and the perpetuation of a species through successive generations.

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّسْل: الخَلْق، والوَلَد والذُّرِّيَّة، والجمع أَنْسَال. ونَسَلَ الوَبَرُ عن البعير: سقط. وتَنَاسَلُوا: وَلَدَ بعضُهم بعضاً.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Nasl: creation, offspring, and progeny; plural: ansāl. The fur shed from a camel: it fell off. They reproduced: some of them begot others.

mufradat.text: النسل: الانفصال عن الشيء. يقال: نسل الوبر عن البعير، والقميص عن الإنسان، قال الشاعر: 437- فسلي ثيابي عن ثيابك تنسلي (4) والنسالة: ما سقط من الشعر، وما يتحات من وإن كنت قد ساءتك مني خليقة الريش، وقد أنسلت الإبل: حان أن ينسل وبرها، ومنه: نسل: إذا عدا، ينسل نسلانا: إذا أسرع. قال تعالى: وهم من كل حدب ينسلون [الأنبياء/ 96]. والنسل: الولد، لكونه ناسلا عن أبيه. قال تعالى: ويهلك الحرث والنسل [البقرة/ 205] وتناسلوا: توالدوا، ويقال أيضا إذا طلبت فضل إنسان: فخذ ما نسل لك منه عفوا.

entries.text: نسل الريش والشعر: سقط نسولا، وأنسله الطائر والدابة. وهذا نسال الطائر، ونسيل الدابة ونسالتها. قال الراعي: أطار نسيله الشتوي عنه ... تتبعه المذانب والقرارا

نسل الولد ينسل إذا ولد لأنه يسقط من بطن أمه إلى الأرض. ونسلت الناقة بولد كثير. وأنسل الرجل نسلا كثيرا. وتوالدوا وتناسلوا. وهو من نسل طيب ونسل خبيث. وما لفلان نسولة. كقولك: حلوبة وركوبة وهي ما يتخذ للنسل من الإبل والغنم. ونسل الذئب إذا أسرع بإعناق، كما يقال: انسل في عدوه وهو الخرو

record.ontological_core: The root's foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) centers on the act of administering a substance into the mouth or throat, specifically forcing a liquid or medicine into someone's mouth, and by extension, the giving of a fee or bribe to a soothsayer to induce speech.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal physical meaning is: 'نشع الصبي الدواء وأنشعه' — he poured the medicine into the boy's mouth, or made him swallow it; the medicine itself is called 'نشوع', and the act is 'انتشعه'. The instrument is 'منشع الصبي' — the device used to administer medicine to the boy, i.e., a syringe or funnel.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and scholastically, the root extends to the soothsayer's fee (جُعْل الكاهن), as in Lisān al-ʿArab: 'النَّشْعُ: جُعْلُ الكاهِنِ، وقد أَنْشَعَه' — the soothsayer's payment, and he gave it to him. This usage is metaphorical because the fee is like medicine forced into the soothsayer's mouth to make him speak or prophesy. The verse by Ru'bah: 'قال الحَوازي، وأَبَى أَن يُنْشَعا' — the diviners spoke, but he refused to be given the fee (or to be made to speak). Thus, the root denotes both the physical act of administering medicine and the transactional act of paying a soothsayer, with the latter being a metaphorical extension.

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّشْعُ: جُعْلُ الكاهِنِ، وقد أَنْشَعَه. ونَشَعَ الصبي الدواء وأنشعه: أوجره وهو النشوع فانتشعه. وهذا منشع الصبي: لمسعطه.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Nashʿ: the soothsayer's fee, and he gave it to him. He administered medicine to the boy, or made him swallow it; the medicine is called nashūʿ, and the act is intashʿa. This is the boy's minshaʿ: a syringe or funnel.

he made someone swallow medicine; he forced a soothsayer to speak by paying him

entries.text: نشع الصبي الدواء وأنشعه: أوجره وهو النشوع فانتشعه. وهذا منشع الصبي: لمسعطه.

نشع فلان كذا وبكذا. قال مرار بن منقذ: إليكم يا لئام الناس إني ... نشعت العز في أنفي نشوعا وقال مغلس الربعي: خليلي إن أصعدتما أو مررتما ... على أهل حنفاء الغضا فاذكرانيا وقولا أثيبي يا علي متيما ... أخا الموت منشوعا بذكراك عانيا وقال عبدة بن الطبيب: لا تأمنوا قوما يشب صبيهم ... بي

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin of the root نضح is the act of sprinkling or scattering water or a similar fluid in fine, dispersed droplets upon a surface, as opposed to a full, drenching pour. This core image underlies all subsequent literal and figurative applications.
record.haqiqah_literal: According to Asās al-Balāghah, the literal meaning is the sprinkling of water upon something (نضح عليه الماء) or the sprinkling of a house with water (نضح البيت بالماء), which is characterized as رش (rashsh), i.e., a light, scattered sprinkling. It also literally denotes the oozing or exuding of sweat from the skin (نضح جلده بالعرق).
record.majaz_scholastic: In metaphorical and scholastic usage, the root extends to any subtle, non-violent diffusion or emanation, such as the gentle spread of moisture, the exudation of perspiration as a sign of bodily function, or the sprinkling of a liquid as a symbolic act of purification or blessing. It may also be applied to the diffuse radiation of light or the soft dissemination of knowledge, always retaining the nuance of fine, dispersed particles rather than a concentrated flow.

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّضْحُ: الرَّشُّ. نَضَحَ عَلَيْهِ المَاءَ يَنْضَحُهُ نَضْحًا، وَنَضَحَ البَيْتَ بِالمَاءِ، وَنَضَحَ جِلْدُهُ بِالعَرَقِ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Naḍḥ is sprinkling. One sprinkles water upon something (naḍaḥa ʿalayhi al-māʾa yanḍaḥuhu naḍḥan); one sprinkles the house with water; and one's skin exudes sweat.

derivations.english_translation: to sprinkle, to scatter (water) lightly
sprinkling, light scattering (of water)
to sprinkle repeatedly or intensively
sprinkled, that which has been sprinkled upon
sprinkling, one who sprinkles; (also) a camel used for drawing water

entries.text: قد نضح الشجر: تفطر. ورأيت نضح الرمان وغيره. قال أبو طالب: بورك الميت الغريب كما بو ... رك نضح الرمان والزيتون ونضح غلته بالماء: بلها، ومنه: النضيح والنضح: للحوض لبله عطش الإبل وكذلك البعير الناضح، ونواضح يثرب، ونضح أديم الود بينهم. قال الكميت: نضحت أديم الود بيني وبينهم ... بآصرة

نضح عليه الماء، ونضح البيت بالماء نضحا وهو الرش. ونضح جلده بالعرق. Metaphorical (Majaz): قد نضح الشجر: تفطر. ورأيت نضح الرمان وغيره. قال أبو طالب: بورك الميت الغريب كما بو ... رك نضح الرمان والزيتون ونضح غلته بالماء: بلها، ومنه:
نضح عليه الماء، ونضح البيت بالماء نضحا وهو الرش. ونضح جلده بالعرق.

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical act of threading beads or pearls onto a single cord, thereby gathering discrete, scattered units into a unified, ordered sequence.
record.haqiqah_literal: To string pearls or beads onto a thread; to arrange individual items in a linear, connected order.
record.majaz_scholastic: The composition of poetry (نَظْمُ الشِّعْر) as a verbal threading of words; the ordering of affairs or arguments upon a coherent model (نَظَمَ الأَمْرَ عَلَى الْمِثَال); and in scholastic theology, the rational coherence and providential ordering of created things (نِظَام).

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّظْمُ: التَّأْلِيفُ. نَظَمَهُ يَنْظِمُهُ نَظْمًا وَنِظَامًا، وَنَظَّمَهُ فَانْتَظَمَ وَتَنَظَّمَ. وَنَظَمْتُ اللُّؤْلُؤَ أَيْ جَمَعْتُهُ فِي السِّلْكِ.
canonical_definition.english: Naẓm is composition. He strung it, he strings it, with naẓm and niẓām; and he organized it, so it became strung and organized. I strung the pearls, that is, I gathered them onto the cord.

نظمت الدر ونظمته، ودر منظوم ومنظم، وقد انتظم وتنظم وتناظم، وله نظم منه ونظام ونظم. Metaphorical (Majaz): نظم الكلام. وهذا نظم حسن، وانتظم كلامه وأمره. وليس لأمره نظام إذا لم تستقم طريقته، وتقول: هذه أمور عظام، لو كان لها نظام، ورمى صيدا افنتظمه

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is a sudden, forceful emission or gust — whether of wind, scent, or a striking limb — characterized by a single, discrete impulse rather than sustained duration.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical meaning is the blowing or wafting of wind or fragrance in a single gust (nafḥah), and the striking or kicking of an animal with its hoof or a person with a sword.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorically and theologically, it denotes a fleeting touch or visitation of good or evil, as in the Qurʾānic phrase 'a nafḥah of your Lord's punishment' (Q 21:46), indicating a slight but perceptible impact. It is also applied to a she-camel whose milk flows without milking, a bow with far-reaching shot, and the rennet (infiḥah) used to coagulate milk — all extensions of the root's core sense of a sudden, forceful emission.

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّفْحَةُ دُفْعَةُ الرِّيحِ، طَيِّبَةً كَانَتْ أَوْ خَبِيثَةً؛ وَلَهُ نَفْحَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ. وَنَفَحَتِ الرِّيحُ: هَبَّتْ.
canonical_definition.english: A nafḥah is a gust of wind, whether pleasant or foul; and it may be said that something has a pleasant nafḥah. The wind nafaḥa means it blew.

derivations.english_translation: to blow, waft, or emit a gust; to strike or kick

mufradat.text: نفح الريح ينفح نفحا، وله نفحة طيبة. أي: هبوب من الخير، وقد يستعار ذلك للشر. قال تعالى: ولئن مستهم نفحة من عذاب ربك [الأنبياء/ 46] ونفحت الدابة: رمت بحافرها، ونفحه بالسيف: ضربه به، والنفوح من النوق: التي يخرج لبنها من غير حلب، وقوس نفوح: بعيدة الدفع للسهم، وأنفحة الجدي معروفة.

entries.text: نفح الطيب نفحا، وله نفحة ونفحات طيبة، ونافجة نافحة، ونوافج نوافح، وجبن اللبن بالإنفحة. قال: كم قد تمششت من قص وإنفحة ... جاءت بذاك إليك الأض Metaphorical (Majaz): لا تزال له نفحات من المعروف. والله النفاح بالخيرات. قال: والله نفاح اليدين بالخير ورجل نفاع نفاح. ونفحه بالمال. ونفحه بالسيف: ضربه ضربة خفيف

نفح الطيب نفحا، وله نفحة ونفحات طيبة، ونافجة نافحة، ونوافج نوافح، وجبن اللبن بالإنفحة. قال: كم قد تمششت من قص وإنفحة ... جاءت بذاك إليك الأضؤن السود وقال الشماخ: وإني من القوم الذين علمتهم ... إذا ألوموا لم يولموا بالأنافح

لا تزال له نفحات من المعروف. والله النفاح بالخيرات. قال: والله نفاح اليدين بالخير ورجل نفاع نفاح. ونفحه بالمال. ونفحه بالسيف: ضربه ضربة خفيفة، ومنه: نفحت عن فلان ونافحت عنه: دافعت. وكان حسان رضي الله تعالى عنه ينافح عن رسل الله صلى الله عليه وسلم. وقال: وكم مشهد نافحت عنك خصومه .

record.ontological_core: The foundational physical origin (Aṣl al-Wadʿ) is the expulsion of a current of air from the mouth or a bellows into a receptive object, producing inflation, agitation, or combustion.
record.haqiqah_literal: The literal physical act of blowing air from the mouth or a bellows into something, such as blowing into a vessel, a fire, or a horn, causing it to swell, kindle, or sound.
record.majaz_scholastic: Metaphorical and scholastic applications include: the divine insufflation of the spirit into the human form (nafkh al-rūḥ); the eschatological blowing of the horn (al-Ṣūr) to signal resurrection; the swelling of the belly from food or drink; the rising of the day (intifākh al-nahār); the blossoming of spring (nafkhah al-rabīʿ); a corpulent man (rajul manfūkh); and the puffing of the cheeks as a gesture of arrogance (nafkh shidqayhi).

canonical_definition.arabic: النَّفْخُ: إِخْرَاجُ الرِّيحِ مِنَ الفَمِ أَوِ المِنْفَاخِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ، فَيَنْتَفِخُ أَوْ يَشْتَعِلُ أَوْ يَصْدَحُ؛ وَمِنْهُ نَفْخُ الرُّوحِ، وَنَفْخُ الصُّورِ، وَانْتِفَاخُ البَطْنِ، وَانْتِفَاخُ النَّهَارِ، وَنَفْخَةُ الرَّبِيعِ، وَرَجُلٌ مَنْفُوخٌ أَيْ سَمِينٌ.
canonical_definition.english: Al-Nafkh: the expulsion of air from the mouth or a bellows into an object, causing it to inflate, ignite, or resound; hence the insufflation of the spirit, the blowing of the horn, the swelling of the belly, the rising of the day, the blossoming of spring, and a corpulent man.
